issues.title: Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
issues.text: Review nutritional status and relevant laboratory assessment; the RYGB review specifically identifies iron, vitamin B12, and folate deficiencies for evaluation.

issues.title: Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
issues.text: Review medications for possible altered absorption after RYGB. Assess GLP-1/GIP therapy individually, considering gastrointestinal symptoms because these agents may delay gastric emptying.

issues.title: Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
issues.text: For bariatric surgery, use lung-protective tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight (PBW). Optimal PEEP and the role of recruitment maneuvers remain uncertain.

issues.title: Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockers have been administered, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. The site recommendation is adductor pollicis, not eye muscles.

issues.title: Sleeve Gastrectomy
issues.text: Review medication effects and comorbidities, including weight-loss therapies that may delay gastric emptying, and plan individually for aspiration risk. The source describes individualized assessment rather than routine discontinuation of GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 therapies.

issues.title: Sleeve Gastrectomy
issues.text: Optimize preoxygenation; a tight-fitting mask with 100% oxygen is standard, and HFNC may be an adjunct. Have video laryngoscopy and advanced airway devices available. Consider rapid-sequence or modified rapid-sequence induction when aspiration risk is significant.

issues.title: Sleeve Gastrectomy
issues.text: Residual neuromuscular blockade is associated with upper-airway obstruction, reintubation, atelectasis, pneumonia, and prolonged PACU stay. Quantitative TOF assessment at the adductor pollicis is recommended when monitoring blockade; confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

issues.title: Sleeve Gastrectomy
issues.text: The ERAS guideline reports associations between both hypervolemia and hypovolemia and worse outcomes. Balanced crystalloids are supported over 0.9% saline; bariatric-specific evidence comparing crystalloids and colloids is sparse.

issues.title: Escharotomy / Fasciotomy for Burns
issues.text: Fluid resuscitation-associated edema develops during the first 48 hours after burn. Escharotomy is usually performed within that period in relation to the injury and resuscitation-associated edema; need and timing depend on clinical assessment and response to treatment, as no objective measure defines the need.

issues.title: Bronchoscopy (Flexible / Rigid)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Cardiac Catheterization / PCI
issues.text: The main catheterization source is a 2014 anesthesia review, not a formal guideline or a procedure-specific trial. It explicitly does not identify one ideal anesthetic technique and describes decisions as patient- and procedure-dependent.

issues.title: Cardiac Valve Repair / Replacement (Open)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Chest Wall Resection and Reconstruction
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies when blockade is used, not to every case or anesthetic technique.

issues.title: Chest Wall Resection and Reconstruction
issues.text: The procedure-specific evidence consists of small retrospective surgical series, not anesthesia guidelines. One is a retrospective single-institution case series of eight patients; another is a retrospective multicenter study of 26 patients.

issues.title: Decortication (Pleural)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, using the adductor pollicis site. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: ECMO Cannulation / Decannulation
issues.text: For adult VA-ECMO weaning, assess the trajectory of myocardial recovery, inotropic requirements, and filling pressures. Weaning is uncommon during the first 72 hours after implantation, but this is contextual guidance rather than a fixed waiting rule.

issues.title: Esophagectomy (Ivor Lewis / McKeown / Minimally Invasive)
issues.text: Use protective ventilation: control tidal volume, minimize driving pressure, optimize compliance, and use reasonable PEEP. The review cites tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight (IBW) for esophagectomy and no more than 5 mL/kg IBW during OLV to avoid volutrauma.

issues.title: Esophagectomy (Ivor Lewis / McKeown / Minimally Invasive)
issues.text: The 2017 review reports that studies are often small or heterogeneous and that outcome evidence for fluid strategies and some monitoring approaches is limited. Reconcile its discussion with the later review: neither supports a universal fluid recipe or vasopressor hierarchy.

issues.title: Heart Transplant
issues.text: Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) is failure of graft function within the first 24 hours after transplantation, in the absence of hyperacute rejection, pulmonary hypertension, or known surgical complications such as bleeding or tamponade.

issues.title: Heart Transplant
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation, measured at the adductor pollicis. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Lobectomy (VATS / Open)
issues.text: Assess pulmonary reserve with spirometry/FEV1 and DLCO; perfusion scanning and exercise testing may be used when appropriate.

issues.title: Lobectomy (VATS / Open)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Lobectomy (VATS / Open)
issues.text: No evidence-supported universal fluid total, arterial-line requirement, OLV setting, extubation threshold based on ppo-FEV1, or prophylactic atrial-fibrillation drug regimen can be derived from the supplied sources.

issues.title: Lung Transplant (Single / Double)
issues.text: Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) is a leading cause of death after lung transplantation and typically occurs within 72 hours. Treatment is supportive, including lung-protective ventilation and early postoperative MCS for severe PGD.

issues.title: LVAD Placement (Left Ventricular Assist Device)
issues.text: One anesthesia review describes transfer to the ICU sedated with propofol and extubation once hemodynamically stable. A surgical review reports that patients are typically extubated within 24 hours after surgery in the CVICU.

issues.title: LVAD Placement (Left Ventricular Assist Device)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm quantitative train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this recommendation is conditional on neuromuscular blocker use, not a requirement for cases without blockade.

issues.title: LVAD Placement (Left Ventricular Assist Device)
issues.text: The LVAD anesthesia source is a 2004 overview focused primarily on DeBakey VAD and Jarvik 2000; its device descriptions and perioperative discussion may not represent current devices or contemporary practice.

issues.title: Mediastinoscopy
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies when blockade has been used, not to local or neuraxial techniques without blockade.

issues.title: Pericardial Window
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Pleurodesis (Chemical / Surgical VATS)
issues.text: Obtain a chest radiograph 24 hours after pleurodesis to check for pneumothorax or fluid reaccumulation. The chest tube may be removed if the radiograph is satisfactory and there is no further fluid output. Follow-up, including chest radiography, is recommended after 4–6 weeks.

issues.title: Pneumonectomy
issues.text: Assess spirometry and DLCO, then estimate predicted postoperative function. NICE recommends counselling patients with ppoFEV₁ or ppoDLCO below 30% predicted about increased risk of postoperative dyspnoea and long-term oxygen therapy, and referring them for formal exercise testing. Another overview describes estimated postoperative FEV₁ or DLCO below 40% predicted as high risk warranting further functional assessment; these are distinct source thresholds, not interchangeable eligibility rules.

issues.title: Pneumonectomy
issues.text: Ensure postoperative-care capacity appropriate to expected risk. The review calls for availability of a level-2 postoperative bed and crossmatched red cells; this is not evidence that every case requires ICU admission or a fixed blood-preparation protocol.

issues.title: Pneumonectomy
issues.text: Post-pneumonectomy pulmonary oedema occurs in 2–5% of cases and is associated with reported mortality above 50%. It typically presents with respiratory distress and hypoxaemia within 72 hours. Treatment is generally supportive, with ventilatory support as required, restrictive fluids, and diuretics.

issues.title: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Repair (TEVAR / Open Descending)
issues.text: For open descending thoracic or thoracoabdominal repair, the review describes ICU monitoring, continued hemodynamic and neurologic assessment, attention to respiratory, renal, and cardiac complications, and ongoing CSF-drain management when used. It states a postoperative MAP target of 80–90 mmHg in this open-repair context; do not generalize this target to TEVAR or other contexts.

issues.title: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Repair (TEVAR / Open Descending)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockers are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are supported by the ASA guideline overview; this applies only when NMB has been used.

issues.title: Thoracotomy (Open) / Exploratory Thoracotomy
issues.text: For pain expected to remain moderate to severe beyond the immediate postoperative period, the review recommends a catheter-based approach; its cited open-thoracotomy guidance specifies postoperative infusion for 2–3 days. This is a source-specific recommendation, not an automatic duration for every patient.

issues.title: Thoracotomy (Open) / Exploratory Thoracotomy
issues.text: If a neuromuscular blocker has been administered, confirm quantitative TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies when neuromuscular blockade is used, not to every anesthetic.

issues.title: Thymectomy (VATS / Open / Robotic)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade was used, quantitative monitoring guidance recommends confirming TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation. Sugammadex is recommended over neostigmine for rocuronium- or vecuronium-induced deep, moderate, or shallow block in the general guideline; this is not an MG-specific comparative recommendation.

issues.title: VATS Wedge Resection
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the supplied guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, measured at the adductor pollicis. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)
issues.text: The APR review gives no emergence or extubation protocol. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirming train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

issues.title: Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)
issues.text: For elective colorectal surgery, offer a regular diet within 24 hours. After mid/lower rectal resection, urinary catheter removal is typically recommended within 24–48 hours, balancing urinary-retention risk after pelvic dissection against UTI risk; apply these recommendations to the operative and patient context.

issues.title: Anal Fistula Repair (Fistulotomy / LIFT / Seton)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is preferred and recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 should be confirmed before extubation; this does not apply to local or neuraxial cases without NMB.

issues.title: Anal Fistula Repair (Fistulotomy / LIFT / Seton)
issues.text: The case-specific evidence is a 2001 surgical review, not an anesthesia reference; it supplies operative discussion but limited anesthetic detail. Its procedural recommendations should be interpreted within that scope.

issues.title: Colectomy (Open / Laparoscopic / Robotic)
issues.text: For elective colorectal resection, the 2023 ASCRS/SAGES guideline supports mechanical bowel preparation combined with oral antibiotics. This differs from the older review's position against routine mechanical preparation; follow applicable current institutional and surgical protocols.

issues.title: Colectomy (Open / Laparoscopic / Robotic)
issues.text: Avoid intraoperative hypotension. The guideline notes association of MAP below 65 mm Hg, even briefly, with myocardial injury and acute kidney injury; this is a risk signal, not a universal individualized target.

issues.title: Colectomy (Open / Laparoscopic / Robotic)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockers are used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Colectomy (Open / Laparoscopic / Robotic)
issues.text: After elective colorectal surgery, offer a regular diet within 24 hours and encourage early progressive mobilization.

issues.title: Colectomy (Open / Laparoscopic / Robotic)
issues.text: The principal procedure-specific source is the 2023 ASCRS/SAGES guideline for elective colon and rectal resections. It is not a dedicated anesthesia reference and does not specify airway management, positioning, vascular access, or detailed intraoperative monitoring protocols.

issues.title: Hemorrhoidectomy
issues.text: A 2007 clinical review advises limiting intraoperative fluids to no more than 500 mL to help decrease urinary retention; this is a source-reported practice, not an individualized target.

issues.title: Hemorrhoidectomy
issues.text: A meta-analysis found lower pain scores at six and 24 hours with local anesthesia plus IV sedation than with spinal anesthesia. The review gives no specific patient-selection criteria.

issues.title: Hemorrhoidectomy
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, confirm quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; the recommendation is conditional on NMB use, not a requirement for local or neuraxial cases without blockade.

issues.title: Hemorrhoidectomy
issues.text: The other procedure review is from 2007, reports inconsistent open-versus-closed findings, and provides no anesthesia-specific airway or monitoring protocol. Its practice statements require cautious interpretation.

issues.title: Low Anterior Resection (LAR)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Low Anterior Resection (LAR)
issues.text: Avoid intraoperative hypotension; the guideline associates MAP below 65 mm Hg, even briefly, particularly with myocardial injury and acute kidney injury. It gives no LAR-specific transfusion threshold.

issues.title: Low Anterior Resection (LAR)
issues.text: In the absence of surgical complications or hemodynamic instability, discontinue IV fluids early postoperatively. Offer a regular diet within 24 hours after elective colorectal surgery.

issues.title: Ostomy Creation / Reversal (Ileostomy / Colostomy)
issues.text: In this practice survey, respondents reported hand-sewn anastomoses in 45.2% of cases and stapled anastomoses in 54.8%; the survey reports practice patterns, not a comparison of their outcomes.

issues.title: Ostomy Creation / Reversal (Ileostomy / Colostomy)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirming train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Ostomy Creation / Reversal (Ileostomy / Colostomy)
issues.text: Avoid intraoperative hypotension in the colorectal guideline’s population; it associates even brief MAP below 65 mm Hg particularly with myocardial injury and acute kidney injury.

issues.title: Ostomy Creation / Reversal (Ileostomy / Colostomy)
issues.text: For patients undergoing elective colorectal surgery, offer a regular diet within 24 hours; early progressive mobilization is associated with shorter length of stay.

issues.title: Ostomy Creation / Reversal (Ileostomy / Colostomy)
issues.text: The closure survey describes Italian surgeons’ practice for loop ileostomy reversal after rectal cancer surgery; 219 SICCR members responded, for a 22% response rate. It is a practice survey, not an anesthesia guideline.

issues.title: Dental Rehabilitation Under General Anesthesia (Adult)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative TOF recovery to at least 0.9 before extubation; the cited recommendation is not a requirement for cases without neuromuscular blocking drugs.

issues.title: Orthognathic Surgery (Bimaxillary Osteotomy)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring rather than clinical assessment alone and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; the guideline specifies the adductor pollicis site.

issues.title: Adrenalectomy (Laparoscopic / Robotic)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockade has been used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation; the recommendation applies to cases in which blockade is used.

issues.title: Awake Fiber-Optic Intubation (AFOI)
issues.text: The 2025 ENT review is narrative and covers diverse airway procedures; it supports planning and shared-airway principles but is not an AFOI-specific guideline. The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general standards, not AFOI-specific management protocols.

issues.title: Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)
issues.text: In the review, Kolia and Man’s 2019 meta-analysis reported that propofol-based TIVA, compared with inhalational anesthesia, improved surgical-field quality, reduced blood loss, and shortened operative time. Findings across studies were incongruent, so these reported benefits should not be treated as guaranteed.

issues.title: Laryngectomy (Total / Partial)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Mastoidectomy
issues.text: Mastoidectomy is generally performed under general anesthesia with tracheal intubation; the bed is typically turned 180 degrees after induction. The operation uses drilling to open mastoid air cells, with the aim of creating a “safe and dry ear.”

issues.title: Mastoidectomy
issues.text: Plan for the operating microscope, drill, and otologic instruments. After induction, the bed is typically turned 180 degrees; confirm the intended arrangement and access with the team.

issues.title: Mastoidectomy
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring guidance recommends confirming a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation, with monitoring at the adductor pollicis. This does not make blockade or quantitative monitoring a mastoidectomy-specific requirement.

issues.title: Maxillofacial Trauma Surgery (Panfacial Fractures)
issues.text: The most procedure-specific source is a retrospective, single-center review of 288 maxillofacial-trauma operations. Its reported techniques and outcomes describe local practice, not comparative effectiveness or a universal standard; some reported counts conflict.

issues.title: Maxillofacial Trauma Surgery (Panfacial Fractures)
issues.text: The 2021 maxillofacial-trauma article is a brief narrative review without evidence grading or comparative outcome data. Its airway options inform planning, but do not establish one preferred approach for all fracture patterns or patients.

issues.title: Microlaryngoscopy / Vocal Cord Surgery
issues.text: A cuffed ETT secures the airway but can obstruct visualization. Use the smallest tube that supports ventilation; the source describes a 5.0- or 5.5-mm microlaryngeal tube as adequate in most cases, while recognizing increased resistance and the need to assess for leaks.

issues.title: Microlaryngoscopy / Vocal Cord Surgery
issues.text: For laryngeal laser procedures, use a laser-resistant ETT compatible with the particular laser if an ETT is selected. Reduce inspired oxygen concentration to less than 30% and discontinue nitrous oxide; allow approximately 5 minutes for equilibration, depending on fresh-gas flow, circuit length, and initial oxygen concentration. Fill the ETT cuff with saline tinted with methylene blue to signal cuff rupture.

issues.title: Microlaryngoscopy / Vocal Cord Surgery
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Neck Dissection (Radical / Modified / Selective)
issues.text: Cranial-nerve injury is a recognized complication. In the retrospective cohort, 14 documented iatrogenic cranial-nerve injuries occurred among 925 cases; documentation-based ascertainment may have missed injuries.

issues.title: Neck Dissection (Radical / Modified / Selective)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, the cited ASA guideline recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this applies to cases receiving blockade, not to all neck-dissection anesthetics.

issues.title: Parotidectomy (Superficial / Total)
issues.text: Assess facial-nerve function immediately in recovery. After hemostasis, a suction drain is placed; the chapter states it remains until output is less than 15 to 50 mL over 24 hours.

issues.title: Septoplasty / Turbinate Reduction
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Septoplasty / Turbinate Reduction
issues.text: In the office-based setting, observe patients for 30 minutes postoperatively to ensure recovery. The review does not establish a general discharge duration for operating-room anesthesia.

issues.title: Septoplasty / Turbinate Reduction
issues.text: The deep-sedation study was retrospective, single-center, and included 40 deep-sedation patients; it cannot establish comparative routine practice or eliminate confounding. The ENT airway chapter and newer airway review are narrative sources covering multiple procedures, so their device discussions require case-specific interpretation.

issues.title: Tracheal Intubation for Epiglottitis
issues.text: The 2012 review describes fibreoptic nasal intubation or rigid bronchoscopy with a substantially reduced-diameter tube as preferred approaches. A later chapter also describes awake fibreoptic intubation in a cooperative patient and allows direct or video-assisted laryngoscopy; these sources do not resolve technique selection for every adult presentation.

issues.title: Tracheal Intubation for Epiglottitis
issues.text: The procedure-specific anesthesia source is a 2012 narrative overview, not a formal guideline or trial; it describes airway management in general terms and does not provide detailed anesthetic regimens or a complete extubation protocol.

issues.title: Tracheal Intubation for Epiglottitis
issues.text: The 2018 chapter is also a narrative review rather than an anesthesia protocol. It supplies adult airway selection and safeguard information but explicitly lacks detailed anesthetic, fluid, analgesic, emergence, and postoperative airway plans.

issues.title: Tympanoplasty
issues.text: Local anesthesia with conscious sedation is an alternative described in a small adult trial, not a universal technique. Its study cohort was ASA I–II adults aged 18–75, and the article does not report an airway device.

issues.title: ASD / PFO Closure (Percutaneous)
issues.text: Review imaging for defect size and location, septal rims, and associated anomalies. TTE is usually adequate initially in children with good windows; adults often require TEE, and 3D TEE, MRI, or CT may also be considered.

issues.title: ASD / PFO Closure (Percutaneous)
issues.text: Assess pulmonary pressure, PVR, and shunt direction before deciding on closure. The review states closure should not be performed with PA systolic pressure or PVR above two-thirds systemic, or net right-to-left shunting. It describes possible consideration in selected patients with Qp:Qs ≥1.5 and lesser pulmonary vascular disease; this requires appropriate specialist assessment.

issues.title: ASD / PFO Closure (Percutaneous)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade was used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation are supported by the cited ASA guideline overview. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: ASD / PFO Closure (Percutaneous)
issues.text: Source 0 notes nonrandomized comparative outcome evidence, practice variation in antiplatelet therapy, and limited longer-term data for some devices. These limitations argue against treating the review’s reported outcomes or postoperative practice as universal standards.

issues.title: Atrial Fibrillation Ablation (Pulmonary Vein Isolation)
issues.text: PFA-specific anesthesia and comparative safety evidence remain limited in the supplied sources; the cited first-human pilot does not establish routine adult practice. The 2025 narrative review also states that it provides no single protocol validated across procedures.

issues.title: Atrial Flutter Ablation (Cavotricuspid Isthmus)
issues.text: For monitored anesthesia care, recovery is guided by the patient's respiratory, circulatory, and consciousness status. After general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this requirement applies when neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used.

issues.title: Cardiac Catheterization (Diagnostic)
issues.text: The cath-lab anesthesia source is a 2014 review covering adult and pediatric catheterization procedures; it is not presented as a guideline and does not identify one ideal anesthetic technique. Pediatric-specific material is not used here to establish adult practice.

issues.title: Elective Cardioversion (DCCV)
issues.text: The procedure-specific cardioversion source is a narrative review published in 2009, not a systematic review or anesthesia guideline; its anticoagulation and energy recommendations require current specialty-protocol verification.

issues.title: Elective Cardioversion (DCCV)
issues.text: This single-centre trial enrolled 60 selected adults undergoing elective cardioversion (ASA I–III, ejection fraction >35%). Its regimens and findings should not be generalized to emergency cardioversion or more unstable patients, who were not enrolled.

issues.title: Electrophysiology (EP) Study
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, confirm quantitative recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: ICD / AICD Placement
issues.text: Cardiac tamponade is a recognized complication of permanent pacemaker and/or ICD implantation; the review reports an incidence of 0.1–5.2%.

issues.title: ICD / AICD Placement
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are supported; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: MitraClip / TEER (Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair)
issues.text: Most patients can be awakened at procedure end and recover in PACU; routine ICU admission is no longer usual. Intermediate-care or coronary-care units are suitable for most. Perform transthoracic echocardiography within 24 h to confirm success and assess residual MR, new mitral stenosis, and any unclosed septal defect’s flow volume and direction.

issues.title: MitraClip / TEER (Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This is a neuromuscular-blockade standard, not a requirement for cases without NMB.

issues.title: MitraClip / TEER (Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair)
issues.text: During recovery, evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature, with monitoring appropriate to the patient’s condition. Monitor access sites for bleeding and haematoma. Perform transthoracic echocardiography within 24 h to confirm success and assess residual MR, new mitral stenosis, and any unclosed septal defect’s flow volume and direction.

issues.title: PCI with Hemodynamic Support (High-Risk PCI)
issues.text: This 2014 review covers multiple catheterization procedures. It describes PCI as usually performed with mild sedation under cardiologist supervision, with anesthesiologist involvement considered for respiratory distress, hemodynamic instability, or sedation rescue; it does not provide a dedicated high-risk PCI anesthetic protocol.

issues.title: Permanent Pacemaker Implantation
issues.text: In the single-center observational study, patients were monitored in the cardiology intensive care unit for at least 30 minutes, remained in hospital for one day with monitoring for hematoma, swelling, and edema, and were scheduled for a one-week wound-healing and infection assessment.

issues.title: SVT Ablation (AVNRT / AVRT)
issues.text: The 2022 review favors general anesthesia for many ablations to support comfort and limit movement, while the 2016 review describes moderate sedation as common and supported for SVT. These positions are reconciled by individualizing technique to inducibility needs, procedural complexity, patient risk, and EP-team goals—not by declaring either approach universal.

issues.title: TAVR (Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement)
issues.text: The detailed anesthesia review is a 2016 narrative review, not a guideline or trial; its MAC-versus-GA evidence was largely observational and reflects practice available at that time.

issues.title: TEE-Guided Cardioversion
issues.text: TEE-guided cardioversion uses transesophageal imaging before nonemergent direct-current cardioversion (DCCV) to assess for intracardiac thrombus, including left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombus. For AF lasting longer than 48 hours, the cited review describes oral anticoagulation for at least three weeks before and four weeks after electrical cardioversion, or TOE to exclude LAA thrombus if the patient is not anticoagulated.

issues.title: TEE-Guided Cardioversion
issues.text: TEE is used before nonemergent direct-current cardioversion to assess for intracardiac thrombus. For AF lasting longer than 48 hours, the cited review describes oral anticoagulation for at least three weeks before and four weeks after electrical cardioversion, or TOE to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus if the patient is not anticoagulated.

issues.title: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) Ablation
issues.text: The procedure-focused 2023 source is a review, not an anesthesia reference, and does not grade evidence. It supports procedural approaches and risk discussion but leaves several anesthesia and recovery details unspecified.

issues.title: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) Ablation
issues.text: The 2025 deep-sedation cohort is observational, single-centre, and has no general-anesthesia comparison. Its findings should not be used to establish universal anesthetic practice or a routine disposition.

issues.title: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) Ablation
issues.text: The 2022 EP anesthesia review is broad rather than VT-specific throughout; it notes evidence limitations and provides no obstetric-specific recommendations. This draft is limited to adult VT ablation and does not infer obstetric practice.

issues.title: Watchman / Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion (LAAO)
issues.text: The airway comparison is a retrospective, single-center adult Watchman study (155 ETT and 42 SGA in the overall cohort). Propensity matching does not remove unmeasured selection bias, and the SGA group was small; findings support feasibility, not a universal airway standard.

issues.title: Abscess Incision and Drainage (I&D)
issues.text: The anorectal source recommends laboratory assessment including CBC, creatinine, inflammatory markers, blood glucose, and HbA1c. Diabetes and other immunocompromised states are identified as risk modifiers; this is not an anesthesia-specific testing protocol.

issues.title: Appendectomy (Laparoscopic/Open)
issues.text: For laparoscopic appendectomy, anticipate CO₂ insufflation. Positioning is not universal: the cited trial used Trendelenburg with a 15° turn, while other laparoscopic procedures may use different positions; insufflation and positioning can have hemodynamic and pulmonary effects.

issues.title: Appendectomy (Laparoscopic/Open)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring when available and confirm adequate recovery before extubation; the cited ASA guideline overview recommends a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9. This does not apply to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Bowel Resection (Small / Large)
issues.text: For elective rectal/pelvic surgery, clear fluids are permitted up to 2 hours and solid food up to 6 hours before induction. A clear fluid containing complex carbohydrates 2 hours before anesthesia is recommended unless aspiration risk is increased, such as with bowel obstruction.

issues.title: Bowel Resection (Small / Large)
issues.text: Acetaminophen/paracetamol and NSAIDs are described as components of multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia. The colorectal review notes concern about increased anastomotic-leak risk with COX-2 inhibitors; it does not justify treating all NSAIDs as interchangeable or universally appropriate.

issues.title: Bowel Resection (Small / Large)
issues.text: The colorectal review does not establish a specific extubation protocol. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, using the adductor pollicis site.

issues.title: Bowel Resection (Small / Large)
issues.text: The main procedure-specific source is a clinical review of colorectal surgery, published in 2012; it is not a dedicated small-bowel resection guideline. The rectal/pelvic ERAS review addresses elective rectal/pelvic surgery, not every bowel-resection population.

issues.title: Breast Biopsy / Lumpectomy / Mastectomy
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are supported by the cited ASA-guideline overview; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Diagnostic Laparoscopy / Lysis of Adhesions
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring when available; the cited ASA guideline recommends confirming TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Feeding Tube Placement (PEG / J-tube)
issues.text: Aspiration is a delayed complication; the review reports it occurs in less than 2% of patients and can increase pneumonia risk. The supplied sources do not specify an airway technique for this procedure.

issues.title: Feeding Tube Placement (PEG / J-tube)
issues.text: For radiologically guided feeding-tube placement, a nasogastric tube is used to insufflate the stomach and facilitate gastric puncture; ultrasound and fluoroscopy guide catheter placement. The review states that the entire procedure is typically performed in less than 20 minutes.

issues.title: Feeding Tube Placement (PEG / J-tube)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, using the adductor pollicis. This is conditional on NMB use, not a requirement for local or neuraxial techniques without blockade.

issues.title: Femoral Hernia Repair
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to cases without blockade.

issues.title: Femoral Hernia Repair
issues.text: For laparoscopic and robotic surgery, the review advises attempting to keep insufflation pressure below 15 mmHg to allow normalization of renal function and urine output. This is general review guidance, not a femoral-hernia-specific target.

issues.title: Femoral Hernia Repair
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockers were administered, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, as described in the guideline overview.

issues.title: Femoral Hernia Repair
issues.text: The femoral-specific comparative study is a small, single-center retrospective study of 41 adult female patients; it is not an anesthesia reference and cannot establish general anesthetic practice or outcomes across populations.

issues.title: Hiatal Hernia Repair / Nissen Fundoplication
issues.text: Laparoscopic hiatal hernia repair generally combines reduction/mobilization, hiatal closure and fundoplication. A 360° Nissen is common, but motility findings can inform selection of a partial wrap.

issues.title: Hiatal Hernia Repair / Nissen Fundoplication
issues.text: A short, loose 360° Nissen is commonly described. Toupet or Dor alternatives are also described; preoperative or intraoperative manometry may help guide wrap selection. This is a surgical choice, not an anesthesia prescription.

issues.title: Hiatal Hernia Repair / Nissen Fundoplication
issues.text: Positioning is not consistent across the supplied procedure-specific account and general laparoscopic review: one describes 30-degree Trendelenburg, while reverse Trendelenburg is commonly used for upper gastrointestinal procedures. Confirm the intended position with the surgical team and protect pressure points.

issues.title: Hiatal Hernia Repair / Nissen Fundoplication
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, ASA guideline recommendations summarized by APSF support quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Hiatal Hernia Repair / Nissen Fundoplication
issues.text: The procedure-specific 2016 article is a technical letter, not an anesthesia reference or comparative study; its brief anesthesia description cannot establish an anesthetic regimen or outcome.

issues.title: Inguinal Hernia Repair (Open/Laparoscopic/Robotic)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Inguinal Hernia Repair (Open/Laparoscopic/Robotic)
issues.text: The hernia-specific sources are narrative clinical reviews, not anesthesia protocols. The 2011 review does not provide airway, positioning, monitoring, fluid, bleeding, or emergence protocols; the minimally invasive repair review also lacks detailed anesthetic regimens and monitoring guidance.

issues.title: Lower Extremity Amputation (Toe / Foot / BKA / AKA)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Perforated Viscus Repair
issues.text: In sepsis present or suspected during emergency laparotomy, the guideline describes norepinephrine as the first-choice vasopressor to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg; epinephrine or vasopressin 0.03 U/min may be added to norepinephrine. Apply this guidance in context rather than as an automatic drug sequence.

issues.title: Perforated Viscus Repair
issues.text: For emergency laparotomy, prefer balanced crystalloids over 0.9% saline for resuscitation and intravascular volume maintenance; the guideline grades this as a weak recommendation based on low evidence and notes that evidence is inferred from other populations.

issues.title: Pilonidal Cyst Excision
issues.text: The surgical reviews do not specify an emergence or extubation plan. For any patient who received neuromuscular blocking drugs, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirming TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply as a routine requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Port Placement / Removal (Mediport / PICC Port)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, the cited guideline recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to local-anesthetic cases without blockade.

issues.title: Robotic Cholecystectomy
issues.text: Use multimodal basic analgesia appropriate to the patient; the review cites paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, with opioids reserved for rescue when needed.

issues.title: Robotic Cholecystectomy
issues.text: Detach robotic arms before reversal of neuromuscular blockade. When a blocker has been used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended by the cited guideline summary.

issues.title: Robotic Hernia Repair / Abdominal Wall Reconstruction
issues.text: For laparoscopic and robotic surgery, a commonly used lung-protective strategy is 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight with PEEP 5–10 cm H₂O, titrated according to driving pressure and respiratory compliance; these are not hernia-specific targets.

issues.title: Robotic Hernia Repair / Abdominal Wall Reconstruction
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred to clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Robotic Hernia Repair / Abdominal Wall Reconstruction
issues.text: Hernia-specific evidence includes a 118-patient surgical cohort and a descriptive technique review. The cohort is not an anesthesia reference, used nonrandom approach selection, and followed patients for six weeks.

issues.title: Soft Tissue Mass Excision
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended and recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 should be confirmed before extubation; this does not apply to cases without blockade.

issues.title: Splenectomy (Laparoscopic/Open)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Thyroidectomy
issues.text: Consider associated endocrine disease in thyroid cancer, including MEN type 2 and possible pheochromocytoma or hyperparathyroidism; the source describes screening for relevant clinical and biochemical clues.

issues.title: Thyroidectomy
issues.text: For any neuromuscular blocker used, quantitative monitoring guidance recommends confirming train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Tracheostomy Placement
issues.text: The COVID-era review recommends multidisciplinary discussion for its population and describes infectious-risk planning. Those recommendations are specific to COVID-19-era practice and do not establish routine timing or testing requirements for other patients.

issues.title: Tracheostomy Placement
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation is conditional on blockade use; it does not impose paralysis for every tracheostomy.

issues.title: Tracheostomy Placement
issues.text: Early tube changes are discouraged unless necessary because the immature tract increases the risk of false passage and airway compromise. The source describes the initial tube change as typically occurring on postoperative days 5 to 7; this is not a universal timing instruction for an individual patient.

issues.title: Tracheostomy Placement
issues.text: The second procedure source concerns COVID-19-associated respiratory failure and is a narrative review combining prior outbreak literature with institutional experience. Its timing and infection-control discussion should not be generalized as routine practice outside its scope.

issues.title: Umbilical / Ventral / Incisional Hernia Repair
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockers were administered, use quantitative monitoring to confirm adequate recovery before extubation. The cited guideline recommends TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 and the adductor pollicis monitoring site; these recommendations do not apply to cases without NMB.

issues.title: Umbilical / Ventral / Incisional Hernia Repair
issues.text: The hernia-specific article is a perspective/review, not an anesthesia guideline or randomized anesthesia trial. It reports no randomized trials comparing LA + MAC with general or regional anesthesia for umbilical hernia repair; its institutional feasibility cohort included 53 veteran patients, limiting generalizability.

issues.title: Wound Debridement
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to local-anesthetic or other cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Wound Debridement
issues.text: For minor procedures, topical lidocaine–prilocaine cream may be sufficient; the position paper specifies an adequate application time of not less than 30–60 minutes.

issues.title: EGD (Upper Endoscopy)
issues.text: Review the last oral intake and assess for impaired gastric emptying or esophageal motility disorders. A review describes minimum fasting periods of 2 hours for clear liquids and 6 hours for food, extended to at least 12 hours for known or suspected delayed gastric emptying or motility disorders and 48 hours in achalasia. The ASGE guideline reports no direct evidence linking fasting duration to pulmonary-aspiration risk and no universally accepted practice standard; it cites ASA guidance of at least 2 hours after clear liquids and 6 hours after light meals.

issues.title: EGD (Upper Endoscopy)
issues.text: The ASGE guideline reports variable sedation practice and notes that evidence for capnography benefit differs by sedation depth. Reconcile this with ASA monitoring standards: use continual ventilation observation and expired-CO2 monitoring for moderate or deep sedation unless precluded or invalidated, while not claiming proven benefit in every moderate-sedation EGD.

issues.title: ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography)
issues.text: Assess comorbidities, airway anatomy, aspiration risk, prior sedation or anesthesia difficulties, anxiety and analgesia needs, and the anticipated procedure and position. The 2025 narrative review calls for anesthesiologist evaluation of all ERCP patients; this is review guidance, not a society standard.

issues.title: ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography)
issues.text: The supplied ERCP reviews do not provide a detailed ERCP-specific emergence or postoperative monitoring protocol or discharge criteria. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation are recommended.

issues.title: ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography)
issues.text: The evidence includes a 2011 sedation review, a 2025 narrative review focused on ERCP airway management, a 2018 ASGE sedation guideline, and general ASA monitoring and recovery standards. The 2025 review reports that its methodology was not systematic or standardized and that evidence quality was not formally assessed.

issues.title: ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography)
issues.text: The 2018 ASGE guideline addresses sedation across GI endoscopy and includes ERCP context; the ASA documents establish general monitoring and postanesthesia-care requirements rather than ERCP-specific procedural management.

issues.title: Cervical Cone Biopsy / LEEP
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred to clinical assessment alone; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. This is conditional and does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Cervical Cone Biopsy / LEEP
issues.text: The ACOG consensus is the most procedure-specific supplied source for in-office LEEP and cervical procedures. Its literature search ended in September 2023 with a bridge search in October 2024, and the source notes limited or conflicting evidence for many interventions.

issues.title: Dilation and Curettage (D&C)
issues.text: When local anesthesia is used, 1% lidocaine is most commonly injected into the cervix and lower uterine segment. Anesthesia personnel are required if IV sedation or general anesthesia is used.

issues.title: Dilation and Curettage (D&C)
issues.text: When local anesthesia is used, 1% lidocaine is most commonly injected into the cervix and lower uterine segment; IV sedation and general anesthesia are also described as options. The D&C review does not specify drug regimens.

issues.title: Dilation and Curettage (D&C)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not imply that blockade is routine for D&C.

issues.title: Dilation and Curettage (D&C)
issues.text: The procedure-specific source is an educational clinical review that includes pregnant and nonpregnant patients and focuses on first-trimester procedures before 14 weeks; it is not a detailed anesthesia protocol.

issues.title: Gynecologic Oncology Staging Laparotomy
issues.text: Use postoperative bladder drainage for a short period where clinically suitable; the guideline prefers less than 24 hours, while noting limited gynecologic-surgery evidence.

issues.title: Gynecologic Oncology Staging Laparotomy
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Gynecologic Oncology Staging Laparotomy
issues.text: Encourage mobilization within 24 hours where appropriate. Start oral fluids and food on the day of surgery whenever possible; in uncomplicated recovery, IV fluids beyond 12–24 hours are rarely needed once oral intake and analgesia are tolerated.

issues.title: Gynecologic Oncology Staging Laparotomy
issues.text: The most procedure-relevant source is a 2016 ERAS postoperative-care guideline covering open general gynecologic and major oncologic surgery. It explicitly does not supply an intraoperative anesthetic protocol for this case.

issues.title: Hysteroscopy
issues.text: The ACOG consensus addresses in-office pain management, not general anesthesia or comprehensive perioperative care. Its literature search covered English-language human studies through September 2023, with a bridge search in October 2024, and reports heterogeneous or limited evidence for many interventions.

issues.title: Hysteroscopy
issues.text: The 2025 office-hysteroscopy article provides procedural guidance and discusses evidence from reviews, trials, observational studies, and case reports, but it is not an anesthesia reference and lacks airway, emergence, and detailed recovery protocols.

issues.title: Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (TLH / LSH)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Laparoscopic Ovarian Cystectomy / Oophorectomy
issues.text: The supplied trial enrolled elective patients aged 18–65 years with ASA I–II status; that narrow population does not establish eligibility or risk estimates for other adults. It gives no detailed exclusion criteria or comorbidity assessment.

issues.title: Laparoscopic Ovarian Cystectomy / Oophorectomy
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockers are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred and recovery to TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis should be confirmed before extubation. This applies to cases using neuromuscular blockade, not to local or neuraxial techniques without it.

issues.title: Laparoscopic Ovarian Cystectomy / Oophorectomy
issues.text: In an ovarian-cystectomy randomized trial, nausea/vomiting and the QoR-15 pain domain were reported as recovery outcomes, with QoR-15 assessed at 24 hours. The abstract does not describe an emergence protocol, PACU management, discharge criteria, or postoperative-care protocols.

issues.title: Laparoscopic Ovarian Cystectomy / Oophorectomy
issues.text: The most procedure-specific evidence supplied is an abstract-only randomized trial in 80 elective ASA I–II patients. It addresses analgesia and recovery outcomes, not airway, positioning, monitoring, fluids, bleeding, or detailed hemodynamics.

issues.title: Myomectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: Use an individualized multimodal, opioid-sparing approach where appropriate. The gynecologic ERAS review describes combinations of non-opioid agents, NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors, but does not establish a universal regimen or dose.

issues.title: Myomectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: Regional blocks are an option, not a required technique. In a single-center randomized trial of laparoscopic myomectomy, TIVA alone was compared with TAPB+RSB or QLB-LSAL; resting and movement pain scores were lower in the block groups. Follow-up was limited to 48 hours, and the trial was underpowered to detect rare complications.

issues.title: Myomectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation.

issues.title: Myomectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: The most directly procedure-specific anesthesia article is a 2011 narrative overview of laparoscopic myomectomy, without formal evidence grading or comparative outcome data; treat its recommendations as limited and not as current universal standards.

issues.title: Myomectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: The randomized analgesia trial concerns selected elective laparoscopic patients and reports only 48-hour follow-up; it cannot establish long-term benefit, rare-event safety, or practice for open myomectomy.

issues.title: Ovarian Cancer Debulking (Cytoreductive Surgery)
issues.text: Ovarian cancer debulking aims to reduce residual tumor as much as possible, with R0 resection described as the operative aim; the supplied sources do not define the surgical access or extent.

issues.title: Ovarian Cancer Debulking (Cytoreductive Surgery)
issues.text: The described operations are primary or interval tumor-debulking procedures intended to reduce postoperative residual tumor burden, with R0 resection as the aim.

issues.title: Ovarian Cancer Debulking (Cytoreductive Surgery)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockers are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation apply; these recommendations do not impose paralysis or extubation monitoring on cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Postpartum Tubal Ligation
issues.text: ACOG categorizes PPTL as urgent and ideally performed within 24 hours after delivery. Individualize timing and anesthetic technique according to anesthetic and obstetric risks and patient preference.

issues.title: Postpartum Tubal Ligation
issues.text: Before elective PPTL, avoid solid food for 6 to 8 hours depending on food type and consider aspiration prophylaxis. For laboring patients with aspiration risks, consider additional oral-intake restrictions case by case.

issues.title: Postpartum Tubal Ligation
issues.text: Consider aspiration prophylaxis with a nonparticulate antacid, an H2-receptor antagonist, and/or metoclopramide as appropriate. The guideline reports effects on gastric acidity and peripartum nausea, but does not establish that prophylaxis changes aspiration frequency or outcomes.

issues.title: Postpartum Tubal Ligation
issues.text: A labor epidural is an option only if it is functional and provides an adequate surgical block. A T4 pinprick level is identified as indicated for surgical anesthesia in the OpenAnesthesia review; confirm block adequacy before proceeding.

issues.title: Postpartum Tubal Ligation
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies when blockade is used, not to neuraxial or local techniques without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Robotic Hysterectomy
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Robotic Hysterectomy
issues.text: Pneumoperitoneum-related increases in intra-abdominal pressure can affect airway pressure, cerebral and ocular pressures, and hemodynamics. The review reports that mean arterial pressure may decrease at pressures over 15 mmHg; this is a reported physiologic effect, not a stated intervention threshold.

issues.title: Robotic Hysterectomy
issues.text: The 2025 respiratory-mechanics study is retrospective and single-institution, with historical practice data; its findings do not establish current ventilation recommendations. The general robotic/laparoscopic review is educational and not a procedure-specific guideline.

issues.title: Sacrocolpopexy (Open / Robotic)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not imply paralysis is required for every approach.

issues.title: Sacrocolpopexy (Open / Robotic)
issues.text: In a prospective series of 132 laparoscopic sacrocolpopexies beyond the learning curve, reported blood loss was 185 mL (SD 124). A separate cohort estimated blood loss from the difference between pre- and postoperative hemoglobin and did not report a separate measured quantity. These observational series results are not an individualized blood-loss prediction.

issues.title: Sacrocolpopexy (Open / Robotic)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockers have been used, confirm quantitative TOF recovery to at least 0.9 before extubation; this guidance applies to NMB use, not to cases performed without it.

issues.title: Sacrocolpopexy (Open / Robotic)
issues.text: Procedure-specific evidence is limited: one source is a retrospective cohort with 110 patients and six-month follow-up; the laparoscopic procedural review is narrative and reports observational experience. Neither is an anesthesia guideline.

issues.title: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH)
issues.text: When IV fluids are needed, balanced crystalloids such as Ringer’s lactate are preferred over large volumes of 0.9% saline. Stop IV fluids within 24 hours when oral intake is adequate.

issues.title: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH)
issues.text: Use judicious opioids when appropriate and emphasize stepwise, multimodal, nonopioid strategies. For women undergoing TAH, preemptive acetaminophen, gabapentin, NSAIDs, and COX-2 inhibitors have been shown to reduce total narcotic requirements and improve pain and satisfaction.

issues.title: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH)
issues.text: TAP blocks are an option, but findings are mixed. A small randomized TAH trial found lower 24-hour morphine use in its TAP group than in its epidural and parenteral groups; its protocol and population do not establish a universal preferred technique.

issues.title: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm quantitative TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation. This guidance addresses neuromuscular blockade generally, not TAH specifically.

issues.title: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH)
issues.text: The TAH randomized trial is narrow evidence: 60 selected patients, with exclusions including BMI of 30 or greater, and study-specific analgesia regimens. Its comparative results should not be converted into routine doses or a universal technique.

issues.title: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH)
issues.text: The AHRQ anesthesiology evidence-review material supplied here is only an abstract and does not state specific recommendations or regimens. Adult-focused applicability is not consistently defined across sources; the TAH trial includes adults aged 18–60, while the broader guidance does not explicitly define an adult-only population.

issues.title: Vaginal Hysterectomy (VH)
issues.text: ERAS guidance favors balanced crystalloid over normal saline when IV fluids are required and recommends oral fluids and food on the day of surgery whenever possible. In uncomplicated recovery, postoperative IV fluids beyond 12–24 hours are rarely needed once oral intake and analgesia are tolerated.

issues.title: Vaginal Hysterectomy (VH)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, quantitative monitoring is recommended, with confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This applies when blockade is used, not to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Vaginal Hysterectomy (VH)
issues.text: Monitor for pain, hemorrhage, and urinary retention. ERAS recommends short-duration postoperative bladder drainage, preferably less than 24 hours; the guideline notes limited gynecologic-surgery evidence.

issues.title: Vulvar / Vaginal Procedures (Excision / Repair)
issues.text: For vulvar punch biopsy, reported complications are rare (less than 1%). Reported events include bleeding, infection, pain from inadequate anesthesia, vagal response, scarring, keloid formation (especially in skin of colour), and rare argyria associated with topical silver nitrate or silver-coated wound dressings. Do not extrapolate this rate to larger operations.

issues.title: Vulvar / Vaginal Procedures (Excision / Repair)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirming TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, using the adductor pollicis site; this does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Cubital Tunnel Release
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring and confirmation of recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis apply; these requirements do not imply that blockade is needed for this operation.

issues.title: Dupuytren Contracture Release
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA guideline recommends quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. This is conditional on NMB use, not a requirement for local-anesthetic cases.

issues.title: Ganglion Cyst Excision
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to local-only cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Hand Infection Incision and Drainage (Felon / Flexor Tenosynovitis)
issues.text: For felon I&D, pack the wound and splint the finger; remove packing 24 to 48 hours after the procedure and have a physician re-examine the finger.

issues.title: Nerve Repair (Digital / Peripheral)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply as a routine requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Hepatic Resection (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: CT or MRI can estimate future liver remnant (FLR) volume; interpret it alongside liver function and post-hepatectomy liver failure risk. The review cites minimum FLR volumes of 20% with normal liver function, 30–40% with severe steatohepatitis or prior hepatotoxic chemotherapy, and at least 50% with cirrhosis.

issues.title: Hepatic Resection (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: Optimize relevant comorbidities and consider chemotherapy-related hepatic and cardiac effects; the review states surgery should be delayed until 4–6 weeks after neoadjuvant treatment.

issues.title: Hepatic Resection (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: Monitor for PHLF, bile leak, postoperative haemorrhage, renal dysfunction, and metabolic disturbance. The review describes PHLF by rising INR and bilirubin on or after postoperative day 5.

issues.title: Liver Transplant
issues.text: In liver transplantation, post-reperfusion syndrome is defined as a 30% decrease in MAP for at least one minute within the first five minutes after graft reperfusion; it can cause severe arrhythmias or asystole.

issues.title: Liver Transplant
issues.text: When a neuromuscular blocking drug has been used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Open Cholecystectomy
issues.text: The open-cholecystectomy source does not specify an emergence or extubation approach. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation.

issues.title: Whipple Procedure (Pancreaticoduodenectomy)
issues.text: The procedural review does not specify emergence or extubation criteria. For patients who receive neuromuscular blocking drugs, confirm a TOF ratio of ≥0.9 before extubation.

issues.title: Whipple Procedure (Pancreaticoduodenectomy)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, ASA guideline recommendations summarized in the supplied source support quantitative monitoring and confirming a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: ACDF (Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, quantitative monitoring is recommended, with adductor pollicis monitoring preferred and a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 confirmed before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: ACDF (Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion)
issues.text: The largest ACDF-specific source is a retrospective database study of adults receiving general anesthesia. It reports associations with 30-day outcomes, not causal effects or a detailed anesthesia-management protocol; important ACDF outcomes and blood-loss volume were not captured.

issues.title: Cervical Laminectomy / Laminoplasty
issues.text: SSEP/MEP monitoring may support detection of cord compromise; recovery priorities include a prompt neurological assessment and attention to new root-level weakness, particularly C5 palsy.

issues.title: Cervical Laminectomy / Laminoplasty
issues.text: Segmental root palsy, most often involving C5, is reported after laminoplasty. New postoperative weakness or sensory symptoms warrant prompt neurological assessment and communication with the surgical team.

issues.title: Cervical Laminectomy / Laminoplasty
issues.text: The procedure-specific source is a 2008 narrative review, not an anesthesia guideline, and does not provide a systematic-review method. Its recommendations and numerical outcomes draw on cited studies and author experience.

issues.title: Craniotomy for Brain Tumor
issues.text: If a neuromuscular blocking drug was used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Craniotomy for Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
issues.text: Do not use 30–35 mmHg as a routine PaCO₂ target for every TBI patient. ACS 2024 guidance gives an initial PaCO₂ target of 35–45 mmHg when intracranial hypertension is absent; raised ICP, severe metabolic acidosis and significant pulmonary disease require an individualized strategy. Therapeutic hyperventilation belongs in an ICP-directed rescue or tiered pathway, not a universal ventilation recipe.

issues.title: Craniotomy for Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
issues.text: The Brain Trauma Foundation Level II B recommendation advises against prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 25 mmHg or less. Its older statements on temporary hyperventilation and brain-oxygen monitoring are restated with an explicit warning that they do not meet current evidence standards. Do not present all these statements as equally graded recommendations.

issues.title: Deep Brain Stimulator (DBS) Placement
issues.text: The DBS-specific anesthetic evidence provided consists mainly of reviews rather than procedure-specific society standards. The 2015 source is a narrative review; the 2014 source is a systematic literature review, but it reports institutional variation and unresolved anesthetic effects on MER.

issues.title: Epilepsy Surgery (Temporal Lobectomy / Cortical Resection)
issues.text: Provide postanesthesia care with continuing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative train-of-four recovery to at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation.

issues.title: MEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
issues.text: Volatile anesthetics suppress evoked responses. One review describes concentrations below 0.5 MAC as generally compatible with acceptable MEPs, while another warns that halogenated agents may abolish MEPs even at low doses. Prefer a stable technique and do not treat 0.5 MAC as a guaranteed safe threshold.

issues.title: MEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
issues.text: MEP alarm criteria vary by procedure and practice: one review reports absence of mMEP as an alarm sign for spinal surgery and a greater-than-50% amplitude decrement as a potential alarm sign for brain surgery in the authors’ laboratory. A spine review states that there is no clear consensus on meaningful change and describes a 50% increase in stimulus intensity needed to elicit tceMEPs as significant.

issues.title: MEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
issues.text: The general IOM review does not provide procedure-specific analgesia or detailed postoperative care. A spine-monitoring review describes a balanced TIVA approach including an opioid such as sufentanil and says the infusion is usually stopped 30–60 minutes before the end of surgery to provide analgesia at emergence.

issues.title: MEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockers have been used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone, with TOF ratio at least 0.9 confirmed at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies when blockade is used, not to every MEP case.

issues.title: Neuro-Angiography / Cerebral Angiogram (Diagnostic)
issues.text: After diagnostic cerebral arteriography, achieve common femoral artery hemostasis with manual compression or a percutaneous closure device. At the authors’ institution, pressure is typically held for approximately 20 minutes with a 5-Fr system.

issues.title: SSEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
issues.text: An SSEP amplitude decrease of 50% or greater and/or latency increase of 10% or greater is commonly considered significant when not attributable to anesthetic or temperature changes. Criteria are empirical; changes should be sustained and reproducible, and a physiologically meaningful change should appear in more than one recording and preferably more than one modality.

issues.title: SSEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
issues.text: Volatile anesthetics suppress cortical SSEP amplitude and increase latency in a dose-dependent manner. The review describes cortical monitoring as compatible with concentrations up to 0.5 MAC with nitrous oxide or up to 1.0 MAC without it; these are context-specific compatibility statements, not universal anesthetic targets.

issues.title: SSEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
issues.text: Use a sustained, reproducible SSEP amplitude decrease of 50% or greater and/or latency increase of 10% or greater as a commonly used warning criterion when not attributable to anesthetic or temperature changes. Criteria are empirical; latency changes of 7–10% and amplitude reductions of 45–50% have also occurred without postoperative neurologic change.

issues.title: SSEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative TOF ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this recommendation does not impose blockade or reversal on cases where neuromuscular blockers were not used.

issues.title: Subdural / Epidural Hematoma Evacuation
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Transsphenoidal Pituitary Surgery (TSPS / Endoscopic)
issues.text: Position supine with head-up tilt; the review describes 20–30° to improve venous drainage. Head support may be a horseshoe rest, pillow or Mayfield clamp. Expect restricted access because of the surgical team and equipment arrangement.

issues.title: Transsphenoidal Pituitary Surgery (TSPS / Endoscopic)
issues.text: Monitor urine output and fluid balance, particularly with hormone-secreting or large tumours. The surgical team may request Valsalva to improve visualisation, check for a CSF leak, or ensure haemostasis. Alert the anaesthesia team to a CSF leak because it limits maintenance of a 30° head-up tilt after surgery.

issues.title: Transsphenoidal Pituitary Surgery (TSPS / Endoscopic)
issues.text: CSF leak occurs in 2–12% of transsphenoidal resections and is more common with revision surgery and large adenomas. Prompt repair is essential because of risks including meningitis and pneumocephalus.

issues.title: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) Shunt Placement / Revision
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, apply quantitative monitoring and confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade has been used, assess recovery appropriately; general ASA guidance recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

issues.title: Labor Epidural Placement
issues.text: For thrombocytopenia, weigh the cause, bleeding history, signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation, competing risks, airway factors, and patient preference. SOAP consensus describes risk as likely low at platelet counts of at least 70,000 × 10⁶/L for specified common etiologies when there is no bleeding-history or DIC concern; lower counts require individualized assessment, not an automatic rule.

issues.title: Labor Epidural Placement
issues.text: The ASA obstetric anesthesia guideline is based on searches ending in 2015 and presents recommendations rather than absolute requirements; the 2021 ASA neuraxial guideline and 2021 SOAP thrombocytopenia consensus provide more directly relevant procedural and platelet-assessment guidance.

issues.title: Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS) — Cesarean Hysterectomy
