issues.text: For stable patients, the cited recommendation is planned delivery at 34 + 0 to 35 + 6 weeks; earlier delivery is for obstetric indications. This is a source-based planning range, not an individual timing directive.

issues.title: Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS) — Cesarean Hysterectomy
issues.text: Anesthetic comparisons are uncertain: source 0 notes differing outcomes and selection bias. Technique should therefore be individualized rather than presented as a single mandatory approach.

issues.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage Management
issues.text: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is defined in the supplied summary as blood loss greater than 1000 mL after either vaginal or cesarean delivery. Causes are commonly organized as tone, trauma, tissue, and thrombin.

issues.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage Management
issues.text: For major obstetric hemorrhage, follow a locally appropriate massive-transfusion protocol. The review describes packed red cells and FFP in a 1:1 ratio, with early platelet use, and cautions that large volumes of crystalloids or colloids can cause dilutional coagulopathy.

issues.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage Management
issues.text: The sources present PPH thresholds at different levels of detail: one defines PPH as blood loss greater than 1000 mL after either delivery, while the review classifies 500–1000 mL as minor and more than 1000 mL as major. Interpret these definitions in the applicable clinical context.

issues.title: Preeclampsia / Severe Preeclampsia — Anesthesia Management
issues.text: Use the SOAP thrombocytopenia consensus as a qualified decision framework, not a standalone cutoff: for a known hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, a count at or above 70,000 × 10⁶/L is described as likely low risk when there is no bleeding-history or DIC concern and neuraxial care is clinically indicated. Lower counts require individualized weighing of competing risks.

issues.title: Urgent/Emergent C-Section (Category 1 & 2)
issues.text: The available sources do not define category 1 or 2 criteria or a decision-to-delivery target for this case. No category-specific threshold or time target is asserted here.

issues.title: Blepharoplasty (Upper / Lower Eyelid)
issues.text: The 2009 overview gives brief anesthesia options and surgical details but lacks airway-management guidance, monitoring recommendations, and an anesthetic regimen. Its local/general choices should be interpreted as options, not a decision rule.

issues.title: Cataract Surgery (Phacoemulsification)
issues.text: This 2012 regional-anaesthesia review does not state a formal search method or evidence-grading approach; interpret its technique and risk statements in that context.

issues.title: Retinal Detachment Repair (Vitrectomy/Scleral Buckle)
issues.text: The procedure-specific anesthesia source is a brief 2008 letter, not a comprehensive guideline or comparative study. Its anesthesia detail is limited, so it should not be treated as definitive for current practice.

issues.title: Retinal Detachment Repair (Vitrectomy/Scleral Buckle)
issues.text: The 2023 retinal-detachment review informs surgical selection, tamponade, positioning, and gas-related precautions, but explicitly provides limited anesthesia detail. The adult ophthalmic review supplies broader context rather than a retinal-detachment-specific anesthetic protocol.

issues.title: Strabismus Repair (Adult)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Strabismus Repair (Adult)
issues.text: The review reports adult PONV at 30%, independent of general anaesthetic technique, and notes that ondansetron plus dexamethasone is often given prophylactically to adults.

issues.title: ACL Reconstruction
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, employ quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Ankle ORIF
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are supported. These recommendations do not apply to cases managed without neuromuscular blockade or general anesthesia.

issues.title: Ankle ORIF
issues.text: The risk-and-complications review is a narrative review published in 2014. Its findings are useful for orthopedic complications but do not supply current, procedure-specific anesthesia protocols.

issues.title: External Fixator Placement
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, confirm quantitative train-of-four recovery to at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This requirement does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Irrigation and Debridement (I&D) of Joint / Wound
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade or to every regional anesthetic.

issues.title: Laminectomy (Lumbar / Cervical)
issues.text: For minor spine procedures classified by the review as up to two-level decompression without instrumentation, it describes an 18–20G IV and an arterial line only when medically indicated. Do not generalize access recommendations for major or complex operations to every decompression.

issues.title: Laminectomy (Lumbar / Cervical)
issues.text: Do not infer that NSAIDs are universally appropriate or inappropriate after decompression from fusion-related evidence. The supplied spine review says selective COX-2 effects were reported while non-union and bleeding concerns remained debatable; it does not resolve drug choice for this individual procedure.

issues.title: Laminectomy (Lumbar / Cervical)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm TOF recovery of at least 0.9 before extubation. This applies when blockade is used, not to local-anesthetic or neuraxial cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Long Bone ORIF (Tibia / Femur / Humerus)
issues.text: When a neuromuscular blocking drug is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This guidance applies to neuromuscular blockade, not to every regional or local-anesthetic case.

issues.title: Long Bone ORIF (Tibia / Femur / Humerus)
issues.text: In a retrospective cohort of isolated periprosthetic distal femur fractures, median estimated blood loss was 200 mL (IQR 137.5–250 mL; range 10–1,000 mL). This cohort does not establish expected blood loss or transfusion practice for tibial, femoral-shaft, or humeral ORIF; it reports no fluid administration, transfusions, or specific blood-management measures.

issues.title: Long Bone ORIF (Tibia / Femur / Humerus)
issues.text: Base extubation on the patient's clinical status and adequate recovery from any neuromuscular blockade used; quantitative TOF confirmation of at least 0.9 is recommended before extubation when applicable.

issues.title: Lower Extremity Amputation (Orthopedic) — Toe / Ray / Transmetatarsal
issues.text: The amputation review does not provide an emergence or extubation protocol. If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, the ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Lumbar Discectomy / Microdiscectomy
issues.text: When a neuromuscular blocker has been used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended by the cited ASA guideline overview. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Pelvic Fracture Fixation
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirming a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Rotator Cuff Repair (Arthroscopic)
issues.text: Use multimodal analgesia unless contraindicated: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2-specific inhibitor, with opioids reserved for rescue. Individualize agents to patient factors and local practice.

issues.title: Scoliosis Correction (Posterior Spinal Fusion with Instrumentation) (Adult)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockers were used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery before extubation; the supplied guideline specifies adductor pollicis monitoring and a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9.

issues.title: Scoliosis Correction (Posterior Spinal Fusion with Instrumentation) (Adult)
issues.text: The 2025 blood-pressure review is a narrative clinical review, and the supplied sources do not provide an adult posterior-fusion-specific standard for neuromonitoring rescue, extubation, PONV prevention, or postoperative analgesia.

issues.title: Shoulder Arthroplasty (Total or Reverse)
issues.text: Avoid hypotension that could compromise cerebral perfusion during beach-chair positioning. One study summarized in a 2025 clinical review suggested cerebral blood flow was maintained above a particular MAP; that finding is not a universal patient-specific target or a procedure guideline.

issues.title: Shoulder Arthroplasty (Total or Reverse)
issues.text: No procedure-specific emergence or extubation approach is supplied. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation follow the cited ASA guideline summary.

issues.title: Shoulder Arthroplasty (Total or Reverse)
issues.text: The shoulder-anesthesia source is a 2012 review, not a guideline or trial, and combines evidence from different shoulder procedures. Its technique and analgesia descriptions should not be treated as validated arthroplasty-specific prescriptions.

issues.title: Shoulder Arthroplasty (Total or Reverse)
issues.text: The 2025 blood-pressure article is a clinical review; beach-chair numeric findings and management descriptions rely on cited studies, not a shoulder-arthroplasty-specific trial or society protocol.

issues.title: Shoulder Arthroscopy
issues.text: Beach-chair positioning is associated with reduced cerebral oxygenation and blood flow and neurological complications. The review describes gradual table elevation, pre-emptive vasopressor infusion to stabilize MAP ≥70 mmHg, and continuous cerebral oximetry as a management strategy; this is not a universal MAP target.

issues.title: Shoulder Arthroscopy
issues.text: In patients receiving sevoflurane in the beach-chair position, one study suggested cerebral blood flow was maintained only when MAP exceeded 70 mmHg. This is a study-specific finding, not a universal target.

issues.title: Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA)
issues.text: Fat embolism syndrome may complicate long-bone fractures, intramedullary nailing, or joint arthroplasty. Its classic features are respiratory distress, altered mental status, and petechial rash; onset is typically 12–72 hours after injury or instrumentation.

issues.title: Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA)
issues.text: Use multimodal analgesia to support function and limit opioid exposure. The THA review describes regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, with rescue opioid, as basic multimodal analgesia; select components for the patient's renal, cardiovascular, bleeding, and other risks.

issues.title: Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA)
issues.text: The TKA anesthesia and analgesia sources are reviews, not procedure-specific guidelines. The 2017 review notes conflicting comparative evidence and cautions that larger, robust clinical-outcome studies are needed.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: Trigger finger release is an open division of the A1 pulley. The available sources describe awake local anesthesia, with light sedation also an option; they do not establish a single anesthetic technique for every patient.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: The key procedural priorities are complete A1 release while preserving the A2 pulley and protecting the radial and ulnar neurovascular bundles. Incomplete release may leave triggering; inadvertent A2 release can cause bowstringing.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: Open A1 pulley release is described as definitive treatment, typically considered when symptoms persist despite conservative management, including at least one corticosteroid injection. Symptoms include pain, clicking, locking or catching, reduced range of motion, and tenderness or a palpable A1-pulley nodule.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: The described open technique exposes and divides the A1 pulley, then irrigates and closes the wound. One source describes transverse or longitudinal incisions by surgeon preference; another describes a longitudinal incision. This supports technique variation, not a single required incision.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: A complete release should preserve the A2 pulley. After release, flex and extend the digit to assess for persistent triggering; if clinically significant locking remains, identify its cause rather than extending the pulley release.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: If WALANT is used, the technique article recommends anesthetizing the patient in the preoperative holding area and allowing 20–30 minutes before incision for epinephrine to take effect.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: Protect the neurovascular bundles during exposure and preserve the A2 pulley while completing A1 release. The technique source identifies visualization of the distal volar-plate border as a sign of complete release.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: Incomplete A1 release may cause recurrent triggering; inadvertent A2 release risks bowstringing, with possible reduced digital strength and extensor lag. These are procedural hazards, not evidence of comparative rates between techniques.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: If significant locking persists after A1 release, investigate the cause rather than releasing additional pulley. The technique article describes tendon-directed procedures for selected causes, but does not establish them as routine.

issues.title: Trigger Finger Release
issues.text: The 2025 technique article is a surgical technique guide with a retrospective single-practice series and no comparison cohort; it is not a study of anesthetic regimens or outcomes.

issues.title: Abdominoplasty (Tummy Tuck)
issues.text: Use forced-air warming and monitor temperature because of the large exposed surface area; the procedure-specific review gives a core-temperature goal above 36 °C. Foley catheterization is generally unnecessary, but may be considered for long cases or anticipated significant fluid shifts.

issues.title: Abdominoplasty (Tummy Tuck)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred over clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Breast Reconstruction (Implant-Based)
issues.text: Prioritize temperature above 36°C and balanced fluid management that avoids both over- and under-resuscitation. The sources do not establish a case-specific fluid total or a universal role for invasive monitoring.

issues.title: Breast Reconstruction (Implant-Based)
issues.text: Maintain standard anesthetic monitoring and monitor temperature when clinically indicated; breast-reconstruction guidance recommends active warming and maintaining temperature above 36°C.

issues.title: Breast Reconstruction (Implant-Based)
issues.text: Reduce infection risk with chlorhexidine skin preparation and intravenous antibiotics covering common skin organisms within one hour of incision. Prolonged antibiotics beyond 24 hours have not been proved beneficial.

issues.title: Breast Reconstruction (Implant-Based)
issues.text: Use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia. The consensus lists NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, gabapentin, and local-anesthetic infiltration among options; selection should account for patient factors and operative considerations.

issues.title: Breast Reconstruction (Implant-Based)
issues.text: Treat PONV as an important recovery concern: use preoperative and intraoperative prophylaxis, with combined antiemetic classes supported over a single class in the consensus evidence. Neurokinin-1 antagonists, when selected, must be administered preoperatively; no doses are specified here.

issues.title: Breast Reconstruction (Implant-Based)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation applies when neuromuscular blockade is used, not to every anesthetic technique.

issues.title: Breast Reconstruction (Implant-Based)
issues.text: The 2024 narrative review concerns abdominal-based free-flap reconstruction, not implant-based reconstruction, and describes insufficient evidence and no established consensus for that distinct procedure. Its local practices are not treated here as implant standards.

issues.title: Burn Reconstruction
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockade has been used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are supported by the cited ASA guideline overview; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Craniofacial Reconstruction (Adult)
issues.text: During general anesthesia, continually evaluate ventilation and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of a TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation are recommended.

issues.title: DIEP / Free Flap Breast Reconstruction
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to cases without NMB.

issues.title: Facelift (Rhytidectomy)
issues.text: The article recommends EKG and laboratory testing for patients older than 50. This is a recommendation within a surgical review, not a universal anesthesia-testing rule; testing should be based on the individual’s clinical assessment and applicable policy.

issues.title: Facelift (Rhytidectomy)
issues.text: The review identifies hematoma as the most common reported complication after rhytidectomy, with an incidence of 0.9%–9%; it identifies hypertension as a controllable risk factor. Prompt recognition is emphasized because large hematomas can compromise the airway, and large hematomas require return to the operating room.

issues.title: Hand / Digit Flap Coverage
issues.text: If LAST is suspected, stop injection, call for help, stabilize vital signs, treat seizures (for example, with benzodiazepines), and initiate 20% intravenous lipid emulsion therapy.

issues.title: Hand / Digit Flap Coverage
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is recommended, with recovery to TOF ratio at least 0.9 confirmed before extubation; assess at the adductor pollicis rather than relying on clinical strength tests alone.

issues.title: Local Flap / Rotational Flap Coverage
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, quantitative monitoring and confirmation of a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis apply before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to procedures performed without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Local Flap / Rotational Flap Coverage
issues.text: The WALANT flap evidence is a retrospective series of 21 patients from one surgeon, with no comparison group; it does not report adult-specific outcomes, airway management, or comparative anesthesia outcomes. It cannot establish a general anesthetic standard.

issues.title: Panniculectomy
issues.text: Recovery should include the procedure-specific bent-at-the-waist, semi-Fowler positioning and postanesthesia observation. When neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm quantitative recovery to a TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation.

issues.title: Panniculectomy
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is recommended over clinical assessment alone; confirm TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation. This recommendation applies to blockade management, not to cases without neuromuscular blockers.

issues.title: Panniculectomy
issues.text: For wound protection, patients are instructed to remain bent at the waist 30 degrees in a semi-Fowler position for one week, then slowly return to fully upright.

issues.title: Pressure Ulcer Flap Reconstruction
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Pressure Ulcer Flap Reconstruction
issues.text: In a single-surgeon series of 117 patients with stage III or IV pressure sores, reported minor complications included partial dehiscence and necrosis (20.3%; 28 patients), while major complications included flap failure and dehiscence (7.2%; 10 patients). These are cohort findings, not individualized predictions.

issues.title: Rhinoplasty
issues.text: The procedure review describes multimodal postoperative pain options, including long-acting local anesthetic, COX-2 inhibitors, acetaminophen, and gabapentin, but provides no comparative regimen or doses. Select an approach considering the individual bleeding and medication risks.

issues.title: Scar Revision
issues.text: Nonsurgical or adjunct options include intralesional corticosteroids, 5-fluorouracil, laser resurfacing, fillers, and dermabrasion. Raised scars and depressed scars have different treatment options; avoid treating these methods as interchangeable.

issues.title: Scar Revision
issues.text: Assess whether the scar is mature and whether surgery is appropriate now. The overview describes maturation over about 12–18 months; immature scars may have poor surgical results, so maturity assessment should inform timing rather than relying on a single calendar cutoff.

issues.title: Split-Thickness / Full-Thickness Skin Graft
issues.text: For patients with burn injury, avoid succinylcholine from 48 hours after injury because extrajunctional acetylcholine-receptor upregulation can cause exaggerated hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest.

issues.title: Split-Thickness / Full-Thickness Skin Graft
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended by the cited ASA-guideline overview. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Tissue Expander Placement
issues.text: If a neuromuscular blocking drug was used, use quantitative monitoring rather than clinical assessment alone and confirm TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Damage Control Laparotomy
issues.text: After temporary closure, phase-2 ICU care focuses on resuscitation, rewarming, correction of coagulopathy and acidosis, and reassessment before definitive repair. Timing of the next operation depends on physiologic status.

issues.title: Damage Control Laparotomy
issues.text: Damage-control resuscitation emphasizes early replacement of blood components and avoiding excessive crystalloid. The 1:1:1 ratio is described as supported by military experience with civilian benefit still awaiting prospective-trial confirmation; it is not presented here as a universal prescription.

issues.title: Damage Control Laparotomy
issues.text: Plan postoperative disposition to ICU for phase-2 damage-control resuscitation. The provided sources do not establish routine extubation timing or require that every patient remain intubated.

issues.title: Damage Control Laparotomy
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade was used, quantitative monitoring is preferred and recovery to TOF ratio at least 0.9 should be confirmed at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Emergency Thoracotomy (Resuscitative / Trauma)
issues.text: The procedure may occur in a trauma bay or operating room. For the described clamshell approach, position supine with 360-degree access; team members should work in parallel so airway management and IV access do not delay chest entry.

issues.title: Exploratory Laparotomy (Trauma)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Fasciotomy (Lower Extremity)
issues.text: The leg has four compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, and deep posterior. The review describes medial and lateral incisions, each at least 15 cm; some surgeons propose a single lateral approach. The incision must be large enough to decompress all affected compartments.

issues.title: Artificial Urinary Sphincter (AUS) Implantation
issues.text: Postoperative catheter management and device activation are part of recovery, but the reported schedules differ by source and population. In the adult series, the system was activated 4–6 weeks after surgery; do not treat that cohort protocol as universal.

issues.title: Artificial Urinary Sphincter (AUS) Implantation
issues.text: If general anesthesia includes neuromuscular blockade, use quantitative monitoring and confirm adequate recovery before extubation. The cited ASA guideline overview recommends TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Artificial Urinary Sphincter (AUS) Implantation
issues.text: In a retrospective series of 32 adults undergoing AUS placement, two cases of transient perineal pain were reported; the pain was managed conservatively. The series does not specify an analgesic regimen.

issues.title: Artificial Urinary Sphincter (AUS) Implantation
issues.text: The male series describes activation at 4–6 weeks; the timing is a reported follow-up practice and should be determined with the implanting team. The female terminology report describes gradual activation but does not establish a male protocol.

issues.title: Artificial Urinary Sphincter (AUS) Implantation
issues.text: The male-relevant procedure evidence is a retrospective 32-adult clinical series, mostly men, involving AUS as part of complex urinary reconstruction. It is not an anesthesia trial or general practice guideline.

issues.title: Artificial Urinary Sphincter (AUS) Implantation
issues.text: In the retrospective adult series, the indwelling catheter remained for the first 24 hours, then was replaced by an external urine-collection device until system activation, 4–6 weeks postoperatively. This is the series’ reported practice, not a universal catheter schedule.

issues.title: Hydrocelectomy / Varicocelectomy
issues.text: In a prospective Nigerian study, hematoma occurred in 4 patients (8%) and wound infection in 3 (6%); all were managed conservatively. In a separate office-based series, one patient taking warfarin had a delayed postoperative hematoma, no postoperative infections were reported, and one small recurrence was noted at follow-up. These are cohort-specific outcomes, not general incidence estimates.

issues.title: Kidney Transplant
issues.text: The 2025 review advises dialysis before surgery for volume overload or hyperkalemia and day-before hemodialysis for most recipients, with day-of-surgery reassessment. Apply this in the context of the patient's dialysis course and transplant timing, rather than as a universal instruction for every recipient.

issues.title: Kidney Transplant
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery before extubation. The ASA guideline recommends monitoring at the adductor pollicis and a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to cases without blockade.

issues.title: Kidney Transplant
issues.text: The principal transplant-specific source is a 2025 review that presents recommendations but does not describe a systematic search or grade recommendations. Treat its proposed practices as review-level evidence, not as a procedure-specific society guideline.

issues.title: Kidney Transplant
issues.text: The other recipient-focused transplant source is a 2009 narrative review and is dated. Its reported fluid and CVP targets conflict with the newer review's advice against routine CVP targeting; the newer position is represented here without converting it into a universal fluid prescription.

issues.title: Laser Lithotripsy (Holmium / Thulium Laser)
issues.text: The adult trial was limited to patients aged 18–60 with ASA physical status 1–2 and renal stones. Its selection criteria do not define the broader adult population or a universal threshold for proceeding.

issues.title: Laser Lithotripsy (Holmium / Thulium Laser)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. This recommendation applies when a blocker has been administered, not to regional or local anesthesia without blockade.

issues.title: Laser Lithotripsy (Holmium / Thulium Laser)
issues.text: The 2019–2020 urologic anesthesia article is a narrative review and offers broad context rather than a procedure-specific guideline; the available textbook chapter page is only an abstract and subscription preview.

issues.title: Nephrectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: Consider iron deficiency, with or without anemia, in the context of anticipated blood loss. The general urologic review recommends treating iron deficiency when predicted blood loss exceeds 500 ml; this is not a nephrectomy-specific threshold.

issues.title: Nephrectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred; confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation. These recommendations do not apply to cases without blockade.

issues.title: Nephrectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: When blockade has been used, confirm quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation; the neuromuscular-blockade guidance recommends this site and a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9.

issues.title: Orchiectomy (Radical / Simple)
issues.text: In the Nigerian single-center cohort, the narrative reports scrotal haematoma in five patients (5.0%), while Table 1 reports four (5.00%); neither figure should be treated as a general incidence estimate.

issues.title: Orchiopexy (Adult)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Orchiopexy (Adult)
issues.text: In this single-center observational series of acute testicular-torsion cases with symptom-duration data, salvage was 52.2% (12/23) for presentation within 24 hours and 7.7% (2/26) after 24 hours. These findings are not an elective orchiopexy risk estimate or an anesthetic target.

issues.title: Partial Nephrectomy (Open / Robotic / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: The objective is complete excision of the renal mass while conserving functional parenchyma. Partial nephrectomy is recommended for cT1a–b tumors when technically feasible; the choice of operation remains dependent on tumor and patient characteristics.

issues.title: Partial Nephrectomy (Open / Robotic / Laparoscopic)
issues.text: For open partial nephrectomy, the review describes cold ischemia as valuable when complex resection or prolonged repair is anticipated to take more than 25 minutes. It states cold ischemia is not necessary when resection is expected to take less than 20–25 minutes. These are surgical-review statements, not universal anesthetic targets.

issues.title: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
issues.text: Aim for optimal glucose control; HbA1c above 8.5% is associated with increased postoperative infection. Address smoking cessation early because tobacco use is associated with higher surgical-site infection rates.

issues.title: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
issues.text: The available procedure-specific evidence does not establish a need for neuromuscular blockade. If blockade is used, the cited ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, measured at the adductor pollicis.

issues.title: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
issues.text: Postoperative urinary retention affects up to 27% of patients. Management typically includes Foley catheterization or clean intermittent self-catheterization.

issues.title: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
issues.text: The procedure source provides no emergence protocol. When neuromuscular blockade has been used, follow quantitative monitoring and reversal guidance applicable to the agent and block depth; confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

issues.title: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
issues.text: PCNL is described as an established minimally invasive option for renal calculi generally larger than 2 cm. The review also lists large renal calculi (>1.5–2 cm), staghorn calculi, and upper-tract calculi not responding to other treatment among its indications.

issues.title: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is recommended, with TOF ratio at least 0.9 confirmed before extubation. This recommendation applies when NMB has been used, not to regional or local anesthesia without blockade.

issues.title: Prostate Biopsy (TRUS / MRI-Fusion)
issues.text: The review recommends at least 10 systematically directed cores for an initial biopsy and more for larger glands; this is a biopsy sampling recommendation, not an anesthesia plan.

issues.title: Prostate Biopsy (TRUS / MRI-Fusion)
issues.text: The 2025 local-anesthesia source is a technical report and image-based guide, not a comparative trial; its authors note variable effectiveness across studies and need for further research.

issues.title: Prostate Biopsy (TRUS / MRI-Fusion)
issues.text: The biopsy review is narrative and dates to 2008. Its prophylaxis and complication data should not be read as a current institution-specific antibiotic protocol.

issues.title: Pyeloplasty (Open / Robotic)
issues.text: In this retrospective, single-center cohort, success was 84% after open and 87% after laparoscopic pyeloplasty; the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.631).

issues.title: Pyeloplasty (Open / Robotic)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred, with recovery confirmed at TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases conducted without NMB.

issues.title: Pyeloplasty (Open / Robotic)
issues.text: The principal procedure source is a retrospective, single-center comparative surgical-outcomes study of 113 patients, including children and adults. It is not an anesthesia guideline, and adult-specific outcome values are generally not supplied.

issues.title: Radical Cystectomy with Urinary Diversion
issues.text: Treat iron deficiency, with or without anemia, when predicted blood loss is >500 mL, as recommended in the anesthesia review.

issues.title: Robot-Assisted Prostatectomy (RALP)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm adequate recovery before extubation. The cited guidance recommends monitoring at the adductor pollicis and a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not imply paralysis for every anesthetic technique.

issues.title: Robot-Assisted Prostatectomy (RALP)
issues.text: The main RALP-specific source is an institutional review of approximately 1,500 cases, not a controlled comparative study or guideline. Its observed complications and local practices should not be treated as universal rates or requirements.

issues.title: Robot-Assisted Prostatectomy (RALP)
issues.text: The 2019 urologic source is a narrative review summarizing cited studies. Its RALP content is useful for physiologic considerations but does not establish a complete procedure-specific protocol.

issues.title: Robotic Nephrectomy (Partial or Radical)
issues.text: Patients are commonly positioned lateral decubitus. For robot-assisted partial nephrectomy, the robotic review describes 45° lateral decubitus with flank elevation; it does not specify a corresponding setup for radical nephrectomy.

issues.title: Robotic Nephrectomy (Partial or Radical)
issues.text: Positioning risks include pressure sores, nerve damage, and venous congestion; protect the patient’s head from robot-arm collisions. In one center, positioning injuries occurred in 6.6% of 334 adult robot-assisted urological procedures; this is not a nephrectomy-specific incidence.

issues.title: TURBT (Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade is used, employ quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery before extubation. The cited ASA-guideline overview recommends the adductor pollicis site and a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9.

issues.title: TURP (Transurethral Resection of the Prostate)
issues.text: Spinal anesthesia is an established approach and permits assessment of consciousness and patient-reported symptoms. The cited review notes a T10 level may preserve recognition of pain associated with capsular tear or bladder perforation; this is not a universal prescription.

issues.title: TURP (Transurethral Resection of the Prostate)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is preferred and recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis should be confirmed before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Ureteral Stent Placement / Removal
issues.text: In urgent obstructive-stone cases, infection and acute kidney injury are clinically important indications, and the cohort found associations between infection indication and 30-day mortality. This observational association is not proof of causation or a procedure-specific complication rate.

issues.title: Ureteral Stent Placement / Removal
issues.text: For patients who received neuromuscular blocking drugs, use quantitative monitoring and confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This guidance is conditional on blockade having been used.

issues.title: Ureteroscopy (URS)
issues.text: If a neuromuscular blocking drug is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred and recovery should be confirmed at TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation, using the adductor pollicis site. These recommendations concern blockade management, not a requirement to use blockade for ureteroscopy.

issues.title: Ureteroscopy (URS)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm quantitative TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation. The source recommends PACU attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

issues.title: Urethral Dilation / Stricture Repair
issues.text: Endoscopic treatment is typically performed in dorsal lithotomy, with cystoscopic equipment available. The balloon-dilation report specifies rigid cystoscopy for its described 30F balloon technique.

issues.title: AV Fistula Creation / Revision
issues.text: The procedure-specific sources do not establish an emergence protocol. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring, using the adductor pollicis, and confirming a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS) — Anesthesia Support
issues.text: The CAS cohort’s primary composite outcome included 30-day periprocedural mortality, postoperative ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, and myocardial infarction.

issues.title: Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS) — Anesthesia Support
issues.text: For carotid stenting access, the 2024 CIRSE standards advise ultrasound-guided local-anesthetic application at the anterior arterial wall and arterial puncture to reduce access-related pain and complications. Agent and dose are not specified in this recommendation.

issues.title: Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS) — Anesthesia Support
issues.text: The reported functional-outcome timing is internally inconsistent: the methods list 90-day mRS, while the results describe the comparison at 30 days. Interpret that result cautiously.

issues.title: Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS) — Anesthesia Support
issues.text: Access-site analgesia is supplemented by the 2024 CIRSE CAS Standards of Practice, a best-practice document rather than a clinical practice guideline or systematic review. The SVS sedation statement explicitly applies to TCAR/TFCAS; broader carotid-surgery recommendations are not automatically stenting instructions.

issues.title: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)
issues.text: CEA treats atherosclerotic carotid stenosis, usually at the carotid bifurcation. The cited review describes it as the treatment of choice for symptomatic internal carotid stenosis above 70%; the indication for asymptomatic high-grade stenosis is less clear.

issues.title: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)
issues.text: During carotid cross-clamping, the cited review states that arterial pressure should not fall below the patient’s baseline and describes maintaining it at baseline or up to 20% above baseline. The review cautions that pressure augmentation can precipitate myocardial ischemia; this is not a universal target.

issues.title: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. This recommendation applies when neuromuscular blockade is used; it does not impose paralysis or extubation requirements on local or regional techniques without a secured airway.

issues.title: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)
issues.text: The 2022 Italian-guideline update is a systematic evidence review, but reports that most included randomized and observational studies were low quality; it also identifies insufficient evidence on heparin reversal and non-robust evidence for postoperative blood-pressure management.

issues.title: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)
issues.text: The 2015 anesthesia review is an older narrative review that itself reports uncertainty about comparative anesthetic outcomes. Its detailed practice descriptions should be interpreted alongside the later guideline review and current local policy.

issues.title: Dialysis Graft Placement
issues.text: The procedure-specific PTFE report is a 1987 single-center experience series, with incomplete follow-up and no formal anesthesia protocol. Its technical and complication descriptions should not be assumed to represent current universal practice.

issues.title: Endovascular Aortic Repair (EVAR)
issues.text: The review states AAA surgery is usually offered when the anteroposterior diameter reaches 5.5 cm or growth exceeds 5 mm in 6 months; apply these thresholds in the individual clinical context.

issues.title: Endovascular Aortic Repair (EVAR)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; confirm train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Iliac Artery Bypass / Aortobifemoral Bypass
issues.text: Potential consequences of internal iliac artery occlusion include sigmoid injury and pelvic or gluteal ischemic symptoms. These are risks described in the article's literature discussion, not incidence estimates from its 12-patient series.

issues.title: Iliac Artery Bypass / Aortobifemoral Bypass
issues.text: After anesthesia, patients should be admitted to a PACU or equivalent unless the responsible anesthesiologist orders otherwise; destination should reflect the patient's condition and care plan. In the 12-patient aortoiliac series, all patients were observed in the ICU for at least 24 hours; this observational practice does not establish a routine ICU disposition for all aortobifemoral bypass patients.

issues.title: Lower Extremity Amputation (BKA / AKA)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Lower Extremity Amputation (BKA / AKA)
issues.text: The 2025 source is a narrative review of regional anesthesia, especially peripheral nerve blocks, rather than a guideline or systematic quantitative synthesis. Its authors identify selection bias, heterogeneity, retrospective designs, and limited technique-specific conclusions.

issues.title: Mesenteric Revascularization (Open / Endovascular)
issues.text: After restoration of SMA flow, planned reassessment is required. If bowel viability remains uncertain, re-exploration is most often within 24–48 hours.

issues.title: Mesenteric Revascularization (Open / Endovascular)
issues.text: For acute laparotomy, the operative goals are to restore perfusion, resect non-viable bowel, and preserve viable bowel. When viability remains uncertain, planned reassessment is required; re-exploration is most often within 24–48 hours.

issues.title: Mesenteric Revascularization (Open / Endovascular)
issues.text: When further bowel assessment is planned, temporary abdominal closure can permit second-look surgery; re-exploration is most often within 24–48 hours.

issues.title: Mesenteric Revascularization (Open / Endovascular)
issues.text: If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended; confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Open AAA Repair (Elective)
issues.text: For elective fusiform AAA, the review reports intervention thresholds that vary by sex and growth; it describes intervention for growth greater than 10 mm/year regardless of diameter. These are selection criteria from the cited guideline review, not an individualized operative decision.

issues.title: Open AAA Repair (Elective)
issues.text: When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended by the cited ASA-guideline overview. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

issues.title: Open AAA Repair (Elective)
issues.text: The principal anesthesia source is a 2010 book chapter/review, not a single evidence-graded protocol; it expressly notes areas of limited or conflicting evidence, including fluid choice and intraoperative epidural use.

issues.title: Open AAA Repair (Elective)
issues.text: The 2020 AAA review informs procedure selection and outcomes but is not an anesthesia reference and does not provide an OAR anesthetic regimen or immediate anesthesia-care instructions.

issues.title: Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (rAAA)
issues.text: Plan recovery in an ICU or equivalent critical-care setting capable of ongoing resuscitation and multisystem support. The review describes level 3 care; the institutional guideline recommends postoperative ICU monitoring.

issues.title: Varicose Vein Procedures (EVLA / Phlebectomy / Stripping)
issues.text: The main procedure review is a 2005 narrative overview, not an anesthesia protocol; it explicitly lacks detailed anesthetic and perioperative management information. Treat its procedural descriptions as contextual, not as a contemporary universal standard.

reports.title: Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
reviewNotes: The RYGB surgical review supplies operative anatomy and complication information but explicitly is not an anesthesia reference; anesthesia statements here rely mainly on broader bariatric guidance and general anesthesia standards.
The ERAS guideline reports limited or low-quality evidence for several bariatric interventions. Its broad recommendations should not be mistaken for an RYGB-specific protocol.

Fluid statements have an important tension: the guideline favors individualized goal-directed therapy and cautions against both hypovolemia and hypervolemia, while also reporting possible harm from restrictive administration. No fixed volume is justified.

RYGB-specific NSAID safety is unresolved in the supplied material. The surgical source reports marginal ulcer prevalence, while ERAS describes opioid reduction with NSAIDs across bariatric surgery; neither establishes a universal RYGB NSAID rule.
The operative source describes leak-test methods and defect closure but does not establish that a particular leak test or anesthetic response is mandatory.
The NMB recommendations apply only when neuromuscular blockers are used. TOF recovery guidance should not be generalized to cases without NMB.

Source 1 describes surgical leak-test methods but states that it does not specify airway management technique or monitoring beyond its examples; it does not establish an anesthesia-specific leak-test protocol.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not establish an RYGB-specific anesthetic protocol for airway technique, hemodynamic management, or intraoperative targets.
The supplied sources do not resolve RYGB-specific NSAID safety or provide a procedure-specific analgesia and PONV regimen.
corrections: Removed the Base44 claim that RYGB is the “most effective” bariatric procedure for type 2 diabetes remission; the supplied sources support significant metabolic improvement, not that comparative superlative.

Removed fixed positioning angles, a universal RSI instruction, and the assertion that an OGT is routinely used to decompress the gastric remnant or conduct leak testing; these are not established by the sources as universal anesthetic practice.
Removed a mandatory intraoperative leak-test claim. The RYGB review describes air or methylene-blue techniques but does not establish a universal mandate.
Removed the fixed restrictive fluid volume and claims that blood must always be available; the evidence supports individualized fluid management and gives no universal blood-preparation rule.

Corrected routine full sugammadex reversal to objective neuromuscular monitoring and reversal appropriate to measured blockade; the supplied guidance specifies monitoring rather than automatic reversal for every patient.
Removed the lifetime NSAID prohibition and blanket ketorolac avoidance claim. The supplied material identifies marginal-ulcer concern but does not determine a universal NSAID policy.
Replaced “immediate CPAP for OSAHS” as a universal rule with continuation of preoperative CPAP/BiPAP when indicated and individualized respiratory monitoring.
Omitted unsupported drug lists, fixed medication regimens, and other Base44 details not substantiated by the fetched evidence.

reports.title: Sleeve Gastrectomy
reviewNotes: The Base44 material is unverified and was not treated as evidence. Its fixed fluid total, mandatory RSI, universal videolaryngoscopy-first claim, specific drug regimens, and claims that sugammadex guarantees complete reversal were not carried forward as standards.

The BMI eligibility statement in the Base44 fields reflects older thresholds. The supplied StatPearls review describes 2022 ASMBS/IFSO guidance supporting consideration of metabolic and bariatric surgery at BMI 35 kg/m² or more regardless of comorbidity, with selected lower-BMI cases also considered; this is not an individual eligibility determination.
The ERAS guideline favors individualized goal-directed fluid therapy and reports risks associated with both hypovolemia and hypervolemia; this does not support a universal restrictive fluid total.
Neuromuscular monitoring and TOF thresholds apply when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used. They do not impose paralysis or quantitative TOF monitoring on every anesthetic approach.
The case report of sleeve gastrectomy under spinal anesthesia is a single case and does not establish routine regional anesthesia. Its reported patient outcome does not establish general safety.
The provided sources do not establish routine arterial-line use, mandatory crossmatch, a universal DVT-prophylaxis regimen, fixed PONV prophylaxis, or a universal extubation-support protocol.
evidenceGaps: The available sources do not provide a validated sleeve-specific intraoperative recognition and response pathway for suspected staple-line leak or other acute surgical complication.
The available sources do not establish a sleeve-specific PONV prophylaxis protocol or comparative regimen.
corrections: Removed the claim that videolaryngoscopy must always be first-line and direct laryngoscopy should never be attempted; the sources support availability and potential benefit of videolaryngoscopy, particularly when airway difficulty is anticipated, but describe heterogeneous efficacy.

Removed the assertion that RSI is universally preferred for all bariatric patients; the review says rapid-sequence or modified rapid-sequence induction may be considered when aspiration risk is significant.

Removed the fixed 500–1000 mL fluid prescription and blanket restrictive-fluid approach; the ERAS guideline supports individualized goal-directed therapy and avoidance of both hypovolemia and hypervolemia.
Removed specific induction, neuromuscular-blocker, reversal, and analgesic doses from the Base44 fields; supplied evidence does not support copying them as universal clinical instructions.
Corrected the claim that sugammadex ensures or guarantees complete reversal. Reversal depends on blocker, depth of blockade, dose, and objective monitoring.

Removed a universal reverse-Trendelenburg angle, mandatory arterial line, fixed blood preparation, and mandatory CPAP application; the supplied sources support individualized positioning, monitoring, and respiratory support.
Did not treat the case-report methylene-blue leak test, local anesthetic technique, or other single-case choices as routine standards.

reports.title: Burn Excision and Split-Thickness Skin Grafting
reviewNotes: The supplied acute-burn source is a narrative review with no systematic-review methods or evidence grading. Treat its descriptions of reported practice and expert recommendations accordingly.

The Base44 claims that excision within 72 hours reduces mortality, that one unit of blood is lost per 1% TBSA excised, that an arterial line is mandatory, and that ketamine is the ideal anesthetic are not established by the supplied evidence.
The source-supported blood-loss estimate differs from the Base44 figure and is itself an estimate from a review; it is not presented here as a reliable case-level prediction.

The Base44 fixed hemoglobin goal, mandatory CVP/central access, routine TXA or cell saver, fixed warm-room setpoint, and specified drug infusion recipes are not established as universal procedure requirements by these sources.

The source describes succinylcholine-associated hyperkalemia risk beginning 48 hours after burn injury. This draft retains the hazard as a source-supported consideration without framing it as a universal drug rule for every patient or burn phase.
The supplied material does not support a universal extubation destination, blood-product order, fluid total, or anesthetic regimen; these require individualized clinical judgment.
evidenceGaps: Contemporary adult, procedure-specific evidence comparing excision timing and operative approaches for patient-centered outcomes.
Comparative adult evidence for blood-conservation methods, including the effectiveness of TXA or cell salvage in this procedure.
A validated procedure-specific transfusion strategy or threshold for adult burn excision.
corrections: Removed the unsupported claim that early excision within 72 hours reduces mortality; the source supports early excision and coverage as standard care to reduce wound colonization and systemic sepsis, not that mortality claim.

Removed the estimate of one unit of red cells per 1% TBSA excised and the fixed hemoglobin target; the source provides a different broad estimate and advises transfusion based on physiology and anticipated ongoing loss.
Changed mandatory arterial line and central venous access claims to considerations based on anticipated bleeding, monitoring, and access needs.
Removed the fixed 37°C operating-room requirement; the review describes a temperature range dependent on age and burn severity and recommends active warming.
Removed the claims that ketamine is uniquely ideal and that specified anesthetic infusions are standard; the supplied review describes options and adjuncts without establishing a universal regimen.
Removed routine TXA, cell-saver, and fixed blood-product requirements because the supplied sources do not establish them as universal care.

reports.title: Escharotomy / Fasciotomy for Burns
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as a source. The supplied procedure source supports local anesthetic infiltration of unburnt skin and optional sedation, but not the listed ketamine, propofol, fentanyl, or midazolam doses, ketamine infusion, or drug-specific plan.

The claimed immediate peak-airway-pressure reduction of 10–20 cmH2O is not supported by the supplied sources. Chest release is intended to allow ventilation; response must be assessed rather than promised.

The claim that full-thickness eschar is insensate and therefore requires only sedation is not established in the supplied sources. The source specifically notes local anesthetic for unburnt skin into which the incision extends.
The source supports usual timing within the first 48 hours after injury, but not a fixed 24–48-hour rule or timing independent of clinical assessment.
The source supports bleeding as a possible complication, but not the Base44 assertion that no additional major blood loss is expected.
The supplied evidence does not justify treating loss of a distal Doppler signal as the sole indication, using a universal airway plan, or assuming a specific post-release ventilator response.
evidenceGaps: Adult-specific anesthetic evidence for escharotomy, including comparative evidence for local anesthesia alone versus sedation or general anesthesia.
Procedure-specific adult guidance for airway management when chest-wall release is undertaken in a patient with respiratory compromise.
Escharotomy-specific analgesia and PONV recommendations; the supplied sources do not establish a systemic regimen.
corrections: Removed unsupported ketamine 1–2 mg/kg, propofol/fentanyl, midazolam, and ketamine-infusion recipes.
Removed the asserted 10–20 cmH2O peak airway-pressure decrease and any implication that improvement is guaranteed or immediate.
Corrected the anesthesia description: general anesthesia is not usually required; sedation is optional, and local anesthetic is specified for unburnt skin into which the incision extends.
Removed the unsupported claim that full-thickness eschar is insensate.
Removed the claim that major blood loss is not expected; bleeding is a recognized complication, with no source-supported blood-loss estimate.
Replaced the unqualified “standard ASA” claim with applicable general monitoring standards, including the stated exception conditions for expired-CO₂ monitoring during moderate or deep sedation.

reports.title: Aortic Root / Ascending Aorta Repair
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, its fixed preoperative blood-pressure targets, DHCA safe interval, routine drug bundle, and routine ICU-intubation/extubation timing were not carried forward as universal recommendations.

The proximal-aortic review describes differing institutional approaches and unresolved evidence for temperature and cerebral-perfusion strategies. The draft avoids presenting one strategy or arrest duration as universally safe.

Positioning and procedure-specific extubation criteria are explicitly absent from the proximal-aortic source. The general postanesthesia standards support appropriate PACU or equivalent care but do not establish aortic-repair-specific disposition criteria.
The analgesia consensus applies broadly to adult cardiac surgery, not specifically aortic repair; its recommendations support individualized multimodal care rather than a single regimen.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific evidence to guide selection and monitoring of cerebral-protection strategies, including temperature and perfusion approach, remains limited or conflicting.
Aortic-repair-specific positioning, analgesic/PONV regimen, and extubation criteria are not provided in the fetched sources.
corrections: Removed the Base44 claim that deep hypothermia provides a fixed 45–60-minute safe arrest interval; the sources describe estimates and variable outcomes rather than a universal safe duration.
Removed a universal acute-dissection SBP/heart-rate target; the source supports reducing wall stress while maintaining end-organ perfusion, with clinical circumstances affecting the balance.

Removed blanket claims that bilateral radial lines, a PA catheter, EEG, and specific cerebral-protection drugs are mandatory for every case; the sources describe monitoring choices, limitations, and variation by operation and institution.
Removed the fixed 12–48-hour extubation schedule and mandatory postoperative intubation claim; the aortic review gives no extubation criteria or timing.

reports.title: Aortic Valve Replacement (AVR)
reviewNotes: The supplied case fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. In particular, the asserted induction and maintenance recipes, lesion-specific heart-rate and hemodynamic targets, transfusion threshold, routine monitoring package, and fixed early-extubation window are not supported by the supplied SAVR-specific source.

Do not describe TEE as universally indispensable for SAVR based on the MICS review: that review discusses TEE in minimally invasive procedures and its own scope, while the SAVR overview does not specify an intraoperative imaging protocol.
Do not transfer TAVR-specific access, pacing, or complication-management details to surgical AVR. The sources describe TAVR separately from SAVR.

The Cleveland Clinic source supports general SAVR procedure, valve-choice, and complication information but explicitly lacks detailed anesthesia guidance. The general MICS review is narrative and reports scarce large randomized data; its practice descriptions are not a universal standard.
ASA monitoring and postanesthesia-care standards apply generally, not as AVR-specific instructions. Quantitative TOF guidance applies when neuromuscular blockade is used, not to every anesthetic.
The supplied sources do not establish an AVR-specific troubleshooting sequence for new hemodynamic or rhythm disturbances; the complications bullet was narrowed to the supported communication point.
evidenceGaps: AVR-specific anesthetic physiologic targets and a detailed approach to management by valve lesion and ventricular function are not established in the supplied sources.
A SAVR-specific intraoperative echocardiography protocol, including routine indications and assessment criteria, is not provided.
The supplied material does not provide a detailed CPB, hemostasis, fluid, or transfusion protocol for SAVR.
SAVR-specific emergence criteria, postoperative pacing management, and ICU respiratory or hemodynamic protocols are not provided.
corrections: Removed the unsupported high-dose fentanyl, midazolam, etomidate, and rocuronium induction recipe and the TIVA/volatile maintenance recipe; the supplied sources do not establish these as SAVR regimens.
Removed asserted fixed heart-rate and loading/afterload targets for aortic stenosis and regurgitation; these targets are not established in the supplied evidence.
Removed the unverified routine radial arterial line timing, PA catheter, CVP, cerebral oximetry, external pads, cell-saver, and pacing setup as a universal SAVR package.
Removed the asserted hematocrit transfusion trigger and routine blood-product protocol; available sources provide no SAVR-specific threshold.
Replaced claims of universal TEE use and a fixed 4–8-hour extubation window with approach- and condition-dependent language supported by the available sources.
Removed unverified fixed postoperative drug choices and rescue-treatment claims for low cardiac output, heart block, bleeding, atrial fibrillation, or paravalvular leak.

reports.title: Bronchoscopy (Flexible / Rigid)
reviewNotes: Sources 0 and 1 are narrative/educational reviews, not procedure-specific society guidelines. The ASA monitoring standards are higher-authority for general monitoring; accordingly, this draft states expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring during moderate or deep sedation unless invalidated, despite source 0 reporting that it is usually not done.

The rigid-bronchoscopy review describes multiple ventilation methods. The draft does not turn ETT use or jet ventilation into a universal requirement; source 1 also describes ETT and LMA options for deeper sedation or general anesthesia.

The supplied evidence is adult-applicable in part, but source 0 includes pediatric techniques and source 1 does not define a trial population. Pediatric details and doses were not carried into adult recommendations.

Base44 claims not independently supported by the fetched evidence were excluded or qualified: routine glycopyrrolate, a specific propofol/fentanyl/dexmedetomidine combination, exact topical-lidocaine timing, an ETT size threshold for adult flexible bronchoscopy, mandatory post-transbronchial-biopsy chest radiography, and a universal NPO interval until gag returns.

The Base44 statement that rigid bronchoscopy requires ETT or jet ventilation overstates the evidence: general anesthesia is usual, but the review lists several ventilation approaches. Its claims about EBUS duration/sedation and a mandatory post-biopsy chest radiograph are not established by the supplied sources.
evidenceGaps: Adult procedure-specific guidance for EBUS and other advanced flexible bronchoscopic procedures, including how procedural goals affect anesthetic depth and airway strategy.
A bronchoscopy-specific recovery/imaging pathway after transbronchial biopsy, including indications for post-procedure chest imaging.
Bronchoscopy-specific guidance for oral intake after topical airway anesthesia and assessment of return of protective airway function.
corrections: Removed fixed anesthetic drug combinations and routine glycopyrrolate because the supplied evidence does not establish them as standard adult practice.
Removed the asserted 60–90 second topical-lidocaine timing and the claim that bronchoscopist-administered lidocaine is definitively the most effective technique.
Removed the universal adult ETT size threshold and the claim that rigid bronchoscopy must use an ETT or jet ventilation.
Corrected mandatory post-transbronchial-biopsy chest radiography to acknowledge pneumothorax risk while noting that the sources do not establish a universal imaging protocol.
Removed a fixed fasting interval after topical anesthesia; the sources identify aspiration risk but do not support that specific timing.
Did not include numerical medication doses, infusion rates, or a universal fluid, blood-loss, or recovery target.

reports.title: CABG (Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as clinical evidence. Removed its blanket beta-blocker continuation, ACE-I/ARB hold interval, antiplatelet instructions, mandatory pre-induction arterial line, and LIMA-side access restrictions because these are not established by the supplied sources.

Removed the Base44 induction and maintenance drug recipes, specific opioid doses, lidocaine and dexamethasone dosing, fixed heart-rate target, and claims that one anesthetic technique is required. The consensus advises against routine high-dose opioid anesthesia; the CABG source says outcomes do not differ with a particular anesthetic technique.

Did not adopt the Base44 ACT threshold as a universal target. The CABG source states a range considered adequate in its context; anticoagulation must be confirmed and managed for the individual bypass case.
Removed Base44 transfusion thresholds, hemoglobin goals, fixed extubation timing, and routine analgesic/PCA regimen: the supplied evidence does not support these as universal CABG standards.

Qualified TEE rather than repeating Base44's claim that it is mandatory for every cardiac case: the CABG source reports measurable outcome benefits; the robotic review's mandatory statement applies to minimally invasive cardiac surgery.
The available sources do not provide CABG-specific comparative medication-management instructions, a complete transfusion protocol, or detailed treatment algorithms for postbypass complications.
The source reports a typical MAP goal for its on-pump context, but the numerical target is omitted rather than presented as a fixed clinical target.
The supplied CABG summary does not establish transfusion thresholds, fluid totals, or blood-loss targets.
evidenceGaps: CABG-specific perioperative medication-management guidance for antiplatelet and cardiovascular drugs, including patient- and procedure-specific qualifiers.
A CABG-specific blood-management and transfusion protocol with context-appropriate criteria.
Detailed, validated postbypass complication recognition and escalation pathways beyond the hazards and assessment points described in the supplied summary.
fluids: This is a limitation of the supplied evidence rather than a clinical fluid-management recommendation.
corrections: Removed unsupported universal prescriptions for HR 55–75, ACT greater than 480, hemoglobin thresholds, and transfusion thresholds; did not substitute other fixed targets.
Removed fixed medication stop/continue intervals and drug-dose recipes from the unverified Base44 fields.
Corrected the implication that all CABG patients require the same airway, access, monitoring, anesthetic, fluid, analgesic, or extubation plan.
Corrected the claim that TEE is mandatory for all CABG cases; source support distinguishes conventional cardiac surgery from minimally invasive practice.
Removed fixed 4–6-hour extubation timing and replaced it with individualized ICU fast-track recovery language.

reports.title: Cardiac Catheterization / PCI
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. The 2014 catheterization review is the most directly relevant source, but it is not a formal guideline and provides limited PCI-specific detail.
Distinguished PCI sedation from TAVI practice; TAVI hemodynamic goals and reported extubation practice were not generalized to PCI.
Used ASA standards for general anesthesia monitoring and postanesthesia care, not as evidence for catheterization-specific airway, access, or complication protocols.
The adult cardiac-surgery analgesia consensus was not extrapolated into a PCI analgesia regimen. Pediatric catheterization material was excluded as a basis for adult practice.
No universal arterial line, intubation, blood availability, fluid volume, contrast limit, anticoagulation target, or access-site protocol is asserted.
evidenceGaps: Adult PCI-specific management of vascular-access complications and recovery-site surveillance, including differences by access route.
A fuller adult PCI-specific complication and rescue-management source beyond the review's limited discussion of thrombosis and sedation-related rescue.
PCI-specific analgesia and PONV evidence or guidance; the supplied pain consensus is for cardiac surgery.
corrections: Removed the unsupported claim that lead aprons are mandatory without exception; retained source-supported radiation protection principles and ALARA.
Removed the detailed midazolam, fentanyl, propofol, and dexmedetomidine dose/rate recipes; the supplied material does not validate them as a PCI regimen.
Removed the claim that arterial monitoring is routine; the ASA source requires general monitoring but does not mandate an arterial line for every case.

Removed unsupported claims and protocols concerning radial/femoral approach selection, access-site compression or closure, hematoma and retroperitoneal bleeding surveillance, and post-PCI renal monitoring schedules.

Removed the specific contrast-allergy premedication schedule and the blanket iodine-allergy framing; the supplied review discusses contrast-agent classes and prior reactions but does not establish that recipe.
Removed the assertion of minimal pain with a prescribed acetaminophen/ice plan and all cardiac-surgery analgesic dosing as PCI guidance.

Removed the claim that conversion from MAC to general anesthesia must be expected at any moment as a universal rule; retained the evidence-supported need for rescue readiness when instability or sedation complications arise.

reports.title: Cardiac Valve Repair / Replacement (Open)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unauthenticated material, not evidence. Remove or independently verify its routine high-dose fentanyl/induction recipe, valve-specific HR/SVR/preload rules, mandatory PA catheter and pre-induction arterial line, BIS/ACT list, and fixed ICU intubation or fast-track extubation timing; the fetched sources do not establish these as universal practice.

Do not present the Base44 SAM treatment recipe as a protocol. The mitral review supports optimizing filling, AV pacing to improve synchrony, and reducing hypercontractility, but does not support the listed exact drug choices or instruction to stop inotropes as a universal rule.

The cited ASA neuromuscular-blockade source is an overview of the 2023 guideline, not the full guideline. Its quantitative TOF recommendation applies when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, not to every anesthetic.

The mitral review discusses repair and selected replacement considerations; the aortic review focuses on repair and valve-sparing root procedures. They do not establish a comprehensive anesthetic reference for every valve, lesion, or replacement technique.
The supplied valve-repair reviews are not detailed anesthesia protocols and do not establish universal hemodynamic or fluid-management targets.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific anesthetic planning for open replacement across valve types, including how lesion-specific physiology should alter intraoperative targets and vasoactive choices.
Evidence-supported selection of invasive monitors and vascular access for individual valve procedures and patient risk profiles.
A valve-surgery-specific approach to CPB separation, ventricular dysfunction, and post-CPB hemodynamic management.
Open valve-surgery protocols for bleeding, transfusion, anticoagulation reversal, and fluid management.
Valve-specific airway, ventilation, extubation, and postoperative analgesia/PONV protocols.
corrections: Removed unsupported fixed anesthetic drug doses and induction/maintenance recipes from Base44.
Removed unsupported universal valve-specific heart-rate, SVR, and preload targets.
Removed unsupported claims that PA catheter, pre-induction arterial line, BIS, or ACT monitoring are mandatory for every case.
Removed unsupported fixed ICU intubation, fast-track extubation, and postoperative analgesic schedules.
Qualified SAM management to the measures described in the mitral review; did not retain unsupported drug-specific instructions.
Did not treat the ASA quantitative TOF recommendation as applying when neuromuscular blockade is not used.

reports.title: Chest Wall Resection and Reconstruction
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. The draft retains only claims supported by the supplied sources or general applicable anesthesia standards.

Removed the unsupported claims that thoracic epidural is mandatory or essential, that paradoxical chest-wall movement makes spontaneous ventilation impossible, and that mesh stabilization establishes extubation readiness.

Removed unsupported routine recommendations for arterial line placement, cell saver, TXA, fixed crystalloid volumes, blood products, or mandatory ICU intubation. The procedure-specific sources do not report evidence to support these as universal practices.

Prior radiation, radiation necrosis, subclavian-vessel proximity, flail-chest physiology, and the proposed risks of increased bleeding or impaired healing are not established by the supplied procedure-specific sources.

The paravertebral catheter and reported low discharge pain scores are small-series observations, not a routine technique or outcome guarantee. The cardiac-surgery pain consensus is relevant only by cautious analogy to thoracotomy.
No supplied evidence supports a universal extubation approach, a specific ventilation strategy, or a chest-wall-specific complication-management algorithm.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific anesthetic planning for major resections, including how extent of resection and associated lung resection should inform respiratory risk assessment and postoperative disposition.
Chest-wall-resection-specific evidence for emergence and extubation decision-making, including postoperative respiratory support needs.
Comparative evidence or procedure-specific guidance for analgesic techniques and multimodal regimens after chest-wall resection and reconstruction.
Procedure-specific evidence for intraoperative bleeding/perfusion management and fluid or transfusion strategies.
corrections: Corrected the Base44 statement that thoracic epidural analgesia is mandatory or essential: no supplied chest-wall source supports a universal epidural requirement.

Removed the claim that multi-rib resection predictably causes paradoxical movement or that mesh reconstruction must stabilize the chest wall before extubation; these assertions are not established by the supplied sources.

Removed fixed or routine anesthesia recipes, including propofol/fentanyl/rocuronium, epidural test dosing, arterial line pre-induction, TXA, cell saver, a 1–3 L crystalloid range, and ICU intubation after multi-rib resection.
