Corrected the airway claim to reflect reported practice: double-lumen intubation was used when lung resection was planned and single-lumen intubation otherwise in the multicenter series; this does not establish a universal rule based solely on pleural entry.
Removed claims about radiation-related bleeding or healing risk and specific vascular proximity because the supplied evidence does not support them.

reports.title: Decortication (Pleural)
reviewNotes: Source 0 concerns malignant mesothelioma P/D and reports institutional choices; its DLT, separate-ventilator technique, epidural practice, blood availability, and ICU pathway should not be converted into universal empyema-decortication standards.
Source 1 is a single non-intubated empyema case. It supports noting conversion hazards, but not routine non-intubated management or a general conversion rate as a dependable individual prediction.

The cardiac-surgery sources (2 and 3) do not establish pleural-decortication anesthetic or analgesic protocols. The basic and postanesthesia standards (4 and 6) are general standards, not operation-specific guidance.

The Base44 material is unverified and was not used as evidence. In particular, mandatory epidural, RSI, routine TXA, cell saver, antibiotics/IV antibiotic strategy, mandatory DLT lung isolation for every case, and specific extubation or ICU decisions are not established by the supplied sources.

Base44’s statement that DLT isolation is critical to prevent contamination of the dependent lung and its claim of bilateral pneumonia from contamination are not supported by the fetched evidence. Its average-blood-loss characterization, cell-saver rule, and VATS conversion assertion also are not established by these sources.
The supplied sources do not establish the noted cell-saver, TXA, fluid/vasopressor, or PONV-prevention approaches for this procedure.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific adult anesthesia guidance for empyema decortication, including how infection burden and planned surgical extent should modify anesthetic technique.
A broadly applicable ventilation strategy and extubation criteria for decortication with substantial air leak.
Procedure-specific evidence for fluid and transfusion strategy, blood conservation, and cell-saver use in infected versus noninfected pleural cases.
Procedure-specific comparative evidence for analgesia options and postoperative respiratory-support pathways.
fluids: This is a limitation of the supplied evidence, not a clinical-management recommendation; retain it in the evidence section rather than the clinical bullets.
analgesia: This is a limitation of the supplied evidence, not a clinical-management recommendation; retain it in the evidence section rather than the clinical bullets.
corrections: Removed the unsupported claim that thoracic epidural is mandatory for open decortication; the mesothelioma review describes an institutional practice and does not prescribe it universally.
Removed routine RSI and specified induction-drug choices; no supplied procedure-specific source supports them as universal practice.
Removed routine TXA and cell-saver recommendations, including a categorical prohibition in infected cases; these claims are not established in the supplied evidence.
Qualified DLT use, lateral positioning, arterial line, blood availability, OR extubation, and ICU admission as described practices or context-dependent decisions rather than universal requirements.

Did not carry forward Base44’s specific claims of sepsis-management plans, nutritional support, mandatory OLV, bilateral pneumonia from contamination, or average blood loss because they are not supported by the fetched sources.

reports.title: ECMO Cannulation / Decannulation
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. Removed its mandatory-ETT/RSI framing, specific induction recipe, blanket propofol contraindication, and fixed sedation plan; the VA explant review allows general anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care depending on central versus peripheral approach.

Base44’s ACT target of 160–200 is not adopted. The supplied reviews report differing targets and explicitly tie anticoagulation practice to ECMO mode, circuit, manufacturer guidance and local perfusionist input.

Corrected the claim that a distal perfusion catheter must always be placed: the VA review describes a distal perfusion cannula or graft as options, not a universal requirement. Its supplied content does not substantiate the Base44 limb-ischemia percentage or irreversible-limb-loss claim.
The cited VA review supports right radial blood-gas sampling during peripheral VA-ECMO but does not substantiate Base44’s specific right-hand pulse-oximetry instruction as a universal rule.

The sources principally address VA-ECMO weaning/explantation and VV-ECMO anesthesia considerations; they do not substantiate all Base44 indications, including ECPR, or its detailed cannulation anesthetic regimen.
The supplied sources identify ECMO hazards but do not provide a single troubleshooting algorithm; the immediate-assessment recommendation was therefore not retained.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific adult guideline for initial VA- and VV-ECMO cannulation anesthesia, including selection of anesthetic technique and airway management, was not supplied.

The supplied evidence does not establish a universal adult approach to access-site selection, distal limb perfusion device selection, or management of differential hypoxemia across ECMO configurations.

A current, applicable ECMO anticoagulation guideline covering mode-specific targets and peri-decannulation management was not supplied; the available reviews describe varying targets and local/circuit dependence.
The available sources do not provide standardized adult extubation criteria or a comprehensive post-decannulation surveillance protocol.
corrections: Removed mandatory intubation, routine RSI, and the listed ketamine/succinylcholine induction doses; these are not supported as universal ECMO anesthesia practice by the supplied sources.

Removed the blanket statement that propofol is contraindicated in hemodynamic instability and the specified maintenance-drug combinations; no supplied procedure-specific source establishes these as universal rules.
Removed the fixed ACT target and fixed anticoagulation regimen; the available sources describe differing targets and emphasize circuit-specific and local guidance.
Corrected “always place a distal perfusion catheter” to a qualified description of distal perfusion cannula or graft options for femoral arterial access.
Removed the unsubstantiated limb-ischemia frequency and irreversible limb-loss claim.
Removed the instruction that right-hand SpO2 is the critical measurement; retained the supported preference for right radial blood-gas sampling in peripheral VA-ECMO.
Removed any implication that decannulation routinely permits extubation; the VA explant review describes patients usually remaining intubated and lightly sedated after weaning and decannulation.

reports.title: Esophagectomy (Ivor Lewis / McKeown / Minimally Invasive)
reviewNotes: Base44 claims that phenylephrine or norepinephrine should be avoided, vasopressin is preferred, or alpha-agonists increase anastomotic-leak risk are not supported by these sources. The procedure-specific review instead states that norepinephrine is justified for anesthesia-induced hypotension.

Base44’s fixed restrictive-fluid rates, universal fluid ceiling, and assertion that fluid restriction is the leading modifiable determinant are not supported as universal rules. Reviews describe variable definitions, limited esophagectomy-specific trial evidence, and harm from both hypervolemia and hypovolemia.

A routine DLT-to-single-lumen exchange, fixed phase sequence, routine ICU intubation, and delayed extubation policy are not established by the supplied evidence. Approach, surgical preference, and recovery criteria vary.

The source set does not substantiate Base44’s routine cell-saver, central-venous-access, specific epidural placement timing, TXA, jejunostomy-feeding timing, or immediate bilateral recurrent-laryngeal-nerve injury claims as universal anesthesia guidance.
The reviews conflict or differ in emphasis on fluid restriction and goal-directed therapy; current evidence presented here does not resolve the optimal individualized strategy.

The supplied esophagectomy sources do not establish a procedure-specific PONV prevention protocol; remove this clinical bullet rather than infer one from evidence concerning other surgical populations.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific PONV prevention evidence or an applicable guideline was not supplied.
The supplied sources do not establish a standard postoperative nutrition protocol, including patient selection and timing of enteral feeding.
analgesia: The supplied esophagectomy sources do not establish a procedure-specific PONV prevention protocol.
corrections: Removed the unsupported instruction to avoid norepinephrine or phenylephrine and the claim that vasopressin is the preferred routine vasopressor; retained the source-supported emphasis on avoiding systemic hypotension and considering conduit perfusion.
Removed fixed fluid rates, fluid totals, and a universal restrictive-fluid prescription; replaced with individualized management that avoids both overload and hypovolemia.
Removed universal DLT exchange and routine ICU intubation/extubation claims; presented lung isolation and recovery decisions as approach- and patient-dependent.
Removed unsupported leak-timing, recurrent-laryngeal-nerve, chylothorax, and immediate-stridor assertions from the anesthetic reference.

Removed the unverified claim that thoracic epidural analgesia is universally mandatory or guarantees fewer complications; retained it as a supported option with stated limitations and monitoring considerations.

reports.title: Heart Transplant
reviewNotes: Base44 was treated as unverified. Its specific induction and maintenance drug recipes, routine inhaled nitric oxide, isoproterenol target, atropine claim, mandatory monitoring configuration, transfusion/TXA practices, and fixed extubation interval are not established by the supplied sources and were not carried forward as recommendations.

The supplied evidence does not support a universal 4–6 hour ischemic-time limit or a claim that less than four hours is optimal. Donor coordination and ischemic time are discussed, but no universal threshold is established here.
The transplant anesthesia review is ACHD-specific; Fontan and other congenital-anatomy considerations are explicitly qualified and should not be generalized to all adult recipients.
Denervation-related physiology in source 0 is discussed in the context of anesthesia after transplantation. It should not be misrepresented as a validated transplant-operation emergence protocol.
The POQI/ERAS consensus concerns adult cardiac surgery broadly, not heart transplantation specifically; its analgesia recommendations are labeled accordingly.

The transplant sources describe TEE and Swan-Ganz monitoring but do not establish that either is mandatory in every recipient. ASA monitoring standards are general standards, not transplant-specific setup instructions.
The supplied transplant anesthesia source does not specify patient positioning or a standard access configuration; the setup limitation has been moved to the evidence section.
The source supports the PGD definition but does not provide the stated prompt-assessment recommendation.
evidenceGaps: Transplant-specific anesthetic induction and maintenance guidance, including how to individualize technique for recipient physiology and MCS.
Detailed donor coordination and ischemic-time management guidance, including applicable thresholds for particular donor-recipient circumstances.
A transplant-specific immunosuppression regimen and timing protocol.
Transplant-specific extubation criteria, postoperative analgesia plan, and recovery protocol.
A transplant-specific fluid, transfusion, and bleeding-management protocol.
setup: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a clinical setup recommendation; retain it in the evidence section.
corrections: Removed unverified fixed ischemic-time limits and the assertion that a specific duration is universally optimal.
Removed unverified anesthetic drug doses, infusion rates, and drug-selection recipes.
Changed routine inhaled nitric oxide and isoproterenol claims to source-supported, individualized discussion; removed the unsupported heart-rate target and specific atropine assertion.
Removed the claim that TEE, PA catheter, arterial line, or a particular vascular-access setup is mandatory for every case.
Removed routine massive-transfusion, cell-saver, TXA, and aggressive-hemostasis prescriptions because these practices are not established by the supplied evidence.
Removed the fixed 12–48 hour extubation timetable and unsupported ICU-intubated instruction.

Removed the unsupported claim that opioid minimization in transplant recipients is required because of infection risk; retained relevant adult cardiac-surgery opioid-stewardship guidance with scope qualification.

reports.title: Lobectomy (VATS / Open)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified claims, not evidence. This draft retains only claims supported by the supplied sources and distinguishes general anesthesia standards from lobectomy-specific evidence.

The source-reported atrial-fibrillation frequency (33%) differs from the case-field estimate of 10–20%; rates vary by source and population, so no single rate is used as a prediction or prophylaxis trigger.

The StatPearls source gives pulmonary-risk thresholds and recommendations from cited guidance, but they are not presented here as universal extubation criteria. The case-field ppo-FEV1/ppo-DLCO cutoffs are not supported by the supplied evidence.
The VATS technique article dates from 2013 and is an editorial. Its operative details are useful context, not a replacement for current procedure-specific surgical judgment.
The general ASA monitoring standards support minimum monitoring requirements; they do not establish an arterial-line mandate for lobectomy.
The supplied lobectomy sources do not provide a PONV prophylaxis regimen.
The supplied lobectomy sources do not define emergence or extubation criteria, postoperative ventilation, or oxygen targets.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific anesthetic source defining one-lung ventilation strategy, physiologic targets, and hypoxemia escalation for adult lobectomy.
Current procedure-specific guidance on emergence, DLT exchange, and criteria for postoperative ventilation versus extubation.
Lobectomy-specific fluid, perfusion, and blood-management evidence sufficient to guide practice beyond individualized assessment and preparedness for bleeding.
analgesia: The supplied lobectomy sources do not support a PONV prevention recommendation.
emergence: The source set does not provide lobectomy-specific emergence or extubation criteria.
corrections: Removed the unverified ppo-FEV1/ppo-DLCO risk cutoffs and any inference that they alone determine extubation.
Removed prescribed one-lung ventilation settings and hypoxemia maneuvers; the supplied lobectomy sources do not establish those parameters.
Removed the routine arterial-line claim as a universal requirement; basic monitoring standards do not impose it for this procedure.
Removed the case-field fluid total, restrictive-fluid recipe, and preference for vasopressors over volume as a fixed strategy; procedure sources provide no such protocol.
Removed prophylactic amiodarone or diltiazem recommendations and the case-field atrial-fibrillation rate as routine guidance.
Removed the claim that epidural analgesia is essential for open lobectomy; the sources describe pain control as important but do not establish that claim or a required epidural regimen.
Removed unverified DLT sidedness, mandatory fiberoptic reconfirmation, DLT exchange instructions, and the proposed extubation criteria based on pulmonary function and analgesia.
Removed the case-field PONV drug regimen as procedure-specific guidance; the provided lobectomy sources do not establish it.

reports.title: Lung Transplant (Single / Double)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not support mandatory PA catheter or TEE use for every patient; one source specifies PA catheter use only if there is no contraindication.

The assertion that inhaled nitric oxide should be used routinely is not supported. Sources describe inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol as selective pulmonary vasodilator options, particularly relevant to pulmonary hypertension or RV support.

The Base44 claim that PGD is defined by PaO₂/FiO₂ below 200 is incomplete: the source defines PGD as PaO₂/FiO₂ below 300 and/or pulmonary edema; below 200 with infiltrates corresponds to grade 3 in the review.
The proposed universal FiO₂ 100% during pneumonectomy phases conflicts with guidance to minimize hyperoxia, including low FiO₂ during reperfusion and the lowest level compatible with oxygenation.
The proposed fixed extubation delay of days to weeks is not established by the sources. Early extubation is described when graft function is adequate and hemodynamics are stable.

The source material does not substantiate the Base44 position options, mandatory bronchoscopy details, routine cell-saver or TXA use, or a universal epidural/paravertebral plan. These are not presented as standard recommendations here.

Source 0 and source 1 differ in some ventilation targets and PGD framing; this draft emphasizes shared principles and attributes the specific PGD grading definition to the review rather than presenting a single universal target.
The supplied transplant sources do not specify patient positioning or establish one required room configuration for every transplant.
The supplied transplant-specific sources do not provide a PONV prevention or treatment protocol.
PGD thresholds and grading were omitted because the available definitions and grading details should not be simplified into a single definition or threshold in this draft.
evidenceGaps: Transplant-specific patient positioning and its relationship to the intended surgical approach.
A transplant-specific PONV prevention and treatment approach.
The supplied sources do not establish one standardized monitoring, ventilation, or postoperative pathway; local transplant-team protocols and patient-specific decisions remain relevant.
setup: The supplied transplant sources do not specify patient positioning.
analgesia: This is a source-scope limitation, not a clinical analgesia recommendation.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that PA catheter monitoring and TEE are mandatory for every transplant recipient.
Removed routine inhaled nitric oxide use as a universal instruction; sources describe selective pulmonary vasodilator use.
Corrected PGD definition and grading: PGD is described as PaO₂/FiO₂ below 300 and/or pulmonary edema; grade 3 includes PaO₂/FiO₂ below 200 with infiltrates.
Removed universal FiO₂ 100% during pneumonectomy phases in favor of source-supported avoidance of hyperoxia and individualized oxygenation.
Removed the fixed expectation of ICU intubation for days to weeks; extubation timing is conditional on graft function and hemodynamic stability.
Did not retain unverified position, routine TXA or cell-saver use, or a fixed regional analgesia choice as established practice.

reports.title: LVAD Placement (Left Ventricular Assist Device)
reviewNotes: This is an adult-focused draft, but the two LVAD-specific sources do not state an adult age range. The cited general cardiac-surgery consensus addresses adult cardiac surgery.
The 2004 LVAD overview discusses older and investigational devices; it cannot substantiate contemporary HeartMate 3- or HVAD-specific anesthetic recommendations.

The surgical approaches article reports one institution’s techniques and acknowledges the need for larger studies. Do not promote its particular access, off-pump, or adenosine choices to routine practice.

Base44 claims that RV failure is the '#1 cause' of LVAD-related mortality, that specific CVP/PCWP ratios define risk, and that suction events should be treated by speed reduction and volume are not supported by the supplied evidence. The sources do support RV dysfunction as a major concern and discuss device flow/aortic-valve relationships.

Base44 claims about mandatory pre-induction arterial line, device console, cell saver, IABP standby, specific induction/maintenance drug choices, and a universal anticoagulation plan are not established by these sources. The older overview describes pre-induction pulmonary artery catheter placement, standard TEE, and individualized management; that is not validation of every Base44 setup claim.

The older source’s postoperative propofol sedation and the other source’s typical extubation within 24 hours are descriptive, not universal prescriptions. The evidence supports stability-based extubation, not a fixed 12–48-hour window.

The older source describes device-dependent anticoagulation for devices of its era; the surgical article describes a particular institutional postoperative protocol. Neither supports a universal lifelong warfarin or heparin-bridging rule across current devices.
The supplied sources describe reported practice but do not establish a universal extubation time or complete readiness criteria.
evidenceGaps: Contemporary, device-specific LVAD anesthesia and perioperative guidance, including current device-specific management of flow, alarms, and device complications.
Validated contemporary RV-failure risk assessment and management guidance for LVAD implantation, including actionable perioperative targets and escalation pathways.
Current device-specific anticoagulation and antiplatelet recommendations for implantation and early postoperative care.
corrections: Removed unverified fixed induction and maintenance recipes, including etomidate/fentanyl/rocuronium dosing, blanket propofol avoidance, and specified inotrope or pulmonary-vasodilator regimens.
Removed unsupported routine setup claims for a pre-induction arterial line, device console, cell saver, IABP standby, and mandatory extubation timing.
Corrected universal anticoagulation language: the supplied sources describe device- and protocol-dependent regimens, not one current regimen applicable to every LVAD.
Removed unsupported quantitative claims about RV-failure mortality ranking and CVP/PCWP risk ratios.
Removed the proposed suction-event treatment recipe because it is not established in the supplied evidence.

reports.title: Mediastinoscopy
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its routine recipe-like claims (specific induction drugs, volatile maintenance, ketorolac/acetaminophen plan, and listed key drugs) are not established by the supplied mediastinoscopy sources.
The Base44 statement that a mediastinoscope in the trachea causes airway compromise is not supported by the supplied procedural descriptions; it was omitted.

The Base44 assertion that an anterior mediastinal mass is simply an indication for awake fiberoptic intubation and avoidance of paralysis needs risk qualification: sources describe awake intubation with spontaneous ventilation for major/high-risk airway compromise, not as a universal approach.

The sources differ in how they frame anterior mediastinal mass: one lists it among absolute contraindications but also describes selected procedures despite such a mass. This draft presents it as a major individualized hazard, not an unconditional rule.

The Base44 claims of bilateral arm pulse oximetry/BP comparison, a mandatory right-arm cuff, routine sternotomy tray open and blood in room, routine post-procedure CXR, and a specific extubation/pain plan are not established as universal requirements by the supplied sources.
Cardiac-surgery analgesia sources were excluded from procedure-specific recommendations; their population and focus do not establish a mediastinoscopy analgesic or PONV protocol.
evidenceGaps: Mediastinoscopy-specific evidence does not establish detailed anesthetic regimens, ventilation targets, fluid or transfusion protocols, analgesia/PONV strategies, or routine emergence and postoperative imaging protocols.
corrections: Removed unsupported universal drug combinations, volatile maintenance, and neuromuscular-blocker recipe from Base44.
Removed the unsupported claim that the mediastinoscope is in the trachea and routinely causes airway compromise.
Qualified awake intubation and preservation of spontaneous ventilation to patients with major or high-risk airway compromise.
Corrected the Chamberlain description to access aortopulmonary lymph nodes; the supplied source does not establish that it is for all left-sided nodes.
Removed unsupported mandatory bilateral arm monitoring, routine crossmatch/blood-in-room requirements, routine chest radiography, and fixed pain-management recommendations.

reports.title: Pericardial Window
reviewNotes: Base44’s blanket ETT requirement and fixed induction recipe are not supported as universal practice: the pericardial review says local-anesthetic subxiphoid window drainage may be used in decompensated patients and describes its ketamine choice as author practice, not a trial regimen.

The claim that surgeon decompression must precede induction is stronger than the source: it supports having the surgeon scrubbed and equipment ready before induction, not a universal requirement to decompress before induction.

The proposed fixed preload volume, mandatory vasopressor infusion, N2O prohibition, CVP monitoring, and specific drug combinations are not established as universal pericardial-window recommendations by the supplied sources; they were not retained as clinical instructions.
The source describing approximately 1.5% major complications concerns pericardiocentesis, not open surgical drainage. It cannot establish a complication rate for a pericardial window.

The MAC case series is small, retrospective, and limited to postoperative cardiovascular-surgery patients. Its spontaneous-breathing technique and reported airway events do not establish general adult practice or superiority to general anesthesia.

Analgesia evidence is not fully aligned: the pericardial review says intercostal block may be appropriate depending on approach, while the broader cardiac-surgery consensus says intercostal block is not routinely recommended. This draft presents the choice as conditional, not a standard.
The draft is a source-grounded reference draft, not a patient-specific plan, clinical approval, or production-ready protocol.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific guidance on patient positioning and selection among subxiphoid, thoracoscopic, thoracotomy, or other surgical access for particular effusion characteristics.
Comparative adult evidence on anesthetic technique and airway strategy for pericardial window, including which selected patients may benefit from local anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care.
Window-specific complication rates and detailed surgical bleeding or transfusion evidence; the supplied complication rate is for pericardiocentesis.
Pericardial-window-specific emergence and extubation criteria.
corrections: Removed the unsupported universal requirement for endotracheal intubation and general anesthesia.
Removed fixed ketamine, rocuronium, fluid-bolus, vasopressor-infusion, and other drug-dose recipes from the Base44 material.
Corrected the implication that CVP is a reliable filling-pressure measure in tamponade; the review says chamber compression makes it an inaccurate reflection of true filling pressure.
Removed the unsupported rule that the surgeon must decompress the pericardium before induction; retained source-supported readiness of the surgeon and equipment before induction.
Removed the Base44 claim that the pericardiocentesis complication rate describes open-window complications.
Removed unsupported claims about a universal extubation plan, mandatory N2O avoidance, and a specific postoperative analgesic combination.

reports.title: Pleurodesis (Chemical / Surgical VATS)
reviewNotes: Chemical bedside or catheter pleurodesis and surgical VATS/thoracotomy are distinct pathways; do not carry general-anesthesia assumptions into the chemical procedure.
The reviews differ on NSAID use after pleurodesis. The draft preserves the conflict and does not convert either position into a universal instruction.

Talc-associated ARDS is described as rare and associated particularly with smaller particles or large doses. The sources support concern about particle size but do not establish the Base44 claim of a specific calibrated product requirement.

Several Base44 statements are unsupported by the provided procedure sources, including lateral decubitus as universal positioning, DLT/bronchial blocker and one-lung ventilation, named induction and maintenance drugs, routine arterial line, fixed crystalloid amount, DLT exchange, and specified regional blocks or PONV prophylaxis.
Source 0 describes a drain-output criterion for contraindication and a different preparation criterion; these are not synthesized into a universal threshold here.
General ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards apply to anesthesia care but do not validate a pleurodesis-specific technique or prove the procedure is appropriate for an individual patient.
No pleurodesis-specific PONV prophylaxis regimen is established in the supplied evidence; the flagged prophylaxis bullet was removed.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific VATS airway device, ventilation strategy, and intraoperative physiologic targets are not established in the provided sources.
Pleurodesis-specific positioning, room configuration, and anesthetic monitoring beyond general standards are not established.
A procedure-specific fluid, blood-loss, or transfusion strategy is not established.
Pleurodesis-specific emergence, extubation, and PONV protocols are not established.
The supplied pleurodesis reviews do not define an exclusively adult population or provide adult-specific anesthesia outcomes.
airway: This is a source-scope limitation, not a procedure-specific airway recommendation; move it out of the clinical airway bullets.
fluids: This is a source limitation rather than a clinical fluid-management recommendation; move it out of the clinical fluids bullets.
analgesia: The supplied evidence does not establish a pleurodesis-specific PONV prophylaxis regimen.
corrections: Removed DLT, bronchial blocker, routine one-lung ventilation, fiberoptic confirmation, and brief OLV claims as unsupported by the pleurodesis sources.
Removed universal lateral-decubitus positioning; the available seated/supine guidance concerns catheter drainage, not VATS.
Removed the Base44 induction, maintenance, and PONV drug recipe; the sources do not establish a pleurodesis-specific anesthetic regimen.
Removed routine arterial-line use, fixed crystalloid volume, and DLT exchange/extubation plan as unsupported.
Removed specified paravertebral/intercostal blocks and the claim that they are established pleurodesis standards; the procedure sources do not provide this evidence.
Qualified the large-particle talc statement: reviews describe fewer ARDS reports with larger particles, but do not substantiate a specific calibrated-talc requirement.
Qualified NSAID guidance because the supplied reviews report conflicting conclusions about use after pleurodesis.

reports.title: Pneumonectomy
reviewNotes: Base44's claimed mandatory epidural is not supported: the procedure review lists a mid-thoracic epidural or surgeon-placed paravertebral catheter, and another overview says epidural may be used if appropriate.

Base44's ppo-FEV1/ppo-DLCO >40% rule overstates a universal threshold. The procedure review cites a NICE 30% limit; another overview describes values below 40% as high risk. Assessment should be individualized.

Base44's 6-minute walk test, routine PA catheter, cell saver, DLT cuff occlusion of the bronchial stump, routine ICU intubation after right pneumonectomy, and end-of-case stump leak test as bronchoscopy are not established as stated in the supplied sources.

Base44's <500 mL fluid target and 80–100% RPE fatality claim are unsupported. The procedure review reports RPE mortality above 50% and recommends restriction while avoiding hypovolaemia and kidney injury.

The procedure review supports bronchoscopy-confirmed lung isolation, but DLT side selection is procedure-dependent; right-sided tubes have right-upper-lobe obstruction risk. Confirm position after lateral positioning.

The adult cardiac-surgery analgesia consensus and basic ASA monitoring standards are indirect or general sources; they do not establish a pneumonectomy-specific medication regimen or advanced-monitoring requirement.

The PONV bullet has been moved to evidence because the supplied pneumonectomy sources do not provide a specific prevention regimen; the cardiac-surgery pain consensus is not a pneumonectomy-specific source.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific evidence for EPP and other uncommon variants is limited in the supplied sources; their distinct surgical extent warrants individualized planning.
The supplied sources do not establish a pneumonectomy-specific PONV prevention approach.
analgesia: This is a source-scope note, not a pneumonectomy analgesia recommendation.
corrections: Removed the assertion that thoracic epidural analgesia is mandatory; retained epidural or paravertebral analgesia as described options.
Replaced the universal ppo-FEV1/ppo-DLCO >40% criterion with the differing source thresholds and individualized interpretation.
Removed the fixed intraoperative fluid total, extreme-fluid-restriction wording, and unsupported 80–100% RPE mortality claim.
Removed routine PA catheter, cell-saver, postoperative right-pneumonectomy intubation, stump cuff-occlusion, and bronchoscopic stump-leak-test claims as unsupported by the supplied evidence.
Reframed ICU-level care as postoperative setting appropriate to condition and risk; the sources do not support mandatory ICU intubation for every right pneumonectomy.

reports.title: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Repair (TEVAR / Open Descending)
reviewNotes: The supplied Base44 fields were treated as unverified, not as evidence. Several detailed anesthesia recipes and device-specific claims cannot be corroborated from the fetched sources.
The two aortic reviews give different size criteria and discuss different populations/approaches; the draft reports clinical factors without presenting one threshold as universally determinative.

The TEVAR review is from 2011 and acknowledges evidence limitations, including unsettled left-subclavian management. Its deployment MAP description is explicitly an operator practice, not a universal target.

The 2019 open-repair review includes institutional practices and describes CSF-drain placement after induction; therefore the Base44 claim that awake placement before induction is the standard was not retained.

The Base44 assertion that TEVAR is routinely supine and uses a specified single-lumen airway, as well as its detailed ventilator settings, bilateral arterial-line arrangement, and universal CSF targets, are not established by the supplied TEVAR source.

The Base44 suggestion that epidural analgesia and CSF drainage are categorically mutually exclusive is not established in the fetched material. Regional analgesia also requires attention to bleeding/anticoagulation context.

Generic cardiac-surgery analgesia evidence, basic ASA monitoring standards, and neuromuscular-blockade guidance are used only within their stated scope; none supplies a complete aortic-repair protocol.
Source 1 is a narrative review focused principally on open descending thoracic and thoracoabdominal repair. Its postoperative MAP target should not be generalized to TEVAR or other contexts.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific, contemporary guidance comparing anesthetic management and outcomes for open descending repair versus TEVAR, including how anatomy and patient risk determine approach.
TEVAR-specific airway, ventilation, positioning, hemodynamic-management, emergence, and blood-management protocols; the supplied TEVAR review explicitly omits several of these details.

Approach- and risk-specific criteria for selecting prophylactic CSF drainage and for safely managing, monitoring, and removing a drain; the sources describe risks and differing practices but do not establish one universal protocol.
corrections: Removed the Base44 assertion that CSF drainage is the single most important spinal-protection tool; the open-repair review describes multiple adjuncts and states no single method is entirely effective.

Removed the instruction to place a CSF drain awake under local before induction; the supplied open-repair review describes an institutional practice of placement after induction, and the TEVAR review does not establish the Base44 timing.

Did not retain a fixed TEVAR extubation plan, supine position, single-lumen tube requirement, one-lung ventilation settings, or routine bilateral radial arterial lines because these are not supported by the supplied TEVAR source.
Did not retain the Base44 fixed CSF pressure, MAP, or neurologic-response recipe as a universal plan; sourced targets are approach/context-specific and must not be conflated.

Did not retain a fixed blood-product preparation, medication list, or ketorolac recommendation as a universal aortic-repair regimen; the supplied sources do not establish those as routine requirements.

reports.title: Thoracotomy (Open) / Exploratory Thoracotomy
reviewNotes: This draft is not a patient-specific plan and has not been clinically approved. The source set does not support treating the Base44 fields as verified guidance.
Corrected the Base44 assertion that thoracic epidural is the open-thoracotomy gold standard or essential: the supplied procedure-specific review prefers PVB, with TEA as an effective alternative.

The Base44 OLV settings, hypoxemia sequence, restrictive-fluid prescription, fixed crystalloid range, and routine cell-saver implication are not supported by the supplied thoracotomy sources and were not repeated as recommendations.

The Base44 ppo-FEV1 threshold, routine positioning and setup details, universal DLT selection/confirmation claims, anesthetic drug recipe, and universal extubation instructions are not substantiated by the fetched evidence.
Source 3 concerns adult cardiac surgery pain management, not a general open-thoracotomy protocol; its drug examples and recommendations were not converted into a thoracotomy regimen.
The sources do not establish a thoracotomy-specific PONV strategy, fluid or blood-management protocol, or general OLV troubleshooting algorithm.
The OLV discussion is drawn from a review of tracheobronchial and related airway procedures; the supplied sources do not establish a general OLV protocol or thoracotomy-specific rescue sequence.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific adult guidance for OLV settings and a validated approach to intraoperative desaturation in open thoracotomy.
Procedure-specific adult guidance for fluid, blood-loss, transfusion, and perfusion management in open thoracotomy.
A thoracotomy-specific emergence/extubation protocol and PONV prevention strategy.
corrections: Removed the claim that TEA is mandatory or universally the gold standard; source 0 prefers PVB for open thoracotomy and describes TEA as an effective alternative.
Removed unsupported exact OLV settings and the proposed hypoxemia treatment sequence from the Base44 material.
Removed the Base44 fixed crystalloid total and restrictive-fluid prescription; the supplied thoracotomy source explicitly provides no fluid-management or surgical blood-loss recommendations.
Removed the ppo-FEV1 cutoff, routine lateral-positioning/setup recipe, and blanket DLT confirmation claims because the supplied sources do not establish them for this case.
Removed unverified routine epidural, arterial-line, cell-saver, drug-selection, and extubation directives.

reports.title: Thymectomy (VATS / Open / Robotic)
reviewNotes: The source set is strongest for VATS operative technique and general anesthetic monitoring; it is thin for open or robotic thymectomy and does not establish a comparative anesthetic technique.
The VATS sources differ on reported CO₂ insufflation pressure limits. The draft therefore describes careful, coordinated insufflation without adopting either figure as a universal target.
The neuromuscular-blockade guideline is general perioperative guidance, not MG-specific evidence. Its TOF and reversal recommendations are explicitly limited here to cases in which blockade is used.

Removed or not adopted from the unverified case fields: precise NIF/FVC extubation cutoffs; high-dose remifentanil or other specific induction recipes; a blanket succinylcholine prohibition; claims of MG-specific sugammadex superiority or neostigmine-related cholinergic crisis; mandatory ICU admission; fixed fluid totals; and prescriptive open-surgery analgesic techniques.

The source material includes institutional practices and technical recommendations; it does not establish that every thymectomy requires lung isolation, arterial monitoring, a particular regional block, or a particular postoperative destination.
evidenceGaps: Adult-specific comparative anesthetic evidence for open, robotic, and VATS thymectomy, including approach-dependent airway and ventilation strategies.

An evidence-supported MG-specific anesthesia pathway addressing neuromuscular blocker selection/reversal, postoperative myasthenic or cholinergic crisis recognition and management, and extubation or postoperative-disposition criteria.
Thymectomy-specific comparative evidence for analgesia and PONV prevention, particularly for open and robotic approaches.
corrections: Corrected the unverified assertion that double-lumen intubation is required for VATS: the sources also describe single-lumen ventilation with CO₂ insufflation and, for simple procedures, nonintubated anesthesia.
Did not present one VATS insufflation pressure as a universal target because the technical sources report different limits.
Did not repeat unverified MG-specific drug doses, infusion rates, extubation thresholds, or reversal claims as recommendations.
Did not present institutional intercostal-block practice, arterial catheter use, or postoperative ventilation arrangements as mandatory standards.
Did not retain a fixed crystalloid volume, universal blood availability instruction, or unsupported open-sternotomy analgesia protocol.

reports.title: VATS Wedge Resection
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not support a universal lateral position, left-sided double-lumen tube choice, drug recipe, fluid volume, arterial-line policy, or routine OR extubation for this case.

Source 0 is a practical review of a technique for highly selected non-intubated patients, not a general VATS anesthesia guideline. Source 1 is a selected, single-center trial; its group protocols and outcomes should not be promoted as universal recommendations.

Sources 2 and 3 concern adult cardiac surgery, not VATS wedge resection. General monitoring, postanesthesia, preanesthesia, and neuromuscular-blockade standards were used only within their stated scope.

The supplied evidence is limited for conventional one-lung ventilation settings, conversion frequency, procedure-specific positioning, fluid and bleeding protocols, systemic analgesia, and emergence planning.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific guidance establishing when conventional intubated one-lung ventilation versus a selected laryngeal-mask or non-intubated technique is appropriate.
Source-supported positioning guidance and detailed conventional one-lung ventilation settings or physiologic targets.
A VATS-specific fluid, bleeding, and perfusion strategy, including relevant procedure-specific escalation guidance.
A broadly applicable systemic multimodal analgesia and PONV approach, and detailed extubation or emergence criteria beyond neuromuscular-blockade monitoring.
corrections: Removed the unsupported conversion estimate of 5–10%; no supplied source establishes a general conversion rate.
Removed the asserted routine left-sided double-lumen tube for right-sided resections and the claim that one airway plan is standard for all wedge resections.

Removed the fixed crystalloid volume, universal restrictive-fluid instruction, and arterial-line recommendation; the procedure trial does not report fluid regimen and the evidence does not establish routine arterial monitoring for every case.
Removed the routine OR-extubation statement and fixed DLT-to-single-lumen exchange instruction; the supplied evidence does not establish these as universal practice.
Removed drug combinations and dose-like recipes from the unverified fields, including the fixed induction/maintenance regimen and routine ketorolac-based plan.

Removed a claim that paravertebral block or ESPB is universally preferred. The sources describe options and selected-study outcomes, not a mandatory technique; the non-intubated review's block discussion does not establish ESPB as the routine approach.

reports.title: Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as an evidence source. Its fixed crystalloid volume, routine CVP and arterial-line claims, cell-saver and TXA use, epidural/TAP selection, and named induction or maintenance drugs are not established as APR-wide practice by the supplied sources.

The source-supported discussion of presacral bleeding does not substantiate Base44's specific emergency maneuver, claims about suture ligation, or a prescribed blood-product setup. These details were omitted rather than converted into guidance.
The claimed APR syndrome frequency and recommendation to start gabapentin preemptively are unsupported by the supplied sources. They were omitted.

Base44's claims of routine preoperative chemoradiation, ureteral stents, and particular drug combinations are not universal recommendations in the provided evidence. Stents are described only as a consideration when injury concern is significant, and the source says they do not reduce injury risk.

The applicable colorectal guideline supports individualized fluid management and selected goal-directed therapy; it does not support a fixed fluid total. Epidural analgesia is an option for open surgery with acute-pain-team support, not a universal requirement.
Quantitative TOF monitoring and a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation apply when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used; they are not a requirement for every anesthetic technique.
evidenceGaps: APR-specific anesthesia guidance for airway strategy, anesthetic technique, ventilation, vascular access, and monitoring beyond general anesthesia standards.
A validated anesthetic response and escalation protocol for major presacral hemorrhage, including APR-specific transfusion guidance.
APR-specific postoperative pain, phantom rectal pain, and perineal-wound surveillance guidance.
corrections: Removed fixed crystalloid volumes and routine claims for CVP, arterial line, cell saver, TXA, epidural, or TAP blocks as established APR standards.
Removed unsupported prescribed induction, maintenance, and postoperative drug regimens, including preemptive gabapentin for phantom rectal pain.
Removed the specific thumbtack maneuver and categorical claims about presacral-vein ligation because the supplied sources do not support them.
Corrected the ureteral-stent claim: the APR review says stents may aid earlier identification and repair but do not reduce ureteral-injury risk.
Qualified epidural analgesia as an option for open colorectal surgery with acute-pain-team support, not a routine requirement for all APRs.

reports.title: Anal Fistula Repair (Fistulotomy / LIFT / Seton)
reviewNotes: The supplied Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. The fistula review is old and surgical in scope; it does not substantiate most anesthesia-specific field entries.
The general ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards support applicable monitoring and recovery statements but do not establish a fistula-specific anesthetic plan.
The colorectal enhanced-recovery guideline applies to elective colorectal resections and was not used to import its analgesia, fluid, or recovery recommendations into fistula surgery.

The fistula source is a surgical review, not an anesthesia reference. It mentions regional or general anesthesia for abscess surgery and possible anesthesia for seton placement, but does not provide a fistula-repair anesthetic plan.
evidenceGaps: Fistula-specific evidence establishing anesthetic technique, airway approach, positioning, analgesia/PONV strategy, fluid or bleeding management, and postoperative anesthesia-care priorities is not available in the supplied sources.
Case-specific targets and a preferred anesthetic technique cannot be established from the available sources.
corrections: Removed the unverified saddle-block/MAC/GA airway plan, including specific spinal drug and positioning claims; the fistula review does not provide anesthetic regimens or airway details.
Removed unverified setup and tract-identification claims about prone jackknife or lithotomy positioning and hydrogen peroxide or methylene blue as routine room setup.
Removed unverified fluid total, minimal blood-loss assumption, rapid emergence claim, and case-specific analgesia, wound-care, and PACU concern recipe.
Removed unverified Crohn’s-specific treatment assertions and LIFT-specific content; the supplied fistula review does not establish these as case-specific recommendations.
Corrected any implication that quantitative TOF monitoring is universal: the cited neuromuscular-blockade guidance applies when NMB is used.

reports.title: Bowel Obstruction Surgery (Open / Laparoscopic)
reviewNotes: This is an unapproved reference draft, not a patient-specific plan or checklist.

The unverified Base44 assertion that RSI is mandatory and the stomach is never empty is not supported as a universal rule by the supplied obstruction review; it says many clinicians use RSI and discusses aspiration risk.

Base44 drug combinations and doses, routine cricoid pressure, universal preoperative NG placement, fixed supine positioning, arterial-line requirements, aggressive fluid totals, TXA, and early NG removal are not established by the supplied evidence and were not reproduced.
The elective colorectal recommendation against routine NG tubes does not negate possible decompression in intestinal obstruction; the patient population and clinical purpose differ.
The obstruction review is older narrative evidence without grading. The elective colorectal ERP guideline is more formal but explicitly has limited applicability to nonelective obstruction surgery.
evidenceGaps: Adult obstruction-specific evidence establishing airway technique selection and ventilation management.
Adult obstruction-specific guidance on operative approach, positioning, vascular access, and criteria for invasive monitoring.
Adult obstruction-specific emergence, extubation, and postoperative destination criteria.
corrections: Removed the claim that RSI is mandatory for every patient and that the stomach is always empty-proof; sources describe aspiration concern and common RSI use, not an absolute rule.
Removed unsupported fixed induction drug doses, cricoid-pressure instruction, and claims that an NG tube makes RSI optional or mandatory.
Removed universal setup, fluid, blood-product, TXA, analgesic, and NG-removal prescriptions that were present in unverified Base44 material but not established by the supplied sources.
Qualified elective colorectal guidance so it is not presented as a validated protocol for urgent obstruction surgery.

reports.title: Colectomy (Open / Laparoscopic / Robotic)
reviewNotes: The Base44 claim that mechanical bowel preparation is optional or varies by surgeon is not an adequate summary of the supplied current elective-surgery guideline: ASCRS/SAGES recommends mechanical preparation combined with preoperative oral antibiotics. The older 2012 review disagrees about routine mechanical preparation; this draft gives precedence to the newer procedure-specific guideline for elective resection.

Removed unsupported Base44 claims that ETT is universally required for colectomy, robotic docking necessarily prevents the surgeon from reaching the patient, and all robotic cases require a particular airway or emergence plan. The generic laparoscopy/robotics review prefers ETT but does not establish a colectomy-specific mandate.

Removed Base44 prescriptions for routine crossmatch, CVP, cell saver, arterial line, epidural test dose, TXA, and fixed crystalloid totals: the supplied sources do not establish these as universal colectomy practices.
The source describing an MGH ERAS pathway is institution-specific and conflicts with other supplied evidence on bowel preparation and some pathway details; it was not used as a universal recipe.

The 2012 clinical review is older and itself notes evidence limitations. Generic laparoscopic/robotic physiology is useful for anticipating hazards but is not procedure-specific proof of a required technique.

The supplied sources do not define an adult-only study population for the procedure-specific guideline; this draft uses the requested adult clinical-reference framing without asserting adult-specific trial evidence.
evidenceGaps: Colectomy-specific airway and anesthetic technique recommendations are not established by the supplied procedure-specific guideline.
No source provides a colectomy-specific transfusion threshold or detailed hemorrhage protocol.
corrections: Removed the Base44 statement that bowel preparation is simply surgeon-dependent; the supplied 2023 ASCRS/SAGES guideline recommends mechanical preparation combined with oral antibiotics for elective colorectal resection, while an older review conflicts.
Removed unsupported universal ETT requirement and robotic-airway-access assertion.
Removed unsupported routine CVP, arterial line, cell saver, crossmatch, TXA, epidural test-dose, and fixed-fluid-volume claims.

Corrected routine laparoscopic epidural framing: the 2023 guideline does not recommend thoracic epidural routinely for laparoscopic surgery; it remains an option for open surgery with dedicated acute-pain support.

Did not repeat Base44's asserted ERAS length-of-stay reduction or anastomotic-leak timing as routine anesthetic facts; these are not established as universal case-specific management claims by the selected evidence.

reports.title: Hemorrhoidectomy
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified, not as evidence. The grade III–IV indication, concurrent anorectal-anatomy considerations, bowel-preparation details, and outpatient status are not established by the supplied sources as general rules.
Removed unsupported airway claims: prone-position LMA contraindication, ETT preference, and lithotomy LMA preference. The hemorrhoidectomy sources do not provide airway-device guidance.
Removed the specific saddle-block posture, dose, sacral-level targeting, recovery time, and hemodynamic claims; these are not supported by the fetched sources.

The case-field claim that surgeon local infiltration dramatically reduces opioid use and provides a specified duration of analgesia is not established by the evidence supplied. Local techniques are described, but detailed comparative data are limited.
The fixed low-fluid target appears in the older 2007 review; it is presented only as a source-reported practice and not as a universal target. The 2022 pain review provides no fluid guidance.

The case-field description of metronidazole as an anal-tissue anti-inflammatory was not used as a mechanism. The review reports pain outcomes for topical and oral metronidazole but does not establish that mechanism as the basis for a standard anesthetic plan.
Sitz baths are not presented as reliably analgesic: the systematic review reports that warm sitz baths did not provide better post-hemorrhoidectomy pain relief.
General ASA monitoring and PACU standards are applied only within their stated scope; they do not supply hemorrhoidectomy-specific airway, technique, or discharge protocols.
The supplied sources do not establish anticoagulant-management guidance for hemorrhoidectomy.
The preparation and fluid statements come from a 2007 clinical review; they should not be interpreted as current universal protocols.
evidenceGaps: Hemorrhoidectomy-specific criteria for choosing local anesthesia with sedation, spinal/regional anesthesia, or general anesthesia.
Perioperative anticoagulant and antiplatelet management applicable to excisional hemorrhoidectomy.
Current, procedure-specific bowel-preparation guidance and the relevance of the older cleansing-enema practice.
Hemorrhoidectomy-specific airway and ventilation recommendations for prone or lithotomy positioning.
Contemporary procedure-specific PONV prevention and discharge criteria.
corrections: Removed the unverified Grade III–IV indication and claim of failure of office procedures as a universal indication.
Removed prone-versus-lithotomy airway-device recommendations and the assertion that an LMA is contraindicated in prone positioning.
Removed the saddle spinal dose, positioning duration, targeted sacral levels, and stated spinal recovery time.
Removed a universal crystalloid total and the claim that urinary retention can be prevented by a fixed fluid limit.
Removed specific claims for local infiltration duration, dramatic opioid reduction, surgeon delivery as routine, and guaranteed analgesic benefit.
Removed a universal recommendation for metronidazole, docusate, ketorolac, acetaminophen, or other named medication regimens.
Corrected the sitz-bath claim: the supplied systematic review found no better postoperative pain relief with warm sitz baths.

reports.title: Low Anterior Resection (LAR)
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields were treated as unverified and were not used as evidence. Source-supported claims are qualified where evidence is narrow or non-randomized.

The source guideline’s recommendation for combined mechanical bowel preparation and oral antibiotics is more specific than the single-hospital ERAS protocol’s mechanical-preparation statement; the latter does not establish a contrary general recommendation.

The 40-patient LAR trial supports discussion of possible hemodynamic and pulmonary changes with pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg, but not routine nitroglycerin, universal invasive monitoring, or a fixed anesthetic regimen.

Base44 claims about anastomotic distance, leak-rate estimates and specific risk factors, diverting-stoma protection, routine ureteral stents, lithotomy compartment-syndrome prevention, fixed fluid volumes, cell salvage, and epidural/TAP selection were not established by the supplied sources and were excluded or qualified.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific adult evidence on positioning and prevention or management of positioning-related injury during LAR.
LAR-specific evidence to stratify anastomotic leak risk and guide response to suspected leak; supplied cohort data do not establish individual risk factors or a management pathway.
Procedure-specific guidance for recognition and management of pelvic autonomic nerve or ureteral injury.
corrections: Removed the Base44 definition of a low anastomosis as less than 6 cm from the anal verge; no supplied source supports that cutoff.
Removed the asserted 10–15% leak rate and Base44 risk-factor claims involving low anastomosis, radiation, sex, and obesity; the provided sources do not substantiate those estimates or modifiers.
Removed claims that diverting ileostomy protects an anastomosis from fecal contamination, and that routine ureteral stents improve identification; these are not supported in the supplied sources.
Removed fixed positioning, lithotomy time thresholds, leg-lowering instructions, and compartment-syndrome risk claims; the supplied sources do not establish them as LAR guidance.

Removed routine arterial line, central access, crossmatch, cell-saver, epidural, and fixed crystalloid-volume prescriptions; these are not established as universal LAR requirements by the supplied evidence.
Did not present the trial’s nitroglycerin dose or regimen as a recommended treatment.

reports.title: Ostomy Creation / Reversal (Ileostomy / Colostomy)
reviewNotes: The supplied evidence is strongest for general elective colorectal enhanced-recovery principles and weakest for ostomy creation, colostomy reversal, and procedure-specific anesthesia. Do not present broad colorectal recommendations as ostomy-specific standards.
The loop-ileostomy closure survey is a practice survey with a 22% response rate; its opioid-practice description is internally inconsistent, so no opioid-use conclusion is drawn from it.
The multimodal-pain study is retrospective and single-center. Its protocol and outcomes do not establish a preferred block, drug regimen, or general treatment effect.
No supplied source supports the Base44 claim that LMA is acceptable for reversal alone, or its proposed induction drugs, fluid volume, ketorolac regimen, or stoma-viability return-to-OR rule.
No supplied source establishes a stoma-specific PACU viability assessment method or escalation threshold; the flagged complication bullet was removed.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific adult anesthesia guidance for ileostomy or colostomy creation and for colostomy reversal.
Evidence-based criteria and testing strategy for anastomotic integrity before reversal.
A source-supported PACU method and escalation criteria for assessing stoma viability after creation.
Procedure-specific airway and anesthetic technique selection, emergence criteria, and fluid or bleeding data for ostomy procedures.
complications: The supplied sources do not describe a PACU stoma-viability assessment method or escalation threshold.
corrections: Removed the Base44 LMA-for-reversal suggestion: the supplied sources do not establish airway-device suitability or a preferred technique.
Removed the fixed 500–1500 mL crystalloid amount and blood-products-available instruction: supplied ostomy studies do not report fluid volumes, blood loss, or transfusion requirements.
Removed the routine propofol/fentanyl/rocuronium recipe and ketorolac-plus-acetaminophen plan: these are not established as case-specific regimens by the supplied sources.
Removed the claim that dusky or dark stoma appearance mandates return to the operating room: the supplied sources do not provide a stoma-viability assessment or escalation protocol.
Qualified early feeding, minimally invasive surgery, fluid management, and analgesia as broad elective-colorectal guidance rather than ostomy-specific recommendations.

reports.title: Dental Rehabilitation Under General Anesthesia (Adult)
reviewNotes: The case fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not support mandatory throat-pack placement for every case, a fixed 180-degree table turn, routine atropine or rocuronium, a particular induction or maintenance regimen, a fixed fluid volume, a required awake extubation technique, or lateral-decubitus recovery.

Reconciled the dental review's statement that intubation is highly recommended with its acknowledgement that it is not routine for deep sedation in some jurisdictions; this draft describes nasotracheal intubation as commonly preferred, not mandatory.

Throat-pack safeguards and removal/suction considerations are supported by the orthognathic review and broad OMS material, not by comparative evidence establishing a universal dental-rehabilitation protocol.

The adult special-needs dental review is limited and reports no standardized anesthetic regimen. ADA and ASA standards support general safety and monitoring principles but do not fill procedure-specific gaps.
evidenceGaps: The available sources do not resolve a standardized adult dental-rehabilitation regimen or establish universal pack placement, recovery position, induction drugs, or fluid volume.
analgesia: This is a limitation of the supplied sources, not a clinical analgesia recommendation.
corrections: Removed the unsupported claim that a throat pack is mandatory in every dental anesthetic; retained pack-placement and removal safeguards only when a pack is used.
Removed unsupported fixed room orientation, positioning, recovery position, and extubation instructions from the unverified case fields.
Removed unsourced drug recipes, including routine atropine, neuromuscular blocker, steroid, antiemetic, and postoperative analgesic choices or doses.
Removed the fixed crystalloid volume and unsupported local-anesthetic/volatile-agent arrhythmia warning as case-specific instructions.
Qualified nasotracheal intubation as commonly preferred for oral access rather than an absolute requirement.

reports.title: Orthognathic Surgery (Bimaxillary Osteotomy)
reviewNotes: Base44 material is unverified and was not used as evidence. Unsupported claims not carried forward include mandatory nasal intubation, a fixed head-elevation angle of 15–20 degrees, routine arterial line and Foley placement, a specific MAP target, a quantified TXA blood-loss benefit, and wire cutters as a universal postoperative requirement.

The procedure review contains an internal practical tension: it describes nasal intubation for maxillofacial access while cautioning that nasal tubes may hinder suctioning and ventilation in long procedures. The draft preserves both statements without asserting a universal solution.
The review describes a head-up position of at least 45 degrees as a possible edema-reduction measure; it does not support the Base44 position value or a universal positioning instruction.
The MMF aspiration concern is supported, but the supplied sources do not establish wire cutters at bedside as a required standard or describe a wire-cutting rescue protocol.

The review’s blood-loss and fluid claims vary in procedure specificity. TXA timing and dose are explicitly unresolved; cited regimens and departmental practice should not be converted into universal dosing advice.
The draft is an evidence-grounded reference draft, not a patient-specific plan, checklist, or clinically approved protocol.

The airway source reports videolaryngoscopy findings for particular difficult-airway settings but does not supply a patient-specific airway-device selection algorithm; the revised bullet therefore does not recommend a device or airway plan.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific guidance resolving airway technique and ventilation/suction tradeoffs for prolonged bimaxillary surgery.
A detailed, validated postoperative emergency response protocol for nausea or vomiting with MMF.
corrections: Removed the claim that nasal intubation is mandatory; the review describes nasal intubation for facial access but also flags limitations during long procedures.

Removed the fixed 15–20 degree head elevation and table-turn/shoulder-roll instructions because the supplied sources do not support them; the review’s separate edema-positioning suggestion is not presented as a universal setup requirement.
Removed routine arterial line, Foley, cell-saver, blood-crossmatch, and controlled-hypotension prescriptions because the supplied sources do not establish them as universal requirements.
Removed the unsupported assertion that TXA reduces bimaxillary blood loss by 30–50%, and did not repeat any TXA dose.
Removed mandatory wire cutters and the claim that MMF invariably means liquid diet; the sources support aspiration concern with nausea/vomiting but not those directives.
Corrected extubation guidance to make quantitative TOF recovery applicable when neuromuscular blockade is used, not to all orthognathic cases.

reports.title: Adrenalectomy (Laparoscopic / Robotic)
reviewNotes: Base44 clinical fields were treated as unverified and were not used as evidence. The specific potassium threshold, stress-dose steroid regimen and schedule, fluid total, and blanket arterial-line recommendations were not carried forward.

Pheochromocytoma preparation recommendations conflict in emphasis: older narrative reviews describe routine blockade, while the 2022 critical appraisal reports uncertain outcome benefit, inconsistent targets, and heterogeneous evidence. The draft preserves this uncertainty and does not reproduce medication doses.
Laparoscopic guidance is general rather than adrenal-specific; it supports relevant insufflation and robotic-positioning considerations but not a robotic adrenalectomy-specific protocol.
The Cushing’s and Conn’s anesthesia sources are narrative reviews. No claim of clinical approval or completeness is made.

The supplied robotic-surgery source addresses laparoscopic and robotic surgery generally, not robotic adrenalectomy specifically; the available sources do not establish comparative outcomes or a robot-specific anesthetic protocol.
evidenceGaps: An adrenalectomy-specific evidence-based potassium threshold or target for correction before surgery.
A validated, phenotype-specific perioperative glucocorticoid replacement and postoperative taper protocol.
Comparative evidence or a procedure-specific anesthetic protocol for robotic versus conventional laparoscopic adrenalectomy.

procedure: This is a limitation of the available evidence, not a clinical recommendation. The robotic-surgery source is general rather than adrenalectomy-specific, and the pheochromocytoma review’s approach comparison is laparoscopic versus open.
corrections: Removed Base44 claim that potassium must be corrected to greater than 3.5 mEq/L; that numeric threshold is not supported by the supplied sources.
Removed the fixed hydrocortisone dose, timing, and postoperative schedule; sources support that replacement may be required but do not establish that Base44 regimen as universal.
Removed universal arterial-line, vasopressor, blood-product, crystalloid-volume, and positioning prescriptions; monitoring and resources should reflect tumor function and case circumstances.
Corrected claims implying that all adrenalectomy approaches, positions, or robotic cases share a single anesthetic protocol; available evidence does not establish that.

reports.title: Pheochromocytoma Resection
reviewNotes: Base44 statements asserting mandatory alpha blockade, a fixed 7–14-day course, a universal BP target, orthostatic symptoms as proof of adequate blockade, and mandatory volume expansion were not carried forward as universal rules. Sources describe guideline-supported preparation but also contested outcome evidence and no consensus on targets.

Removed Base44 drug-dose regimens and statements that ketamine is categorically contraindicated, that one volatile agent is universally preferred, or that one vasoactive sequence is required. The sources support cautions and drug options, not a universally applicable anesthetic recipe.

Base44 claims of mandatory central access, routine CVP/PA catheter/TEE, fixed intraoperative fluid totals, routine ICU care, and a required vasopressor infusion before adrenal-vein approach are not established uniformly in the sources. Monitoring and disposition should reflect patient condition and institutional practice.
The Base44 positioning, detailed airway sequence, laryngoscopy drug recipe, and specific analgesia plan lack adequate case-specific support in the fetched evidence and were not adopted.

The 2011 and 2015 narrative reviews contain older practice descriptions and differ from more recent reviews. The 2022 critical appraisal and 2021 review also acknowledge limits and uncertainty; no single source settles preparation or ICU disposition.
The neuromuscular-blockade source is a general ASA-guideline overview, not pheochromocytoma-specific. Its quantitative TOF guidance is included only conditionally when neuromuscular blockade is used.

The sources describe management options for intraoperative instability but note that randomized evidence does not establish the best treatment for hypertensive spikes; no single response algorithm is asserted.
evidenceGaps: No case-specific source establishes an optimal preoperative preparation regimen or blood-pressure target that improves outcomes.
No procedure-specific airway or ventilation protocol, including positioning and insufflation strategy, is established in the available evidence.
No pheochromocytoma-specific postoperative analgesia or PONV prevention regimen is established.
No uniform blood-loss, transfusion, or postoperative destination protocol is established; disposition depends on operative course and clinical stability.
corrections: Removed fixed alpha-blockade duration and target pressure as mandatory universal requirements; retained the source disagreement and guideline context.

Corrected the claim that arterial line, central line, CVP/PA catheter, or TEE are all mandatory: arterial monitoring is emphasized, while advanced monitoring and central access are individualized or vary by review.
Removed fixed fluid quantities, pre-induction fluid instructions, and universal vasopressor timing or infusion requirements.
Removed unsupported specific ETT, induction, maintenance, extubation, and postoperative analgesia recipes.
Corrected routine ICU disposition to monitored recovery with acuity determined by postoperative stability; sources conflict on routine ICU use.
Removed blanket statements that ketamine or other named agents are absolutely contraindicated; presented source-described cautions without converting them into universal rules.

reports.title: Airway Foreign Body Removal
reviewNotes: The supplied case fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. Their pediatric age range, supine neck extension, spontaneous-ventilation inhalational induction, avoidance of neuromuscular blockade, named anesthetic drugs, topical lidocaine, and routine edema treatments are not established as adult standards by the supplied procedure-specific adult sources.

Adult sources describe multiple airway and ventilation approaches. One adult review notes that spontaneous ventilation may worsen airway collapse and that positive-pressure or jet ventilation can cause distal migration; neither supports a universal ventilation mode.

The adult reviews are narrative sources with limited comparative evidence and no standardized anesthetic protocol. The general ENT chapter is not specific to foreign-body retrieval; pediatric-only bronchoscopy details were excluded from adult recommendations.

No fixed fluid total, universal drug regimen, patient position, or emergence technique is recommended. This reflects case-specific selection and source limitations, not a reason to invent a universal target.
evidenceGaps: The available sources do not resolve an adult-specific induction and maintenance strategy, including when to use spontaneous versus controlled ventilation or neuromuscular blockade for a particular obstruction and retrieval scenario.
The available sources do not establish a foreign-body-specific adult emergence, extubation, or airway-edema management protocol.
The available sources do not provide a procedure-specific adult analgesia or PONV regimen.
corrections: Removed the unverified pediatric age distribution and any pediatric-derived technique presented as an adult default.

Removed the asserted universal preservation of spontaneous ventilation and blanket avoidance of muscle relaxants; the adult evidence describes competing ventilation considerations and does not establish either as universal.

Removed unsubstantiated fixed positioning, sevoflurane/N2O induction, topical lidocaine, routine dexamethasone or racemic epinephrine, and a mandatory surgeon-ready-before-induction rule as sourced standards.
Reframed rigid bronchoscopy as preferred in specified adult situations rather than as the universal approach; flexible bronchoscopy is commonly initial for stable adults in the supplied adult review.

reports.title: Awake Fiber-Optic Intubation (AFOI)
reviewNotes: Base44 presents AFOI as the technique of choice for predicted difficult airway with CICO risk. The sources support awake intubation as an option in anticipated difficulty and describe awake approaches for severe compromise, but do not establish that universal wording.

Base44's specific lidocaine, nerve-block, dexmedetomidine, glycopyrrolate, and timing recipes are not reproduced as recommendations. The sources do not validate that combined regimen for a general adult AFOI population.
The claim that dexmedetomidine is ideal because it preserves respiration, and that a patient tolerating scope examination will tolerate intubation, is unsupported by the supplied evidence.
The stated ETT rotation maneuver, fixed tube size, fixed topicalization interval, and blanket extubation distinctions by indication are not established as general standards in the supplied sources.

AFOI-specific fluid access, blood-loss strategy, analgesia, PONV regimen, and postoperative reflex-return interval are not supported; avoid converting their absence into universal practice requirements.

Source 0 is an older narrative review with no reported outcomes or evidence-grading framework. Source 1 concerns a small series of awake supraglottic-airway-guided cases, not conventional AFOI. Source 3 is a broad narrative review, and sources 4 and 6 provide general standards rather than AFOI protocols.
The sources combine reviews of airway anesthesia and ENT practice with a small adult awake SAGFBI case series; the case-series preparation details should not be treated as a universal AFOI protocol.
The supplied material does not define AFOI-specific intraoperative targets, fluid or blood-product thresholds, vascular-access requirements, postoperative analgesia, or extubation criteria.
evidenceGaps: A contemporary procedure-specific guideline establishing adult AFOI selection criteria, contraindications or relative cautions, and escalation criteria.
A validated adult conventional-AFOI sedation and topical-anesthesia protocol, including dose limits and monitoring details applicable to the selected technique.
A procedure-specific rescue pathway for failed awake intubation or deteriorating oxygenation, including criteria for changing approach or proceeding to emergency front-of-neck access.
AFOI-specific postoperative guidance on airway protection and timing of reassessment after topical anesthesia.
intraop: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a clinical-section instruction.
fluids: The sources describe resuscitation priorities in bleeding-airway scenarios but do not provide AFOI-specific thresholds or access requirements.
analgesia: The evidence concerns airway anesthesia and sedation, not postoperative analgesia for the underlying operation.
corrections: Removed the unqualified assertion that AFOI is the technique of choice for all predicted difficult airways or CICO risk; reframed as an option when securing the airway before induction is advantageous.

Removed Base44's exact drug doses, nerve-block injection instructions, fixed timing, and dexmedetomidine preference because they are not validated as general adult recommendations by the supplied evidence.
Removed the claim that tolerance of a scope examination predicts tolerance of intubation; no supporting evidence was supplied.
