Removed fixed ETT sizes, ETT-rotation advice, blanket positioning, and indication-based extubation rules as unsupported general instructions.
Corrected the awake supraglottic-airway-guided case-series technique to a distinct, limited-evidence approach rather than routine conventional AFOI practice.
Did not prescribe a universal fluid total, vascular-access requirement, crossmatch, analgesic regimen, PONV regimen, or topicalization-related recovery interval.

reports.title: Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)
reviewNotes: The supplied material does not support several Base44 claims as universal FESS practice. In particular, the throat-pack source says packs should be recorded and accounted for when used; it does not establish mandatory placement in every case.

The TIVA review favors improved field conditions overall but describes incongruent study results. Its evidence supports individualized consideration, not a guaranteed reduction in bleeding or a universal deliberate-hypotension target.
The base record's exact positioning, fluid volume, MAP target, anesthetic recipes, drug list, and mandatory airway plan are not established by the supplied sources.
The FESS complications review is from 2009 and focused on ophthalmic complications. Its detailed orbital-management statements should not be treated as a current anesthesia protocol.
No supplied source establishes routine preoperative steroid continuation, oral steroid use, asthma-specific planning, anticoagulant interruption, or a specific FESS analgesic regimen.
evidenceGaps: A current, procedure-specific guideline or robust evidence synthesis establishing FESS airway selection and any criteria for throat-pack use.
Applicable specialty guidance for perioperative management of antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy in FESS, including how bleeding risk and thrombosis risk are balanced.
A current, procedure-specific source for preoperative steroid management and other medication decisions in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis or nasal polyposis.
FESS-specific evidence for postoperative analgesia and PONV prevention strategies.
corrections: Removed the claim that a throat pack is mandatory for every FESS case; sources support recording and accounting for packs when used.
Removed the instruction to remove a throat pack first before extubation; the provided sources support end-of-procedure accounting but do not specify that sequence.

Removed the fixed MAP target and assertion that deliberate hypotension is a required technique; sources give no target and describe permissive hypotension only as a possible field-improvement measure.
Removed the prescribed positioning, anesthetic drug sequence, fluid volume, and routine arterial-line recommendation because the supplied evidence does not establish them as FESS standards.
Removed unsupported preoperative steroid, anticoagulant, asthma, and aspirin management instructions.
Reframed TIVA benefits and PONV claims as evidence-supported possibilities rather than guaranteed outcomes or universal requirements.

reports.title: Laryngectomy (Total / Partial)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified. Its specific airway recipes, fixed long-case duration, mandatory arterial or central access, cell-saver and crossmatch claims, fluid volumes, TXA use, PEG planning, and universal ICU disposition are not established by the supplied evidence.
The source comparing total laryngectomy with other procedures concerns aspiration-prevention surgery; it cannot be used to set routine expectations for oncologic laryngectomy.

The sources do not substantiate the Base44 claims that partial laryngectomy preserves voice function or that total laryngectomy necessarily creates the described permanent-stoma and post-resection airway circumstances. These require procedure-specific evidence.

No source supports a universal airway induction method, a claim that one rescue approach is always safest, or a laryngectomy-specific extubation plan. The draft therefore emphasizes shared planning and makes the limits explicit.
The supplied material does not establish laryngectomy-specific arterial or central access requirements.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific airway management for oncologic total versus partial laryngectomy, including airway transition during resection and management of the postoperative airway.
Laryngectomy-specific positioning, vascular access, blood-loss preparation, and postoperative disposition guidance.
Laryngectomy-specific emergence, analgesia, PONV, and postoperative monitoring recommendations.
setup: The sources do not establish procedure-specific vascular-access requirements; this is an evidence-scope limitation, not a clinical recommendation.
corrections: Removed unsupported claims that partial laryngectomy preserves voice and that total laryngectomy necessarily results in the stated permanent-stoma physiology and inability to ventilate by mouth or nose.
Removed the unsupported fixed 8–12-hour duration, mandatory arterial line/CVP, two large-bore IVs, crossmatch quantity, cell saver, crystalloid/colloid volume, TXA, and universal ICU plan.

Removed specific preoperative PEG advice, drug recipes, and the assertion that awake tracheostomy is always the safest option; the provided evidence does not establish these as routine recommendations.
Did not treat aspiration-prevention case reports or their procedural comparisons as routine anesthetic guidance for oncologic laryngectomy.

reports.title: Mastoidectomy
reviewNotes: The supplied Base44 fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. In particular, “facial nerve monitoring is mandatory” overstates the procedure source, which says monitoring is often used but not required.

The Base44 instruction to give no neuromuscular blockers after intubation is more categorical than the source. The source says to discuss monitoring before induction to ensure no long-acting paralytic is used; it does not establish a universal prohibition on all blockade.

TIVA, avoidance of nitrous oxide, deliberate hypotension or a specified MAP, fixed crystalloid volume, particular drug regimens, awake extubation, and aggressive PONV prophylaxis are not supported as routine mastoidectomy recommendations by the provided general procedure source.

The general mastoidectomy source says CT is not required, while the separate endoscopic technique paper calls CT mandatory for its selected technique. These statements concern different approaches and should not be collapsed into a universal imaging rule.
The endoscopic paper’s hypotensive-anesthesia statement is technique-specific and its systolic-pressure wording is explicitly unclear; it should not establish a routine target.

The supplied evidence does not support a mandatory supine/head-turned position, mandatory arterial line, preoperative facial-function documentation protocol, or absolute nitrous-oxide contraindication for mastoidectomy.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific evidence for anesthetic maintenance and physiologic targets, including whether any target improves outcomes in general mastoidectomy; do not infer a universal target from the narrow endoscopic technique report.

Procedure-specific blood-loss characterization and bleeding-management evidence, including fluid or transfusion guidance. These decisions remain individualized; absence of a universal fluid total is not itself a gap.
Mastoidectomy-specific analgesia, PONV prevention, and emergence/extubation evidence.
Adult-specific outcome evidence and obstetric-specific guidance are not supplied; this draft does not establish pregnancy-specific management.
corrections: Changed “facial nerve monitoring mandatory/non-negotiable” to “often used, not required,” consistent with the procedure source.

Removed the categorical prohibition on neuromuscular blockade after intubation; retained the source-supported need to coordinate monitoring and avoid long-acting paralytic use when monitoring is planned.
Removed unsupported routine TIVA, nitrous-oxide avoidance, deliberate hypotension/MAP target, fixed fluid volume, drug list, extubation technique, and PONV regimen.

Corrected the implication that CT is always required: the general mastoidectomy source says it is not required, while a separate endoscopic technique paper describes mandatory CT for its specific approach.
Removed unsupported mandatory arterial-line monitoring, exact positioning beyond the reported bed turn, and routine documentation requirements not stated in the supplied evidence.

reports.title: Maxillofacial Trauma Surgery (Panfacial Fractures)
reviewNotes: The Base44 airway options and perioperative details are not validated facts. The draft retains only choices supported in the fetched sources and frames them as individualized options rather than a fixed recipe.

Corrected the implication that a nasal ETT is required whenever MMF is planned: route selection depends on surgical access and nasal/skull-base injury; oral, nasal, submental, and surgical-airway approaches appear in the sources.
The supplied evidence does not substantiate the Base44 claim that soft-tissue swelling peaks at 48–72 hours or an optimal fixation window. No timing recommendation is made.

The Base44 claims of universal table rotation, head extension, two IVs, arterial line, Foley, crystalloid volume, TXA, and particular analgesic drugs are not supported as routine case-specific recommendations in the supplied sources and were not carried forward.

The categorical Base44 statement that vomiting with MMF will cause death is not adopted. The cited review identifies severe nausea/vomiting as a concern and supports bedside wire cutters or scissors and staff instruction.
The source series includes pediatric patients and does not provide a separate adult-only analysis. This draft is adult-scoped and does not use pediatric-specific evidence to establish adult practice.

The sources disagree or are not uniform on nasotracheal intubation in skull-base injury: one review advises avoiding blind nasal instrumentation when certain fractures are possible, while another notes a published contrary view. The draft avoids endorsing nasal intubation in that setting.

Specific instructions about tube fixation, circuit position, access after draping, and suctioning or airway assessment immediately before MMF were not supported by the supplied sources and were omitted.
The sources support MMF-related monitoring and wire-cutter preparedness but do not provide a procedure-specific antiemetic regimen.
evidenceGaps: Adult-only comparative evidence for airway-route selection and outcomes in panfacial fracture repair.
Case-specific criteria for positioning and when invasive monitoring or particular vascular access is indicated.
Procedure-specific evidence for analgesia and PONV prevention in patients with postoperative MMF.
Evidence establishing an optimal interval from injury to fixation; the supplied sources do not support the Base44 48–72-hour swelling or fixation-window claim.
corrections: Removed fixed airway recipes such as awake nasal fibreoptic intubation whenever the mandible is intact, routine RSI, or mandatory preoperative tracheostomy; the sources describe individualized selection.
Removed the assertion that nasal intubation is categorically safe or required for MMF; nasal and skull-base injury may make it unsuitable.
Removed fixed positioning, table rotation, number of IVs, routine arterial line/Foley, fluid totals, blood-product protocol, TXA, and drug lists as unsupported routine recommendations.
Removed fixed extubation instructions based solely on MMF; the sources support individualized ventilation and extubation decisions based on edema, airway maintenance, associated injuries, and status.
Replaced absolute statements about aspiration-related death with source-supported airway-risk language and bedside cutter/scissor preparedness.

reports.title: Microlaryngoscopy / Vocal Cord Surgery
reviewNotes: The source material supports considering general anesthesia for microlaryngoscopy, but also describes awake approaches for other phonosurgical procedures; do not generalize one approach to all voice surgery.

Laser precaution details are supported in broad terms, including reduced FiO₂, discontinuing nitrous oxide and a dyed saline cuff. The supplied sources do not support the case-field assertion that even one second at a higher FiO₂ can ignite, nor do they supply a complete fire-response protocol.

The case-field claims that dexamethasone is mandatory, remifentanil is uniquely ideal, all cases require awake extubation, and a particular airway-fire sequence is universal are not established by the supplied sources and have been omitted or qualified.

The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia-care sources are standards applicable to their stated scope, not microlaryngoscopy-specific technique recommendations. Neuromuscular-blockade guidance applies only when such drugs are used.
evidenceGaps: A complete, authoritative operating-room airway-fire response protocol applicable to laryngeal laser surgery is not included in the supplied sources.
The sources do not establish a procedure-specific emergence/extubation protocol or postoperative analgesia and PONV regimen for microlaryngoscopy.
corrections: Removed the case-field-specific position and shoulder-roll instruction because the supplied sources do not establish a position for this procedure.
Removed the fixed crystalloid amount and minimal-blood-loss assertion; the sources provide no case-specific fluid or quantified blood-loss recommendation.
Removed mandatory dexamethasone, routine racemic epinephrine, voice-rest and humidified-air prescriptions because these are not supported by the supplied sources.

Replaced the blanket awake-extubation instruction with individualized emergence planning; a source reports awake extubation is usual in ENT practice, while the procedure-specific chapter supplies no general protocol.

Removed the claim that remifentanil is uniquely effective or ideal and the assertion that a longer-acting opioid transition is required; the sources describe anesthetic options but do not establish these claims.
Qualified laser-fire troubleshooting because the supplied evidence does not substantiate the case-field's full immediate-response sequence.

reports.title: Myringotomy with Tube Placement (Adult)
reviewNotes: The supplied procedure-specific source is pediatric-focused for general anesthesia; pediatric mask-only practice cannot establish adult practice.

The adult anesthesia approach is not consistent across the supplied descriptions: StatPearls describes adults often tolerating clinic local anesthesia, while Cleveland Clinic says general anesthesia is usual overall and adults may receive local anesthesia depending on circumstances.
The broad ENT airway chapter discusses ear procedures but is not a dedicated adult myringotomy anesthesia reference; its SGA description should not override patient- and setting-specific judgment.

The Base44 claims about a usual pediatric age range, sevoflurane/N2O recipe, mask-only airway, no IV, spontaneous ventilation, specific positioning, emergence position, and parent presence are not supported as adult guidance by the supplied sources.
No source establishes the Base44 claims that this is the fastest anesthetic, that surgical time is a fixed five minutes, or that a particular depth at incision is an adult standard.
evidenceGaps: Adult-specific comparative evidence or guidance for selecting local anesthesia versus general anesthesia and, when general anesthesia is used, choosing an airway technique.
Adult myringotomy-specific anesthesia complication rates and detailed perioperative monitoring, emergence, and analgesia guidance.
corrections: Removed pediatric age range, parent-at-induction recommendation, and other pediatric-specific workflow claims from adult guidance.
Removed the fixed sevoflurane/N2O induction and maintenance regimen, no-IV assertion, and blanket mask-only/no-LMA airway plan.
Removed unsupported fixed positioning, surgical duration, total anesthetic duration, spontaneous-ventilation prescription, and emergence-position instruction.
Removed the claim that the procedure has a single usual adult anesthetic approach; sources describe both adult local anesthesia and general anesthesia without resolving a universal preference.
Did not carry forward the Base44 analgesic drug list or claim that a named ear-drop product is routinely used for adult postoperative analgesia.

reports.title: Neck Dissection (Radical / Modified / Selective)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as factual evidence. In particular, claims about bilateral IJV ligation causing cerebral venous hypertension, specific head-up angles, routine arterial lines, deliberate hypotension, airway edema from bilateral dissection, and mandatory ICU disposition are not supported by the supplied sources.

The source set supports surgical anatomy and complications more strongly than procedure-specific anesthesia management. Generic ENT airway statements are explicitly not equivalent to a neck-dissection protocol.
The cohort on neuromuscular blockade is retrospective, single-center and underpowered; its non-significant association must not be presented as proof that blockade has no nerve-injury risk.

The source’s mention of postoperative hematoma is retained as a complication, but the Base44 bedside evacuation/reintubation instructions are not reproduced because they are not established in the supplied evidence.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific postoperative airway-risk assessment and escalation pathway, including how operative extent, airway findings and neck swelling should influence disposition.
Neck-dissection-specific fluid and blood-product management guidance and analgesia/PONV recommendations.
corrections: Removed unsupported Base44 claims that bilateral IJV ligation requires a particular carbon-dioxide target, head position or ICU pathway.
Removed unsupported routine recipes for crystalloid volume, type-and-crossmatch, cell salvage, controlled hypotension, arterial-line placement, drug selection and cervical plexus block.

Removed unsupported claims that bilateral dissection predictably causes airway edema or that smooth extubation, awake extubation in every case, or a specific bedside hematoma procedure is established by the supplied procedure evidence.

Corrected the implication that nerve monitoring universally requires avoidance of neuromuscular blockade; the supplied study describes case-by-case decisions and does not establish a universal approach.

reports.title: Parotidectomy (Superficial / Total)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not as evidence. Removed or qualified its claims of mandatory facial nerve monitoring, a particular RAE tube, intubation-only neuromuscular blockade, TIVA, controlled hypotension to a fixed MAP, and routine fluid volumes; the supplied sources do not establish these as universal parotidectomy practice.

The source does not support the Base44 postoperative analgesic regimen, smooth-extubation prescription, or claim that parotid-region hematoma compresses the airway. Hematoma prevention and possible surgical reintervention are supported; a specific airway-compression claim is not established in the fetched evidence.

The source describes loss of ear sensation as a possible complication, not as an expected outcome. Nerve monitoring is described as standard in many centers, not mandatory for every procedure or approach.
The MAC series is a six-patient, single-center retrospective report in selected patients. It does not justify routine MAC or define standard parotidectomy anesthesia.
The adult clinical material does not address pregnancy-specific management. Obstetric decisions should not be inferred from non-obstetric sources.
The supplied parotidectomy chapter does not establish a procedure-specific postoperative nausea-and-vomiting strategy.
evidenceGaps: No procedure-specific evidence establishes anesthetic drug selection, hemodynamic targets, fluid or blood-management approach, emergence/extubation technique, postoperative analgesia, or PONV management.
No pregnancy-specific evidence addresses parotidectomy anesthesia, maternal-fetal considerations, or obstetric monitoring.
analgesia: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a clinical analgesia recommendation; moved it to evidence.
corrections: Removed universal claims that facial nerve monitoring is mandatory and that NMB must be limited to intubation; sources advise avoiding relaxants when monitoring facial nerve function and describe monitoring as standard in many centers.
Removed routine Oral RAE, TIVA, fixed MAP 65, 500–1000 mL crystalloid, and routine blood-availability instructions as unsupported recipes.
Removed the specific acetaminophen/ketorolac/opioid regimen and smooth-extubation instruction as unsupported by the procedure-specific source.
Removed the claim that postoperative parotid hematoma compresses the airway; retained source-supported concern for hematoma, hemostasis, and potential surgical reintervention.
Corrected auricular numbness from an expected effect to a possible complication described by the source.

reports.title: Septoplasty / Turbinate Reduction
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not as evidence. The fetched material does not support a mandatory oral RAE tube, mandatory throat pack, fixed head elevation, or a universal choice between general anesthesia and a supraglottic airway.

The supplied sources do not support the Base44 claims that injected epinephrine has a defined arrhythmia risk in this procedure, that one volatile agent is safer than another, or that a particular fluid total is routine. Local anesthetic/vasoconstrictor use is described, but no procedure-specific dose or hemodynamic target is established.

The sources do not establish routine nasal packing, mandatory mouth-breathing counseling, pack-removal timing, or a specific postoperative analgesia regimen. A study's medication protocol is not a recommendation.
The review's 30-minute postoperative observation applies to the office-based procedures it discusses, not as a universal PACU duration.
The clinical material is an evidence-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan or a clinically approved reference.
The supplied procedure-specific review addresses office-based functional nasal procedures; it does not establish an operating-room position or case-specific operating-room setup protocol.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific comparative evidence to guide airway-device selection and airway-protection strategy across septoplasty and turbinate-reduction case complexity.
A procedure-specific bleeding, fluid, and postoperative nasal-packing protocol, including evidence-based pack counseling and removal practices.
corrections: Removed unverified fixed positioning, table rotation, oral RAE, and mandatory throat-pack claims; sources do not establish these as universal for the case.
Removed unsupported epinephrine-arrhythmia and volatile-agent safety comparisons; no supplied source substantiates those claims for this procedure.
Removed fixed fluid totals and blood-management assumptions; available sources do not provide a septoplasty-specific fluid or blood-loss protocol.
Reframed the retrospective deep-sedation study's anesthetic and medication protocols as study observations, not recommendations or standards.
Removed unsupported claims about routine nasal packing, obligatory postoperative mouth breathing, and a fixed pack-removal interval.

reports.title: Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy (T&A) (Adult)
reviewNotes: The pain guideline is the most procedure-specific source for analgesia. Its finding that included NSAID studies did not show increased bleeding should be reported with its evidence limits, not converted into a guarantee of no bleeding risk.

The airway sources describe both tracheal tubes and FLMA use. The FLMA tonsillectomy discussion is explicitly experience-dependent; the supplied evidence does not establish one device as universally preferred.

Adult scope is maintained. The prominent opioid/OSA desaturation warning in the tonsillectomy pain review is specifically pediatric; it is not used here to assert an adult-specific effect size or blanket opioid restriction.

Base44 claims about indications, pediatric prevalence, recent-URI deferral intervals, position, room layout, tube-size recipes, induction and maintenance drugs, specific drug doses, lateral extubation as essential, emergency RSI, and codeine warnings are not supported by the fetched material as adult T&A recommendations and have not been carried forward.

The Base44 characterization of ketorolac as controversial or commonly avoided is not adopted: the procedure-specific guideline supports NSAIDs and reports no increased bleeding in included studies, while individual contraindications and clinical judgment remain relevant.
evidenceGaps: Adult-specific preoperative selection and risk-stratification guidance for tonsillectomy and adenotonsillectomy, including procedure-specific assessment of OSA.
Adenoidectomy-specific adult anesthetic and airway details; the provided procedure-specific evidence centers on tonsillectomy.
Adult tonsillectomy-specific management of significant postoperative or intraoperative hemorrhage, including airway and hemodynamic escalation pathways.
corrections: Removed unsupported Base44 procedural indications and the claim that T&A is the most common pediatric surgical procedure; the supplied sources do not establish either as adult reference facts.

Removed the stated URI deferral interval, NPO rule, table rotation, Rose position, shoulder roll, routine throat-pack placement, and prescribed tube-size formula because the provided evidence does not support these as adult T&A instructions.

Removed Base44 drug doses and its fixed induction, maintenance, analgesia, and laryngospasm medication recipe; the procedure-specific pain guideline supplies recommendations but no dosing instructions.

Removed claims that lateral extubation is essential, that bleeding tonsil cases universally require RSI, and that particular drugs are categorically avoided in specified age groups; these were not established by applicable adult evidence in the supplied sources.

Corrected any implication that NSAIDs are categorically inappropriate after tonsillectomy: the guideline recommends NSAIDs and reports no increased bleeding in included evidence, without guaranteeing safety for every patient.

reports.title: Tracheal Intubation for Epiglottitis
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its statement that every case requires immediate controlled intubation is too broad: the adult chapter says airway intervention may not be necessary in many adults, while emphasizing close monitoring and the possibility of deterioration.

The supplied sources do not substantiate the Base44 pathogen-frequency claims or its specific antibiotic combination. The 2018 chapter describes empiric antibiotic coverage, but a current, applicable infectious-disease guideline was not supplied; no regimen is recommended in this draft.

The Base44 sevoflurane concentration, ketamine dose, fixed ICU intubation duration, CRP/temperature extubation criteria, and proposed analgesic drugs are unsupported by the supplied evidence and were excluded. The available source supports a cuff-leak test and usually a second-look laryngoscopy, not the full proposed criteria.

The Base44 instruction to have a surgeon with a scalpel in hand is not established by the sources. The supported requirement is experienced airway personnel and immediate surgical-airway readiness; the chapter distinguishes cricothyroidotomy readiness from tracheotomy preparation.

The 2012 overview's preferred fibreoptic nasal or rigid-bronchoscopy approach and the 2018 chapter's options (including awake fibreoptic and direct/video laryngoscopy) are not a direct, evidence-based comparison. Technique selection remains dependent on presentation, expertise, and available resources.
The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards support general monitoring and recovery principles, not a specific epiglottitis airway protocol.
evidenceGaps: A current adult-specific decision framework for selecting observation versus airway intervention, including validated thresholds or criteria; the supplied sources identify risk associations but do not establish a definitive rule.
Comparative adult evidence or a current specialty guideline to select among awake fibreoptic, direct/video laryngoscopy, rigid bronchoscopy, and awake surgical airway for differing presentations.
A current adult epiglottitis guideline covering antimicrobial selection and adjunctive treatment; the supplied narrative sources do not establish a contemporary regimen for this draft.
A validated adult extubation and post-extubation airway protocol, including how to combine cuff-leak assessment, laryngoscopic reassessment, and clinical recovery.
corrections: Removed the assertion that all adults with epiglottitis require immediate intubation; intervention is case-dependent and may not be required in many adults.
Removed unsupported adult pathogen prevalence claims and the Base44 antibiotic regimen.
Removed specific induction drug concentrations and doses, fixed 24–72-hour intubation duration, CRP and fever criteria, and the proposed analgesic regimen.

Replaced an absolute prohibition on lying flat with the sourced caution that suspected adults should be kept sitting and should not be asked to lie down; forced supine positioning may precipitate obstruction.
Replaced 'ENT with a scalpel in hand' with sourced requirements for experienced personnel and immediate surgical-airway readiness.
Did not present a single airway technique, neuromuscular-blockade rule outside this airway context, or fixed extubation protocol as universally established.

reports.title: Tympanoplasty
reviewNotes: The case fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. Removed unsupported fixed plans, drug choices, doses, fluid total, position details, and claimed mandatory monitoring or recovery practices.

The claim that nitrous oxide is absolutely contraindicated, diffuses into the middle ear at a particular rate, and physically displaces a graft is not established by the supplied sources. The procedure review only says possible effects were discussed; the sedation study does not report its use.

The claims that PONV is the primary threat to graft success, that vomiting causes graft disruption, and that multimodal antiemesis is mandatory are not supported here. The trial's vomiting reporting is internally inconsistent.

Facial-nerve monitoring as required, avoidance of all neuromuscular blockade after intubation, and the proposed ETT/oral RAE plan are not established as tympanoplasty-specific requirements. Generic ENT airway statements should not be converted into procedure-specific rules.
The trial's selected adult population, local-anesthetic sedation methods, and reported outcomes should not be generalized into recommended dosing or routine anesthetic technique.
The supplied study content does not establish whether neuromuscular blockade was used; do not infer that it is required or prohibited.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific anesthesia guideline or comparative evidence addressing anesthetic technique, airway selection, and the role of facial-nerve monitoring or neuromuscular blockade in tympanoplasty.
Reliable tympanoplasty-specific evidence on nitrous oxide and middle-ear pressure or graft outcomes, and on whether PONV or coughing meaningfully affects graft success.
intraop: This is an evidence-scope note rather than a supported intraoperative practice recommendation; move it out of the clinical bullets.
corrections: Removed the unsupported absolute N2O contraindication and asserted mechanism of graft displacement.
Removed claims that TIVA, scopolamine, specific antiemetic combinations, or particular emergence drugs are mandatory or preferred for tympanoplasty.
Removed fixed ETT/oral RAE, no-further-NMB, reverse-Trendelenburg, shoulder-roll, table-rotation, and facial-nerve-monitor requirements as unsupported procedure-specific rules.
Removed the asserted fixed crystalloid volume and minimal-blood-loss expectation; supplied procedure sources give no fluid regimen or blood-loss estimate.

Removed the claim that deep extubation is acceptable under specified conditions and the proposed propofol/lidocaine doses; these are not supported as tympanoplasty recommendations by the supplied evidence.

reports.title: ASD / PFO Closure (Percutaneous)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, the specified drug combinations, TIVA preference, ETT/MAC rules, pediatric anesthesia claim, arterial-line/Foley use, fixed fluid amount, analgesics, and specific antiplatelet combination are not established by the supplied ASD closure evidence.
The case field’s PFO indication and prior-stroke selection criteria are not verified by the ASD-focused procedural review; PFO-specific guidance is not supplied.

Source 0 is the most procedure-specific source but is a review, not an anesthesia guideline. Source 1 is a patient-facing overview. Source 3 concerns broader EP procedures and should not be used to impose AF-ablation or other EP protocols on ASD/PFO closure.

Antiplatelet therapy after ASD closure is described as lasting at least six months, while the same review notes substantial practice variation and need for further study. A fixed drug combination should not be inferred.
The case-field air embolism warning is not substantiated as a closure-specific complication by the ASD sources; it was not presented as routine ASD closure guidance.
The supplied ASD closure sources do not establish routine arterial-line or Foley-catheter use, patient positioning, or procedure-specific fluid and analgesia plans.
The supplied sources enumerate ASD closure risks but do not provide an ASD-specific anesthesia response algorithm for the complications named in the removed bullet.
evidenceGaps: PFO-specific indications, patient selection, technique, and perioperative management.
Closure-specific anesthesia and airway evidence, including factors for choosing sedation versus general anesthesia.
Closure-specific anticoagulation and intraprocedural ACT guidance.
Procedure-specific recognition and rescue guidance for major events such as tamponade, air embolism, or device embolization.
setup: This is a source-scope note rather than a procedure-specific setup recommendation.
complications: The supplied ASD closure sources describe potential complications but do not provide an ASD-specific anesthesia response algorithm for tamponade, device embolization, or air embolism.
fluids: This is a source limitation, not a clinical fluid-management recommendation.
analgesia: This is a source limitation, not an analgesic recommendation.
corrections: Removed the case-field assertion that cryptogenic stroke history establishes PFO closure candidacy; no supplied source supports those criteria.
Removed the fixed propofol, fentanyl, rocuronium, dexmedetomidine, and TIVA recipes because the supplied ASD sources do not establish them.
Removed mandatory ETT, pediatric GA, continuous TEE, arterial line for large ASD, Foley, and fixed fluid-volume claims as unsupported by the procedure-specific evidence.

Corrected the case-field aspirin-plus-clopidogrel six-month regimen to the narrower source-supported statement that antiplatelet therapy is used for at least six months, with practice variation and further study needed.
Removed routine acetaminophen/ketorolac analgesia and fixed PACU arrhythmia-management claims because these are not established in the supplied sources.

reports.title: Atrial Fibrillation Ablation (Pulmonary Vein Isolation)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unaudited material, not evidence. Corrected its categorical claim that an ETT is required: supplied sources describe several airway approaches and allow sedation in selected cases.
Did not endorse TIVA as preferred or as guaranteeing catheter stability; sources describe both TIVA and volatile maintenance and report mixed, technique-specific evidence.

Removed universal arterial-line, Foley, esophageal-probe, PaCO₂-target, apnea, and fixed fluid-volume claims. The sources support selective use or identify unresolved practice, not blanket requirements.

Did not retain Base44's fixed ACT range, esophageal temperature alert threshold, or routine posterior-wall/additional lesion-set claims as universal practice; supplied sources conflict on ACT targets or describe individualized lesion strategies.
Kept phrenic-nerve assessment during right-sided cryoablation and the need to avoid paralysis during that assessment; quantitative TOF recovery applies only when neuromuscular blockade is used.
No routine ketorolac/NSAID regimen or PONV protocol is asserted. Analgesia is individualized, and the supplied sources do not provide a PVI-specific PONV plan.

The supplied sources do not establish a universal PVI fluid total, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion threshold. One review discusses substantial irrigation fluid in AF ablation, but does not establish a universal target.
The supplied sources do not support the removed renal or anticoagulation-related analgesia-selection claims or a PVI-specific PONV prevention regimen.
The supplied sources do not establish neurologic findings, access-site hemostasis, or symptoms of tamponade or phrenic-nerve dysfunction as required elements of routine recovery assessment.
evidenceGaps: Adult comparative evidence establishing a routine anesthesia and airway strategy specifically for pulsed-field AF ablation is not provided; the available cited human evidence is an early pilot.
The supplied sources do not resolve whether routine esophageal temperature monitoring, or a particular probe type, improves outcomes across AF ablation practice.
fluids: This is an evidence-scope limitation, not a clinical-section recommendation.
corrections: Corrected “ETT required” to individualized airway management; the sources describe facemask, supraglottic airway, endotracheal tube, and sedation approaches.
Removed “TIVA preferred” as a universal recommendation and any claim that it guarantees catheter stability.
Removed universal arterial-line and Foley requirements; use depends on patient and procedural factors.
Removed a fixed PaCO₂ target and routine intermittent apnea instruction; ventilation strategies require procedural coordination and individualization.
Removed a fixed 1–2 L crystalloid prescription; irrigated ablation can contribute substantial additional fluid, so total administration is individualized.
Removed a universal ACT target and fixed esophageal temperature alert threshold because supplied sources differ or do not establish a universal threshold.
Corrected routine posterior-wall isolation and additional lesion sets to case-specific operator strategy.
Removed the claim that NSAIDs are universally appropriate or that one postoperative analgesic regimen is standard.

reports.title: Atrial Flutter Ablation (Cavotricuspid Isthmus)
reviewNotes: Base44's specific dexmedetomidine, midazolam, fentanyl, and propofol regimen—including boluses timed to lesion delivery—is not supported as a routine CTI anesthetic technique by the supplied sources; the flutter source says approaches vary and provides no specific regimen.

The Base44 claims of therapeutic anticoagulation as a universal preoperative requirement, heparin by the cardiologist, and renal function assessment for contrast confirmation are not established for typical CTI ablation in the supplied evidence. Left-sided ablation anticoagulation statements should not be generalized to this right-sided procedure.

The claimed CTI success rate above 95%, specific 3D-mapping setup, 500–1000 mL crystalloid, and routine groin rhythm/recurrence-check protocol are not established by the supplied sources as universal CTI standards.

The EP source's broad complication estimates are not CTI-specific. The low tamponade-risk description for flutter and general EP/RF-ablation risk statements are presented with their differing scope rather than merged into a single estimate.
This is an evidence-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan or a declaration of clinical approval.
The supplied flutter review does not provide a CTI-specific peri-procedural anticoagulation regimen or ACT target; the ACT range cited in the other review is explicitly for left-sided ablation.
The sources recommend endpoint checks and postoperative monitoring but do not supply a specific recurrence-surveillance protocol.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not establish a CTI-specific anesthetic drug regimen, airway technique, anticoagulation plan, or ACT target.
The supplied sources do not define CTI-specific fluid or blood-loss targets, a PONV regimen, or detailed recovery and discharge criteria.
corrections: Removed the fixed dexmedetomidine–midazolam–fentanyl induction recipe and propofol bolus timing because these are not supported as routine CTI practice in the fetched evidence.
Removed the greater-than-95% success claim because no supplied source substantiates that figure.
Removed the fixed crystalloid volume, routine contrast/renal-function premise, and universal therapeutic-anticoagulation assertion because the procedure-specific sources do not establish them.
Corrected the airway framing: sedation or general anesthesia may be used; routine intubation, paralysis, or general anesthesia is not imposed.
Corrected anticoagulation framing so left-sided ablation targets are not presented as universal for right-sided CTI ablation.

reports.title: Cardiac Catheterization (Diagnostic)
reviewNotes: Base44 was treated as unverified and not used as evidence. Several of its specific clinical recommendations are not substantiated by the supplied sources.
The 2014 cath-lab review is broad, lacks formal evidence grading, and mixes adult and pediatric material; only its applicable general adult-context statements were used.
The RHC review is procedure-specific but is not an anesthesia source. RHC acquisition and position details are explicitly limited to RHC rather than extrapolated to coronary angiography.
Generic ASA monitoring and recovery standards are retained as general anesthesia standards, not represented as cath-specific protocols.

The supplied sources discuss complications in other contexts, including PCI, right-heart catheterization, and electrophysiology procedures, but do not establish the stated diagnostic coronary-catheterization-specific recognition and escalation pathway.
evidenceGaps: Adult diagnostic coronary angiography-specific anesthetic guidance, including selection of anesthetic technique and access strategy.
A source-supported approach to contrast allergy risk assessment and premedication, and to medication management such as metformin when contrast is used.
Diagnostic coronary-catheterization-specific recognition and escalation guidance for coronary injury, arrhythmia, air embolism, and access-site complications.
Cath-specific postprocedure access-site surveillance, mobilization, and discharge guidance.
complications: This is a source-scope limitation, not a supported clinical complication-management recommendation.
corrections: Removed the unverified preference for radial access and the claim that it enables earlier ambulation; the supplied sources do not establish that as a universal diagnostic-cath recommendation.

Removed fixed midazolam and fentanyl dosing and the assertion that a particular MAC regimen is usual; sources support case-dependent technique and, for diagnostic RHC, often local anesthesia without sedation.
Removed the specified saline prehydration rate and timing; the source supports adequate hydration in the context of contrast-related renal risk but does not establish that recipe for all patients.
Removed the metformin hold interval, contrast-allergy premedication drugs, and claims of specific prophylaxis because the supplied evidence does not support them.
Removed specific RCA-injection bradycardia and femoral retroperitoneal-hematoma management claims as routine diagnostic-cath guidance; those claims are not supported by applicable supplied evidence.
Removed the source-independent claim that recovery is necessarily rapid and the radial-band/femoral-dressing instructions; no supplied source establishes these as a general recovery protocol.

reports.title: Elective Cardioversion (DCCV)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified claims. Do not carry forward its exact drug doses, fixed shock timing, fixed emergence time, or instructions for jaw thrust, bag-mask ventilation, atropine, pacing, or succinylcholine as routine case standards.

The supplied sources do not substantiate the Base44 claims that NPO status must follow a particular rule, AP pads are preferred, electrolyte or thyroid tests are universally required, or a particular anesthetic drug is best for all patients.

The cardioversion review identifies digitalis toxicity as a contraindication, but this does not substantiate routine digoxin levels for all patients. The sources do not establish a universal repeat-shock energy sequence or a standard fluid, analgesic, or skin-burn protocol.

The 2009 narrative review is older than the ASA standards supplied and is not a current full society guideline for elective cardioversion anticoagulation. The more recent EP review concerns AF ablation and must not be treated as a cardioversion guideline.
The elective anesthetic trial has limited applicability to patients outside its selected study population, and its abstract and results section conflict on statistical significance for hypotension.
evidenceGaps: A current, full society guideline specifically addressing elective cardioversion anticoagulation eligibility and post-cardioversion management was not supplied; use the applicable cardiology guidance and local protocol.
The supplied sources do not establish an adult cardioversion-specific airway technique or comparative anesthetic protocol for patients with substantial hemodynamic instability or major comorbidity.
corrections: Removed unsupported fixed propofol, fentanyl, methohexital, and etomidate doses and the claim that cardioversion should occur within a fixed interval after induction.

Removed fixed 3–5-minute emergence, mandatory natural airway, routine avoidance of intubation, and specific airway maneuvers as universal directions; airway management is individualized and the cardioversion review specifies no airway technique.
Removed the unsupported universal pad-position preference, electrolyte correction thresholds, thyroid testing, digoxin-level testing, and fixed anticoagulation criteria or intervals.
Removed routine atropine, transcutaneous pacing, asynchronous defibrillation-mode, repeat-shock energy, acetaminophen, and skin-burn instructions as unverified case recipes.

reports.title: Electrophysiology (EP) Study
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not support a universal dexmedetomidine-preferred regimen, routine medication-hold plan for standalone diagnostic EP studies, fixed fluid volume, or standardized recovery protocol.

Evidence about propofol and inducibility is not uniform: focal atrial tachycardias and ventricular ectopy may be suppressed, while the review reports that propofol did not suppress inducibility in most SVT cases. Avoid a blanket claim that one agent suppresses all arrhythmias.
ACT guidance in the sources is tied to particular ablation procedures. No universal EP-study ACT target is stated here.
Sources discuss different populations and procedures, including ablation, device implantation, and cardioversion. Do not treat their procedure-specific recommendations as interchangeable.
The adult-focused draft does not use pediatric findings to establish adult practice. No pregnancy-specific management recommendation is supported by the supplied sources.
This is an evidence-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan, checklist, or statement of clinical approval.
Fluid-management and analgesia guidance in the supplied material pertains to other EP procedures or is not stated; do not treat those gaps as evidence for a diagnostic-study protocol.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific description of standalone diagnostic EP-study workflow, access, and which phases require inducibility or mapping.
An applicable diagnostic EP-study medication-management protocol, including how to individualize decisions about antiarrhythmic continuation or interruption.
Diagnostic-study-specific anticoagulation and access-site management guidance, including which patients or procedural features require anticoagulation.
Diagnostic EP-study-specific recovery and disposition criteria.
procedure: This is a limitation of the evidence base, not a procedure instruction.
fluids: The fluid-overload warning is supported in the context of ablation, while the lack of a diagnostic-study fluid protocol is an evidence-scope limitation.
analgesia: This is an evidence gap; the sources do not support a diagnostic-study-specific analgesic or PONV recommendation.
corrections: Removed the unsupported fixed preference for dexmedetomidine and the claim that propofol uniformly suppresses arrhythmias; available evidence describes effects that vary by rhythm and procedure.
Removed the blanket instruction to hold many antiarrhythmics preoperatively; the cited medication-holding information is specific to AF ablation and does not establish a diagnostic EP-study regimen.
Removed the fixed crystalloid amount and routine medication dosing from the unverified fields; the sources do not support these as universal diagnostic-study practice.

Removed the assertion that MAC with a natural airway is universally appropriate; technique and airway management are individualized, and the sources describe possible escalation to airway intervention.
Removed any universal ACT target, positioning instruction, or EP-study-specific emergence and extubation protocol not established by the supplied evidence.

reports.title: ICD / AICD Placement
reviewNotes: Base44’s blanket requirement for endotracheal intubation, general anesthesia, full paralysis, and arterial line during DFT is not supported as a universal ICD approach. The EP review says anesthetic choice depends on the patient and that DFT is performed less often; testing may cause hemodynamic compromise.

The supplied evidence does not establish the Base44 drug recipes, mandatory 100% oxygen protocol, intentional VF procedure sequence, or external-defibrillator rescue algorithm for ICD placement. These have not been reproduced as clinical instructions.

The Base44 claims for routine ACT monitoring, postprocedure chest radiography, device interrogation/programming details, and activity restrictions are not established by the supplied ICD-specific evidence and were not presented as recommendations.

The source mentioning S-ICD general anesthesia uses qualified wording (“probably”) and should not be elevated into a standard. The other review says local infiltration may be insufficient and that evidence for regional adjuncts is limited.
The output is an evidence-grounded draft, not a patient-specific anesthetic plan or a clinically approved protocol.

The supplied sources do not provide ICD-specific troubleshooting guidance for failed device testing, lead displacement, pneumothorax, or air embolism. The replacement complication statement is limited to reported tamponade risk; it does not address those other events.
Fluid guidance in the supplied sources concerns ablation or other procedures, not ICD placement. No ICD-specific PONV-prevention strategy is established.
evidenceGaps: Adult ICD-specific criteria and protocol for selecting, conducting, and responding to defibrillation testing, including failed-test rescue steps.
ICD-specific postimplant device interrogation, imaging, lead/pocket surveillance, and activity-restriction guidance.
Procedure-specific guidance for identifying and managing lead displacement, pneumothorax, and other implant complications.
fluids: The supplied sources do not establish an ICD-specific fluid strategy; fluid guidance pertains to other procedures.
analgesia: The supplied sources do not establish an ICD-specific PONV prevention strategy.
corrections: Removed universal ETT/GA/paralysis and mandatory arterial-line requirements; anesthetic depth and monitoring are individualized.
Removed unsupported induction and maintenance drug combinations, including etomidate thresholds and vasopressor or epinephrine instructions.
Removed an asserted mandatory DFT workflow, 100% oxygen instruction, and external-defibrillator rescue sequence because the provided sources do not establish these as an ICD protocol.
Removed routine ACT testing, CXR, interrogation, and activity-restriction claims as unsupported by the supplied ICD-specific material.
Removed a fixed postoperative analgesic regimen and unsupported fluid-management recipe; the sources support anticipating S-ICD and pocket pain but do not establish a universal regimen.

reports.title: Implantable Loop Recorder (ILR) Placement
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as evidence. Removed the stated 10–15 minute duration, supine position, and minor procedure room/EP lab setup because the supplied ILR sources do not establish them.
Removed the proposed midazolam dose and specific lidocaine-with-epinephrine recipe; the ILR sources support usual local anesthesia and optional conscious sedation but do not give these regimens.
Corrected the claim that anticoagulation typically continues: available ILR evidence identifies bleeding diathesis as a relative contraindication but does not specify anticoagulant management.

Did not retain a routine PACU device-programming, wound-check, or acetaminophen protocol; the source supports device activation and general follow-up information but not those specific recovery prescriptions.
Placement landmarks differ between the clinical review and a device-specific case report. The draft avoids presenting a single rib-level landmark as universal.
No obstetric-specific ILR evidence was supplied. This draft is adult-focused and does not establish pregnancy-specific practice.
evidenceGaps: ILR-specific anesthesia guidance for patient positioning, airway planning, and monitoring when sedation is used beyond general ASA standards.
ILR-specific perioperative anticoagulant management and practical bleeding-management guidance.
ILR-specific recovery workflow, including wound assessment, device interrogation/programming, and discharge criteria.
ILR-specific analgesia and PONV guidance.
corrections: Removed unverified 10–15 minute procedure duration.
Removed unverified supine positioning and room assignment.
Removed midazolam dosing and the specific lidocaine-with-epinephrine regimen.
Removed the unsupported statement that anticoagulation does not need to be held; no general hold or continuation recommendation is made.
Removed unverified fluid management, acetaminophen plan, and routine PACU programming claims.
Qualified device migration as a single case-report hazard rather than a routine complication estimate.

reports.title: Lead Extraction (Transvenous)
reviewNotes: Base44 claims that general anaesthesia and TEE are mandatory for every extraction are overstated: the procedure-specific review describes GA as common, TOE monitoring for high-risk cases, and sedation as possible for low-risk cases when rapid conversion to GA is available.
The claim that ICU admission is standard is not supported: the principal review describes routine ward disposition after PACU for uncomplicated cases and higher-acuity care for complications.

The specified propofol–fentanyl–rocuronium regimen, mandatory pre-induction arterial line, universal cell saver/Level 1 infuser, TXA, and fixed vasopressor or reversal-drug readiness are not established as universal practice by the supplied extraction evidence. Avoid presenting them as protocol.

The statement that SVC injury causes exsanguination 'in seconds' is not supported by the sources. They describe potentially rapid collapse and emphasize urgent surgical management; avoid overstating a precise timeline.

The sources differ in emphasis: the BJA Education overview describes GA as common and sedation as an option for low-risk cases, while the three-case series used deep sedation and the later narrative review favors GA for specified higher-risk features. None establishes a universally preferred technique.

The 2025 narrative review is broad and lacks formal review methods; the 2022 case series has only three patients. Neither should override the procedure-specific overview or be treated as definitive practice guidance.
The draft is an evidence-grounded reference draft, not a patient-specific plan, institutional protocol, or clinically approved product.
evidenceGaps: Comparative adult evidence sufficient to select GA, deep sedation, and TOE use across clearly defined extraction-risk groups.
A locally validated, procedure-specific major-haemorrhage and rescue pathway covering surgical response, CPB readiness, and any SVC balloon strategy.
Extraction-specific evidence for PONV prevention and a detailed postoperative analgesia approach.
corrections: Removed the Base44 assertion that GA and TEE are mandatory for every case; source 0 allows sedation in low-risk cases and specifies TOE monitoring for high-risk cases.
Corrected 'ICU admission standard' to risk- and complication-dependent disposition; source 0 describes ward transfer after PACU for routine cases.
Removed unsupported fixed anaesthetic drugs, neuromuscular blockade, fluid regimen, TXA, cell-saver and Level 1 infuser requirements, and blanket vasopressor/reversal-drug claims.
Removed the claim that SVC tear causes exsanguination in seconds; the available sources support urgent recognition and surgical escalation, not that exact characterization.
Did not retain a universal venoplasty, temporary pacing, arterial-line, or central-access requirement; the sources describe planning and access choices that depend on patient and procedural factors.

reports.title: MitraClip / TEER (Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair)
reviewNotes: Base44’s claim that general anesthesia is mandatory is too absolute. The TEER review calls tracheal intubation typical and describes non-routine alternatives; the APSF article recommends GA with ETT for TEE-guided placement.

Base44’s TIVA-preferred wording is not established as a universal preference. The TEER review describes institutional maintenance with remifentanil plus either volatile anesthetic or propofol infusion.

The proposed fixed crystalloid volume, routine Foley, intermittent apnea, esophageal-temperature monitoring, and acetaminophen-plus-ketorolac plan are not supported as universal TEER practices by the supplied procedure-specific evidence.
An ACT value reported as an author or institutional target should not be presented as a universal target. Anticoagulation and ACT management require coordination with the procedural team.

The evidence base is chiefly narrative review and institutional practice, rather than TEER-specific comparative trials or formal anesthesia guidelines. Generic ASA standards inform monitoring and recovery, not procedure-specific management.

The supplied TEER review does not establish a universal recovery checklist covering routine rhythm, neurologic-status, or renal-function assessment; those claims were omitted from the overview bullet.
The TEER-specific sources do not address PONV prevention or treatment, so the analgesia bullet was removed rather than presenting a general recommendation as TEER-specific evidence.
evidenceGaps: TEER-specific comparative evidence establishing optimal anesthetic maintenance technique and airway strategy.
A TEER-specific analgesia and PONV strategy; the supplied procedure-specific source says pain is uncommon but provides no preferred regimen.
A broadly applicable TEER anticoagulation and antiplatelet protocol; the supplied review describes practice choices but does not establish one universal schedule.
analgesia: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a clinical-section recommendation.
corrections: Corrected “GA mandatory” to “GA with tracheal intubation is typical”; non-intubated approaches are reported but not routine.
Removed “TIVA preferred” as a universal claim; the cited review describes both volatile-agent and propofol-infusion maintenance in institutional practice.
Removed the fixed 1–2 L crystalloid plan; sources caution that fluid loading may worsen MR and that flushing fluid can be substantial.
Removed routine Foley catheterization; the TEER review states urinary catheterization is not routine.
Removed routine intermittent apnea and the proposed universal nasal RAE tube approach; these are not established by the supplied TEER sources.
Removed routine esophageal-temperature monitoring for TEER; the supplied temperature-probe discussion concerns AF ablation, not TEER.
Removed the fixed acetaminophen-plus-ketorolac plan and any implied PONV regimen; the TEER-specific sources do not establish these treatments.
Reframed ACT management as procedural-team coordinated rather than treating a review’s institutional target as universal.
Limited quantitative TOF guidance to cases in which neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.

reports.title: Pacemaker / ICD Generator Change
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its claims that generator change routinely replaces a depleted generator while retaining functional leads, commonly occurs at a stated battery-life interval, or may include specified upgrades are not established by the supplied sources.

Removed the unsourced default anesthetic recipe, drug doses, procedure duration, ETT indication, atropine preparation, named analgesic regimen, and arm restrictions. The sources do not validate these as generator-exchange standards.

External pacing pads and device-status review are supported as general CIED precautions; the specific instruction to have pads on before generator disconnection, and the asserted disconnect-related asystole interval, are not established in these sources.
The battery-life discussion is general preoperative pacemaker guidance, not a generator-replacement timing or urgency rule.

The anticoagulation trial summaries concern pacemaker/ICD surgery generally. They support recognizing pocket-hematoma risk, not a universal anticoagulant continuation or interruption plan for an individual exchange.
General postanesthesia standards support monitoring and recovery processes but do not supply generator-specific discharge criteria or wound/device instructions.

The supplied sources do not describe the generator-exchange sequence, generator-disconnect pacing contingency, generator-exchange-specific lead injury or infection management, or an analgesic regimen for generator exchange.
The general EP anesthesia discussion supports individualized planning but does not establish a default anesthetic approach specifically for generator exchange.
evidenceGaps: Generator-exchange-specific operative sequence, indications and urgency criteria, including how to distinguish generator-only exchange from lead revision or upgrade.
Exchange-specific management of pacing during generator disconnection and lead manipulation, including the frequency and duration of any loss of pacing.
Procedure-specific anesthetic technique, analgesia, infection-prevention approach, wound care, device interrogation/programming workflow, and discharge instructions.
intraop: No supplied source describes the generator-disconnect phase or a generator-exchange pacing contingency.
complications: The supplied sources do not establish generator-exchange-specific lead injury risks, generator-disconnect asystole frequency, or infection-management guidance.
corrections: Removed the claim that functional leads are routinely retained and that generator exchange is routinely performed at a particular battery-life interval; neither is established by the fetched evidence.
Removed upgrade examples as a routine feature of generator exchange; the supplied sources do not provide exchange or upgrade criteria.
Removed the unverified MAC/local-anesthetic regimen, natural-airway default, conditional ETT recommendation, induction drug doses, and stated procedure duration.

Removed generator-disconnect-specific asystole claims and the instruction to have atropine drawn; the sources support assessing pacemaker dependence and having external pacing capability, but not these specific claims.
Removed the stated routine analgesic drugs and postoperative arm restrictions; these are not supported for generator exchange by the supplied sources.
Replaced a single anticoagulation recipe with a caution that device-surgery evidence identifies pocket-hematoma risk and does not establish an individualized exchange plan.

reports.title: PCI with Hemodynamic Support (High-Risk PCI)
reviewNotes: The Base44 case includes specific induction and maintenance drug recipes, propofol avoidance thresholds, vasopressor instructions, invasive monitoring requirements, access assumptions, MCS timing claims, and postoperative recommendations that are not established by the supplied high-risk PCI evidence. They have not been adopted as routine guidance.
The VA-ECMO registry describes selected elective cases and local practice; its support and anesthesia patterns should not be generalized to Impella-, IABP-, or ECMO-supported PCI overall.
The general catheterization anesthesia review dates to 2014. Its PCI discussion is broad and does not resolve management of contemporary planned MCS-supported PCI.
Basic ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards support general monitoring and recovery principles, but do not supply procedure-specific high-risk PCI targets or protocols.
The supplied review describes PCI sedation and selected reasons for anesthesia involvement, but does not provide a dedicated high-risk PCI anesthetic protocol.
evidenceGaps: Comparative adult evidence or current procedure-specific guidance on selection and timing of Impella, IABP, and VA-ECMO for high-risk PCI.
High-risk PCI-specific anticoagulation and ACT protocols by support device and procedural context.
High-risk PCI-specific anesthetic and airway strategy, including criteria for planned general anesthesia, extubation, and postoperative ventilation.
Procedure-specific hemodynamic targets and fluid, bleeding, and transfusion protocols for supported PCI.
corrections: Removed the assertion that Impella or other MCS must always be running before PCI; the supplied registry does not establish a universal timing rule.

Removed the Base44 drug-dose recipes and blanket recommendations to avoid propofol or maintain continuous vasopressor infusions; the provided sources do not support these as universal high-risk PCI practice.

Removed routine requirements for pre-induction arterial line, PA catheter/CVP, Foley catheter, bilateral femoral access, ECMO perfusionist, or cardiac-surgery backup in every case; these are not established across the applicable sources.
Removed claims of universal ICU admission, planned intubation, or cath-lab extubation; the registry describes variable anesthesia and selected ICU admissions but provides no extubation protocol.
Corrected the implication that the supplied sources substantiate a specific high-risk PCI analgesia, PONV, fluid, or blood-management plan; these areas are not adequately described.

reports.title: Permanent Pacemaker Implantation
reviewNotes: This is an evidence-limited reference draft, not a patient-specific anesthetic plan or a clinically approved protocol.

The two most directly relevant sources are a small observational anesthesia study and a broad narrative EP review. Their findings differ in scope and should not be treated as a single validated pacemaker pathway.
The review’s reported tamponade incidence range combines permanent pacemaker and ICD implantation and is broad; it is not a precise individual risk estimate.

The anticoagulation evidence supports rejecting routine heparin bridging as an assumed default for warfarin-treated device patients, but does not supply one plan for every anticoagulant or clinical circumstance.
The regional-block case report is not a basis for routine practice. Its reported case and author experience are insufficient to establish comparative safety or efficacy.

The supplied sources do not specify pacemaker-specific postprocedure imaging, device interrogation or programming, wound instructions, or activity restrictions. The reported follow-up details come from a small, single-center observational study and should not be treated as a universal protocol.
evidenceGaps: Pacemaker-specific management of device programming, pacemaker dependence, and temporary pacing during implantation.
Procedure-specific guidance for lead displacement or perforation recognition and management beyond general tamponade assessment.
Pacemaker-specific postimplant imaging, device interrogation/programming, wound care, and activity restrictions.
Implant-specific airway and sedation comparisons, positioning recommendations, and monitoring beyond general anesthesia standards.
Pacemaker-specific postoperative analgesia and PONV guidance.
corrections: Removed the supplied fixed midazolam, fentanyl, and propofol doses and the prescribed MAC induction/maintenance recipe; the available implant study does not report an IV regimen.

Removed the asserted routine supine position, shoulder roll, contralateral head turn, natural airway, and routine ETT indications; the procedure-specific study does not report positioning or airway management.

Removed claims that lead manipulation predictably causes PVCs, VT, or VF, and that transcutaneous pacing pads, atropine, or epinephrine must be available in every case; these claims are not supported by the supplied pacemaker sources.

Removed the claims that postprocedure chest radiography is mandatory, that an arm sling and six-week movement restrictions are routine, and that specific wound instructions are established; the supplied sources do not substantiate them.
Removed the prescribed acetaminophen/ketorolac plan and subclavian air-embolism positioning advice; no applicable pacemaker-specific evidence was provided.

Corrected the blanket heparin-bridging implication: the cited device-surgery trial found fewer clinically significant pocket hematomas with continued warfarin than with heparin bridging, while DOAC continuation was not superior to interruption.

reports.title: SVT Ablation (AVNRT / AVRT)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. Its specific dexmedetomidine, midazolam, fentanyl, and propofol regimens and doses were not carried forward as recommendations.

Base44 claims that dexmedetomidine is ideal, that propofol should be avoided during induction, and that deeper sedation should be used during ablation energy delivery are not established as universal SVT practice by the supplied evidence.

Base44-specific claims about para-Hisian ablation, pacemaker capability in the room, phrenic-nerve pacing during cryoablation, routine fluids, heparin, groin pressure, and postoperative analgesics are not adopted as SVT standards here; the supplied sources do not establish those details for this case.

The sources differ in emphasis on general anesthesia versus moderate sedation. The draft preserves that uncertainty and prioritizes case-specific coordination rather than selecting an unsupported universal technique.
The supplied sources are mainly narrative reviews with varying evidence quality; the ASA sources provide general monitoring and recovery standards, not an SVT-specific anesthetic protocol.
The supplied sources do not specify an SVT-specific analgesic dosing regimen or a PONV-prevention strategy.
evidenceGaps: AVNRT- and AVRT-specific procedural workflow and any subtype-specific anesthesia implications.
SVT-specific medication reconciliation and antiarrhythmic medication-hold instructions.
SVT-specific anticoagulation, ACT, access management, and postprocedure rhythm-monitoring or discharge criteria.
corrections: Removed Base44's fixed sedation and analgesic doses and its characterization of dexmedetomidine as universally ideal.
Removed the blanket instruction to avoid propofol during arrhythmia induction; the sources describe possible effects but do not support a universal prohibition.
Removed Base44's implied standard timing for deeper sedation during energy delivery.
Removed unsupported routine fluid volumes, blanket heparin instruction, and universal postoperative pain-medication choices.
Did not present para-Hisian AV-block precautions or cryoablation phrenic-nerve pacing as established SVT-specific standards from the supplied sources.

reports.title: TAVR (Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified. The claim that MAC is now preferred at most centers and improves hemodynamics is not established by these sources; GA remains common in the APSF review, while MAC comparisons are limited and potentially confounded.

The supplied evidence does not support a universal arterial-line mandate, MAC sedative recipe, fixed fluid volume, fixed temporary-pacing-wire duration, or a stated 10–20% permanent-pacemaker rate. These have not been carried forward as general rules.

The source reports higher AV-block association with CoreValve and increased pacing risk with specified baseline conduction abnormalities, but does not establish that every patient needs a permanent pacemaker or a fixed monitoring interval.

The 2016 review's procedural and anesthetic discussion is older; the APSF review gives no publication/update date in the supplied content. Local contemporary TAVR pathways and the heart-team plan remain important.
The review’s description of pain-control drug classes is not a prescribing recommendation for an individual patient; renal function and bleeding risk may affect drug selection.
evidenceGaps: Contemporary, procedure-specific guidance or randomized evidence resolving comparative outcomes and selection criteria for MAC versus GA in current TAVR practice.

Patient-specific assessment is unavailable, including AS severity and symptoms, ventricular function, renal function, baseline conduction, vascular anatomy, planned valve/access route, and institutional rescue capability.
The supplied sources do not define a detailed postoperative conduction-monitoring schedule or discharge criteria; these should follow the procedural team's current pathway.
corrections: Removed the Base44 assertion that MAC is preferred at most centers and is associated with better hemodynamics; the evidence supports selected use, not a universal preference or causal advantage.
Removed fixed dexmedetomidine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, and neuromuscular-blocker recipes and all numerical drug dosing.
Corrected the claim that an arterial line is mandatory: the review describes invasive monitoring, but the supplied sources do not state a universal arterial-line requirement for every TAVR case.

Removed the fixed 500–1500 mL crystalloid amount and blanket claims about avoiding all fluid; sources instead describe maintaining perfusion, renal-protective hydration, and limiting contrast as appropriate.
Removed the 10–20% permanent-pacemaker rate and the fixed 24–48-hour pacing-wire retention instruction because those claims are not supported by the supplied sources.
Did not carry forward ketorolac as a routine analgesic or PONV plan; the source supports only broad analgesic classes and does not provide a TAVR-specific PONV regimen.

reports.title: TEE-Guided Cardioversion
reviewNotes: The Base44 case fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not establish mandatory NPO language, left-lateral positioning, return to supine, a specific propofol/fentanyl regimen, dexmedetomidine as ideal, or expected apnea with a shock bolus.

The sources describe lidocaine topicalization as an option and note historical benzocaine use with methemoglobinemia concern; they do not support presenting benzocaine as routine or specifying a universal topical anesthetic.
The claim that LAA thrombus automatically cancels cardioversion is not explicitly stated in the supplied evidence. The draft instead calls for pausing and cardiology reassessment.
The asserted gag-reflex recovery interval, prohibition on oral intake until a fixed time, ice chips, throat pain treatment, and aspiration protocol are not established in the supplied sources.
The cardioversion review gives anesthetic drug examples and emergency medications, but these are not reproduced as recommended dosing or as a universal medication protocol.

The source set is educational/review material plus general ASA standards. The TEE/DCCV-specific evidence is limited, and the sources do not establish one preferred sedation depth or airway technique for all adults.
The supplied sources do not specify positioning for these procedures or a procedure-specific postoperative analgesia/PONV regimen for cardioversion or diagnostic TEE.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific adult protocol for patient positioning and transitions during the combined TEE and cardioversion workflow is not provided.
TEE-specific recovery criteria after pharyngeal topicalization, including safe timing for oral intake, are not provided.
setup: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a procedural positioning recommendation.
analgesia: Retains the source limitation as evidence context rather than presenting an unsupported regimen or clinical instruction.
corrections: Removed unsupported Base44 fasting/NPO assertion; the supplied sources do not state a TEE-cardioversion fasting protocol.
Removed unsupported default left-lateral position and supine repositioning instruction; source material explicitly lacks a procedure-specific positioning protocol.
Removed unverified drug doses, infusion rates, and claims that dexmedetomidine is ideal or that apnea is expected with a particular shock bolus.
Removed fixed gag-reflex/oral-intake timing and specific throat-discomfort treatment because these are not supported by the supplied evidence.
Replaced categorical cancellation for LAA thrombus with cardiology reassessment because the sources establish thrombus assessment but do not explicitly state a management disposition.
Did not impose a universal fluid volume, invasive line, airway device, or anesthetic technique.

reports.title: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) Ablation
reviewNotes: Base44 states that an endotracheal tube is required, an arterial line is mandatory before induction in all cases, and ICU admission is standard for complex VT ablation. The supplied sources do not support these as universal requirements; they describe choices based on case characteristics, and the cohort transferred patients according to clinical status.

Base44’s specific induction and maintenance recipes, EF-based propofol avoidance, fixed MAP target, routine MCS thresholds or pre-placement, and postoperative ketorolac plan are not established as universal VT-ablation guidance by the supplied sources. Drug doses and fixed physiologic thresholds were therefore not carried forward.
