Source 1 reports a deep-sedation cohort, not a comparison of deep sedation with general anesthesia; its local protocol and observed outcomes should not be converted into routine recommendations.
Source 3 is a narrative EP anesthesia review with heterogeneous evidence. Its general recommendations are used only when relevant to VT ablation, not as a substitute for a VT-specific guideline.

No supplied source establishes a universal position, airway device, anesthetic recipe, fluid quantity, blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, analgesic regimen, or postoperative destination for every VT ablation.
The supplied VT-specific sources do not state a routine patient position.

The sources do not provide a VT-specific protocol for device review or antiarrhythmic-drug interruption. The source material supplied for this bullet also does not support the draft’s phrenic-nerve injury or stroke statements as written.
evidenceGaps: Adult VT-ablation-specific society guidance or a validated protocol for anesthetic technique selection, airway strategy, and extubation criteria was not supplied.
VT-specific evidence for routine analgesia and PONV prevention was not supplied.
setup: The supplied VT-specific sources do not specify a routine patient position.
corrections: Removed the claim that endotracheal intubation is required for every VT ablation; sources describe both general anesthesia and monitored anesthesia care.
Changed the claim that arterial-line monitoring is mandatory before induction in every case to a case-sensitive recommendation supported by the EP review.
Removed the claim that ICU admission is standard; disposition is described as dependent on respiratory status, hemodynamic stability, and catecholamine requirement.

Removed fixed anesthetic drug choices and doses, EF-based propofol prohibition, fixed MAP threshold, routine MCS EF threshold, and routine pre-placement assertions because the supplied evidence does not establish them as universal practice.
Removed the unsupported specific postoperative analgesic regimen and did not infer a PONV protocol.
Did not specify supine positioning because the VT sources do not report a routine position.

reports.title: Watchman / Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion (LAAO)
reviewNotes: The supplied fields assert that GA is mandatory, ETT is required, TIVA is preferred, and arterial-line monitoring is routine. These are not established as universal LAAO requirements by the sources; the evidence includes ETT, SGA, and selected conscious-sedation approaches.

The supplied fields specify an ACT range and a postimplant antithrombotic regimen. Source descriptions vary in ACT targets, and the sources do not establish one universal anticoagulation or postimplant medication plan; defer to the procedural protocol and patient-specific prescribing team.

The supplied fields list routine Foley use, a fixed crystalloid volume, specific analgesics, and immediate availability of pericardiocentesis supplies. These details are not supported as universal requirements by the provided LAAO-specific evidence.

The source set includes a small retrospective airway comparison, a five-patient feasibility series, and a narrative review. None establishes that a particular anesthetic or discharge pathway is appropriate for every patient.
The supplied air-embolism discussion concerns AF ablation and does not specifically establish air entry as an LAAO acute concern, so that claim was omitted.
evidenceGaps: Prospective comparative evidence and validated criteria for selecting ETT, SGA, or conscious sedation in adult TEE-guided LAAO.
A validated, broadly applicable post-LAAO recovery and same-day-discharge pathway, including standardized criteria for surveillance imaging and postimplant antithrombotic management.
corrections: Removed the Base44 assertion that general anesthesia is mandatory and that an ETT is required; sources describe alternatives and do not establish a universal airway technique.
Removed the assertion that TIVA is preferred or uniquely provides stable conditions; supplied evidence does not establish that as a universal LAAO recommendation.
Removed routine arterial-line and Foley requirements because the procedure-specific study reports standard ASA monitors and does not establish either as routine.
Removed fixed crystalloid volume and routine acetaminophen/ketorolac claims; the Watchman comparison does not report a fluid regimen or establish a postoperative analgesic protocol.
Reframed ACT and postimplant antithrombotic details as procedural-team decisions because source targets and descriptions vary and do not establish one universal regimen.

reports.title: Abscess Incision and Drainage (I&D)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. The stated propofol, fentanyl, ketamine, and maintenance recipes are not established by the supplied sources; the cutaneous review only reports that various agents appeared in emergency-department studies without comparative recommendations or specified regimens.

The suggested sub-dissociative ketamine dose is unsupported by the provided evidence and was omitted. The recommendation to consider spinal anesthesia for painful perianal lithotomy cases is also not established in these sources.

The Base44 claim that rapid recovery is expected, and its specific wound-care/antibiotic-plan framing, are not established as universal anesthesia or postoperative protocols. Antibiotic decisions in the anorectal source are condition-specific, not a general anesthesia plan.

The cutaneous review and anorectal review differ on packing: the former describes variable expert practice and insufficient evidence, while the latter advises against routine anorectal packing except for hemostasis. The anorectal-specific recommendation is retained for anorectal cases; neither supports universal packing.
The supplied ASA monitoring and PACU standards support general monitoring and recovery statements, but not the Base44 procedure-specific room, anesthetic, or emergence claims.
evidenceGaps: Comparative adult anesthesia techniques and airway strategies for deep, extensive, or otherwise complex abscess drainage are not established by the supplied procedure-specific sources.
Procedure-specific evidence for anesthetic drug selection, PONV management, and emergence planning is not provided.
corrections: Removed the Base44 agent and infusion recipes, including the ketamine dose; the sources do not validate those as routine regimens.
Removed the unsupported blanket implication that MAC/sedation is usual for most cases or that spinal/general anesthesia is specifically indicated for perianal lithotomy.
Did not carry forward a universal minimal-fluid claim, expected rapid recovery, or routine antibiotics as established practice; the provided sources do not support those universal statements.
Qualified local anesthesia as generally sufficient only for the superficial cutaneous population specified in the review, and separated anorectal guidance from general soft-tissue abscess care.

reports.title: Appendectomy (Laparoscopic/Open)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields are unverified. They are not used as clinical evidence; case-specific medication doses and fixed fluid amounts were excluded.
The claim that an ETT is required for every laparoscopic case was softened: the educational review calls it preferred, not universally mandatory.
The supplied evidence does not support treating perforation alone as an automatic full-stomach designation or a universal indication for RSI. No RSI rule is asserted here.

The fields’ routine laboratory list, pregnancy testing, cefoxitin choice, fixed induction regimen, PONV drug combination, analgesic regimen, and 500–1000 mL fluid amount were not substantiated by the fetched sources and are not presented as recommendations.
The neuraxial appendectomy evidence is limited to selected study populations and should not be generalized to complicated appendicitis, obesity, or patients with significant comorbidity.
The 2026 open-appendectomy cohort is nonrandomized, single-center, and small; its site protocols and comparative outcomes are not treated as standards.

The general laparoscopic review is educational rather than appendectomy-specific, and the ASA sources address general monitoring, preanesthesia, postanesthesia, or neuromuscular-blockade practice rather than appendicitis-specific care.
evidenceGaps: Appendicitis-specific perioperative management for perforation, peritonitis, or sepsis, including how aspiration risk and antimicrobial decisions should be assessed and coordinated, is not established by the supplied sources.
corrections: Removed the unverified assertion that perforated appendicitis inherently means full stomach and requires RSI.
Removed the unverified claim that an ETT is required in every laparoscopic appendectomy; the available review describes it as preferred.
Removed unsupported routine laboratory requirements, pregnancy-testing instructions, and cefoxitin selection.
Removed Base44 induction and maintenance drug doses, reversal assumptions, and specific analgesic and antiemetic recipes.
Removed the fixed 500–1000 mL crystalloid amount and avoided implying a universal fluid total.
Recast laparoscopic and open anesthetic approaches as context-dependent; the available neuraxial studies do not establish a universal alternative to general anesthesia.

reports.title: Bowel Resection (Small / Large)
reviewNotes: The procedure-specific foundation is an older colorectal clinical review and a later elective rectal/pelvic ERAS review; neither establishes a comprehensive adult small-bowel-resection anesthetic protocol.
The sources differ on bowel preparation for rectal resection with a diverting stoma. This draft preserves the stated exception and uncertainty rather than presenting routine preparation as universal.

The colorectal review reports mixed comparative anesthetic findings and insufficient evidence for a specific laparoscopic postoperative analgesic method. No preferred general anesthetic agent is asserted.
ASA monitoring, postanesthesia-care, and neuromuscular-blockade sources provide general standards, not procedure-specific setup, airway, fluid, or recovery algorithms.
The review's positioning injury reports are retained as a hazard signal, not evidence of incidence or a standardized prevention protocol.
The supplied procedure-specific review evidence is colorectal-focused and does not establish small-bowel-specific recommendations.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific adult small-bowel resection evidence, including how recommendations differ from colorectal surgery.
A current, procedure-specific source for airway and ventilation strategy, including how obstruction-related aspiration risk should modify technique.
Procedure- and patient-specific guidance for vascular access and blood preparation; the available sources do not establish universal requirements.
A current detailed protocol for managing suspected anastomotic leak, postoperative ileus, or major intraoperative contamination.
corrections: Removed the Base44-specific cefoxitin recommendation; the colorectal review supports aerobic and anaerobic antimicrobial prophylaxis but does not establish cefoxitin as the required agent.
Removed routine ETT and RSI assertions. The supplied procedure-specific sources do not specify an airway device or universal induction technique.
Removed the fixed 1–3 L crystalloid estimate and blood-management recipe; sources instead describe individualized fluid management and provide no fixed fluid formula or transfusion threshold.
Removed claims that epidural or TAP block universally speeds recovery or significantly reduces opioid needs. Evidence is approach-dependent, and the TAP evidence is described as limited.

Removed any implication that ketorolac or another NSAID is appropriate for every anastomosis; the colorectal review notes a COX-2/anastomotic-leak concern and does not establish universal suitability.
Removed fixed room setup, routine arterial-line, and universal ICU disposition claims; the available sources do not support them as requirements for every case.

reports.title: Breast Biopsy / Lumpectomy / Mastectomy
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. Several specific recommendations in them are not supported by the fetched sources.

The breast sources support procedural details for image-guided biopsy and localization, but explicitly state they are not anesthesia references; their complication data should not be generalized to lumpectomy, mastectomy, or reconstruction.
ASA sources support applicable general anesthesia monitoring, postanesthesia care, and neuromuscular-blockade standards, not breast-specific airway, anesthetic, fluid, or analgesic choices.
Sources 2 and 3 address gastrointestinal ERAS and do not substantiate breast-surgery management. Source 7 is relevant only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.
The cited procedural sources concern percutaneous image-guided breast biopsy; they do not provide an analgesic regimen or anesthesia protocol for lumpectomy or mastectomy.
evidenceGaps: Breast-surgery-specific anesthetic technique and airway management for lumpectomy, mastectomy, and reconstruction.
Breast-surgery-specific analgesia, regional-block evidence, and PONV prevention strategy.
Operative blood-loss, fluid-management, and complication-management guidance for excisional breast surgery and reconstruction.
corrections: Removed the Base44 LMA-for-simple-case and ETT-for-complex-case recommendations: the provided breast sources do not establish an airway-device algorithm.
Removed the Base44 induction, maintenance, and PONV drug recipes, including the asserted TIVA benefit for this case: the supplied sources do not support these breast-surgery recommendations.
Removed the Base44 PECS/serratus block and multimodal analgesia claims: no supplied source establishes those interventions for this case.
Removed the Base44 ipsilateral-arm IV/BP restriction and sentinel-node injection allergy assertions: these are not supported by the supplied sources.
Removed the Base44 positioning, warming, fluid-volume, and blood-loss expectations for operative breast surgery: the available evidence does not establish them.
Qualified biopsy complication findings as percutaneous-procedure evidence rather than applying their rates to lumpectomy or mastectomy.

reports.title: Diagnostic Laparoscopy / Lysis of Adhesions
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified. The supplied evidence does not establish prior abdominal surgery as a quantified conversion risk, mandatory RSI for obstruction, routine Foley use, a fixed crystalloid volume, or a universal extubation endpoint based on reflexes.
The source material does not validate the Base44 induction and maintenance drug recipe, specific analgesic combination, or fixed fluid plan as standards for this case.

The diagnostic gynecologic series used face-mask anesthesia in a selected elective population and excluded emergency cases and known recent food intake; its local technique must not be promoted as routine practice.

General laparoscopic physiology and airway considerations are useful but do not supply adhesiolysis-specific evidence or a universal technique. No source supports a blanket conversion, aspiration, or safety conclusion.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific guidance for adhesiolysis, including bowel-injury recognition, conversion considerations, and anesthetic implications of anticipated complex dissection.

Evidence-based assessment and airway strategy for suspected bowel obstruction or full stomach in this procedural context; the available sources do not establish the Base44 claim that RSI is mandatory.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that RSI is mandatory whenever bowel obstruction is the indication; no supplied applicable guideline supports this absolute.
Removed the fixed 500–1000 mL crystalloid recommendation; available review favors individualized, goal-directed fluid administration and the case series reports no fluid volume.
Removed the claim that prior abdominal surgery necessarily increases conversion risk; the supplied sources do not substantiate it for this case.
Removed universal Foley, drug regimen, and fixed emergence instructions as unsupported by the provided evidence.
Qualified the ETT statement: the general laparoscopic reference prefers ETT for ventilatory support, but the available sources do not establish a uniform airway requirement for every diagnostic case.

reports.title: Feeding Tube Placement (PEG / J-tube)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified. Its specific MAC/propofol/fentanyl plan, RSI or ETT triggers, supine positioning as a universal rule, rapid recovery claim, acetaminophen recommendation, and topical pharyngeal anesthetic pearl are not established by the supplied sources.

The claim that aspiration risk in neurologically impaired patients should routinely trigger ETT is not supported as a procedure-specific recommendation. The available sources identify aspiration risk but do not specify airway management.
The source-supported laparoscopy position is technique-specific; it should not be generalized to radiologic placement, PEG, or every jejunostomy.
The radiologic review favors its approach over PEG on several reported outcomes, but this does not establish a universal approach preference for every patient or procedure.
General ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards support monitoring requirements; they do not supply a feeding-tube-specific anesthetic plan.
evidenceGaps: Procedure- and patient-specific airway and anesthetic technique guidance across PEG, radiologic gastrostomy, and surgical or endoscopic jejunostomy.
Feeding-tube-specific anesthetic fluid, perfusion, and blood-loss management guidance.
corrections: Removed propofol, fentanyl, midazolam, lidocaine, and acetaminophen as recommended regimens because the supplied evidence does not establish them for this case.
Removed universal MAC, RSI, ETT, and supine-positioning instructions; the sources either do not specify these or describe positioning only for a particular laparoscopic approach.

Removed the Base44 transillumination-failure and colon-interposition claims as routine anesthesia guidance; the supplied material describes transillumination as part of direct endoscopic jejunostomy but does not establish these as routine findings.
Reframed tube malposition and aspiration as procedural and recovery concerns supported by the feeding-tube reviews, without implying a specific anesthetic response.

reports.title: Femoral Hernia Repair
reviewNotes: The Base44 claim that femoral hernias have a higher incarceration risk than inguinal hernias is not supported by the supplied sources; the sources mention strangulation and difficult reduction but provide no comparative rate.

Base44's routine ETT, RSI escalation, propofol/fentanyl recipe, succinylcholine or rocuronium choices, volatile maintenance, crystalloid total, awake-extubation direction, and specific analgesic recipe are not established by the femoral-specific evidence. They are not reproduced as recommendations.

The reported open anesthetic is internally inconsistent across the study: methods specify continuous epidural block, while discussion describes local anesthesia. The draft preserves this discrepancy rather than resolving it by assumption.
The study's observed lower pain and foreign-body sensation with TAPP than UHS is limited to its small retrospective comparison and does not establish a universal open-versus-laparoscopic outcome.
General laparoscopic recommendations and ASA standards are scoped to their stated contexts; they do not validate every case-specific claim or supply a femoral-hernia-specific protocol.
evidenceGaps: Femoral-hernia-specific comparative evidence to guide anesthetic approach selection, including open versus laparoscopic repair across broader adult populations.
A validated femoral-hernia-specific preoperative protocol for identifying bowel compromise and its anesthetic implications.
Femoral-repair-specific evidence for airway strategy in open cases, analgesic regimen, and postoperative recovery beyond general postanesthesia standards.
corrections: Removed the unsupported claim that femoral hernias have a higher incarceration rate than inguinal hernias; no comparative rate is supplied.
Removed unsupported routine CBC/BMP testing, aspiration precautions, and universal RSI escalation for strangulation or incarceration.
Removed drug selection and doses, maintenance-agent directions, and the fixed crystalloid volume because the supplied femoral sources do not establish these as practice recommendations.
Removed the claim that spinal anesthesia is specifically acceptable as a general rule; the femoral study describes continuous epidural block in its methods and local anesthesia in its discussion.
Removed routine extubation, bowel-resection fluid/blood requirements, and specific PACU concerns as femoral-specific directives because the supplied sources do not substantiate them.

reports.title: Hiatal Hernia Repair / Nissen Fundoplication
reviewNotes: Base44 content is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its RSI mandate, specified induction drugs/doses, sodium citrate/H2-blocker recipe, fixed 8.0 ETT, mandatory triple PONV prophylaxis, deep extubation or IV lidocaine recipe, fixed fluid total, and claim that vomiting will disrupt the wrap are not established by the supplied sources.

Positioning evidence conflicts: the hiatal repair technical letter describes 30-degree Trendelenburg, while the general laparoscopic review says reverse Trendelenburg is often used for upper GI procedures. Do not silently resolve this conflict as a case-specific rule.

The claim that smooth emergence is critical to avoid tearing the repair, and that dysphagia should be expected for a fixed 4–6 weeks, is not established by the fetched evidence. The sources describe common early dysphagia and provide no emergence protocol.

Source 0 is a brief technical letter and source 1 an educational review; neither provides comprehensive anesthesia guidance. The general laparoscopy review (source 8) is broader than this operation. ASA standards and the APSF summary apply within their stated monitoring, recovery and neuromuscular-blockade scopes, not as a procedure-specific anesthetic recipe.
This is an adult-oriented reference draft, but the supplied procedure sources do not define an adult-only study population. The provided evidence does not support pregnancy-specific management.
The supplied hiatal hernia source does not detail how positioning alters ventilation or hemodynamics; those broad claims were omitted.
evidenceGaps: Case-specific aspiration-risk assessment and airway/RSI strategy for hiatal hernia repair are not established by the supplied sources.
Case-specific positioning preference and emergence/extubation strategy are unresolved in the supplied evidence.
corrections: Removed the unsubstantiated universal RSI requirement and specific induction/pretreatment drug recipes; general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation is supported, but the sources do not specify RSI.
Removed the fixed ETT size, fixed crystalloid volume, and mandatory triple antiemetic regimen; the sources support individualized care and PONV prophylaxis, not those universal prescriptions.
Removed deep extubation and lidocaine as prescribed techniques; the procedure-specific sources provide no emergence protocol.
Corrected the claim that vomiting is established to disrupt the wrap: sources report impaired ability to vomit after Nissen but do not establish that vomiting disrupts the repair.
Replaced a fixed 4–6 week dysphagia expectation with source-supported descriptions of common early, usually transient dysphagia and variable recovery.

reports.title: Inguinal Hernia Repair (Open/Laparoscopic/Robotic)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as clinical evidence. Its claim that laparoscopic/robotic repair requires an ETT is too categorical: the general laparoscopic review prefers an ETT, while the hernia-specific review does not specify an airway device.

The Base44 RSI/full-stomach assertion for incarcerated or strangulated hernia is not established by the supplied sources. Preserve the risk as a preoperative concern for individualized assessment rather than a universal induction instruction.
The Base44 spinal recipe, induction drug doses, short-case crystalloid volume, and drug-specific postoperative plan are unsupported by these sources and were omitted.
The 2011 hernia review reports comparative anesthesia outcomes but is older, narrative, and not anesthesia-focused; its claims do not establish a complete contemporary anesthetic protocol.

The general laparoscopic/robotic review is relevant to insufflation physiology but is not procedure-specific. Its general recommendations are presented as considerations, not universal hernia targets.
Local anesthesia is supported for open repair; this does not establish that spinal anesthesia is universally preferable or that every open repair should avoid airway management.
The source set does not justify a universal fluid total, transfusion threshold, fixed duration, mandatory arterial line, or routine central access; these have not been treated as evidence gaps.
evidenceGaps: Case-specific evidence for aspiration-risk assessment and airway/induction strategy in incarcerated or strangulated hernia.
Procedure-specific evidence for anesthetic choice and airway management in individual open repairs beyond the comparative options described in the review.
A hernia-specific emergence, discharge, and postoperative respiratory-care protocol.
corrections: Removed the unsupported categorical claim that ETT is required for every laparoscopic or robotic repair; retained the general-review preference for ETT while noting the hernia review does not specify a device.
Removed the unsupported universal RSI/full-stomach instruction for incarcerated or strangulated hernia.
Removed Base44 induction and spinal drug doses, fixed crystalloid volume, and specific postoperative medication recipe.
Removed the unsubstantiated claim that mesh placement may increase postoperative pain; the provided sources do not support that specific statement.

Qualified the claim that laparoscopic/robotic approaches are preferred for all bilateral or recurrent hernias; approach selection depends on patient and surgical factors, and recurrence after prior minimally invasive repair is generally described as favoring open repair.

reports.title: Lower Extremity Amputation (Toe / Foot / BKA / AKA)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its claims that spinal anesthesia is preferred, reduces phantom limb pain, and should use specified intrathecal drug doses are not established by these sources.

Removed unsupported Base44 specifics including routine propofol sedation, ETT/LMA selection, Foley use, warming, arterial-line indications, crystalloid totals, blood availability rules, and emergence instructions.

The supplied evidence supports considering regional analgesia but does not justify blanket ketamine or nerve-block prevention claims for phantom limb pain, or a universal multimodal medication recipe.

Regional-anesthesia outcome comparisons are largely observational and sometimes pool neuraxial and peripheral techniques; findings should not be converted into a universal anesthesia preference or mortality claim.
No source establishes a patient-specific anesthetic plan. The draft is an evidence-grounded reference draft and is not patient-specific or clinically approved.

The supplied procedure-specific sources do not establish whether arterial or Foley catheter placement, or other additional access or monitoring, is routine; determine those needs from the patient and operative context.
evidenceGaps: Adult, procedure-specific guidance for selecting among general, neuraxial, and peripheral regional anesthesia in relation to amputation level and patient-specific contraindications.
Detailed airway and ventilation strategy for this procedure and patient population.
Procedure-specific guidance on anticoagulant/antiplatelet management and regional-anesthesia eligibility.
setup: This is a limitation of the source, not a procedure-specific clinical recommendation about whether additional access or monitoring is routine.
corrections: Corrected the claim that spinal anesthesia is preferred for all amputations: the available chapter lists general or regional anesthesia and advises case-by-case selection.
Removed specified spinal bupivacaine and intrathecal fentanyl doses; no supplied applicable source supports those recipes.

Removed claims that spinal anesthesia reduces phantom limb pain; the sources discuss regional analgesia and phantom pain prevention but do not establish that spinal anesthesia has this specific effect.
Removed routine propofol infusion, volatile-agent maintenance, and ETT/LMA plan because the sources do not prescribe them.
Removed routine Foley, warming, arterial-line, fluid-volume, and blood-availability instructions because those claims are unsupported by the supplied procedure-specific evidence.
Reframed ketamine, nerve blocks, and multimodal analgesia as evidence-described considerations rather than guaranteed or mandatory phantom-pain prevention.

reports.title: Perforated Viscus Repair
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. Removed or qualified its asserted mandatory RSI, ketamine as the preferred induction agent, specific induction doses, and the claim that patients can arrest on induction; the supplied sources support aspiration risk and hemodynamic-stability considerations, not those universal claims.

Did not carry forward unsupported claims for a required supine position, suction/rapid-infuser setup, pre-induction arterial line, CVP monitoring, aggressive crystalloid totals, volatile-MAC reduction, ICU intubation, or a specified opioid infusion.

The perforation-specific letter challenges a hemoglobin target near 11 g/dL. The emergency-laparotomy consensus supports restrictive transfusion with individualized exceptions; this draft avoids a numeric threshold and does not present the letter as a full protocol.
Antibiotic timing is drawn from the emergency-laparotomy guideline; specific drug selection and duration remain subject to local or national guidance and operative findings.
The sources do not support declaring one operative approach, anesthetic technique, or postoperative destination appropriate for every perforation case.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not provide a complete adult perforation-specific preoperative optimization and resuscitation pathway, including case-specific assessment of evolving shock and organ dysfunction.
The sources do not establish case-specific selection of induction agent or a detailed anesthetic plan for particular perforation etiologies and degrees of physiologic compromise.

The sources provide antibiotic timing and refer drug choice to local or national guidance, but do not supply a perforation-specific antimicrobial regimen tailored to microbiology, contamination, or source control.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that RSI is mandatory for every patient; retained the guideline-supported aspiration-risk assessment and RSI option.
Removed the unverified ketamine preference and induction drug doses; the guideline supports selecting induction drugs to maintain hemodynamic stability without naming a universally preferred agent.
Removed claims of inevitable induction arrest, mandatory pre-induction arterial access, routine CVP monitoring, and a universal vasopressor or fluid recipe.

Removed unsupported fixed volatile-anesthetic reduction, aggressive crystalloid resuscitation, routine ICU intubation, and routine ICU admission; postoperative destination and extubation are individualized.
Corrected the unsupported fixed hemoglobin target near 11 g/dL; the emergency-laparotomy guideline supports a restrictive strategy with individual exceptions.

reports.title: Pilonidal Cyst Excision
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not substantiate its MAC-versus-spinal recommendations, airway-device selection, airway/positioning hazard claims, anesthetic drug choices, fluid amount, local analgesic regimen, or extubation suggestions.

The surgical literature reports heterogeneous techniques and outcomes; the 2019 review notes there is no generally accepted recurrence definition or treatment algorithm and does not establish superiority among off-midline procedures.
ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards support general monitoring requirements, not pilonidal-specific airway, positioning, fluid, analgesia, or emergence choices.
The supplied quantitative neuromuscular-blockade guidance is relevant only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used; it does not imply paralysis for this operation.

The surgical reviews do not establish a preferred anesthetic or airway technique across pilonidal procedures; the general-anesthesia description applies to the authors’ modified Bascom cleft-lift technique.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific adult anesthesia evidence addressing anesthetic technique and airway planning for definitive pilonidal surgery performed prone.
Pilonidal-specific evidence on anesthesia-related positioning hazards and their prevention or management.
Procedure-specific evidence for intraoperative fluid/blood-loss expectations, analgesia and PONV strategies, and emergence/recovery planning.
corrections: Removed the unverified prone LMA-versus-ETT recommendations and claims about obesity-based airway selection; the supplied pilonidal sources specify no airway technique.
Removed the unverified spinal anesthetic dose, anesthetic maintenance drugs, local anesthetic infiltration, and medication regimen.
Removed the unverified fixed crystalloid volume and claims about expected minimal blood loss.
Removed unsupported prone complications and extubation recommendations, including deep extubation in the prone position.
Corrected the notion that one anesthesia approach applies across pilonidal procedures: source material distinguishes acute drainage, minimally invasive procedures, and definitive excision/closure.

reports.title: Port Placement / Removal (Mediport / PICC Port)
reviewNotes: The Base44 field suggestions are unverified and were not used as evidence. In particular, its drug recipes, rapid-recovery claims, routine postoperative CXR requirement, and guidewire-withdrawal instruction are not adopted as universal recommendations.
The prospective placement study has conflicting complication counts and pneumothorax descriptions; complication rates from it require caution.
The observational audit reports general anesthesia but omits airway and anesthesia details; it cannot establish that general anesthesia is preferable.
This is an adult-focused reference draft. The supplied studies concern oncology or breast-surgery populations; applicability beyond those settings is not established.
evidenceGaps: Port removal: procedural technique, anesthetic approach, and procedure-specific complication profile are not described in the supplied sources.
Port-specific anesthetic selection, airway management, and intraoperative anesthetic targets are not established.
Port-specific fluid, bleeding, analgesia, and PONV strategies are not established.
corrections: Removed the unsupported fixed MAC/propofol/fentanyl/midazolam plan and the claim that an LMA or ETT is rarely needed; available sources do not establish a preferred regimen or airway plan.
Removed the Base44 platelet threshold and unsupported claims about prior ports, central-line stenosis, SVC syndrome, and cardiac-history screening as case-specific evidence.
Corrected routine postoperative CXR language: imaging was used in the reports, but the supplied evidence does not establish a universal requirement.
Removed the assertion that a guidewire entering the right heart should be withdrawn slightly; it is unsupported by the provided source evidence.
Removed fixed recovery duration, fluid bolus, and postoperative analgesic prescriptions.

reports.title: Robotic Cholecystectomy
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified. The source set supports broad laparoscopic/robotic considerations, but not a fixed anesthetic recipe for robotic cholecystectomy.

Neuromuscular-blockade advice is not uniform across the supplied reviews: one describes continuous blockade as indispensable for robotic surgery, while another calls continuation or redosing controversial and the first review notes uncertainty about deep blockade. The draft states the coordination and monitoring principles without imposing a universal regimen.
The robotic references are narrative reviews/educational summaries; emergency cart removal should be locally rehearsed because the supplied sources do not provide an institution-specific sequence.
evidenceGaps: The supplied evidence does not provide a procedure-specific robotic cholecystectomy emergency undocking sequence or comparative outcomes against conventional laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
corrections: Removed the unsupported fixed crystalloid total of 500–1000 mL; the supplied educational source instead describes goal-directed fluid administration.

Removed the unverified induction, maintenance, and PONV drug recipe, including specific doses and mandatory triple prophylaxis; sources support individualized technique and PONV prophylaxis, not that fixed regimen.
Removed unsupported case-specific preoperative claims about LFT/bilirubin testing, anticoagulation management, and Foley use.
Corrected the blanket ETT/NMB framing: tracheal intubation is commonly described for laparoscopic surgery, while continuation or depth of blockade is not uniformly supported as mandatory.

reports.title: Robotic Hernia Repair / Abdominal Wall Reconstruction
reviewNotes: The Base44 field covers inguinal, ventral, and incisional hernias, but the hernia-specific sources supplied here principally address ventral and incisional repairs. No inguinal-specific anesthesia conclusions are inferred.
Base44's fixed propofol/fentanyl/rocuronium induction recipe and RSI suggestion for obesity or GERD are unsupported by the supplied sources and were removed.

Base44's 1–2 L crystalloid total, minimal-blood-loss assumption, routine Foley threshold of cases over 90 minutes, and specific analgesic drug bundle are not established by the sources. One technique review describes catheterization when a procedure is expected to exceed two hours; this is not a universal threshold.

Base44's routine Trendelenburg description is not generalized to ventral/incisional repair. The sources describe supine positioning and possible slight Trendelenburg in particular setup circumstances; they do not establish a universal position.
Base44's emergency-undocking protocol, smooth-emergence recipe, and claim of significant TAP-block opioid reduction lack support in the supplied sources.

The general laparoscopic/robotic review includes useful physiologic and complication information but is not a hernia-specific guideline. Its ventilation and fluid statements are presented as review-level guidance, not mandatory targets.
The quantitative neuromuscular monitoring recommendation is conditional on use of neuromuscular blocking drugs; it is not a requirement for every anesthetic technique.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific anesthesia evidence for robotic inguinal hernia repair is not supplied.
A validated emergency-undocking and patient-access protocol for the specific robotic platform and room setup is not supplied.

Hernia-specific evidence does not establish individualized ventilation targets, fluid strategy, or emergence/extubation criteria; these must not be inferred as fixed protocols from the available sources.
No pregnancy-specific evidence for robotic hernia repair is supplied; this draft cannot establish obstetric management.
corrections: Removed the unsupported fixed induction drug and dose recipe, including the Base44 rocuronium dose.
Removed the blanket RSI recommendation based on obesity or GERD alone.
Removed the fixed 1–2 L crystalloid plan and presumed minimal blood loss.
Corrected the Foley timing claim: the supplied technique review describes catheter use when duration is expected to exceed two hours, not a universal 90-minute threshold.
Removed the claim that TAP block reduces opioid requirements significantly; the general review only describes TAP blocks as an option for laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches.
Removed a routine Trendelenburg assumption for all robotic hernia procedures and an unsupported emergency-undocking protocol.
Did not assert that prolonged Trendelenburg requires leaving the patient intubated; available sources identify edema risk but do not provide that routine extubation rule.

reports.title: Soft Tissue Mass Excision
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, its suggested MAC-versus-general selection, drug recipes, fluid total, monitoring description, frozen-section capability, and postoperative analgesic plan are not substantiated as routine practice by the supplied sources.

The lipoma technique study reports local anesthesia or monitored controlled anesthesia but gives neither selection criteria nor a monitored-anesthesia regimen. Its single-surgeon retrospective results should not be generalized as comparative effectiveness or broad complication rates.

The excisional-biopsy educational review concerns lesion excision and biopsy rather than anesthesia; its melanoma-specific diagnostic and therapeutic margin discussion was not applied as a soft-tissue sarcoma margin recommendation.

The supplied ERAS sources concern gastrointestinal surgery and do not provide usable procedure-specific recommendations for this case. The anesthesia standards are general standards and do not establish a particular anesthetic technique.

No supplied evidence supports routine general anesthesia, intubation, neuromuscular blockade, invasive monitoring, a fixed fluid amount, or a specific medication regimen for all soft-tissue mass excisions.
evidenceGaps: Anesthesia technique selection criteria and airway strategy for deep, large, or anatomically difficult soft-tissue masses.
A reliable multidisciplinary diagnostic and operative pathway for suspected soft-tissue sarcoma, including staging, biopsy planning, definitive margins, and the role of frozen section.
Procedure-specific fluid, postoperative analgesia, and PONV recommendations.
corrections: Removed the unverified Base44 drug selections and induction, maintenance, and postoperative analgesia recipes; the sources do not establish these as a protocol.
Removed the Base44 fixed 250–500 mL crystalloid suggestion; the supplied procedure source provides no intravenous-fluid guidance.
Removed the claim that frozen section capability or a particular margin plan is routinely required; the provided sources do not establish this for suspected sarcoma.
Did not assert that MAC is often sufficient for small superficial masses as a universal rule; the procedure study does not specify anesthesia selection criteria.
Reframed seroma, hematoma, and nerve-injury figures as outcomes from one retrospective lipoma series, not general rates for all soft-tissue mass excisions.

reports.title: Splenectomy (Laparoscopic/Open)
reviewNotes: Base44's assertion that platelet transfusion in ITP should follow splenic artery ligation is not established by the supplied sources; do not retain it as a clinical instruction.
Base44's fixed crystalloid volume, Level 1 infuser setup, routine blood availability, and routine arterial line claims are not supported as universal splenectomy practice by the provided evidence.
The procedure review describes laparoscopic positioning as debated and dependent on surgeon preference; right lateral decubitus should not be presented as mandatory.

Base44 lists trauma and lymphoma staging among indications, but the supplied procedure-review content does not substantiate that complete indication list. Avoid presenting the unverified list as source-confirmed.
The review reports differing lifetime OPSI estimates in different sections; this draft avoids repeating a numerical lifetime risk.
The retrospective fast-track study concerns a selected cohort with hypersplenism and portal-hypertension-related features and cannot establish general anesthetic, analgesic, or transfusion standards.
evidenceGaps: Splenectomy-specific anesthetic drug selection and dosing, hemodynamic targets, transfusion strategy, and case-specific monitoring criteria are not established in the available sources.
The provided sources do not establish a splenectomy-specific extubation, ICU disposition, or postoperative analgesia protocol.
corrections: Removed the unverified instruction to transfuse platelets after splenic artery ligation in ITP; source evidence does not support this timing claim.
Removed fixed crystalloid totals, mandatory Level 1 infuser use, universal blood-product preparation, and routine arterial-line claims as general requirements.
Reframed right lateral positioning as one surgical option rather than the default for every laparoscopic splenectomy.
Did not include numerical platelet thresholds or drug doses from the source material.

reports.title: Thyroidectomy
reviewNotes: Base44's statement that elective patients must be euthyroid is consistent with the sources' optimization goal, but the sources also discuss patients who may not be fully stabilized; avoid implying an absolute rule without clinical context.

Base44 proposes checking calcium at six hours postoperatively. The supplied sources do not support that exact timing: one describes PACU PTH measurement and symptoms commonly arising 24–72 hours after surgery.

Base44's instruction to avoid succinylcholine after NIM-tube placement is unsupported. Sources describe short-acting blockade to facilitate intubation, recovery before monitoring, and avoiding paralytics during nerve monitoring.

Base44 specifies a fixed shoulder-roll position, routine warming, thyroid-storm drugs prepared, remifentanil-based conditions, dexmedetomidine, and a fixed analgesic/steroid regimen. These are not uniformly established as routine requirements by the supplied evidence.

The instruction to open the neck wound at bedside is supported for life-threatening hematoma with airway compression, but it should be framed as urgent escalation/decompression rather than a routine bedside action for every hematoma.
Sources do not support universal fluid restriction, a fixed blood-loss estimate, mandatory NIM monitoring, or a single extubation approach. Individualize these decisions to the operation and patient.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not resolve an optimal thyroidectomy-specific postoperative calcium/PTH surveillance and supplementation pathway, including timing and thresholds; local endocrine and surgical protocols may be needed.
The source set does not provide a comparative, procedure-specific evidence base for selecting airway technique or extubation strategy across degrees of tracheal compression and long-standing goiter.
corrections: Removed the Base44 claim that calcium should always be checked at six hours; the supplied evidence supports PACU PTH measurement in one review and describes typical hypocalcemia symptoms at 24–72 hours, not a universal six-hour calcium check.

Corrected the blanket NIM-related instruction to avoid succinylcholine after tube placement. Evidence supports short-acting neuromuscular blockade for intubation when appropriate, with recovery before monitoring and avoidance of paralytics during monitoring.
Did not present TIVA, remifentanil, dexmedetomidine, corticosteroids, NSAIDs, or any analgesic regimen as mandatory or universally preferred.
Did not retain unsupported routine fluid restriction, a universal blood-loss figure, or an assumption that every thyroidectomy requires general anesthesia, NIM monitoring, or neuromuscular blockade.
Qualified bedside wound release as emergency management for airway-threatening hematoma, consistent with the procedure-specific review evidence.

reports.title: Tracheostomy Placement
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as clinical evidence. The source-supported reference distinguishes open from percutaneous procedures and does not impose intubation, general anesthesia or neuromuscular blockade on every case.

The Base44 FiO₂ <30% instruction is not supported by the supplied tracheostomy sources. They identify fire risk from high oxygen concentrations plus electrocautery and recommend team coordination, but provide no universal oxygen threshold.

The claims that 100% oxygen is required during airway exchange, that ventilation must always be suspended, that bronchoscopy is non-negotiable in every technique, and that the original ETT must always be ready for re-advancement are not established as universal practice by the supplied evidence.

The Base44 cuff-pressure statements conflict in the procedure source itself and use different units; no target was reproduced. The source-supported early tube-change discussion is presented as typical care, not an individual-patient instruction.
The COVID-era review is a limited, context-specific narrative review and should not be used to impose its timing, testing, paralysis or infection-control recommendations on all tracheostomy patients.
The source-supported evidence does not establish tracheostomy-specific fluid, PONV, analgesia, or anesthetic emergence protocols.
evidenceGaps: Tracheostomy-specific adult anesthetic emergence and ETT-removal strategies are not detailed in the available procedure sources.
A procedure-specific analgesia and PONV approach is not established in the available sources.
The available sources do not resolve a universal cuff-pressure target; one source contains conflicting values and units.
corrections: Removed the unsupported blanket FiO₂ <30% rule; retained only the source-supported airway-fire hazard and need for team coordination.
Removed blanket requirements for 100% oxygen, routine neuromuscular blockade, mandatory ventilation suspension, and a specific RSI strategy.
Replaced the claim that bronchoscopic guidance is universally non-negotiable with the narrower source-supported description of its role in percutaneous placement.
Removed the unsourced instruction to re-advance the original ETT if placement fails and the blanket first-week suture/tie rule.
Did not reproduce contradictory cuff-pressure values or assert a universal tracheostomy-tube change date.
Did not include unsupported drug lists, fluid prescriptions, or procedure-specific pain regimens.

reports.title: Umbilical / Ventral / Incisional Hernia Repair
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified claims, not as evidence. The supplied hernia-specific source is limited to primary umbilical hernia and does not validate the full combined umbilical/ventral/incisional case scope.

The source supporting LA + MAC is a perspective/review with a small institutional feasibility cohort; it does not establish superiority or a universal technique. The general laparoscopic/robotic review is educational and not hernia-specific.
The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards and the neuromuscular-blockade guideline support general monitoring and recovery principles, not a hernia-specific anesthetic recipe.

Base44 claims of routine RSI for incarceration, fixed induction drugs/doses, Foley use based on duration, specified crystalloid totals, neuraxial vasopressor management, tight-closure ventilation effects, and routine full NMB reversal were not adopted as case-specific facts. Quantitative TOF guidance is stated only when NMB is used.

The claim that robotic/laparoscopic hernia repair significantly reduces postoperative pain is not established by the supplied hernia-specific evidence; the general MIS review describes broader advantages but does not verify that case-specific claim.
The postanesthesia requirements are general anesthesia-care standards, not a hernia-specific recovery protocol.
evidenceGaps: Direct anesthesia evidence for adult ventral and prior-incisional hernia repair, including large defects and component-separation procedures.
Hernia-specific evidence on abdominal-wall closure effects on ventilation and postoperative respiratory compromise.
Procedure-specific evidence for airway strategy, anesthetic technique, and recovery in incarcerated or bowel-containing ventral/incisional hernias.
corrections: Removed the Base44 drug doses and induction recipe; no supplied source supports a hernia-specific dosing regimen.
Removed routine RSI for incarcerated hernia; the source discusses urgency and bowel-content caution but provides no anesthesia induction protocol.
Removed fixed crystalloid volumes and duration-based Foley criteria as unsupported by the supplied evidence.
Removed the claim that abdominal closure is necessarily tight or that large defects predictably cause a specified ventilation problem; this is not established in the supplied sources.
Restricted the TAP-block statement to the source-supported context of laparoscopic-assisted or hybrid approaches; it is not presented as universally required for open repair.
Restricted quantitative TOF recovery guidance to cases in which neuromuscular blockers are used.

reports.title: Wound Debridement
reviewNotes: Base44 material is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its proposed MAC/ETT/RSI choices, ketamine preference, septic-induction warning, vasopressor plan, arterial-line trigger, fluid volume, blood-product plan, hypothermia concern, ICU intubation disposition, wound-VAC use, and necrotizing-fasciitis emergency claims are not established by the supplied sources.

The wound sources concern chronic or general wound care and do not establish anesthesia management for necrotizing fasciitis, sepsis, unstable patients, or large debridements. Those Base44 assertions should not be presented as source-supported clinical guidance.

The source-supported topical analgesia option and application-time statement are wound-paper recommendations, not a universal anesthetic regimen. Procedure and patient factors still determine technique.
The ASA basic monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general guidance, not procedure-specific recommendations. The neuromuscular-blockade material is relevant only when blockade is used.

Sources 2 and 3 are GI ERAS material and do not substantiate wound-debridement-specific claims. No supplied source supports a fixed procedure-specific fluid total, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion threshold.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific anesthesia guidance for necrotizing fasciitis, sepsis, hemodynamic instability, and extensive debridement, including relevant airway and peri-induction risk management.

Procedure-specific criteria for choosing local anesthesia, monitored anesthesia care, regional anesthesia, or general anesthesia, and corresponding positioning, access, and intraoperative physiologic management.
Debridement-specific fluid, blood-loss, transfusion, emergence, and postoperative disposition recommendations.
corrections: Removed as unsupported: fixed 1–3 L crystalloid, aggressive septic resuscitation recipe, routine blood-product availability, and any implied transfusion threshold.
Removed as unsupported: routine arterial line, universal RSI or endotracheal intubation, ketamine preference, and claims that patients will crash on induction.
Removed as unsupported: routine warming or fluid warmer requirements, vasopressor plan, ICU intubation for necrotizing fasciitis, and PACU disposition based solely on debridement category.
Removed as unsupported: wound VAC as common postoperative management and specific opioid or multimodal analgesic plans.

Corrected scope: surgical debridement may involve general anesthesia or local infiltrate, but the sources do not establish a default technique; local/minor procedures do not imply intubation, paralysis, invasive monitoring, or general anesthesia.

reports.title: EGD (Upper Endoscopy)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and were not used as evidence. The propofol/fentanyl/midazolam doses, infusion rate, Ramsay target, lidocaine-for-injection-pain instruction and medication list are not adopted as clinical recipes.

The claim that nasal-cannula ETCO2 is universally mandatory or the single most important safety monitor is not supported as stated: ASA calls for expired-CO2 monitoring during moderate or deep sedation unless precluded or invalidated, while ASGE says benefit in moderate sedation has not been demonstrated and supports considering it for deep sedation.

The claim that ETCO2 detects apnea 20–30 seconds before SpO2, and that jaw thrust is the most effective intervention in the lateral position, is not established by the supplied evidence. These are omitted.

A natural airway, left-lateral position, routine topical anesthetic, and fixed sedation depth are not universal requirements in the sources. Position, sedation depth and airway protection are individualized.

The stated 4–6-hour solid and 2-hour clear fasting formulation is narrowed: the review describes 6 hours for food and 2 hours for clear liquids, while ASGE notes no direct evidence linking fasting duration to aspiration risk and no universal practice standard.

The Base44 gag-reflex return interval, prohibition on oral intake until sensation returns, lozenges/acetaminophen plan, bloating timeline, routine minimal-fluid approach and injection-pain regimen are not supported by the supplied sources and are omitted.
Atropine for vagal bradycardia and ondansetron as a routine EGD medication are not established by the supplied evidence; no treatment recipe is inferred.

The supplied evidence is predominantly adult, but includes broad endoscopy guidance rather than a single adult EGD anesthesia protocol. Pediatric observations are not used to establish adult practice.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not establish comparative effectiveness of specific oxygen-delivery devices during adult EGD or a procedure-specific oxygenation protocol.
The sources do not establish one optimal adult EGD sedation regimen or a standard position and airway technique across patient risk groups and procedural complexity.
No EGD-specific routine emergence protocol, oral-intake timing after topical pharyngeal anesthesia, or standard postprocedure observation schedule is provided.
corrections: Removed unsupported specific sedative doses, infusion rates and target sedation score from the unverified Base44 fields.

Corrected the universal claim for mandatory nasal-cannula ETCO2 monitoring: the supplied standards distinguish moderate/deep sedation and acknowledge exceptions; ASGE evidence for benefit in moderate sedation is not established.
Removed the claim that ETCO2 detects apnea a fixed 20–30 seconds before desaturation and the claim that jaw thrust is categorically the most effective maneuver.
Removed fixed gag-reflex return timing, oral-intake prohibition interval, routine throat-pain/bloating treatments, fluid totals and medication instructions not supported by these sources.
Replaced a presumed natural-airway, left-lateral-only approach with source-supported recognition of shared airway, limited access and individualized positioning and airway protection.

reports.title: ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified claims, not evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not support mandatory endotracheal intubation for all prone ERCP; the 2025 review describes individualized options, while noting position-related airway-access and aspiration concerns.

The 2011 review prefers deep sedation, but the newer 2025 narrative review states that no anesthetic approach is conclusively superior. The draft avoids presenting either preference as a universal standard.
The claims that cholangitis requires RSI, an arterial line, a fixed crystalloid volume, or immediate ERCP as a universal anesthetic instruction are not established by the provided sources.

The supplied evidence does not establish routine OGT placement, routine dexamethasone or ondansetron, a fixed analgesic regimen, mandatory rectal indomethacin, or a universal extubation technique for ERCP.
Source 1 includes pediatric feasibility information, but this draft uses no pediatric evidence to establish adult practice.
The clinical draft is not patient-specific and has not been clinically approved.

The complications and fluids bullets are unsupported absence-of-evidence notes, so they were removed from the clinical sections. The supplied sources provide no ERCP-specific complication recognition/management protocol or fluid, transfusion, and hemodynamic resuscitation algorithm.
evidenceGaps: ERCP-specific prevention, recognition, and management guidance for post-ERCP pancreatitis.
ERCP-specific recognition and escalation guidance for perforation and cholangitis-related perioperative instability.
Procedure-specific bleeding management beyond airway considerations for massive bleeding.

complications: This is a source-limitations statement rather than a clinical-section bullet. The supplied sources do not provide an ERCP-specific recognition or management protocol for post-ERCP pancreatitis, perforation, or cholangitis.

fluids: This is a source-limitations statement rather than a clinical-section bullet. The supplied sources do not establish ERCP-specific fluid targets, transfusion thresholds, or a hemodynamic resuscitation algorithm.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that an endotracheal tube is mandatory for every prone ERCP; supplied reviews describe individualized airway choices and identify limitations and risks for both spontaneous ventilation and supraglottic devices.
Removed unverified routine RSI, OGT placement, arterial-line placement, fixed crystalloid volume, and routine blood availability claims.
Removed unverified routine drug recipes, including fixed induction and maintenance combinations, routine rectal indomethacin, and a mandatory NSAID/acetaminophen postoperative plan.
Removed unverified categorical statements that prone natural-airway management has no safe alternative and that a particular extubation approach is required.

reports.title: Cervical Cerclage
reviewNotes: The two cerclage-specific sources are educational summaries, not a procedure-specific society guideline. Source 0 describes regional anesthesia as preferred in its discussion but also reports no long-term outcome difference between carefully performed regional and general anesthesia; the draft preserves both points without claiming spinal is mandatory or uniquely safest.

Source 1 says intraoperative monitoring is not specified, while source 0 explicitly supports fetal heart-rate assessment before and after and says continuous intraoperative monitoring is generally not performed. The draft follows the more specific statement without implying that no fetal assessment is needed.
The ASA obstetric anesthesia guideline at source index 8 explicitly excludes surgery during pregnancy; it was not used as a cerclage-specific authority.

Base44 statements that spinal is the safest approach, that a particular low-dose recipe or block height is required, that fluid should be fixed at 500 mL, that benzodiazepines must be avoided, or that pregnant patients are never NPO-safe are not retained as established recommendations. The supplied procedure-specific sources do not support those claims as universal rules.
This is a source-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan, clinical approval, or production-ready reference.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not establish procedure-specific escalation algorithms for significant bleeding, membrane rupture, fetal bradycardia, or maternal deterioration during cerclage.
No cerclage-specific discharge criteria or detailed postanesthesia monitoring protocol is supplied.
corrections: Removed the claim that spinal anesthesia is categorically safest for every patient; the sources support regional preference in discussion but also describe both regional and general anesthesia as options when carefully performed.
Removed specific intrathecal drug doses, spinal block-height targets, and a fixed crystalloid volume; these are not presented as universal procedure-specific requirements in the sources.
Removed the claim that continuous fetal monitoring is required during placement; source 0 instead describes assessment before and after and says continuous monitoring is generally not performed.
Removed unsupported universal claims about avoiding benzodiazepines, mandatory RSI or intubation, and pregnancy being never NPO-safe.

Corrected postoperative care to reflect obstetric reassessment and observation for contractions, bleeding, membrane rupture, infection, and neuraxial recovery without inventing universal discharge criteria.

reports.title: Cervical Cone Biopsy / LEEP
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not establish MAC with a natural airway, propofol/fentanyl use, routine rapid recovery, or a specific postoperative analgesic regimen.

The Base44 claims about vasopressin-induced hypertension/reflex bradycardia and having labetalol or nicardipine ready are not substantiated by the supplied evidence; no related claim is presented as established guidance.

The supplied material does not verify the Base44 claims about LEEP smoke plume, smoke evacuation, cervical bleeding control with Monsel’s solution or suture, preoperative anemia assessment, pregnancy status, or lithotomy positioning.

Source 0 is procedure-specific for pain management but is not an anesthesia management reference; its findings should not be used to infer airway technique or general anesthetic practice. Its LEEP evidence should not be assumed to establish cold-knife cone practice.
Source 1 is abstract-limited and source 2 covers heterogeneous gynecologic surgery rather than this procedure. Neither resolves the case-specific anesthetic gaps.
The supplied evidence does not address vasopressin-associated hypertension or bradycardia during cervical procedures, so no clinical recommendation on that topic can be retained.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific anesthesia approach and perioperative management for cold-knife cone biopsy.
Case-specific airway and ventilation guidance when sedation or general anesthesia is used for LEEP or cone biopsy.
Source-supported guidance on bleeding risk and management, LEEP plume controls, and procedure-specific postoperative surveillance and discharge instructions.

reports.title: Laparoscopic Ovarian Cystectomy / Oophorectomy
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. The ovarian cystectomy trial is narrow and abstract-only. Its opioid-free and opioid-based trial arms and outcomes must not be converted into recommended drug choices or doses.
ASA standards and the neuromuscular-blockade guideline support general monitoring and recovery principles, not procedure-specific ovarian-surgery management.

reports.title: Myomectomy (Open / Laparoscopic)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, routine TXA at induction, routine cell saver, preoperative GnRH therapy, RSI for a large uterus, fixed fluid volumes, and routine arterial-line use are not established by the supplied sources.

Sources vary in relevance and quality: the direct myomectomy anesthesia article is an older narrative overview; the newer randomized trial addresses analgesia in selected laparoscopic patients, not open-case anesthesia or bleeding management.

The general laparoscopy reference supports physiologic and airway context but is not myomectomy-specific. The ERAS systematic review covers diverse gynecologic procedures and is not an anesthesia guideline.
The older myomectomy article contains specific drug and fluid suggestions without formal evidence grading; these were not reproduced as routine treatment instructions.

reports.title: Ovarian Cancer Debulking (Cytoreductive Surgery)

reports.title: Pelvic Organ Prolapse Repair / Colporrhaphy
reviewNotes: Base44 material was treated as unverified. The cohort's catheter outcomes do not support universal retention: catheter reinsertion was numerically different between groups but not statistically significant. The study excluded some patients with relevant retention risk factors.

reports.title: Postpartum Tubal Ligation
reviewNotes: This is a source-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan or a clinically approved reference. Individualize decisions to patient status, preferences, and institutional practice.

reports.title: Robotic Hysterectomy
reviewNotes: Base44 material was treated as unverified and not as clinical evidence. evidenceGaps: The sources say to know the emergency undocking process but do not provide the actual robotic-hysterectomy undocking procedure; the local team protocol is needed for operational use.

reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified. reports.title: Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (TAH)

reports.title: Vaginal Hysterectomy (VH)
reviewNotes: The unverified Base44 claim that spinal anesthesia is the preferred technique for vaginal hysterectomy is not supported. reports.title: Hepatic Resection (Open / Laparoscopic)
reviewNotes: The case fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. The supplied sources support usual general anaesthesia with tracheal intubation, but not a mandatory arterial line, CVP catheter, cell saver, central catheter, or crossmatch quantity for every resection.

The case field calling low CVP the most impactful intervention overstates the evidence. The procedure review describes reduced blood loss/transfusion without demonstrated clinical-outcome improvement and cites a retrospective analysis finding no blood-loss effect from CVP monitoring; minimally invasive pneumoperitoneum can also make CVP unreliable.

A fixed 20–30 minute Pringle tolerance is not supported as a universal rule. The procedure review describes intermittent occlusion and different prolonged-occlusion cautions for normal versus pathological liver; technique and duration require case-specific surgical coordination.

Routine epidural placement/continuation is not supported: the ERAS summaries do not recommend routine TEA for open liver resection and describe alternatives. Coagulation and hemodynamic concerns require individualized assessment.

Routine TXA, nitroglycerin, dexamethasone, epidural, ICU intubation for all major cases, a particular extubation category rule, and hourly glucose checks are not established as universal prescriptions by the supplied sources.

The source set includes general standards and educational reviews, not a complete liver-resection society guideline. The generic monitoring, postanaesthesia-care, and neuromuscular-blockade standards apply within their stated scope, not as a substitute for procedure-specific judgment.

The source also states in its key points that a hepatic remnant of 20–30% is the minimum safe volume, without specifying the same liver-quality categories. The supplied content does not reconcile that general statement with the category-specific estimates.
evidenceGaps: No standardized adult liver-resection extubation criteria or procedure-specific emergence protocol is provided.

A detailed standardized postoperative neurologic-monitoring and disposition protocol specific to awake craniotomy.
corrections: Removed fixed dexmedetomidine doses and claims that it does not impair speech or motor testing; sources describe it as an option with minimal respiratory depression, but also report variable or prolonged sedation and possible delayed neurocognitive responses.

Corrected the implication that arterial line and BIS monitoring are mandatory; sources describe arterial access as dependent on patient/procedure factors and EEG-derived monitoring as potentially useful.
Removed the fixed 1–2 L crystalloid total, routine ketorolac, and blanket ICU-admission claim because the provided sources do not establish these as universal awake-craniotomy practice.
Reframed scalp block as a mainstay of analgesia without claiming a particular local-anesthetic recipe or guaranteed duration of analgesia.
Replaced blanket statements about patient contraindications with individualized selection language because source reviews differ on absolute contraindications.

reports.title: Burr Holes (Exploratory / Therapeutic)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified. The supplied sources do not substantiate its combined indication list (including acute epidural evacuation, EVD/ICP-monitor access, or biopsy) as one burr-hole anesthesia pathway.

Removed the unverified fixed RSI drug regimen, video-laryngoscopy preference, routine arterial line and Foley, specified reversal agents, mannitol/hypertonic-saline instructions, and routine ICU or seizure-prophylaxis claims. These sources do not establish them as routine burr-hole practice.

Removed the claimed abrupt hemodynamic collapse at decompression and middle meningeal artery bleeding as characteristic burr-hole events: the supplied evidence does not establish either claim as a procedure-specific expectation.

The cSDH anesthesia evidence compares local and general anesthesia but does not establish selection criteria, acute hematoma management, or a preferred anesthetic protocol. Do not infer that an association in observational studies determines the best approach for an individual.
This is an adult-focused draft. The supplied sources provide no obstetric-specific evidence or recommendations; they do not establish pregnancy as a contraindication to medically necessary surgery.

The supplied sources do not describe a characteristic physiologic response at the moment of burr-hole decompression or provide a source-grounded response algorithm; the unsupported clinical bullet was removed.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific anesthesia reference for emergency burr-hole decompression, including acute subdural or epidural hematoma indications, is not supplied.
No source establishes a burr-hole-specific approach to anticoagulant or antiplatelet reversal, including timing or agent selection.
No source establishes criteria for choosing local anesthesia, sedation, or general anesthesia in emergency or neurologically deteriorating patients, or criteria for conversion between approaches.
No burr-hole-specific guidance is supplied for positioning, vascular access, raised-ICP management targets, intraoperative bleeding response, or postoperative neurologic monitoring and ICU selection.
intraop: This is a source limitation rather than a clinical procedure standard.
intraop: The supplied sources do not support a specific hemodynamic response or response algorithm for burr-hole decompression.
corrections: Corrected the impression that all burr-hole procedures require general anesthesia or intubation: local anesthesia is described as a feasible cSDH alternative, while case selection is not established.
Removed fixed induction drugs and doses, RSI as a universal approach, and a universal airway plan.

Removed routine arterial-line, Foley, blood-availability, reversal, hyperosmolar-therapy, hyperventilation, and ICU instructions where the supplied evidence did not support a burr-hole-specific standard.
Excluded extrapolation of chronic-subdural-hematoma evidence to acute hematoma, epidural hematoma, EVD/ICP access, brain biopsy, or other exploratory indications.

reports.title: Cervical Laminectomy / Laminoplasty
reviewNotes: Base44 was treated as unverified and not used as evidence. Its fixed MAP target, drug recipes, routine fluid volume, analgesic regimen, and MEP-drop alarm threshold are not established by the supplied procedure-specific sources and were not carried forward.

The procedure-specific review is dated 2008 and describes surgical selection and positioning more fully than anesthetic care. The separate cervical-surgery anesthesia summary is broader than laminoplasty.
Do not conflate posterior surgery with anterior-approach airway edema or anterior-specific considerations. This draft focuses on posterior decompression.
The procedure review says no blood-pressure target is established; perfusion priorities are stated without adopting a universal numeric target.
The source does not provide an anesthetic-coordination protocol or a universal neuromonitoring alert threshold or response algorithm; those claims were omitted.
evidenceGaps: A current, procedure-specific source defining anesthetic management and response criteria for SSEP/MEP changes during cervical laminoplasty.
A laminoplasty-specific extubation and postoperative airway-management protocol.
A procedure-specific comparative evidence base for postoperative analgesia and PONV prevention.
corrections: Removed the fixed MAP >80 target: the procedure-specific review states that no blood-pressure target guidelines are established.
Removed the claimed >50% MEP-amplitude alert threshold: no supplied source establishes that cutoff.

Removed the prescribed crystalloid volume, dexamethasone dose, routine relaxant restriction, ketorolac-based analgesia recipe, and universal collar/PCA plan because the supplied sources do not support them as standard care.
Removed unsupported routine claims about vertebral-artery injury, C7–T1 pneumothorax, postoperative hematoma, and anterior-approach airway edema as specific hazards of posterior laminoplasty.
Reframed TIVA and volatile-agent considerations as source-supported cervical-spine monitoring guidance rather than a laminoplasty-specific mandate.

reports.title: Craniotomy for Brain Tumor
reviewNotes: The supplied Base44 fields are unauthenticated and were not treated as evidence. Several specific recipes or thresholds in those fields—including induction doses, a fixed MAP range, a hemoglobin transfusion threshold, and routine NSAID avoidance—are not established by the supplied sources and are omitted.

Do not present TIVA as mandatory for all tumor craniotomies: the awake-craniotomy review discusses propofol–remifentanil in its specific context, while the educational manual describes other approaches.

The older educational manual’s recommendations, including routine arterial cannulation for full craniotomy and hypocapnia, are reported with their source context rather than elevated to universal contemporary standards.

The ASA basic monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general standards, not tumor-craniotomy protocols. The neuromuscular-blockade recommendations apply only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.
evidenceGaps: A contemporary adult tumor-craniotomy guideline or comparative evidence establishing case-specific ventilation and cerebral-perfusion targets.
A validated procedure-specific postoperative neurological-observation schedule and criteria for escalation.
Current procedure-specific evidence for fluid selection, bleeding preparation, and transfusion decision thresholds.
corrections: Removed unsupported fixed induction drug doses and other numerical medication regimens.
Removed the unsubstantiated fixed MAP target, hemoglobin transfusion threshold, and blanket NSAID prohibition.
Reframed TIVA as a possible technique in relevant contexts rather than a universal requirement.
