Replaced an unqualified claim that arterial monitoring is mandatory with a qualified report of the educational manual’s recommendation.

Did not retain the case-field claims for a specific airway tube type, routine Foley catheter, hourly neurological checks, or a fixed postoperative blood-pressure range because the supplied sources do not establish them as universal practice.

reports.title: Craniotomy for Cerebral Aneurysm (Clipping)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. Do not carry forward its specific induction drug doses, lidocaine timing, fixed MAP ranges, volatile concentration limits, mannitol dose, or hyperventilation target as universal recipes.

Adenosine is discussed as a selected flow-arrest adjunct, but the clipping review reports no consensus dose or delivery guideline; the Base44 dose and assertion of a predictable duration of standstill were not reproduced.

The sources conflict on pre-induction arterial-line use and temporary-clipping pressure/duration strategies. The draft preserves monitoring importance while avoiding a universal line-placement rule or safe occlusion-time claim.

The source review states that prophylactic antiseizure medication is not routinely recommended, though it may be reasonable in selected high-risk patients. The Base44 blanket statement of seizure prophylaxis was therefore not adopted.

The Base44 claims on Fisher grading, routine CVP, cell saver, EVD status, specific post-clip MAP ranges, codeine avoidance, and a fixed analgesia plan are not sufficiently supported by the supplied clipping sources and were not presented as standard practice.
This is a source-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan, checklist, or clinically approved reference.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not establish a validated clipping-specific emergence and extubation protocol, including selection criteria for postoperative ventilation.
The supplied clipping sources do not provide a postoperative analgesia or PONV prevention regimen.
corrections: Removed fixed propofol, fentanyl, lidocaine, and rocuronium induction doses and the asserted lidocaine-before-laryngoscopy protocol; the sources support hemodynamic stability and adequate depth, not those exact recipes.

Removed universal pre-clip and post-clip MAP ranges, a universal volatile-agent ceiling, and fixed mannitol and PaCO2 targets; pressure, ventilation, and brain-relaxation choices require contextual individualization.
Corrected the claim that adenosine dose and standstill duration are established: sources describe selected use but report variable practice and no consensus guideline.
Removed routine seizure prophylaxis as a blanket recommendation; supplied evidence supports selective use in higher-risk patients and says it is not routinely recommended.
Removed unsupported routine CVP monitoring, mandatory cell saver, fixed blood availability, and specified postoperative opioid/PCA or codeine instructions.

reports.title: Craniotomy for Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. In particular, its mandatory RSI and preferred ketamine recipe are not established by the sources: the review says RSI may reduce aspiration risk and describes several induction agents as common and safe.

The Base44 fixed pressure claims (MAP above 80, CPP above 60, and never allowing SBP below 100) are not presented as universal targets here. The review describes varying severe-TBI systolic thresholds, support for a higher target or MAP-based alternative, and notes that hemodynamic thresholds are lacking for moderate TBI.

The Base44 exact induction and hyperosmolar drug doses, routine pre-laryngoscopy lidocaine, and a fixed Hgb target were omitted. The review supplies no basis for a universal recipe and explicitly says there is no standard transfusion threshold.
The Base44 PaCO₂ target of 35 is not represented as a single exact target: the review describes 30–35 mmHg and reserves PaCO₂ below 30 mmHg as a bridge to definitive treatment of high ICP.
The scalp-block source supports an adjunctive rationale, not a complete TBI analgesia or PONV protocol. The general ASA monitoring and recovery standards are applied only within their stated scope.
Manual spot-check superseded the review’s generic 30–35 mmHg PaCO₂ statement with qualified ACS 2024 and BTF guidance. Source text matching alone did not catch this problem.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific criteria for choosing craniotomy versus decompressive craniectomy and timing/selection thresholds are not supplied.
A TBI-specific, evidence-based PONV and complete postoperative analgesia regimen is not established in the supplied sources.
corrections: Removed the unsupported claim that RSI is mandatory for every TBI craniotomy; source 0 describes RSI as an option that may reduce aspiration risk.

Removed a preferred ketamine-based induction prescription and the claim that ketamine is universally preferred; source 0 describes several induction approaches and does not establish a single preferred regimen.
Removed fixed drug doses, including lidocaine, mannitol, and induction-agent doses, as well as the unsupported Hgb target.
Corrected rigid MAP, CPP, SBP, and PaCO₂ claims to reflect source 0's qualified, differing thresholds and the absence of a moderate-TBI hemodynamic threshold.
Did not present supine positioning, a universal arterial-line requirement, routine central access, or a mandatory ICP monitor as established for every case.

Omitted unverified Base44 claims about diabetes insipidus management, seizure prophylaxis, and other postoperative treatments because the supplied sources do not support them as routine case guidance.

reports.title: Deep Brain Stimulator (DBS) Placement
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as clinical evidence. Its absolute awake-only framing is too categorical: the supplied reviews describe awake mapping as common, while also reporting selected general-anesthetic approaches with limitations.

Base44's claims that dexmedetomidine is uniquely suited, that no sedatives/opioids/benzodiazepines may be used during all recording, and that these drugs uniformly suppress neuronal firing are not supported as universal rules. The reviews describe variation, target-dependent effects, and conflicting reports.

The fixed medication hold interval and immediate postoperative levodopa restart in Base44 are not established by the supplied sources. Medication decisions require coordination with the treating team.

The source material does not establish a universal Phase II general-anesthesia technique, fixed fluid restriction, or immediate CT for every patient. Postoperative imaging is commonly described; the clinical trigger and timing are not standardized in these sources.

Source 0 is an older narrative review and source 1 is a 2014 systematic review; neither is a current DBS-specific society guideline. General ASA standards support monitoring and recovery principles, not DBS-specific anesthetic choices.
evidenceGaps: No DBS-specific society guideline or contemporary comparative evidence is supplied to resolve how anesthetic technique and drug exposure affect MER and clinical testing across targets.
No evidence here establishes a universal postoperative medication restart schedule, imaging timing, or detailed response pathway for suspected intracranial hemorrhage.
No obstetric-specific evidence is supplied; pregnancy-related DBS management cannot be inferred from these sources.
corrections: Removed the Base44 absolute claim that every patient must remain awake throughout electrode placement; retained awake mapping as common while acknowledging selected alternatives and their limitations.
Removed the Base44 blanket prohibition on all sedatives, opioids, and benzodiazepines during all phases; described phase- and recording-dependent tradeoffs instead.
Removed the claim that dexmedetomidine uniquely preserves mapping without neuronal suppression; the supplied reviews report conflicting findings and caution against assuming neutrality.
Removed the fixed Parkinson-medication hold interval and immediate postoperative restart instruction because the supplied evidence does not establish either as universal.
Removed fixed phase-specific airway and anesthetic recipes, including a universal GA technique for generator implantation.
Removed the instruction for immediate CT after every neurologic deficit and reframed imaging as commonly obtained, with unexpected change requiring prompt clinical assessment.

reports.title: Epilepsy Surgery (Temporal Lobectomy / Cortical Resection)
reviewNotes: The supplied case fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, mandatory ETT use, arterial line and Foley, specific positioning, fixed fluid volume, routine dexamethasone, and particular rescue or maintenance drug choices are not established as universal epilepsy-resection practice by the supplied sources.

The claim that benzodiazepines should be categorically avoided because they suppress ECoG is not supported by the supplied evidence. The epilepsy review says anesthetics depress ECoG and also says premedication may include a benzodiazepine; the draft therefore does not make a blanket avoidance claim.

The source material does not support describing valproate as an enzyme inducer. It discusses hepatic enzyme induction by some antiepileptic drugs generally, without attributing that effect to valproate.
The review's comments on ketamine and other anesthetics are not a procedure-specific comparative protocol. They should not be converted into universal safe/unsafe rules for epilepsy resection.

The source describing train-of-four monitoring applies when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used; it does not imply paralysis or quantitative TOF monitoring for awake or other non-paralyzed approaches.

The supplied sources do not provide epilepsy-resection-specific positioning or invasive-monitoring choices, or a procedure-specific PONV regimen; these limitations have been moved to the evidence section.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific, contemporary protocol for coordinating anesthetic technique and ECoG/stimulation mapping, including how anesthetic changes affect interpretation.
Epilepsy-resection-specific recommendations for airway strategy, positioning, invasive monitoring, and postoperative level of care.
Procedure-specific comparative evidence for anesthetic regimens, seizure outcomes, and postoperative analgesia/PONV management.
setup: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a clinical setup instruction.
analgesia: This is a source-scope limitation, not a clinical analgesia recommendation.
corrections: Removed the unsubstantiated universal requirement for an endotracheal tube and fixed supine or lateral positioning.
Removed fixed fluid totals, routine mannitol use, routine arterial line/Foley placement, and a universal crossmatch or blood-availability prescription.
Removed the categorical benzodiazepine avoidance claim and the claim that valproate is an enzyme inducer.
Removed unsupported routine AED-level testing, postoperative seizure-frequency claims, and specific medication/dose recipes.

reports.title: External Ventricular Drain (EVD) Placement
reviewNotes: The case fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not establish routine MAC, a natural airway, specific propofol/fentanyl/midazolam regimens, or a universal head-of-bed angle for anesthesia.

A claim that rapid CSF decompression is not a concern because an EVD is pressure-regulated is not supported: the placement review specifically cautions about rapid drainage in unsecured aneurysmal SAH.
The transport instructions conflict: one review says to keep the drain unclamped during transport, while another says to clamp it. This draft does not choose between them.

Reported EVD infection estimates differ (5–20% versus 0–22%) and are from reviews with differing scope; they are not presented as a pooled estimate. The supplied sources do not substantiate a universal 5–7-day infection threshold.

The anesthesia-specific evidence is thin. The EVD placement review is not an anesthesia reference; ASA monitoring and recovery standards do not fill the gap in procedure-specific airway or anesthetic technique.
evidenceGaps: Adult EVD-specific guidance for selecting local anesthesia, monitored anesthesia care, or general anesthesia, including airway strategy and anesthetic drugs.
A directly applicable EVD-specific preoperative protocol for anticoagulation/coagulation assessment and reversal.
An authoritative, procedure-specific transport and clamping protocol to resolve the conflicting review recommendations.
EVD-specific analgesia and PONV guidance, and an emergence or extubation approach.
corrections: Removed the unverified MAC and drug recipe; the EVD sources do not prescribe an anesthetic technique or anesthetic agents.
Removed the unverified 30-degree head-of-bed position; the placement review describes a different procedural position, which is not treated here as an anesthesia mandate.
Corrected the claim that rapid drainage is not a concern: the review identifies a rebleeding concern with rapid CSF drainage in unsecured aneurysmal SAH.
Removed the asserted 5–7-day infection threshold; the supplied evidence notes duration as a possible risk factor but does not establish that threshold.

Did not recommend routine antibiotic-impregnated catheters or systemic antibiotic prophylaxis as a universal practice; the reviews describe these approaches but do not establish a single procedure-specific standard.

reports.title: Intracranial Aneurysm Coiling (Endovascular)
reviewNotes: Base44's claim that GA and an ETT are required is too absolute: the sources describe GA as common and useful for immobility, but coiling may be performed under local or general anesthesia.

A pre-induction arterial line, a specific MAP range, and a single ACT target are not universal requirements established by the supplied evidence. Select monitoring and anticoagulation in coordination with the interventionist and patient-specific plan.

The blanket instruction to reverse heparin immediately for every suspected perforation omits the review's caution that protamine may be skipped when rapid mechanical hemostasis is achievable and should not delay it.
The provided sources do not establish nimodipine prophylaxis for all SAH patients, nor do they establish the Base44 analgesia, extubation, or access-site surveillance recipe as a universal protocol.
evidenceGaps: Contemporary, procedure-specific guidance for individualized blood-pressure and cerebral-perfusion goals across ruptured aneurysm, unruptured aneurysm, and vasospasm states.
A standardized anesthetic and recovery pathway, including patient-selection criteria for local anesthesia versus general anesthesia and criteria for extubation or ICU disposition.
Current guidance for antiplatelet and anticoagulant management in ruptured aneurysm coiling, especially when stent-assisted treatment is planned.
Procedure-specific analgesia and PONV guidance; the supplied sources explicitly do not provide a coiling analgesia regimen.
corrections: Removed the assertion that GA and ETT are required for every case; source evidence allows local or general anesthesia and does not prescribe a universal airway device.
Removed fixed MAP targets and a universal ACT target; the supplied evidence supports individualized pressure and anticoagulation management rather than one target for all cases.
Qualified protamine reversal: mechanical hemorrhage control should not be delayed, and the review describes circumstances in which protamine may be skipped.
Removed the unsupported claim that nimodipine is given to all SAH patients; the provided sources do not substantiate that prophylaxis claim.
Removed unverified routine Foley, femoral-access-site, and minimal-pain claims as universal requirements.

reports.title: Lumbar Laminectomy / Decompression
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. The exact MAP threshold, routine Foley, routine SSEP use, fluid volume, expected blood loss, ketorolac/acetaminophen regimen, and specific intrathecal-morphine duration were not adopted as general recommendations.
The claim that cauda equina syndrome is emergent is not supported by the supplied sources; do not infer or repeat it as a sourced reference statement.

The prone abdominal-free positioning claim is supported by the regional-anesthesia review, which describes increased epidural venous pressure and bleeding risk; it does not quantify the effect or establish a blood-loss protocol.

Source 0 is a narrative review with heterogeneous evidence and no consensus on optimal anesthetic choice. Source 1 is also a narrative review and institutional-experience report, not a clinical practice guideline.
Source 2 is an educational manual with no stated publication date or evidence grading; its spinal-reconstruction material was not used to set routine lumbar-laminectomy practice.
The supplied material includes no obstetric-specific lumbar-decompression guidance. This adult reference does not establish pregnancy-specific anesthetic recommendations.

The supplied sources do not provide a complete preoperative assessment protocol specific to adult lumbar laminectomy/decompression. The spinal-anesthesia eligibility factors are from a narrative review and should not be treated as a comprehensive assessment or universal exclusion criteria.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not address urgency or anesthetic implications for lumbar decompression in cauda equina syndrome.
The sources do not provide a detailed, procedure-specific postoperative neurologic assessment or escalation pathway for lumbar decompression.
corrections: Removed the Base44 assertion that cauda equina syndrome with bowel/bladder involvement is emergent: it is not substantiated in the supplied evidence.
Removed the fixed MAP target, routine SSEP statement, and routine Foley claim because the supplied evidence does not establish them as universal practice for lumbar decompression.
Removed the fixed crystalloid volume and single-level blood-loss characterization; the spinal-anesthesia review explicitly provides no fluid regimen or lumbar blood-loss data.
Removed the fixed postoperative ketorolac/acetaminophen/opioid regimen and the claimed 12–24-hour intrathecal-morphine duration because the supplied sources do not support those details.
Qualified spinal anesthesia as an option for selected elective cases rather than treating it as interchangeable with general anesthesia for every lumbar decompression.

reports.title: Mechanical Thrombectomy for Ischemic Stroke
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, the claim that MAC is strongly preferred and improves neurologic outcomes is not supported by the supplied review, which describes unresolved choice and no significant difference in cited functional outcomes.

The supplied review states a preoperative blood-pressure range of 140–160 mmHg, while another source describes permissive hypertension before recanalization. These statements do not establish a universal phase-specific target; the Base44 targets of 140–180 before and below 160 after recanalization were not adopted.

Specific sedative or induction recipes, heparin use, and a blanket BP threshold are not supported as universal thrombectomy practice by these sources. Trial regimens in the review are reported study protocols, not recommendations.

The manual's detailed interventional-neuroradiology material includes other procedures and is older, lacks stated publication date and references, and includes content not specific to thrombectomy. It was used only cautiously for general procedural-catastrophe context.
Source 1 is an educational summary last updated in 2026; its broad statements about common anesthesia practice do not override procedure-specific uncertainty in source 0.

The supplied sources do not substantiate the flagged list of procedural complications for mechanical thrombectomy; source 2 discusses some complications in other neurointerventional procedures, which does not establish them for this procedure.
The supplied mechanical-thrombectomy source does not specify repeat-imaging timing or a universal repeat-imaging protocol.
evidenceGaps: A thrombectomy-specific, phase-specific blood-pressure target, particularly after recanalization, is not established in the supplied sources.
The supplied sources do not establish a thrombectomy-specific anticoagulation strategy or management protocol for procedure-related hemorrhage.
complications: The supplied sources do not support this list of mechanical-thrombectomy complications or the proposed response guidance.
corrections: Removed the Base44 claim that MAC is strongly preferred and associated with better neurologic outcomes; evidence supplied supports individualized choice and reports no significant functional-outcome difference in cited reviews.
Removed the Base44 pre-recanalization SBP 140–180 and post-recanalization SBP below 160 targets; these exact targets are not established by the supplied sources.
Removed the specified dexmedetomidine/propofol and ketamine/succinylcholine recipes; the sources do not support them as recommended universal regimens.
Removed the claim that each 10-minute delay costs approximately one million neurons; that numerical claim is unsupported by the supplied source content.
Did not impose supine positioning, two large-bore IVs, routine arterial-line placement, or a specific fluid regimen as universal requirements.

reports.title: MEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
reviewNotes: Base44's categorical claim that neuromuscular blockade must never be used is stronger than the sources: one review says blockers decrease or abolish MEPs, while the spine authors generally avoid them. The draft advises minimizing or avoiding blockade during recording and coordinating its use with the monitoring team.

The sources conflict on volatile-agent tolerance: one review warns that low doses can abolish Tc-mMEPs; another reports that below 0.5 MAC should generally allow acceptable signals. The draft presents no concentration as a guaranteed threshold and favors a stable propofol-based technique.

A greater-than-50% amplitude decrement is not established as a universal surgical emergency criterion. The cited review describes it as one laboratory's potential alarm criterion for brain surgery and says criteria remain debated.

The supplied evidence does not support Base44's mandatory bite block, universal ETT requirement, MAP greater than 80 target, or claims of MEP-specific tongue injury, seizures, or cardiac arrhythmia. These claims were not carried forward as clinical instructions.

The pacemaker/device issue is unresolved in the supplied sources: one older review lists devices among contraindications, while Base44 suggests checking compatibility. The draft flags consultation rather than asserting a universal prohibition or clearance.
The supplied excerpts do not establish a postoperative nausea and vomiting regimen.
evidenceGaps: No supplied source establishes device-specific safety or eligibility criteria for TES in patients with pacemakers, ICDs, or other implanted devices.
No supplied source substantiates the case-specific bite-block and TES-related oral injury claim or establishes a universal airway plan for MEP-monitored surgery.
No procedure-specific adult source establishes an MEP monitoring protocol or case-specific alarm threshold for the operation intended by the case record.
corrections: Removed Base44's absolute prohibition on all neuromuscular blockade; retained the supported point that blockade can degrade or abolish muscle MEPs and is generally minimized or avoided during recording.
Removed the fixed volatile-anesthetic threshold as a guaranteed safe boundary; sources differ on tolerance, and one reports suppression or abolition even at low doses.
Removed the universal greater-than-50% MEP-drop emergency claim; the threshold is reported as laboratory practice for a limited context, not consensus.
Removed unsupported assertions that an ETT, bite block, MAP above 80, or TIVA is mandatory in every case.
Removed unsupported MEP-specific complication claims and drug adjunct dosing.

reports.title: Neuro-Angiography / Cerebral Angiogram (Diagnostic)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. Its propofol-based MAC/maintenance plan, dexmedetomidine adjunct, fixed airway-selection rules, and routine anesthetic drug recipe are not supported by the neuroangiography sources.

The source-supported conscious-sedation description is fentanyl plus midazolam; the sources do not establish that combination as mandatory or provide doses. General anesthesia is described as an option for complex intervention or inadequate cooperation, without a specified regimen or airway technique.

Base44's radial positioning, fixed saline volume, specific ACT monitoring instruction, and sheath-removal timing are not presented as universal diagnostic-angiography practice in the applicable reviews. No universal systemic anticoagulation or ACT target is asserted.
Contrast-allergy prophylaxis is described by the reviews, but exact drug doses were omitted. The fetched material does not provide a specific contrast-anaphylaxis response protocol.

The 2013 and 2020 procedure reviews are narrative reviews and contain institutional preferences; the undated neuroanesthesia manual is educational material without evidence grading. Generic ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards support monitoring and recovery requirements but do not resolve neuroangiography-specific anesthetic choices.
evidenceGaps: A current, adult diagnostic-neuroangiography-specific protocol for recognition and management of severe contrast reactions.

A current, procedure-specific anticoagulation and access-site management guideline that addresses how decisions vary with access route, patient risk, and planned intervention; the available material does not establish a universal target.
Comparative or guideline-level evidence for anesthetic technique and airway strategy in adult diagnostic neuroangiography, including thresholds for choosing general anesthesia.
corrections: Removed the unsupported fixed MAC/propofol induction and maintenance recipe and dexmedetomidine adjunct.
Removed automatic ETT use for specified patient groups and any implication that diagnostic neuroangiography routinely requires general anesthesia.
Removed the fixed IV hydration volume and replaced it with source-supported saline hydration for renal insufficiency without a specified volume or rate.
Removed fixed radial positioning, routine ACT target/monitoring assertions, and a universal femoral sheath-removal protocol.
Omitted exact contrast-allergy premedication doses and unsubstantiated claims about a specific postoperative analgesic or PONV regimen.

reports.title: Spinal Cord Stimulator (SCS) Implantation
reviewNotes: Base44 is unauthenticated case material, not evidence. Removed its fixed dexmedetomidine/propofol plan, ketorolac and acetaminophen regimen, and claim that MAC with a natural airway is the universal approach; supplied sources do not establish these as routine SCS prescriptions.

Corrected the implication that every lead placement requires an awake patient: feedback is important for traditional paresthesia mapping, but paresthesia-free anatomical placement and selected deep-sedation or GA circumstances are described.
Did not reproduce the fixed anticoagulant stop intervals or bridging advice. The SCS review refers to ASRA guidance but the applicable detailed guideline is not among the supplied sources.

Did not repeat the blanket statement 'no MRI after permanent implant.' The supplied material does not establish MRI restrictions for all implanted systems; device-specific compatibility and instructions are unresolved.
Did not assert a routine prone-to-supine sequence for IPG pocket work, a specific anesthetic drug or dose, or postoperative analgesic recipe; the sources do not establish these as universal practice.

The survey's reported complication experience is not a reliable estimate of incidence: total case denominators and details were unavailable, and the article itself describes substantial survey limitations.
evidenceGaps: Current, applicable antithrombotic/neuraxial-procedure guidance is needed for case-specific interruption, restart, and coordination decisions; the provided SCS review only refers generally to ASRA guidance.
Device-specific MRI compatibility and postimplant instructions are not established by the supplied sources; verify against the implanted system's labeling and specialist guidance.

SCS-specific anesthetic drug selection, airway strategy, postoperative analgesia/PONV approach, and discharge criteria are not defined by the supplied sources; these remain individualized rather than universal prescriptions.
corrections: Removed Base44's specific dexmedetomidine and propofol infusion recommendations; no source supplies an SCS anesthetic drug regimen or doses.
Removed fixed warfarin, LMWH, and antiplatelet holding intervals and bridging instructions; these are not supported by a supplied full applicable guideline.
Removed the universal 'no MRI after permanent implant' instruction; MRI compatibility is device-specific and is not resolved by these sources.
Removed the Base44 postoperative acetaminophen-plus-ketorolac and minimal-opioid prescription; the SCS sources do not provide a postoperative analgesic protocol.
Qualified the requirement for patient wakefulness: it applies to feedback-dependent paresthesia mapping, not every SCS system or placement technique.
Removed claims of a universal natural-airway MAC technique and fixed positioning sequence; prone airway access and anesthetic choice require individualized assessment.

reports.title: Spinal Fusion (TLIF/PLIF)
reviewNotes: Base44 material was audited, not treated as evidence. Claims that TIVA is the standard, that neuromuscular blockade must never be used after intubation, or that a fixed MAP target protects the cord are not established for all TLIF/PLIF cases by the supplied sources.

Do not label cell salvage mandatory, prescribe a fixed TXA regimen, fluid balance, transfusion trigger, or universal arterial-line requirement. The complex-fusion review supports consideration according to extent and clinical circumstances.

The orientation manual describes controlled hypotension for spinal reconstruction, whereas the more focused complex-fusion review advises against deliberate hypotension because of cardiac and neurologic risks. This draft follows the latter and emphasizes individualized perfusion goals.

Base44’s liposomal-bupivacaine claim is not supported for complex multilevel procedures in the review; the source describes benefit as unestablished. A specific postoperative MRI directive for new deficits is not established in the supplied evidence.
evidenceGaps: A TLIF/PLIF-specific airway and prone-turn management reference, including case-specific extubation considerations, is not provided.
The sources do not specify a TLIF/PLIF-specific pathway for urgent evaluation and imaging of a new postoperative neurologic deficit.
corrections: Removed fixed MAP targets and the claim that one numeric pressure threshold universally protects spinal cord perfusion; sources support avoiding hypotension and individualizing perfusion goals.
Corrected “TIVA is the standard” to TIVA is often chosen; the review also describes a balanced technique that can preserve monitoring in many cases.
Removed routine prohibition of neuromuscular blockade with EMG and blanket claims about drug selection; the sources do not establish those as universal TLIF/PLIF rules.
Removed mandatory cell salvage, a fixed TXA dose, fixed transfusion threshold, target fluid balance, and universal arterial-line requirement.
Removed specific prone airway-device, eye-taping, and repositioning prescriptions not established by the supplied TLIF/PLIF sources.

reports.title: SSEP Monitoring — Anesthesia Considerations
reviewNotes: Base44’s proposed MAP >80 is not supported as a universal SSEP target. The review describes signal effects relative to autoregulatory thresholds and says safe combined blood-pressure and hematocrit thresholds cannot be precisely defined.

The claim that 50–60% nitrous oxide is an acceptable, minimally suppressive adjunct is misleading for cortical SSEPs: the review reports substantial amplitude reduction and potentiation of other anesthetic effects.

The claim that more than 1 MAC necessarily makes all SSEP interpretation unreliable is overbroad. The review distinguishes volatile agent, nitrous oxide use, and cortical versus subcortical responses; it describes different compatibility conditions.
TIVA is not a guarantee of stable signals. Propofol–opioid infusion without nitrous oxide is described as appealing, but some intravenous regimens can reduce amplitude substantially.
Muscle relaxants do not directly influence SSEPs, but this is modality-specific and must not be generalized to MEP monitoring, where blockade can impair recordings.

The proposed routine ETT, unrestricted use of muscle relaxants, fixed MAP target, and specific postoperative neurologic assessment timing are not established as universal SSEP requirements by the supplied evidence.
evidenceGaps: The case record does not identify the specific operation or neural structures at risk; therefore a procedure-specific airway, positioning, access, and critical-phase plan remains unresolved.
SSEP warning criteria remain empirical, with no clear consensus or definitive multicenter evidence establishing predictive performance.
corrections: Removed the unsupported universal MAP >80 target; perfusion goals must be individualized to the procedure and patient.
Corrected the description of nitrous oxide as an acceptable, minimally suppressive SSEP adjunct; supplied evidence reports substantial cortical amplitude depression and potentiation of other agents.
Replaced the categorical >1 MAC interpretation claim with qualified, modality- and combination-dependent volatile anesthetic effects.
Recast propofol–opioid TIVA as an appealing option rather than the guaranteed most stable or interpretable technique.
Limited the no-effect muscle-relaxant claim to direct SSEP effects; it does not apply to MEP monitoring.
Did not adopt the unsupported universal ETT, free use of paralysis, or fixed baseline timing claims as mandatory practice.

reports.title: Subdural / Epidural Hematoma Evacuation
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. The draft omits unsupported fixed anesthetic drug recipes, a universal MAP/CPP target, routine mannitol dosing, and a blanket extubation plan.
The supplied TBI review summarizes CPP 50–70 mmHg and avoidance of SBP below 90 mmHg; the Base44 target of MAP above 80 and CPP above 60 is not adopted as a universal target.
The review cautions that ketamine has been associated with increased CBF and ICP in raised-ICP risk; the Base44 ketamine-based induction recipe is not supported by this source and is omitted.
The Base44 claim that anticoagulation must be reversed before incision is not supported by the supplied sources as a specific protocol. No agent, timing, or reversal threshold is prescribed here.

The supplied evidence does not substantiate a middle-meningeal-artery-specific EDH management protocol, bridging-vein rebleeding protocol, seizure-prophylaxis regimen, or a predictable hemodynamic drop after decompression.
The review is from 2011 and notes limited research in immediate perioperative TBI management. The source set does not include a current procedure-specific society guideline for SDH/EDH evacuation.
evidenceGaps: Current procedure-specific adult guidance differentiating perioperative management of acute versus chronic SDH and EDH, including surgical approach and positioning.
A current, indication-specific anticoagulant and antiplatelet reversal protocol for intracranial hematoma evacuation.
Procedure-specific guidance for postoperative seizure prophylaxis and management of anticoagulation resumption.
Contemporary evidence for postoperative disposition and extubation criteria specific to adult SDH/EDH evacuation.
corrections: Removed the unsupported Base44 ketamine-plus-succinylcholine induction recipe and lidocaine pretreatment instruction.
Removed fixed MAP/CPP goals, mannitol dose, and routine hyperventilation as universal directions; retained source-supported principles and clinical qualifiers.
Removed blanket statements that anticoagulation must be reversed before incision and that all acute cases should remain intubated.
Removed unsupported EDH middle meningeal artery and SDH bridging-vein-specific operative claims, as well as the claimed predictable hemodynamic drop following decompression.
Did not present seizure prophylaxis, postoperative anticoagulation management, or PONV treatment as established by the supplied evidence.

reports.title: TLIF / OLIF / ALIF (Lumbar Interbody Fusion)
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields were treated as unverified, not as evidence. Much of the supplied procedure-specific evidence concerns MIS-TLIF; OLIF- and ALIF-specific anesthesia claims cannot be confirmed from these sources.

Do not retain as established recommendations the Base44 claims for a particular TXA dose or benefit, a fixed MAP target, mandatory TIVA, dexamethasone, no neuromuscular blockade after intubation, or a fixed fluid volume. The procedure-specific review does not report these protocols or targets.

The supplied sources do not substantiate routine vascular-surgeon participation, bowel preparation for OLIF, a universal massive-transfusion setup, or a claim that one approach has a particular dominant feared complication. Major-vessel injury is identified only as a possible hazard of anterior longitudinal ligament violation during TLIF work.

The Base44 analgesic suggestions (including ketorolac, intrathecal morphine, and erector spinae plane block) and PONV plan are not established as procedure-specific recommendations by the supplied sources. A general review discusses selected regional and neuraxial options, with limitations including possible impairment of neurologic assessment.

The awake endoscopic technique is described in a technical note and should remain a selected reported technique, not a default for lumbar fusion. The source also reports conversions to general anesthesia, supporting careful selection and conversion planning rather than broad adoption.
The neuroanesthesia manual is educational and not approach-specific; its spinal reconstruction discussion should not be treated as direct guidance for TLIF, OLIF, or ALIF.
evidenceGaps: Approach-specific anesthesia and complication evidence for OLIF and ALIF, including access-related vascular, neural, and visceral risks and team requirements.
Procedure-specific airway, ventilation, neuromonitoring anesthetic-management, and physiologic response protocols for TLIF, OLIF, and ALIF.
Approach- and extent-specific blood-management evidence, including when blood conservation resources or blood products are appropriate.
Procedure-specific evidence for postoperative analgesia, PONV prevention, and recovery pathways.
corrections: Removed unverified fixed TXA dosing, asserted blood-loss reduction, fixed MAP goal, mandatory TIVA, dexamethasone dosing, and blanket prohibition on neuromuscular blockade.
Removed fixed crystalloid volume, routine cell-saver or blood-availability requirements, and universal arterial-line requirements.
Removed unsubstantiated OLIF bowel-prep and lumbar-plexus-injury claims, and ALIF vascular-surgeon, aorta/IVC mobilization, massive-transfusion activation, and greatest-feared-complication claims.
Removed unsupported routine ketorolac, intrathecal morphine, erector spinae plane block, and PONV medication recommendations.
Corrected the scope: supplied procedural sources chiefly describe MIS-TLIF and do not establish perioperative practice for OLIF or ALIF.

reports.title: Transsphenoidal Pituitary Surgery (TSPS / Endoscopic)
reviewNotes: The case fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. The source material supports transsphenoidal surgery for pituitary tumours/adenomas, but does not substantiate every tumour indication listed in the case fields.

The newer procedure-specific review generally advises avoiding NSAIDs because of bleeding concerns; this conflicts with the case field’s ketorolac suggestion. The draft reports the conflict rather than endorsing a regimen.
Do not use the case field’s fixed crystalloid volume or its urine-output threshold as a universal target. The supplied review gives a DI monitoring approach but no routine fluid regimen.
The case-field claim that SIADH typically occurs on days 7–10 is not substantiated by the supplied sources. Postoperative SIADH/hyponatraemia surveillance remains an evidence gap here.

The source’s institutional hydrocortisone regimen is not presented as a universal recommendation; steroid management varies, and ACTH-secreting Cushing’s disease is specifically treated as an exception to routine stress-dose replacement.

Source 1 is the most detailed procedure-specific review; source 0 is an educational summary. Source 4 supplies general monitoring standards, not a pituitary-specific protocol. No source establishes that any single URL makes an individual case safe.
The supplied review does not specify a routine fluid regimen, transfusion threshold, or case-specific blood-loss target.
evidenceGaps: A postoperative SIADH/hyponatraemia surveillance and management protocol specific to pituitary surgery is not established by the supplied sources.
There is no uniform perioperative steroid-replacement regimen in the supplied evidence; local protocol and endocrinology input remain necessary.
corrections: Removed the unsupported routine indication for craniopharyngioma from the case-field procedure description; the supplied procedure-specific review principally describes pituitary tumours and adenomas.
Did not repeat a fixed crystalloid volume, routine ketorolac plan, or specified DI urine-output trigger from the unverified case fields.

Corrected any implication that all patients require an arterial line, Foley catheter, central line, awake intubation, or the same airway device; the sources support consideration according to risk and case complexity.
Did not present TIVA, dexamethasone, glycopyrrolate, cocaine, or oxymetazoline as mandatory routine choices; the supplied evidence does not establish those case-field recipes as universal practice.
Did not repeat the claimed SIADH day 7–10 timing, which is absent from the supplied evidence.
Did not present a single postoperative CPAP rule; the source reports no clear guidance or consensus.

reports.title: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) Shunt Placement / Revision
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not substantiate its specific induction drugs, airway-device options, fixed fluid volume, analgesic regimen, or MRI/OR-equipment-related programmable-valve reset and reprogramming claims.
The VP-shunt source discusses pediatric patients as well as adults but supplies no adult-specific anesthetic regimen; pediatric details were not used to establish adult practice.

The general neuroanesthesia manual is an educational source spanning several operations. Its raised-ICP and pneumocephalus statements are qualified rather than converted into universal VP-shunt requirements.

The scalp-block review concerns craniotomy and does not establish a VP-shunt analgesic technique. The quantitative neuromuscular monitoring recommendation is included only when neuromuscular blockade is used.
No source establishes a universal airway device, drug recipe, fluid total, blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, perfusion target, or emergence protocol for adult VP-shunt surgery.
The supplied VP-shunt source does not establish a procedure-specific fluid or perfusion target; no clinical target or management recommendation is supported by the provided evidence.
evidenceGaps: Adult VP-shunt-specific anesthetic guidance for airway strategy, anesthetic technique, ventilation targets, and intraoperative monitoring beyond general anesthesia standards.
Adult VP-shunt-specific guidance for fluid, bleeding, and perfusion management; analgesia and PONV; and emergence and postoperative neurologic-care planning.
Evidence-based perioperative management of programmable valves, including whether and when programming checks are needed after relevant imaging or equipment exposure.
Source-supported management of shunt infection and decisions about infected hardware in the perioperative setting.
fluids: This is a source limitation, not a clinical fluid-management recommendation, so it belongs in the evidence section.
corrections: Removed Base44-specific drug combinations and dosing, lidocaine before laryngoscopy, LMA use for selected revisions, and a fixed fluid volume because the supplied sources do not support these as adult VP-shunt recommendations.
Removed the claim that nitrous oxide must be avoided in every VP-shunt case; the neuroanesthesia source makes the precaution conditional on pneumocephalus or decreased intracranial compliance.
Removed the claim that programmable shunts are reset by MRI or OR equipment and require postoperative reprogramming; this is not supported by the supplied evidence.
Did not carry forward Base44’s specific postoperative analgesic regimen, mandatory Foley, or other case-specific setup assertions as source-established practice.

reports.title: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not as evidence. Omitted unsupported fixed positioning, IV gauge, room equipment, hyperventilation and ETCO₂ targets, fluid assumptions, and specific drug regimens.

The Base44 seizure-duration claims are not carried forward as universal targets. The ECT review reports motor seizure duration of 25–50 seconds; EEG duration is approximately 5 seconds longer than motor duration. These measures should not be conflated.

Base44’s claimed typical course of 12–15 sessions differs from the ECT review’s 6–12 treatments per course; the draft states the sourced range and notes that treatment continues according to response.

Base44 advises holding benzodiazepines and makes specific antihypertensive exceptions; the ECT review instead says usual medications are generally continued, with listed exceptions, and notes that beta-blockers and other antihypertensives may interfere with seizure generation but may be indicated.
No source supports routine hyperventilation to a specified ETCO₂, a universal ECT airway device, a fixed fluid regimen, or a standard ECT discharge time.
Drug doses appearing in the supplied sources have been excluded from the clinical reference.
The NORA source is a general narrative-review abstract and does not provide ECT-specific setting recommendations.
The ECT review does not specify positioning or vascular-access recommendations.
evidenceGaps: The ECT-specific sources do not establish a standardized vascular-access, fluid-management, or bleeding-management protocol; these details remain dependent on the individual setting and patient.
setup: Preserves the source limitation as evidence-scope information and removes commentary about unverified case fields.
corrections: Removed unverified Base44 drug doses, medication-holding instructions, and fixed hemodynamic treatment regimens.
Removed the unverified claim that a specified level of hyperventilation or ETCO₂ is essential for seizure optimization.
Removed fixed positioning, airway, bite-block timing beyond placement before stimulation, and vascular-access claims not established by the supplied ECT sources.
Corrected the seizure-duration summary to distinguish the review’s motor-duration range from EEG duration.
Did not assert same-day discharge, rapid orientation by a fixed time, or a universal recovery duration.

reports.title: ICU Bedside Procedures Under Anesthesia / Sedation
reviewNotes: The case-field drug doses, preferred-agent claims, and infusion suggestions are not supported by the supplied sources; they are not reproduced as clinical recommendations.
The assertion that ICU patients are never fasted, and the blanket RSI implication, are not established by these sources. Airway decisions are described only in limited, procedure-specific contexts.
The mandatory bronchoscopic-guidance/two-person-team claim for PDT, and specific chest-tube, tracheostomy, and wound-debridement management claims, lack supporting evidence in the supplied sources.

The ASA monitoring standards are applicable general standards; they do not validate a specific portable equipment kit, arterial/CVP line requirement, defibrillator-in-room rule, or universal bedside setup.
The ICU endoscopy mini review and bedside procedural-anesthesia abstract are limited in scope. Remote-location closed-claims concerns are not an ICU-procedure-specific quantified risk estimate.

The supplied sources do not establish a case-wide blood-product threshold, crossmatch policy, fluid total, or procedure-specific bleeding plan; the relevant source summaries state that fluid and bleeding guidance is not specified or addressed.
The supplied sources do not establish a universal return-to-prior-sedation or ventilator-setting protocol; the source summaries do not provide a specific emergence or ventilator-transition protocol.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific anesthesia and airway guidance for ICU bedside tracheostomy/PDT, chest tube placement, feeding tube placement, and wound debridement, including any proposed bronchoscopic-guidance requirement.
Case-specific anesthetic regimen, procedure-specific ventilator management, and procedural physiologic targets for this heterogeneous set of bedside procedures.
Procedure-specific fluid, bleeding, and recovery recommendations beyond the general anesthesia and postanesthesia standards provided.
fluids: This is an evidence-scope limitation, not a supported clinical instruction.
emergence: This is an evidence-scope limitation, not a supported clinical instruction.
corrections: Removed the case-field propofol, ketamine, fentanyl, and infusion doses because no supplied source supports those regimens or doses.
Removed the claim that ketamine is generally preferred for vasopressor-dependent ICU bedside procedures; the supplied sources do not compare agents for that indication.
Removed universal full-stomach/RSI language, automatic adjustment of pre-existing sedation, and mandatory return to a prior sedation level because the sources do not establish those as general rules.
Removed unsupported universal arterial line/CVP, defibrillator-in-room, reversal-agent, blood-product, and bedside drug-kit requirements.
Corrected the broad claim that PDT must always use bronchoscopic guidance and a two-person team: no supplied source supports it.

reports.title: MRI Under Anesthesia (Adult)
reviewNotes: Base44’s proposed named drug preferences (including propofol target-controlled infusion and dexmedetomidine as 'ideal'), and its specific airway-by-population recipes, are not established by these sources; the ASA advisory explicitly does not address specific drug choices.

The claim that nasal-cannula ETCO2 is universally mandatory for every adult in the bore is too absolute. The supplied ASA monitoring advice calls for expired-CO2 monitoring in deep sedation and in moderate sedation when ventilation cannot be directly observed, subject to limitations of patient, procedure, or equipment.

The Base44 fixed 60–90-second emergency extraction claim, named anesthesia-machine examples, and assertion that a battery-equipped laryngoscope is necessarily ferromagnetic/projectile are not supported by the supplied evidence. Equipment status must be verified for the specific device and location.

Do not convert the advisory’s conditional emergency instructions into automatic quench or evacuation directions. It describes following institutional protocol, removing the patient from zone IV if possible, and persistent magnetic-field hazards after some environmental emergencies.

Pediatric sedation and temperature findings in the sources were not used to establish adult practice. General adult-relevant safety principles were retained only where supported by the MRI advisory or general standards.
evidenceGaps: The supplied evidence does not provide a device-by-device adult MRI clearance protocol or the local operational criteria for managing particular implanted devices; these require the facility’s MRI safety process and relevant device expertise.
The supplied evidence does not establish comparative adult-specific anesthetic drug selection or dosing for MRI.
corrections: Removed universal claims that one anesthetic drug is most reliable or ideal; sources do not establish a preferred MRI drug regimen.
Corrected universal mandatory nasal-cannula capnography to the source-supported sedation monitoring qualification for expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring.
Removed unsupported 60–90-second extraction timing and categorical claims about specific named equipment or battery-containing laryngoscopes.

Replaced categorical device prohibitions with screening and device-specific compatibility assessment; the advisory describes some devices as generally hazardous while recognizing conditional devices and planned exceptions.
Removed pediatric-specific technique and recovery claims from adult guidance.

reports.title: Radiation Oncology Anesthesia (SBRT / SRS / Proton) (Adult)
reviewNotes: The Base44 assertion that anesthesia personnel cannot be present in the room during radiation is not a stand-alone safety instruction: the textbook describes evacuation, while ASA standards require continuous qualified-personnel presence and separately address direct hazards requiring remote observation. Site-specific radiation safety and anesthesia leadership must reconcile the workflow.

Base44 claims that TIVA is preferred, that propofol/dexmedetomidine/remifentanil regimens are ideal, and that a particular ETCO₂ alarm mandates immediate entry are not established as adult radiation-specific recommendations by these sources. The textbook's drug descriptions and pediatric proton series do not establish routine adult regimens.

The supplied sources do not substantiate a universal SBRT/SRS/proton airway device, vault equipment layout, emergency-stop-button specification, MRI-linac protocol, fixed duration, or adult proton anesthetic plan.

The claim that Gamma Knife frame placement should occur before anesthesia and that blood thinners must be held is not established as a general anesthetic instruction by the supplied evidence. The AANS source describes frame placement with local anesthetic but gives no anticoagulant holding protocol.
The case record's broad pediatric-dominant framing cannot be used to infer adult practice. AANS supports adult SRS being commonly awake, while adult-specific anesthesia details remain sparse.
evidenceGaps: Adult-specific anesthesia approach and outcomes for SBRT and proton beam therapy are not resolved by the supplied sources; the proton-series evidence is explicitly pediatric.

A validated, site-specific radiation-vault workflow reconciling radiation-room evacuation, remote observation, emergency access, and applicable anesthesia personnel-presence standards is not supplied.
corrections: Removed Base44's preferred-TIVA and named-drug recipe claims as unsupported adult case-specific recommendations.

Removed the asserted universal immediate-entry response to any loss of capnography waveform; retained ventilation monitoring and coordinated access as priorities without inventing an emergency algorithm.
Removed unsupported claims for specific equipment placement, emergency-stop controls, radiation-team entry rules, and MRI-linac precautions.
Corrected the implication that all SRS requires general anesthesia: the supplied sources describe adults as often awake or lightly sedated, with general anesthesia for selected circumstances.
Did not carry forward the instruction to confirm blood thinners have been held; no applicable anticoagulant-management evidence was provided.

reports.title: Cesarean Section (Elective)
reviewNotes: The Base44 claim that oxytocin must never be given as an IV bolus is overbroad: SOAP describes context-specific regimens that include a small, slow bolus and cautions against large, rapidly administered boluses. This draft avoids drug doses and directs use of applicable guidance.

The Base44 claim that a fixed crystalloid preload or total is required conflicts with obstetric guidance: fluid preload or coload may be used, but spinal anesthesia should not be delayed for a fixed volume.

Claims that a particular phenylephrine regimen is universally standard, that a specific block level or drug recipe is mandatory, or that a specific monitoring interval applies to every elective cesarean were not carried forward as universal prescriptions.
The supplied pain-statement pages have blank best-practice sections; they support attention to pain, communication, and possible supplementation, not a complete algorithm.
The general-anesthesia dosing and airway statements come from a review, not a procedure-specific guideline. No general-anesthesia recipe or universal airway technique is reproduced.
The ASA basic-monitoring and postanesthesia standards apply broadly, while obstetric neuraxial guidance addresses the relevant population. Their scopes should not be conflated.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not provide a complete, current obstetric hemorrhage-resuscitation or transfusion protocol; institutional obstetric hemorrhage guidance is needed for operational detail.
The supplied excerpts refer to SOAP neuraxial-morphine monitoring recommendations but do not reproduce the detailed monitoring protocol for delayed respiratory depression.
No complete obstetric general-anesthesia airway and ventilation algorithm is provided in the supplied sources.
corrections: Removed Base44 spinal anesthetic, intrathecal opioid, vasopressor, oxytocin, and other medication doses and infusion rates.
Removed the absolute statement that oxytocin must never be given by IV bolus; reconciled it with SOAP guidance against large, rapidly administered boluses.
Removed fixed fluid volumes, fixed blood-product availability claims, and universal crossmatch requirements; blood preparation is individualized to risk and policy.

Removed the universal assertion that an obstetric airway is always more difficult and the prescriptive difficult-airway recipe; retained readiness for airway complications and possible conversion to general anesthesia.

Removed unverified routine details including fixed fetal-monitoring timing, universal block targets, a guaranteed duration of spinal anesthesia or intrathecal analgesia, and specific PACU treatment instructions.

reports.title: Epidural Blood Patch
reviewNotes: The supplied Base44 fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. In particular, routine CBC/coagulation testing, IV access and BP monitoring, lateral or sitting positioning, optional midazolam, and a fixed 15–20 mL injection recipe are not established as universal practice by the applicable non-retracted EBP review.

The primary review describes prone positioning and fluoroscopic guidance; this draft does not claim those are mandatory in every clinical setting or that other positions are validated by the supplied evidence.

The Base44 claims of a 70–98% first-patch success rate, a 90%+ second-patch success rate, and a 20–30% repeat-patch rate are not carried forward as general expectations. The primary review reports variable estimates across studies.
The Base44 caffeine amount, optional midazolam dose, and specific medication recipe were omitted. The source material does not establish them as a universal EBP regimen.
The retracted source (index 1) was not used for clinical claims. Sources on cesarean recovery, obstetric anesthesia, and general anesthesia standards were not used to fill EBP-specific gaps.
evidenceGaps: The supplied non-retracted EBP review does not provide a complete decision pathway for evaluating atypical postpartum headache or distinguishing PDPH from other urgent diagnoses.
The supplied sources do not establish an EBP-specific consensus protocol for routine monitoring, sedation selection, or recovery/discharge criteria.
Platelet-threshold recommendations remain uncertain in the primary review: it reports safety findings above one threshold while its author advises against EBP below a higher threshold.
corrections: Removed universal confirmation of PDPH based on a fixed onset window and symptom list; the applicable non-retracted source supports individualized selection based on headache severity, conservative-treatment response, incapacitation, and patient activities.
Corrected routine conservative hydration language: the primary review finds no evidence for routine prophylactic fluid supplementation for PDPH.
Removed the claim that patients necessarily receive no sedation or require no monitoring; the review does not describe a sedation or routine monitoring protocol.
Removed the claim that caffeine plus acetaminophen and NSAIDs is a defined post-patch analgesia plan, and removed all unsupported medication doses.
Removed fixed EBP success-rate claims and the assertion that headache resolution should occur within a specific number of hours.
Clarified that supine positioning and activity restrictions are recommendations reported by the review, not evidence of a universal recovery or discharge protocol.

reports.title: External Cephalic Version (ECV)
reviewNotes: The supplied case fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, the stated neuraxial success increase of 30–40%, specified spinal bupivacaine regimen, routine pre-spinal fluid volume, nitroglycerin tocolysis, and fetal-bradycardia one-minute trigger are not supported as universal ECV recommendations by the supplied sources.

The claimed blanket contraindication for prior uterine surgery is overbroad: the review distinguishes prior classical cesarean from prior low-transverse cesarean. Oligohydramnios is a risk modifier in the sources, not uniformly a strict contraindication; polyhydramnios is not established as a contraindication in the supplied material.

The source describing immediate cesarean after failed ECV is an institutional procedural guide. The other review permits later or same-admission repeat attempts. The draft therefore does not present failed version alone as an automatic indication for immediate cesarean.
ECV complication estimates and neuraxial success estimates vary by source and context. No single percentage has been used as a guaranteed outcome or as a basis for routine anesthetic selection.

The ECV literature provided does not supply a standardized anesthesia protocol, fluid regimen, airway plan, or fixed recovery duration. Generic anesthesia standards support baseline monitoring but do not resolve ECV-specific choices.
evidenceGaps: Comparative, broadly applicable evidence to determine which ECV patients benefit sufficiently from neuraxial analgesia to justify routine use.
ECV-specific fluid and hemodynamic management guidance, including how best to prevent or treat neuraxial hypotension in this setting.

A broadly applicable ECV-specific escalation pathway defining fetal-status thresholds and timing for urgent delivery; the supplied sources advise abandoning significant bradycardia but do not establish a universal numerical trigger.
fluids: This is a source-scope limitation, not a clinical fluid-management recommendation.
corrections: Removed the fixed spinal bupivacaine dose and claim that it is the most common or established regimen; the ECV sources do not establish a universal anesthetic recipe.
Removed the assertion that neuraxial anesthesia increases success by 30–40%; the source review describes evidence as insufficient for universal recommendation and does not support that exact claim.
Removed routine 500 mL pre-spinal fluid and specific vasopressor instructions; ECV-specific fluid and vasopressor protocols are not supplied.
Removed nitroglycerin as an ECV preprocedural tocolytic; the ECV review explicitly does not support it for that indication.
Corrected the blanket prior-uterine-surgery contraindication and the claim that oligo/polyhydramnios are categorical contraindications.
Removed a fixed fetal-bradycardia duration threshold and universal immediate-cesarean rule after failed version; the supplied sources do not establish these as universal ECV triggers.

Removed a fixed post-ECV monitoring duration from clinical recommendations because the exact interval is supported here by a narrative review rather than an applicable full society guideline. The sources' differing follow-up approaches are described without presenting an institution's practice as universal.

reports.title: High-Risk Obstetric Anesthesia — Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy
reviewNotes: Audited the supplied case fields rather than treating them as evidence. Corrected the blanket claim that an arterial line is mandatory: the cardiac review says monitoring should be individualized and that arterial pressure monitoring may help selected lesions.

Removed the unsupported blanket requirement for ICU admission and fixed 24–48-hour monitoring. The supplied cardiac review says postpartum monitoring depends on disease and delivery events; the other cardiac review likewise describes condition-specific postpartum surveillance.

Reconciled the cardiac review’s advice to titrate oxytocin by infusion pump against the ERAC consensus statement’s scheduled-cesarean regimens. The latter is not cardiac-specific; this draft does not reproduce its dosing or apply it as a cardiac recommendation.

Did not reproduce the supplied field’s specific neuraxial aliquot volumes, general-anesthetic drug recipe, or universal vasopressor selection as routine prescriptions. The sources support individualized technique and lesion-specific goals, not one regimen for all cardiac disease.

The source evidence supports different priorities across lesions; it does not support treating severe aortic stenosis, HOCM, pulmonary hypertension, shunts, cardiomyopathy, and mechanical valves as physiologically interchangeable.
The cardiac sources do not provide a cardiac-specific postoperative analgesia or PONV regimen; the analgesia bullet was removed.
evidenceGaps: Patient-level lesion diagnosis, severity, ventricular function, symptoms, prior interventions, and current obstetric status are not supplied; these are necessary to establish an individual anesthetic plan or postpartum care location.

The available sources acknowledge limited evidence for cardiac anesthesia in pregnancy and do not resolve comparative outcomes for lesion-specific anesthetic techniques or a single integrated management pathway.
analgesia: The sources do not establish a cardiac-specific postoperative analgesia or PONV regimen; general cesarean recovery recommendations do not substantiate that cardiac-specific statement.
corrections: Removed the supplied claim that cardiac disease is the leading cause of maternal mortality in developed countries; the provided source content does not substantiate it.
Corrected “arterial line mandatory” to individualized consideration for selected lesions and circumstances.
Removed the claim that ICU admission and 24–48 hours of ICU monitoring are mandatory for every patient with cardiac disease.

Replaced “oxytocin bolus is contraindicated” with the cardiac review’s qualified support for infusion-pump titration because rapid bolus dosing can decrease systemic vascular resistance; generic ERAC dosing is not carried over.
Did not retain the supplied universal labor/cesarean neuraxial recipe, general-anesthetic induction recipe, or fixed vasopressor approach as source-supported routine practice.

reports.title: Labor Epidural Placement
reviewNotes: Base44 platelet wording was corrected: the SOAP consensus does not make platelet counts below 70,000 × 10⁶/L a general contraindication. It supports individualized decisions by etiology, bleeding history, DIC concern, competing risks, and patient preference.

Base44’s mandatory test-dose claim and its specific test-dose recipe are not established by the supplied obstetric guideline excerpts. The draft instead uses the supported safeguards of aspiration, incremental administration, and monitoring for intrathecal or intravascular signs.

Base44 anticoagulation stop intervals, PCEA volumes and lockout settings, fixed fluid volumes, and a universal T10 target were not adopted as prescriptions. The sources do not establish these as universally applicable labor-epidural instructions.

Base44’s blanket preference for phenylephrine was narrowed: the obstetric guideline says ephedrine or phenylephrine may be used and advises considering phenylephrine in the absence of maternal bradycardia.
Source 0 is a review with no stated systematic search or formal evidence-quality assessment. Its drug regimens and reported practice patterns are not treated as society standards.

The provided postanesthesia monitoring standard explicitly excludes its initial pulse-oximetry requirement for obstetrical patients receiving regional analgesia for labor and vaginal delivery; the draft relies on the obstetric neuraxial guideline for labor monitoring instead.
evidenceGaps: Specific anticoagulant or antithrombotic timing decisions for labor epidural placement and catheter removal are not established in the supplied labor-epidural sources; consult applicable current specialty guidance.
A detailed local-anesthetic systemic toxicity rescue pathway is not supplied; the available review describes recognition and broad support but not a complete obstetric rescue protocol.
corrections: Removed the unsupported Base44 claim that platelet counts below 70,000 are generally contraindicated; replaced it with the qualified SOAP consensus approach.
Removed the asserted mandatory epinephrine-containing test-dose recipe and its numeric interpretation criteria because the supplied sources do not establish them.

Removed fixed anticoagulation hold intervals, epidural loading and maintenance recipes, and fluid-volume recommendations that were not supported as universal instructions by an applicable full society guideline.
Removed the blanket claim that fever alone is never a contraindication; the supplied review describes epidural-related fever and infectious surveillance but does not establish that categorical rule.
Removed the broad claim that phenylephrine is always preferred; the obstetric guideline qualifies its consideration by maternal bradycardia and context.

reports.title: Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS) — Cesarean Hysterectomy
reviewNotes: Base44's automatic spinal-to-GA transition and RSI/drug recipes are not established as universal PAS practice. The sources describe several anesthetic options and one sequential strategy; they leave selection individualized.

Base44's TXA timing and repeat-dose schedule, 1:1:1 transfusion ratio, fibrinogen target, calcium-per-unit rule, and mandatory TEG/ROTEM schedule are not supported by the supplied PAS-specific sources. The review states that no standard PAS transfusion protocol is established.

A mandatory cordis, arterial line before induction, two anesthesia providers, MTP activation, and a hybrid OR are not established as universal requirements. The PAS recommendation describes access and monitoring as surgical preparation, while resources depend on the case and center.
REBOA is not supported in the supplied case-specific material. The sources discuss arterial balloon occlusion and embolization, with uncertain patient-specific benefit and risks.
Ureteral stents are not established as routine: the source says they may benefit selected percreta with lower invasion; it also says cystoscopy is not routinely recommended.

Base44's universal postoperative intubation, fixed extubation conditions, and prolonged ICU stay are not established. Sources support intensive postoperative care and note that ventilatory support is often necessary, without universal extubation criteria.

The ketorolac, acetaminophen, PCA, and epidural statements in Base44 are not a PAS-specific postoperative analgesia plan. Scheduled-cesarean ERAC guidance does not establish a regimen for cesarean hysterectomy with major hemorrhage or coagulopathy.

The blanket statement that epidural analgesia is not applicable because of coagulopathy is overbroad. The thrombocytopenia consensus calls for contextual risk-benefit assessment and does not establish a universal prohibition.
The source describes postoperative monitoring and reported risks, but does not supply a detailed PAS-specific postoperative treatment algorithm.
evidenceGaps: Institution-specific PAS hemorrhage activation criteria, product selection, transfusion endpoints, and coagulation-testing strategy are not resolved by the provided sources; no universal ratio or threshold is assumed here.
The PAS-specific criteria for choosing primary general, neuraxial, or sequential anesthesia—and when to convert—remain incompletely specified.
A PAS-specific airway and ventilation plan, including extubation criteria, is not provided.
A detailed postoperative analgesia and PONV regimen validated for cesarean hysterectomy with major hemorrhage is not provided.
Patient-selection criteria and comparative outcome evidence for balloon occlusion or embolization remain uncertain in the supplied sources.
corrections: Removed fixed TXA doses and timing, fixed 1:1:1 transfusion ratio, fibrinogen target, calcium-per-unit rule, and mandatory TEG/ROTEM schedule.
Recast automatic neuraxial-to-GA conversion, RSI, and specified induction drugs as individualized choices; no drug recipe is supplied.
Removed universal REBOA, hybrid-OR, MTP-running, two-provider, and cordis requirements.
Qualified arterial and central venous access as described preparation rather than universal mandates.
Qualified ureteral stents as potentially useful in selected invasion patterns; corrected the implication that cystoscopy is routine.
Removed universal ICU intubation, prolonged ICU stay, and fixed extubation criteria.
Removed Base44's PAS postoperative analgesic recipe and blanket epidural exclusion based on coagulopathy.

reports.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage Management
reviewNotes: Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. This draft omits the asserted vaginal threshold greater than 500 mL, mandatory QBL wording, TXA dose and repeat interval, fixed 1:1:1 component ratio, fibrinogen-first-factor claim and numeric target, fixed uterotonic/intervention sequence, induction and neuraxial drug recipes, routine CVP/cordis, q30-minute laboratory schedule, fixed position, and stated extubation criteria because the supplied evidence does not support them as universal PPH practice.
The hemorrhage review supports packed red cells and FFP in a 1:1 ratio with early platelet use; it does not establish the Base44 1:1:1 ratio as a universal protocol.
The evidence supports early TXA within three hours after birth, but the supplied major-hemorrhage review does not provide the Base44 dose or repeat-dose regimen.

The PPH review describes rapid fibrinogen decline and replacement options, but does not support the Base44 claim that fibrinogen is the first factor to decline or its specific target as a universal threshold.
The PPH-specific sources do not substantiate the Base44 ketorolac-based postoperative regimen, ICU sedation prescription, norepinephrine preference, or ketamine/succinylcholine induction recipe.
evidenceGaps: PPH-specific evidence for choosing and conducting airway management, induction, ventilation, and emergence beyond the broad guidance to favor general anesthesia in hemodynamic instability.
PPH-specific analgesia and PONV recommendations, including how to adapt them to ongoing hemorrhage, coagulopathy, and the procedure performed.
Procedure-specific patient positioning and detailed postoperative ventilation or extubation criteria.
corrections: Corrected the unverified distinction of greater than 500 mL for vaginal birth and greater than 1000 mL for cesarean: the supplied sources give differing definitions, including greater than 1000 mL after either delivery and a review classification of 500–1000 mL minor and greater than 1000 mL major.
Removed the claim that quantitative blood loss is mandatory; the sources support that visual estimation is often inaccurate but do not specify a mandatory quantitative measurement protocol.
Removed the specified TXA dose and repeat interval; retained only source-supported early IV use within three hours.
Replaced the asserted universal 1:1:1 transfusion ratio with the review’s description of packed red cells and FFP in a 1:1 ratio with early platelet use, while noting local protocol.
Removed unsupported fixed fibrinogen targets, the claim that fibrinogen is always the first factor to fall, and a prescribed uterotonic/intervention escalation order.
Removed unsupported fixed position, central venous access, serial laboratory interval, anesthetic drug recipes, and extubation triggers.

reports.title: Preeclampsia / Severe Preeclampsia — Anesthesia Management
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. Its fixed epidural platelet rules, mandatory video laryngoscopy, specified 6.0-mm tube, fixed neuromuscular-block reduction, magnesium serum thresholds, urine-output target, fluid-challenge prohibition, and fixed postpartum magnesium duration were not carried forward as general instructions.

The platelet discussion uses the SOAP consensus qualifiers for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy; it does not imply that one platelet value alone establishes safety. Bleeding history, DIC concern, etiology, trend, competing risks, and clinical indication remain relevant.
The preeclampsia review and general obstetric sources differ in scope. Generic cesarean enhanced-recovery fluid and medication suggestions are not represented as preeclampsia-specific protocols.

The 2024 review is informative but remains a clinical review; the anesthetic choices described in its illustrative scenarios do not establish routine practice. The older survey source describes clinician preferences, not patient outcomes or recommendations.
This is an evidence-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan, approved protocol, or assurance of completeness.
The supplied sources do not establish the listed neurologic, urine-output, magnesium-effect, and evolving-edema concerns as specific postanesthesia observation requirements.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not establish a preeclampsia-specific airway rescue, ventilation, or extubation protocol; these decisions require individual assessment and applicable local difficult-airway guidance.
Optimal frequency of repeat platelet testing in preeclampsia outside the specified HELLP scenario remains uncertain in the consensus source.
corrections: Removed the claim that a platelet count above 70,000 alone makes neuraxial anesthesia safe; retained only the consensus statement’s qualified recommendation for specified etiologies and absence of bleeding-history or DIC concern.
