Removed fixed airway device and endotracheal-tube-size instructions; available evidence supports difficult-airway preparation and video laryngoscopy as an option, not a universal device or size.
Removed fixed neuromuscular-block dose reductions and magnesium serum thresholds as general instructions; source-specific monitoring and guideline-directed management are retained.

Removed the fixed fluid restriction, urine-output target, and categorical prohibition on fluid challenge as a general protocol because the preeclampsia review does not provide a specific fluid regimen.
Corrected the blanket caution against postpartum NSAIDs: the review reports inconclusive clinical-trial results and says the evidence does not justify changing practice.
Did not present a fixed magnesium continuation duration as a universal anesthesia instruction; refer to the applicable obstetric protocol and clinical context.

reports.title: Urgent/Emergent C-Section (Category 1 & 2)
reviewNotes: The Base44 record is unverified and contains precise emergency timing and drug recipes not substantiated by the supplied evidence. These have not been carried into the clinical reference.

The obstetric anesthesia guideline provides general selection principles and examples of emergencies, but is based on literature searched through 2015; it should not be represented as a current category-specific emergency algorithm.
The SOAP ERAC consensus is primarily for scheduled cesareans. Its pathway elements may inform nonscheduled care, but its example regimens are not emergency-specific orders.

The COVID-era review is context-specific and was not used to establish routine airway or anesthetic technique. The newer ASA pain statements have supplied background content but blank best-practice tables.
The thrombocytopenia consensus supports individualized neuraxial risk assessment, not a universal platelet-based rule. The general monitoring standards are not obstetric-procedure-specific.
This is a source-grounded draft, not a patient-specific anesthetic plan, clinical approval, or claim of completeness.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not define the category 1/category 2 classification or establish category-specific decision-to-delivery timing targets.
The supplied sources do not provide a complete emergency cesarean general-anesthesia induction, airway, and ventilation protocol tailored to urgency and maternal/fetal condition.
A detailed obstetric hemorrhage and transfusion protocol for urgent cesarean delivery is not provided; use of institutional protocols is referenced but their contents are absent.
corrections: Removed the Base44 claim of delivery within 30 minutes for category 1 and its category 1/category 2 definitions: the provided sources do not establish these criteria or timing targets.
Removed specified epidural top-up and spinal drug mixtures, doses, volumes, and claimed time-to-surgical-anesthesia; the sources do not support those recipes as universal emergency practice.

Removed mandatory RSI, mandatory video laryngoscopy, and a blanket prohibition on supraglottic airways. The obstetric guideline lists mask ventilation and supraglottic airway devices among possible failed-intubation options.
Removed the asserted volatile-anesthetic MAC target, ketamine adjunct regimen, and extubation details not supported by the supplied case-specific evidence.

Removed the fixed 500–1000 mL preload/co-load and any universal fluid total; the obstetric guideline explicitly says a fixed volume is not required before neuraxial anesthesia and says not to delay spinal initiation for one.

Corrected the implication that intrathecal morphine is always omitted in extreme urgency or that IV PCA is the default alternative; source guidance supports individualized multimodal analgesia and consideration of neuraxial opioids.
Removed claims that fetal heart rate must be monitored continuously until delivery and that the supplied sources establish a particular monitoring schedule for every emergency case.

reports.title: Blepharoplasty (Upper / Lower Eyelid)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields are not treated as evidence. The cited material supports local anesthesia and possible sedation or general anesthesia depending on procedure and patient, but does not validate the listed midazolam, fentanyl, propofol, or dexmedetomidine recipes or doses.

The Base44 recommendation to hold anticoagulants is not supported as a blanket blepharoplasty instruction. The regional-block review advises consultation before stopping anticoagulants; it does not supply a procedure-specific interruption plan.

The listed MAC natural-airway plan, exact positioning/head support, head elevation, ETCO2 via nasal cannula for every case, IV-access-only approach, and specific extubation/recovery plan are not established by the blepharoplasty sources.

Oculocardiac reflex is recognized in the ophthalmic block review, which advises atropine or glycopyrrolate availability; this does not support an automatic atropine instruction for every bradycardic event.

The orbital hematoma source supports emergent decompression with lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis. It does not establish the Base44 wording of a specific bedside workflow or a quantified time window.
CO2 laser use, laser airway-fire precautions, corneal protection setup, insurance coverage, and the listed postoperative drug plan are not supported by the supplied case-specific sources.

The 2012 regional-anesthesia review is older and covers ophthalmic blocks broadly, not blepharoplasty anesthesia specifically. Its block-specific statements should not be converted into a universal blepharoplasty technique.
evidenceGaps: The supplied evidence does not establish a blepharoplasty-specific method for choosing local anesthesia, sedation, or general anesthesia, including how patient cooperation and procedure extent should be weighed.
No blepharoplasty-specific airway, intraoperative positioning, or room-setup protocol is supplied.
No procedure-specific antithrombotic interruption/continuation protocol is supplied; management requires individualized assessment and coordination.
No blepharoplasty-specific postoperative vision-assessment schedule, discharge criteria, or recovery surveillance protocol is supplied.
corrections: Removed unsupported fixed drug combinations, doses, infusion rates, and a claim that dexmedetomidine is an established preferred regimen.
Replaced blanket preoperative blood-thinner withholding with individualized medication reconciliation; the sources do not support universal cessation.
Removed unsupported universal natural-airway MAC, head-on-donut positioning, head elevation, IV-only access, and procedure-specific airway-fire precautions.
Corrected automatic atropine wording to source-supported availability for possible oculocardiac reflex; no universal treatment instruction is inferred.
Retained emergent orbital decompression as a source-supported response to retrobulbar hematoma, without adding a bedside timing protocol.
Removed unsupported insurance, fluid, routine laboratory, blood-product, and fixed analgesic/PONV claims.

reports.title: Cataract Surgery (Phacoemulsification)
reviewNotes: The supplied Base44 fields are unverified. Their detailed MAC drug recipe, infusion rate, exact patient-stillness interval, breathing-hole setup, and asserted mandatory under-drape ETCO₂ setup are not substantiated as cataract-specific recommendations by the fetched sources.

The Base44 claim to continue anticoagulation universally is not retained. The adult review reports sub-Tenon’s block appears safer for patients taking certain antithrombotic agents, while the regional review discusses individualized consultation; neither supports a blanket continuation policy for every patient and technique.

The claim that movement is the “#1 cause” of cataract complications, the specific 0.1 mm injury threshold, and claims of rapid CO₂ accumulation under the drape are not established by the fetched evidence.

The case-specific source material does not establish supine positioning, routine IV access for all topical cases, a universal airway device, or a specific cataract recovery-room visual-testing protocol.
The cited basic anesthesia monitoring and postanesthesia-care standards apply broadly; they support monitoring and recovery requirements, not every procedure-specific detail in the Base44 fields.
The supplied sources do not establish a universal cataract-surgery room configuration or vascular-access setup.
evidenceGaps: Cataract-specific evidence establishing positioning, room setup, and any procedure-specific monitoring arrangement beyond applicable general anesthesia standards.
Cataract-specific evidence defining anesthetic depth or sedation targets and the relative benefits and risks of the available techniques for distinct patient groups.
corrections: Removed the unverified assertion that cataract surgery is the most common surgical procedure in the world.
Removed fixed midazolam, fentanyl, and propofol doses/rates and the claim that a particular MAC recipe is standard.
Replaced universal anticoagulant continuation with individualized technique- and patient-specific assessment.
Removed the asserted universal need for ETCO₂ monitoring under a surgical drape; retained the applicable ASA requirement for moderate/deep sedation and airway-device management.

Removed the blanket preference for an endotracheal tube over a supraglottic airway; the review describes supraglottic devices as widely used and associated with fewer emergence problems, without establishing a universal device choice.
Removed unsupported claims about a fixed 15–20 minute cooperation period, a 0.1 mm movement threshold, movement being the leading cause of complications, and complete analgesia from topical drops.

reports.title: Eye Trauma Repair (Open Globe)
reviewNotes: The supplied case fields are unverified and were not used as clinical evidence. In particular, the claims that open globe necessarily means a full stomach, mandatory RSI or ETT, prohibition of an LMA, avoidance of succinylcholine, and specific rocuronium, propofol, fentanyl, lidocaine, or sugammadex regimens are not established by the supplied sources.

The proposed fixed systemic-fluid maximum, specific emergence drug boluses, triple-agent PONV prophylaxis, and specified postoperative analgesics likewise lack support in the supplied evidence and are not reproduced.

The generic ophthalmic review describes supraglottic airways as widely used and associated with fewer emergence problems than laryngoscopy and intubation. This is not open-globe-specific and should not be converted into a device recommendation for OGI; the procedure-specific sources do not resolve the airway choice.

The OGI surgical review supports minimizing eye pressure and describes surgical risks of air and OVD, but does not provide anesthetic targets or establish that any anesthetic technique guarantees prevention of pressure rises or extrusion.
The provided material is not pregnancy-specific and does not establish obstetric anesthesia management for a pregnant adult undergoing this procedure.
evidenceGaps: An open-globe-specific adult anesthesia reference addressing airway selection, aspiration-risk assessment, induction strategy, and emergence/extubation options.
Procedure-specific evidence for anesthetic drug selection, PONV prophylaxis, and postoperative analgesia in open-globe repair.
fluids: This is a source-scope limitation, not a clinical fluid-management recommendation; move it out of the clinical bullets and remove the internal-import commentary.
analgesia: This is a limitation of the supplied sources, not a clinical medication recommendation; move it out of the clinical bullets and remove the internal-import commentary.
corrections: Removed unsupported claims of mandatory ETT, mandatory RSI, universal full-stomach status, and blanket LMA prohibition.
Removed the stated succinylcholine IOP increase and associated fixed rocuronium dose and sugammadex plan; these claims and dosing are not supported by the supplied sources.
Removed specific induction and emergence drug doses, a fixed systemic-fluid cap, and mandated triple-agent PONV prophylaxis.
Corrected any implication that the generic ophthalmic airway review establishes a preferred airway for open-globe repair.
Did not impose a fixed patient position, systemic fluid total, blood-loss estimate, or postoperative medication regimen.

reports.title: Retinal Detachment Repair (Vitrectomy/Scleral Buckle)
reviewNotes: There is a meaningful difference in emphasis between the 2008 letter, which says general anesthesia is used for most retinal-detachment surgery (with a stated exception), and the later adult vitreoretinal reviews, which describe regional anesthesia as predominant and general anesthesia as selective. The latter is used here for the usual contemporary approach, without implying that it suits every patient or operation.

The 2023 retinal-detachment review is principally surgical and does not establish an anesthetic regimen. The adult ophthalmic narrative review and the regional-anesthesia review add general context but are not procedure-specific anesthesia guidelines.

The regional-anesthesia review is from 2012 and includes broad ophthalmic block guidance. Its complication information is retained only as context when a block is selected, not as a mandate for block technique.
ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards apply generally; they support baseline anesthesia-care requirements, not retinal-specific monitoring, positioning, or physiologic targets.

Base44 material was treated as unverified. Its specific drug recipes, doses, timing claims, fixed positioning and setup claims, and categorical technique preferences are not supported by the supplied evidence and are not adopted.
evidenceGaps: A current procedure-specific anesthesia guideline or comparative evidence for anesthetic technique in adults undergoing combined vitrectomy and scleral buckle.
Operation-specific intraoperative positioning, access arrangements, and ocular-perfusion or blood-pressure targets.
Procedure-specific fluid and bleeding management, postoperative analgesia, and PONV prevention recommendations.
corrections: Removed the fixed supine, head-down or tilted intraoperative position and fixed table orientation; the sources do not specify these as general requirements.

Removed the claim that an LMA is universally preferred; sources describe flexible laryngeal masks as usual in one older letter and supraglottic devices as widely used in broader adult ophthalmic practice, with airway choice dependent on context.
Removed the specific induction regimen, drug doses, and blanket avoidance of succinylcholine; the supplied evidence does not support those case-specific prescriptions.

Corrected the N2O instruction: do not administer it while intraocular gas remains. The asserted instruction to stop it a fixed period before gas injection and the stated gas-expansion multiplier are not established by the supplied evidence.

Removed a fixed atropine dose and a prescribed oculocardiac-reflex treatment sequence; the regional-anesthesia review supports recognition of the reflex and availability of anticholinergic medication, not the supplied algorithm or dose.
Removed claims that PONV is very common in this procedure, that a specific prophylactic antiemetic regimen is required, and that a particular analgesic combination is standard.
Removed unsupported claims about minimal blood loss, fixed postoperative IOP monitoring arrangements, universal postoperative positioning, and a universal intraoperative IOP target.

reports.title: Strabismus Repair (Adult)
reviewNotes: The Base44 assertion that strabismus in children is associated with elevated malignant-hyperthermia risk and that TIVA is mandatory is contradicted by the strabismus anaesthesia review. The adult draft does not retain that claim or infer that volatile agents must be avoided.

The Base44 statements that PONV is the highest of any procedure and that triple prophylaxis is a minimum standard are unsupported. The review reports adult PONV of 30%, independent of general anaesthetic technique, and describes prophylaxis without establishing a universal adult regimen.

The Base44 instruction that atropine is mandatory at bedside and its fixed treatment dose are not adopted as universal adult instructions. Sources support OCR recognition, traction release, and possible anticholinergic treatment, but not a single mandatory protocol for all cases.

The source evidence on which extraocular muscle is most provocative is not uniform: one review says medial rectus surgery is most likely to induce OCR, while the anaesthesia review reports similar reflexogenicity among muscles under comparable stimulus. No muscle-specific claim is used to set a different universal plan.

The anaesthesia review is narrative and predominantly based on paediatric literature; the adult ophthalmology review is not an anaesthesia guideline. Neither establishes a complete adult anesthetic protocol.
evidenceGaps: Adult-specific comparative evidence establishing a preferred general, regional, or topical anaesthetic strategy for routine strabismus surgery and adult OCR/PONV outcomes.
Procedure-specific adult guidance for positioning and access arrangements; the anaesthesia review expressly does not specify them.
setup: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a procedure-specific setup recommendation; move it to the evidence section.
fluids: This is a source-scope limitation; move it to the evidence section and omit advice not established by the cited review.
corrections: Removed the unverified Base44 claim that strabismus is an elevated malignant-hyperthermia risk condition and that TIVA is mandatory.
Removed fixed LMA preference, mandatory prophylactic atropine, and a fixed atropine treatment dose as universal adult requirements.
Removed unsupported claims that strabismus has the highest PONV burden of any procedure and that triple prophylaxis is a minimum standard.
Removed unsupported routine fluid total, blood-loss estimate, and specific room/table setup.
Qualified muscle-specific OCR risk because the supplied reviews do not make fully concordant claims.

reports.title: ACL Reconstruction
reviewNotes: The Base44 material is unverified and was not used as factual evidence. In particular, its LMA preference, spinal drug recipe, block drug concentrations/volumes, routine muscle-relaxant rationale, room/C-arm setup, fixed fluid amount, specified blood-loss assumption, and emergence claim are not supported as ACL standards by the supplied evidence.

The claim that adductor canal block is preferred over femoral block with equivalent analgesia is overconfident: the review reports mostly similar pain scores, mixed analgesic-use results, and less quadriceps strength with femoral block.

The Base44 claim that patellar tendon graft harvest is the primary pain source is not established by the supplied sources. The ACL review supports a comparison of acute pain and breakthrough pain by graft type, but does not identify a universal primary pain source or mandate surgeon infiltration.

The Base44 claims about preoperative swelling requiring delay, popliteal cyst rupture, and particular ACL room equipment/positioning lack supporting evidence in the supplied sources and were not retained as clinical facts.

The cohort study’s reported associations between anesthetic categories and outcomes are observational, have potential residual confounding, and cannot distinguish regional blocks from local infiltration. They do not establish causal benefit or dictate technique.

The tourniquet discussion in the orthopedic blood-pressure review concerns limb surgery generally; it is not ACL-specific. No ACL-specific tourniquet thresholds or management protocol are asserted here.
The supplied ACL sources do not establish room setup or positioning, or provide an ACL-specific emergency-management algorithm.
evidenceGaps: ACL-specific guidance on operative positioning, room setup, and procedure-linked equipment requirements is not supplied.
ACL-specific airway selection, anesthetic technique protocols, intraoperative physiologic targets, and emergence guidance are not supplied.
ACL-specific evidence for tourniquet use and management, fluid requirements, blood loss, or transfusion practice is not supplied.
The sources do not establish a single ACL analgesia or PONV regimen; comparative evidence remains variable and does not settle an optimal approach.
setup: This is a source-scope limitation, not an operative setup instruction.
complications: The supplied sources do not support the popliteal-cyst rupture claim or provide an ACL-specific emergency algorithm.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that LMA is preferred for ACL reconstruction; sources do not provide an ACL-specific airway preference.
Removed specific spinal, induction, block, and local-infiltration recipes and drug doses; the sources describe heterogeneous study regimens, not a universal clinical prescription.

Corrected the claim that adductor canal block is categorically preferred and analgesically equivalent: motor preservation is supported relative to femoral block, but comparative analgesia findings are mixed.
Removed the claim that femoral block should be avoided in all cases; evidence supports a quadriceps-weakness and mobility concern requiring individualized assessment.

Removed unsupported routine positioning, arthroscopic tower/irrigation/C-arm requirements, tunnel-drilling relaxation requirements, fixed crystalloid volume, minimal blood-loss assertion, and stated block-duration guarantee.
Removed the claims that swelling requires delaying surgery, popliteal cyst rupture is a recognized routine concern, and patellar tendon harvest is universally the primary pain source.

reports.title: Ankle ORIF
reviewNotes: The source set supports ankle-fracture surgical considerations more strongly than it supports anesthesia choices. Do not present a particular regional, spinal, or general anesthetic as the standard for ankle ORIF.

Source 0 reports fixation usually within 24 hours while allowing delay for swelling; source 1 emphasizes soft-tissue monitoring when treatment is delayed. These statements are reconciled by making soft-tissue integrity and clinical context—not a fixed timing rule—the determinant.

Source 1 is a 2014 narrative review; source 3 is a broad regional-anesthesia review. Neither should be treated as a current ankle-ORIF-specific anesthesia guideline. ASA sources support general monitoring and postanesthesia standards, not an ankle-specific protocol.
The generic blood-pressure review (source 2) covers diverse orthopedic procedures and populations. Its specific targets and drug regimens are not carried over as ankle-ORIF instructions.

Unverified case-field claims not established by the supplied evidence include exact spinal and peripheral-block drug doses, a fixed block duration, routine LMA or MAC selection, a specific position or tourniquet setup, tourniquet-pain thresholds, fixed fluid volumes, ketorolac-based analgesia, mandatory PONV prophylaxis, and a fixed PACU DVT-prophylaxis plan.
This is an evidence-limited reference draft, not a patient-specific anesthetic plan or a statement of clinical approval.
evidenceGaps: No ankle-ORIF-specific comparative evidence establishes the preferred anesthetic technique, block combination, or criteria for conversion between regional and general anesthesia.
No supplied ankle-ORIF source establishes positioning, tourniquet setup or management, expected blood loss, or an operation-specific fluid and bleeding approach.
No supplied source establishes an ankle-ORIF-specific PONV strategy or a standardized postoperative neurovascular-check frequency.
corrections: Removed exact intrathecal bupivacaine and fentanyl doses, peripheral ropivacaine volumes and concentrations, and proposed sedation-drug recipes because the ankle-fracture sources do not support them.

Removed the claim that popliteal sciatic plus saphenous block is universally complete ankle anesthesia or is strongly recommended for every patient; the regional review says it is commonly combined for foot/ankle surgery but does not establish it as universally sufficient or preferred.

Removed the asserted 12–18-hour block duration, fixed fluid volume, routine ketorolac and acetaminophen schedule, and blanket PONV prophylaxis because these are not supported by the supplied ankle-specific evidence.

Did not retain a fixed supine or lateral position, hip bump, thigh tourniquet, or routine fluoroscopy setup as anesthesia recommendations; ankle-fracture sources do not establish an anesthesia setup plan.
Corrected the source-field spelling 'bimeallolar' to the source-supported term 'bimalleolar' in this draft.

reports.title: Carpal Tunnel Release
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. Its WALANT-specific claims (no IV, no sedation, no tourniquet, surgeon-only management, and epinephrine as tourniquet replacement) are not established by the supplied sources; retain only the guideline-supported option of local anesthesia alone.

Base44’s wrist-block recipe, local-anesthetic and MAC drug doses, minimum local-only monitoring claims, and claim that many centers require no anesthesia-provider involvement are not supported by the fetched evidence and were removed.

The base’s postoperative sensory/motor and wound checks are not specified in the supplied CTR sources. General PACU observation standards are retained without presenting a CTR-specific examination as evidence-based protocol.

The CTR guideline characterizes anticoagulation continuation and office-based release as limited-evidence options, not universal assurances. Individual selection and drug-specific management remain unspecified.

The blood-pressure orthopedic review is not a CTR-specific source and was not used to create procedure-specific targets. The regional-anesthesia review is broad and supports only general considerations; the sedation study is narrow and does not establish routine dosing.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific local-anesthetic agent, concentration, injection technique, dose, and criteria for choosing local anesthesia, IV regional anesthesia, or sedation.
Evidence-based criteria for tourniquet use versus a no-tourniquet technique, and CTR-specific patient-selection criteria for sedation or office-based release.
CTR-specific positioning and setup details, and a postoperative sensory/motor and wound-assessment protocol.
corrections: Removed unsupported assertions that WALANT is the established or required approach, that epinephrine replaces a tourniquet, and that no IV, sedation, tourniquet, or anesthesia-team involvement is needed.
Removed all unverified local-anesthetic, wrist-block, midazolam, and propofol recipes and doses.
Corrected anticoagulation from a broad continuation claim to a limited-evidence option without drug-specific instructions.
Removed unsupported CTR-specific fluid, blood-loss, airway, monitoring-minimum, and recovery-examination claims.

reports.title: Distal Radius ORIF
reviewNotes: Base44 material was treated as unverified and not used as evidence. Removed its specific anesthetic recipes, block drug doses, tourniquet setup claims, screw-check instruction, fluid amount, analgesic schedule, and asserted distal-radius neurovascular/PACU protocol where the fetched sources do not support them.

The registry comparison supports that regional and general anesthesia were studied and showed no statistically significant difference in reported complications; it does not establish equivalence, a preferred block, or safety for every patient. Its classification excluded regional anesthesia combined with MAC/IV sedation.
The WALANT report is a small uncontrolled retrospective series. Its local technique and outcomes are not generalized into routine care.
The tourniquet physiology statement comes from a broad orthopedic blood-pressure review, not a distal-radius-specific study. It is qualified accordingly.
The review of regional anesthesia is broad and lacks formal evidence grading in the supplied text; procedure-specific block selection and complication prevention cannot be settled from it alone.
The setup limitation belongs in the evidence section because the supplied study does not establish a standard table, arm position, tourniquet arrangement, vascular access plan, or fluoroscopy setup.
evidenceGaps: No supplied source establishes a preferred anesthetic technique or a comparative, distal-radius-specific selection protocol that accounts for fracture pattern, surgical approach, and patient factors.
No supplied source defines routine distal-radius ORIF positioning, hand-table or fluoroscopy workflow, tourniquet use, access, or procedure-specific intraoperative monitoring.
No supplied source provides a distal-radius-specific emergence, operative neurovascular examination, splint assessment, or postoperative surveillance protocol.
setup: This is a source-scope note, not a supported clinical setup recommendation.
corrections: Removed claim that brachial plexus block is the ideal or universally preferred anesthetic; sources support regional anesthesia as an option, not a universal choice.
Removed unverified claims about specific blocks or wrist blocks being adequate for particular cases and the unverified LMA/GA pathway.
Removed all unverified drug doses and fixed fluid, blood-loss, tourniquet, and analgesia prescriptions.
Removed the claim that intraoperative C-arm screw-length checking is mandatory; no supplied source supports that surgical instruction.
Removed unverified acute carpal tunnel release criteria and postoperative radial pulse, median nerve sensation, and finger-motion checks as source-backed protocol.
Corrected implications that regional anesthesia guarantees complete anesthesia, avoids airway management in all cases, or provides a fixed duration of postoperative analgesia.

reports.title: External Fixator Placement
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as clinical evidence. The source set supports external-fixation principles and general anesthesia standards, but not the supplied field-by-field anesthetic recipes.

The ED open-fracture statements differ in scope: the technical article contraindicates open fracture for its described ED technique, while the broader review includes complex open fractures among possible ED uses. Neither supports a universal setting rule.

The ED technical article is based on two cases and is not an anesthesia reference; the broader ED review also lacks an anesthesia protocol. Do not elevate local technique details or reported case outcomes into routine anesthetic practice.
ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards support general monitoring and recovery requirements; they do not establish external-fixator-specific targets or replace clinical judgment.
evidenceGaps: External-fixator-specific anesthesia selection and airway guidance, including criteria for general, regional, local anesthesia or sedation.
Procedure-specific fluid, blood-loss and transfusion management guidance; the supplied fixation sources do not provide these protocols.
Procedure-specific analgesia and PONV prevention guidance.
corrections: Removed the Base44 airway and induction recipes, including routine LMA/ETT selection, RSI claims and named induction drugs; no supplied external-fixation source establishes these as a standard.

Removed Base44 claims for routine TXA, antibiotic selection, muscle relaxation, ketorolac/acetaminophen, PCA, and blood-product use; these are not established by the supplied procedure-specific evidence.

Removed the asserted 1–2 hour procedure target and routine ICU disposition. Sources describe rapid damage-control stabilization and deferment of other procedures until physiology improves, but do not establish a universal duration or destination.

Corrected the blanket open-fracture implication by distinguishing the ED technical article’s contraindication for its described technique from the broader review’s discussion of complex open fractures.
Removed a universal arterial-line or Foley-catheter requirement and the hourly compartment-check interval; the sources do not establish these as universal external-fixator practices.
Retained later pin-site planning because the review supports avoiding interference with definitive fixation, but did not reproduce unsupported or overly specific pin-placement recipes.

reports.title: Hardware Removal
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, the proposed routine LMA, propofol/fentanyl induction, regional block, fluoroscopy, expected minimal blood loss, and fixed crystalloid volume are not established by the supplied hardware-removal sources.

The claims about broken-screw extraction, prolonged cases, re-fracture through a stress riser, wound dehiscence, and activity restriction after femoral implant removal have no supporting evidence in the supplied sources and are not presented as established clinical facts.
Pediatric growth-plate considerations were excluded from adult guidance. The maxillofacial cohort’s pediatric statements do not establish adult orthopedic practice.
The WALANT findings are limited to distal-fibula removal and a brief abstract; they do not establish a standard technique, dosing regimen, broad safety claim, or expected effect at other sites.
The clinical draft is an evidence-limited reference draft, not a patient-specific plan or a clinically approved protocol.

The supplied evidence does not establish an adult orthopedic hardware-removal-specific preoperative risk protocol or room-setup requirements. The distal-fibula study does not specify participant ages, and the other hardware-removal study is maxillofacial.
The hardware-removal sources do not provide procedure-specific airway, fluid, blood-loss, or analgesia protocols. The WALANT abstract reports a hemostatic rationale but no numerical results.
The distal-fibula study reports no difference in postoperative complication rates, but does not report complication types or counts.
evidenceGaps: Adult orthopedic hardware-removal evidence beyond distal-fibula cases, including procedure-specific anesthetic selection, patient selection, and comparative outcomes.

Source-supported incidence, recognition, and management evidence for hardware-specific complications such as broken components, re-fracture after implant removal, wound problems, and postoperative activity restrictions.
Procedure-specific information on positioning, imaging, equipment, blood loss, fluid requirements, analgesic regimens, and PONV outcomes.
preop: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a clinical preoperative recommendation.
setup: The source reports no hardware-removal-specific setup protocol; retain this as an evidence limitation, not a clinical setup instruction.
airway: The available material provides no support for a preferred airway device or anesthetic technique.
fluids: This is a limitation of the available evidence, not a case-specific fluid-management recommendation.
analgesia: The cited sources do not establish a hardware-removal-specific multimodal analgesia or PONV regimen.
corrections: Removed the Base44 assertion that LMA is the usual airway and ETT is indicated for prone or prolonged cases; the supplied hardware-removal sources do not establish an airway default.

Removed the proposed propofol/fentanyl induction, routine regional block, volatile/TIVA maintenance, and fixed drug list as procedure-specific recipes; the sources do not support them as standard hardware-removal practice.
Removed the Base44 room setup claims for fluoroscopy, original fixation instruments, and broken-screw extraction tools because the supplied sources do not substantiate them.
Removed the fixed 250–500 mL crystalloid estimate and the claim of minimal blood loss; the supplied sources provide no hardware-removal-specific fluid or blood-loss data.

Removed claims that broken screws commonly prolong surgery, that implant removal creates a stress-riser re-fracture risk, and that a specific activity restriction period is required; these claims are unsupported by the provided evidence.
Did not present pediatric routine removal or growth-plate considerations as adult recommendations.

reports.title: Hip Fracture Repair (ORIF/Hemiarthroplasty)
reviewNotes: Corrected the Base44 claim that spinal anesthesia is preferred because of a demonstrated mortality benefit: the procedure-specific source reports a randomized trial with no superiority for survival or ambulation. Other review and database findings do not resolve the conflict or establish universal superiority.

The Base44 claims specifying spinal drug doses, intrathecal morphine, sedation and dexmedetomidine regimens, phenylephrine infusion, fluid preload, transfusion thresholds, TXA dose, and delirium-prevention effects are not adopted as routine recommendations. The supplied sources do not support those recipes for this reference.

The claim that FICB or PENG specifically reduces delirium risk is not supported by the supplied source material. Evidence supports considering femoral or fascia-iliacus blocks to facilitate early ambulation; block selection and motor effects remain individualized.

The case fields' fixed setup items, Foley use, warming blanket, arterial-line indications, and emergence instructions are not presented as hip-fracture-specific source-supported requirements. Basic monitoring standards are included separately.

The fragility-fracture review is older and describes regional cognitive benefits as controversial; its database outcome associations should not be read as causal trial evidence. The supplied regional-anesthesia review also reports cognition benefits, so this draft does not assert a cognitive benefit from neuraxial anesthesia.
evidenceGaps: Current, agent-specific anticoagulation and neuraxial eligibility guidance applicable to the individual patient, including the effect of renal function and any planned postoperative anticoagulation.
A procedure-specific delirium prevention and management protocol; available sources identify delirium and contributing conditions but do not establish a complete protocol.
A hip-fracture-specific blood-loss, transfusion, and postoperative anemia protocol; the supplied sources do not provide a validated threshold or regimen.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that spinal anesthesia is universally superior to general anesthesia or has an established mortality benefit in hip-fracture repair.
Removed unsubstantiated medication and fluid recipes, including fixed spinal doses, intrathecal morphine, sedation infusions, pressor infusions, preload volume, and TXA dose.
Removed the fixed transfusion thresholds and unqualified blood-loss assumptions from the case fields.
Removed claims that FICB or PENG blocks and dexmedetomidine reliably reduce delirium; the supplied evidence does not substantiate these as routine effects for this case.
Removed categorical avoidance of NSAIDs, routine Foley catheter and arterial-line claims, and specific airway/emergence instructions where not supported as procedure-specific requirements.
Reframed anticoagulation and neuraxial planning as individualized and subject to applicable current specialty guidance rather than copying medication interruption intervals.

reports.title: Irrigation and Debridement (I&D) of Joint / Wound
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, the provided sources do not support a universal LMA or ETT plan, RSI, ketamine preference, vasopressor plan, fixed crystalloid volume, antibiotic timing rule, or red-man-syndrome prevention regimen for I&D.

The knee study reports different anesthesia techniques for open arthrotomy and arthroscopic debridement, but its retrospective design and narrow population do not establish a routine technique for other joints, wounds, PJI, or osteomyelitis.

The knee study describes culture collection before irrigation, but does not establish that antimicrobial treatment should always be withheld until intraoperative cultures, particularly in a systemically ill patient.

Regional-anesthesia guidance identifies infection and sepsis as selection concerns; this should be reconciled with the patient’s condition and the actual operation rather than converted into a universal rule.
The blood-pressure review concerns varied orthopedic procedures and populations; it does not provide I&D-specific blood-pressure, fluid, or vasopressor targets.
evidenceGaps: Procedure- and population-specific guidance for PJI, infected wounds, and osteomyelitis, including anesthetic management when systemic sepsis is present.
I&D-specific evidence for airway and anesthetic technique selection, hemodynamic management during source control, and postoperative disposition in patients with persistent systemic illness.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that LMA is appropriate for most I&D cases and that ETT or RSI should be selected using the listed triggers; the procedure source does not report airway management.
Removed the unverified instruction to hold antibiotics until intraoperative cultures; the source supports culture collection before irrigation, not a universal antibiotic-delay rule.
Removed unverified routine ketamine preference, pre-induction vasopressors, norepinephrine use, fixed fluid volume, and routine arterial-line or Foley recommendations.
Removed unverified vancomycin infusion instructions and blanket drug coverage claims; the supplied sources do not establish I&D-specific antimicrobial selection or administration protocols.
Removed the claim that joint drainage releases bacteria systemically and causes predictable hemodynamic deterioration; the supplied sources do not establish this as a routine event.
Removed the unverified I&D pain regimen and generalized PACU claims; recovery monitoring is described using the applicable postanesthesia-care standard.

reports.title: Knee Arthroscopy
reviewNotes: Base44 details such as preferred LMA, specific spinal drug doses, tourniquet sensory-level targets, fixed fluid amounts, intra-articular bupivacaine/ketorolac efficacy claims, and a defined outpatient recovery timeline are not substantiated by the supplied knee-arthroscopy sources and were not carried forward as recommendations.
The local-anesthetic review is older and its series/regimens are not standards; use it only to describe selected-case feasibility and reported limitations.
The tourniquet hemodynamic discussion comes from a broad orthopedic blood-pressure review, not a knee-arthroscopy-specific management protocol.
General ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards are applied within their stated scope; they do not resolve procedure-specific airway selection, positioning, or discharge criteria.
This draft is source-limited and is not a patient-specific plan, checklist, or statement of clinical approval.
The supplied sources do not provide an arthroscopy-specific postoperative nausea and vomiting prophylaxis regimen.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific positioning and room setup are not described in the supplied knee-arthroscopy sources.
No procedure-specific airway-device selection or anesthetic technique comparison establishes a preferred approach.
The supplied sources do not provide arthroscopy-specific recognition and management guidance for clinically important irrigation-fluid extravasation or compartment syndrome.
No arthroscopy-specific PONV prophylaxis or validated outpatient discharge criteria are provided.
corrections: Removed the unsupported Base44 claim that LMA is preferred for knee arthroscopy.
Removed spinal and intrathecal drug-dose recipes, including low-dose spinal claims and timing claims for turnover or discharge.
Removed unsupported tourniquet sensory-level, pressure, duration-documentation, and pain-breakthrough claims as arthroscopy-specific standards.

Removed the claim that intra-articular bupivacaine plus ketorolac or morphine is a proven or universally preferred analgesic regimen; sources only describe possible surgeon-performed intra-articular blocks.
Removed fixed crystalloid volumes, minimal-blood-loss assumptions, and specific PACU motor-resolution timelines.

reports.title: Laminectomy (Lumbar / Cervical)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its claims that awake fiberoptic intubation is mandatory for cervical instability, neck extension can cause quadriplegia, and TXA or dexamethasone should be given are not supported by the supplied material.

The supplied sources do not support universal arterial access, Foley catheterization, neuromonitoring, TIVA, an armored endotracheal tube, a specific prone frame, a fluid total, or cell salvage for every laminectomy.
The source set does not establish urgent imaging or surgical evacuation timelines for a new postoperative deficit, nor a specific management protocol for durotomy or CSF leak.

There is a tension between the broad orthopedic review's spinal perfusion strategies and the spine review's caution against deliberate hypotension. The draft avoids prescribing a universal MAP target and does not treat deliberate hypotension as routine.

The case describes both cervical and lumbar procedures, but the strongest procedure-specific evidence concerns elective lumbar surgery. Cervical airway technique and cervical-specific anesthetic management remain weakly supported.

The erector spinae plane block finding is reported for lumbar surgery generally; the supplied evidence does not establish its efficacy specifically for laminectomy or define a procedure-specific analgesia regimen.
evidenceGaps: Cervical-laminectomy-specific airway technique and neurologic-risk mitigation, including evidence for or against awake intubation in defined instability or myelopathy subgroups.
Procedure-specific thresholds and escalation pathways for new postoperative neurologic deficits, including the choice and timing of imaging or re-exploration.
Laminectomy-specific management of incidental durotomy, persistent CSF leak, and postoperative monitoring.
Comparative evidence for anesthetic technique and neuromonitoring strategy in cervical versus lumbar decompression.
corrections: Removed the Base44 claim that awake fiberoptic intubation in neutral position is mandatory for significant cervical instability; the sources only identify cervical and upper-thoracic airway management as potentially challenging.
Removed the claim that any neck extension during intubation can cause quadriplegia; no supplied source supports that absolute statement.

Removed the proposed fixed laminectomy fluid volume, routine TXA, routine dexamethasone, routine arterial line, Foley, and universal cell-saver use because the supplied sources do not establish them for all decompressions.

Removed the Base44 NSAID assurance that ketorolac is generally acceptable after decompression; supplied evidence leaves bleeding and non-union considerations unresolved and does not make a procedure-specific recommendation.
Replaced universal hypotension avoidance targets with individualized perfusion management; the sources do not support one blood-pressure target for every laminectomy.
Did not reproduce the Base44 emergency timelines for cauda equina surgery or postoperative hematoma evacuation because the supplied sources do not substantiate those claims.

reports.title: Long Bone ORIF (Tibia / Femur / Humerus)
reviewNotes: Base44's claims about routine TXA at induction and repeat dosing, routine cell salvage or crossmatch quantities, standard fluid totals, and a universal FiO2 increase during reaming are not supported by the supplied evidence and were excluded.

Base44's fracture-specific estimates of femoral and tibial blood loss, routine arterial line/Foley placement, mandatory endotracheal intubation, fracture-table and tourniquet prescriptions, and routine regional-block choices are not established by these sources.
The source cohort's 94.4% endotracheal-anesthesia observation applies to isolated periprosthetic distal-femur ORIF and should not be generalized as a universal airway requirement.
Base44's compartment-syndrome signs, pressure thresholds, and fasciotomy recommendation are not supported by the supplied sources; they were not reproduced as clinical guidance.

The 2025 blood-pressure review includes long-bone FES discussion but is a broad narrative review. Its procedure-specific or population-specific statements should not be promoted to universal long-bone ORIF targets.
Basic ASA monitoring standards and postanesthesia-care standards apply generally; they do not fill the procedure-specific setup, blood-management, or complication-management gaps.
evidenceGaps: Long-bone ORIF-specific evidence for approach and fixation selection, positioning, traction or imaging setup, and procedure-specific anesthetic technique.
Long-bone ORIF-specific evidence for blood-loss prediction, transfusion planning, cell salvage, and TXA use.
Reliable supplied-source guidance on compartment-syndrome surveillance and escalation after fracture fixation.
Comparative, procedure-specific evidence for regional analgesia choices and PONV prevention in tibial, femoral-shaft, and humeral ORIF.
corrections: Removed routine TXA dosing and timing; no supplied source supports the Base44 regimen.
Removed routine 100% oxygen during reaming; the supplied sources discuss FES recognition and supportive oxygenation but do not establish that intraoperative prescription.
Removed fixed fracture blood-loss estimates, crystalloid totals, cell-saver use, and crossmatch quantities as routine recommendations.
Removed blanket ETT, arterial-line, Foley, tourniquet, fracture-table, and nerve-block requirements.
Removed the Base44 compartment-pressure threshold and fasciotomy directive because they are not evidenced in the supplied sources.

reports.title: Lower Extremity Amputation (Orthopedic) — Toe / Ray / Transmetatarsal
reviewNotes: The supplied amputation review is not a toe/ray/transmetatarsal anesthesia reference and focuses primarily on major lower-extremity amputation. Regional technique details come from a broad orthopedic review, so they support options, not a mandatory or preferred plan.

The orthopedic blood-pressure review discusses tourniquet physiology across limb surgery but does not establish targets or interventions specific to this operation. Do not import its numerical targets into this draft.

The ASA monitoring, preanesthesia, and postanesthesia sources are general standards. The neuromuscular-blockade source summarizes a guideline and applies only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.

Base44 statements about block drug concentrations and volumes, spinal dose, a glucose target, insulin infusion, fixed crystalloid volume, avoiding lactated Ringer’s in ESRD, block duration, and drug-specific postoperative analgesia are not established by the supplied evidence and are not reproduced.
The supplied sources do not provide a procedure-specific PONV prevention or treatment regimen.
evidenceGaps: Direct procedure-specific evidence for anesthetic technique and adequacy of regional anesthesia in toe, ray, or transmetatarsal amputation.
Procedure-specific guidance for PONV management and discharge readiness.
analgesia: This is an evidence-scope limitation, not a clinical analgesia recommendation.
corrections: Removed the claim that regional anesthesia is preferred or that diabetic/ESRD patients necessarily tolerate it better; the amputation review describes GA or RA and recommends case-by-case selection.
Removed unsourced local-anesthetic and spinal dosing, dexamethasone use, and claims of fixed block duration.
Removed unsupported glucose threshold, intraoperative glucose-check interval, and insulin-infusion recommendation.
Removed the fixed fluid volume and the blanket instruction to avoid lactated Ringer’s in ESRD.
Removed unsupported claims about routine wound cultures, bone cultures, and specific PACU wound-edge tests as mandatory steps.
Corrected the block claim: popliteal and saphenous blocks are described for foot/ankle surgery, but the supplied sources do not establish them as sufficient sole anesthesia for every case.

reports.title: Lumbar Discectomy / Microdiscectomy
reviewNotes: Base44 material was treated as unverified and not used as evidence. In particular, the fetched sources do not substantiate its knee-chest/Wilson frame claims, mandatory fluoroscopic level confirmation, TXA or dexamethasone choices, fixed fluid volume or blood-loss estimate, dural-tear repair details, wrong-level risk characterization, immediate dramatic radicular-pain relief, or specific foot-dorsiflexion and urinary-retention checks.

The adult microdiscectomy study reports prone positioning and tracheal intubation for its GA group, but these study details do not establish that GA, intubation, a specific frame, or an extubation location is required for every discectomy.

The endoscopic review's anesthetic comparisons are limited and should not be treated as direct evidence for every conventional open or microscopic technique. The observational adult study is non-randomized and single-center.

The broad orthopedic blood-pressure review includes spine-surgery considerations, but its physiologic targets and interventions are not discectomy-specific; no target has been imported as a routine instruction.
The ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards and the neuromuscular-blockade guideline overview provide general standards, not lumbar-discectomy-specific workflows.
The supplied sources do not establish a lumbar-discectomy-specific requirement for documenting baseline motor or sensory findings, or criteria for cauda equina syndrome urgency.
The supplied sources do not provide procedure-specific recognition or management instructions for dural tear, retained fragment, wrong-level surgery, or postoperative epidural hematoma.

The supplied sources do not define a discectomy-specific postoperative neurological examination, urinary-retention protocol, or discharge criteria; the cited PACU requirements are general postanesthesia-care standards.
evidenceGaps: Approach-specific surgical workflow and the relationship between open, microscopic, and endoscopic techniques and anesthetic selection.
Discectomy-specific surgical localization and wrong-level prevention practices.
Procedure-specific recognition and management of dural tear, retained disc material, and new or worsening postoperative neurologic deficit.
Discectomy-specific expected blood loss and fluid-management evidence.
corrections: Removed mandatory knee-chest or Wilson-frame positioning and claims that a particular position reduces epidural venous pressure or blood loss; the supplied endoscopic review provides no positioning protocol.
Removed a mandatory fluoroscopy statement and wrong-level surgery assertions because the supplied sources do not substantiate them.
Removed copied induction, maintenance, TXA, dexamethasone, analgesic, and fixed fluid-volume recipes; study regimens are not presented as universal recommendations.
Removed routine neuromonitoring claims; the endoscopic review notes limited procedure-specific IONM evidence.
Removed claims of immediate dramatic relief of sciatica and the specified postoperative foot, sensation, and urinary-retention assessment because these are not established by the fetched evidence.
Qualified prone positioning, intubation, and operating-room awakening as findings from one adult observational study rather than general requirements.

reports.title: Pelvic Fracture Fixation
reviewNotes: Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, the sources do not support a universal RSI plan, ketamine as mandatory induction, a categorical propofol prohibition, routine vasopressors, or mandatory arterial, central venous, or pulmonary-artery catheter placement.

The supplied sources do not establish the stated 1:1:1 transfusion recipe, calcium dosing rule, TXA timing claim, fixed transfusion thresholds, permissive-hypotension range, or a universal hemorrhage-control sequence for adult pelvic fixation. These claims were omitted rather than presented as clinical instructions.

The proposed routine ICU intubation, prohibition on acute extubation, and fixed return-to-OR interval are not established by the supplied pelvic-fracture sources. Recovery and disposition require patient- and course-specific assessment.

The pregnancy review is not generalized to adult practice. The broad regional-anesthesia review and orthopedic blood-pressure review are not pelvic-fixation-specific; ASA standards support only their stated monitoring, postanesthesia, and neuromuscular-blockade scopes.

The source set is limited: the principal polytrauma source is a narrative review with heterogeneous evidence and no formal quality assessment or meta-analysis. This draft is not a validated protocol or clinical approval.
The supplied sources do not address PONV prevention or treatment specifically for pelvic fracture fixation.
evidenceGaps: Adult pelvic-fixation-specific evidence establishing anesthetic technique, airway strategy, and ventilation approach.
Procedure-specific room setup, positioning, vascular access, and invasive-monitoring indications.
A validated adult pelvic-trauma hemorrhage-control and transfusion protocol, including applicable product selection and resuscitation endpoints.
Pelvic-fixation-specific emergence, extubation, and postoperative disposition criteria.
analgesia: The supplied sources do not support a pelvic-fixation-specific statement about PONV prevention or treatment.
corrections: Removed unsupported categorical statements that propofol is contraindicated and ketamine is the required induction drug.
Removed unverified numerical drug doses, TXA timing instructions, transfusion ratios and thresholds, calcium replacement schedule, and permissive-hypotension targets.
Removed universal requirements for central access, CVP or PA monitoring, pre-induction arterial lines, vasopressors, RSI, and two anesthesia providers.
Removed a universal instruction to leave patients intubated in ICU and a fixed staged-fixation interval.

Corrected recovery language to distinguish ASA postanesthesia monitoring standards from pelvic-fracture-specific recovery guidance; retained quantitative TOF guidance only when neuromuscular blockade is used.

reports.title: Rotator Cuff Repair (Arthroscopic)
reviewNotes: This is an adult-focused clinical reference draft, not a patient-specific plan or an approved protocol. Apply patient-specific judgment and applicable institutional guidance.

The source supporting irrigation-related airway risk is a review; it supports recognition and monitoring precautions but does not provide a validated extubation algorithm or quantified universal threshold for delaying extubation.
The PROSPECT guideline provides procedure-specific analgesia recommendations, but its evidence base is heterogeneous and some interventions were not compared with optimized multimodal analgesia.

The 2025 orthopedic blood-pressure review includes procedure-specific observations, but these do not supersede the rotator-cuff pain guideline's warning against routine controlled hypotension or establish a universal beach-chair target.
Arterial-line use, cerebral oximetry, and vasopressor selection should not be presented as mandatory for every repair on the available evidence.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not establish a validated rotator-cuff-specific protocol for quantifying irrigation-fluid extravasation or deciding when airway findings require delayed extubation.
corrections: Removed the Base44 fixed interscalene drug recipe and perineural adjunct regimen; the supplied guideline recommends intravenous rather than perineural dexamethasone and does not establish that recipe.

Removed the claim that a continuous interscalene catheter for a fixed 48–72 hours is strongly recommended. The procedure-specific guideline favors continuous over single-shot block, but does not support that fixed duration in the supplied text.

Removed a mandatory arterial line, mandatory cerebral oximetry, and the fixed beach-chair MAP target in the Base44 material; sources support individualized monitoring and caution about hypotension, not a universal requirement or target.
Removed the Base44 fixed crystalloid volume and infusion/vasopressor recipe; the procedure-specific review explicitly provides no fluid replacement regimen.

Corrected the procedure description: the supplied review lists biceps tenotomy with or without acromioplasty, but does not establish biceps tenodesis or distal clavicle excision as routine components of this case.
Removed the claim that a specific ketorolac schedule, sling instruction, or exact PONV regimen is established by the supplied sources.

reports.title: Scoliosis Correction (Posterior Spinal Fusion with Instrumentation) (Adult)
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. The draft avoids its specific TXA dose, fixed MAP and hemoglobin targets, mandatory neuromonitoring claims, wake-up-test assertions, and routine ICU disposition.

Adult evidence supports avoiding succinylcholine in significant neuromuscular disorders, but the supplied sources do not establish the Base44 claim that volatile agents are categorically contraindicated in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. That assertion was omitted.

The claim that ketorolac must be avoided after fusion, and the proposed intrathecal morphine, PCA, and diazepam regimens, are not established by the supplied sources. Analgesia and PONV recommendations remain deliberately general.

Neuromonitoring is discussed as a useful technique, not as mandatory for every adult deformity procedure in the supplied evidence. Signal changes require coordinated assessment; no single rescue protocol is endorsed here.

Source 2's controlled-hypotension discussion is in tension with source 1's caution against induced hypotension in spinal cord compression or neurologic deficit. This draft reports the tension without imposing a universal pressure target.

Source 0 includes adolescent idiopathic scoliosis evidence; it is not used to establish adult practice. Adult application is limited to findings supported by adult deformity or general adult spine sources.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not establish a contemporary, adult posterior-fusion-specific neuromonitoring alert and rescue protocol, including a standardized threshold for intervention.
The supplied sources do not provide a procedure-specific emergence and extubation pathway or criteria for postoperative ICU versus ward disposition.
The supplied sources do not establish a posterior-fusion-specific evidence-based analgesia and PONV regimen, including the role and timing of NSAIDs in fusion healing.
corrections: Removed unsupported scoliosis Cobb-angle thresholds and adolescent indications as criteria for adult surgery.
Removed fixed TXA dosing and the claim that a particular high-dose protocol is required.
Removed universal deliberate-hypotension targets and fixed transfusion/hemoglobin thresholds; perfusion and resuscitation decisions are individualized.
Corrected 'SSEPs/MEPs mandatory' to describe their use and limitations without claiming a universal requirement.
Removed the characterization of Stagnara wake-up testing as a gold-standard routine backup; supplied sources do not establish that claim.
Removed routine ICU admission, expected prolonged ventilation for neuromuscular patients, and fixed postoperative monitoring plans as universal recommendations.
Removed unsupported claims of categorical volatile-agent avoidance in Duchenne muscular dystrophy and the specific ketorolac, intrathecal morphine, PCA, and muscle-spasm drug recipes.

reports.title: Shoulder Arthroplasty (Total or Reverse)
reviewNotes: Base44 was treated as unverified and not used to establish clinical facts. Its laryngeal-mask preference, routine mandatory cerebral oximetry, arm-to-brain correction value, block drug recipes, complication percentages, blood-loss estimate, and block-duration claims are not adopted as universal shoulder-arthroplasty guidance.

The supplied sources describe phrenic blockade as near-universal with interscalene block in one review and identify respiratory compromise as a concern; they do not substantiate a universal statement that every patient experiences clinically consequential palsy or a blanket bilateral-block rule.

The arthroplasty review's recommendation favoring combined regional and general anesthesia is qualified by other included studies finding no significant complication-rate difference. The draft presents technique selection as individualized rather than settled.
The older shoulder-anesthesia review reports analgesia and block-duration data from varied procedures and studies. No doses or duration promises are carried into this draft.
General ASA standards apply to anesthetic monitoring and recovery, not shoulder-specific selection, positioning, or treatment protocols.
The supporting shoulder-surgery source is a 2012 review without formal evidence grading; its stated preferences are not standardized protocols.
evidenceGaps: Shoulder-arthroplasty-specific airway-device and ventilation recommendations.
A validated procedure-specific beach-chair positioning and cerebral-perfusion protocol, including how to interpret pressure at the brain relative to the measured site.
Reliable shoulder-arthroplasty-specific blood-loss estimates and transfusion or fluid-management guidance.
Current procedure-specific comparative evidence establishing an optimal regional analgesia regimen and recovery observation protocol.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that an LMA is appropriate for most shoulder arthroplasties; the supplied sources do not establish a preferred airway device.
Removed the claim that NIRS is mandatory for all beach-chair cases. A clinical review describes continuous cerebral oximetry, but the supplied sources do not provide a universal mandate.
Removed the unverified fixed hydrostatic-gradient correction and routine MAP target; available beach-chair numerical findings are review-level and should not be treated as universal targets.
Removed interscalene local-anesthetic recipes, additive doses, and fixed analgesia-duration claims; the task sources do not establish a patient-specific regimen.
Removed the Base44 pneumothorax percentage, routine blood-loss range, and associated universal type-and-screen implication; these are not established for this procedure by the supplied evidence.
Replaced absolute claims about universal phrenic palsy and block contraindications with qualified discussion of phrenic effects, pulmonary reserve, and individualized technique selection.

reports.title: Shoulder Arthroscopy
reviewNotes: Base44 is unauthenticated and was not used as clinical evidence. Removed its unsupported case-specific procedure list, exact block recipe, mandatory ETT/LMA by position, fixed fluid volume, mandatory arterial line, and routine infusion claims.

Corrected the blanket claim of 100% phrenic nerve palsy: one review describes near-100% incidence for interscalene block generally, while another reports markedly different rates by volume and technique. Avoid treating severe pulmonary disease as a universal categorical contraindication; assess reserve and technique-specific risk.

Corrected the unsupported beach-chair MAP ≥80 mmHg and MAP <65-at-brain-level stroke claims. The supplied clinical review discusses MAP ≥70 mmHg in its management strategy and reports a study finding; no supplied source validates an ear-level cuff reference rule or universal arterial-line requirement.
The sources do not substantiate that phenylephrine must be running before positioning, nor establish a standard airway device for beach-chair versus lateral positioning.
Continuous interscalene catheter duration and drug regimens are not made routine recommendations here. The reviews describe benefits alongside respiratory, catheter, and infection concerns.
Case reports establish that severe airway edema can occur but do not define incidence or a validated rescue protocol. The arthroscopy extravasation incidence is explicitly unknown.
The beach-chair blood-pressure and cerebral-monitoring information comes from a clinical review; it does not establish a universal MAP target or a required arm-to-head reference correction.
The shoulder-arthroscopy review describes fluid-related airway risk but does not provide a formal airway-management or emergence protocol.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific, current guideline addressing shoulder-arthroscopy airway selection and management of irrigation-related airway edema is not included.
The supplied sources do not establish a validated shoulder-arthroscopy-specific cerebral-perfusion monitoring protocol, including a universal blood-pressure reference-level correction.
No case-specific irrigation pump settings, fluid accounting protocol, or validated threshold for concern about extravasation is provided.
corrections: Removed unsupported indications and pathology list from the unauthenticated Base44 fields.
Removed Base44's fixed interscalene local-anesthetic dose, concentration, adjunct regimen, and claimed block duration as recommended dosing.
Removed categorical claims that beach-chair cases require an ETT, lateral cases permit an LMA, and interscalene block is always placed pre-induction.
Removed unsupported MAP ≥80 mmHg, MAP <65 mmHg at brain level as a defined stroke threshold, ear-level BP reference instruction, and routine arterial-line mandate.
Removed unsupported fixed crystalloid quantity, routine phenylephrine infusion, fixed continuous-catheter duration, sling instruction, and prescribed PACU counseling as universal case requirements.
Replaced the universal 100% phrenic palsy statement with technique- and volume-dependent risk language supported by the sources.

reports.title: Spine Fusion (Posterior / TLIF / ALIF)
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. The draft removes unsupported claims that TIVA is mandatory for MEP monitoring and that even low-concentration volatile anesthetic necessarily invalidates signals; the complex-fusion review describes TIVA as often chosen and balanced low-concentration volatile techniques as generally preserving monitoring in most cases.

The Base44 numeric rules combining a minimum MAP and hemoglobin threshold, along with a fixed 30-minute eye-check interval, are not presented as clinical instructions. The source evidence supports visual-loss risk awareness and individualized perfusion management, but not those exact rules as a universally applicable protocol.

The claimed dramatic opioid reduction from liposomal bupivacaine is corrected: the complex-fusion review says benefit in complex multilevel procedures is unsupported. Erector spinae blocks have supportive thoracolumbar evidence, not a universal mandate.

The case fields include ALIF and detailed airway, prone-positioning, equipment, and postoperative imaging assertions that are not established by the provided procedure-specific sources. No universal ICU disposition, Foley use, or airway device is asserted.

The general orthopedic blood-pressure review's description of controlled hypotension conflicts with the more procedure-specific complex-fusion review's advice against deliberate hypotension. The draft explicitly notes the conflict and adopts the latter's perfusion-focused caution.
This is an adult clinical reference draft based only on supplied evidence. It is not a patient-specific plan and has not been clinically approved.
evidenceGaps: Approach-specific anesthetic planning for ALIF, including access-related considerations, is not established by the supplied sources.
The supplied sources do not establish a detailed airway and ventilation strategy for prone spine fusion or a specific perioperative visual-loss prevention and response protocol.
corrections: Removed the claim that TIVA is mandatory whenever MEP monitoring is used; evidence supports TIVA as a common option and allows that low-concentration balanced volatile anesthesia generally preserves monitoring in most cases.

Removed the fixed combined blood-pressure and hemoglobin rule and the instruction to check and document eyes every 30 minutes; those exact operational thresholds and intervals are not established as universal practice by the supplied sources.
Corrected the claim that liposomal bupivacaine dramatically reduces opioid requirements in complex multilevel fusion; clinical benefit in that setting is unsupported in the focused review.
Removed unsupported fixed airway-device requirements, prone emergency equipment claims, and a universal ICU disposition.
Did not include a universal TXA regimen, transfusion threshold, fluid total, or blood-pressure target.

reports.title: Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its fixed spinal recipe and claim that spinal is simply 'preferred' were not reproduced; the consensus recommendation applies to primary unilateral THA when no significant contraindication or special circumstance precludes neuraxial anesthesia.

Corrected the claim that spinal anesthesia reduces transfusion by approximately 30%: the consensus source reports a pooled odds ratio for transfusion and lower mean transfusion volume, not that specific percentage.
Removed a routine PENG-as-technique-of-choice claim. The THA review describes mixed comparisons, limited evidence for newer motor-sparing blocks, and potential motor-fiber spread.
Removed the claim that liposomal bupivacaine provides established 24–48-hour block coverage; the supplied sources do not support that claim.
Removed routine gabapentin from the proposed multimodal regimen. The THA review states that routine gabapentin is not recommended.
Removed fixed blood-loss estimates, transfusion thresholds, and TXA dose recipes from Base44. Available sources do not support presenting those as universal case instructions.

BCIS mechanism and management details are attributed to a broad clinical review, not elevated to a society-endorsed THA protocol. No Trendelenburg recommendation is included because the fetched sources do not support it.
No universal airway device, arterial line, fluid volume, blood preparation, or anesthetic recipe is asserted.
Source 0 does not substantiate the flagged post-reaming warning features; source 2 describes fat embolism syndrome as typically presenting 12–72 hours after injury or instrumentation.
evidenceGaps: A current, procedure-specific institutional or society pathway for cemented THA BCIS prevention and escalation, including coordination with the surgical team.
A THA-specific airway and positioning protocol; the supplied THA review explicitly does not provide these.

Patient-specific coordination of neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques with current antithrombotic guidance; the supplied regional review's timing table is not a substitute for current guidance.
corrections: Removed unsupported THA indications and detailed replacement anatomy from the unverified Base44 field; the provided sources do not establish those details as a clinical reference claim.
Removed Base44's blanket preference for spinal, fixed intrathecal drug doses, sedation doses, and GA drug recipes.
Removed unsupported LMA-versus-ETT selection rules and routine positioning/room setup claims.
Removed Base44's cementing treatment claims of epinephrine readiness and Trendelenburg as a standard response; retained recognition of BCIS and cautious escalation language.
Removed fixed blood-loss and transfusion thresholds, including the hemoglobin threshold, and the fixed TXA regimen.
Removed the assertion that PENG is the regional technique of choice and that liposomal bupivacaine guarantees a stated duration of coverage.
Removed the unqualified claim of a 30% transfusion reduction with spinal anesthesia and clarified that pooled associations do not predict an individual outcome.
Removed routine gabapentin and ketamine recipes; ketamine's inclusion in Base44 is not a THA-specific recommendation in the supplied sources.

reports.title: Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and were not used as evidence. The supplied sources do not substantiate its specific spinal drug doses, target level, sedation recipe, ACB local-anesthetic recipe, or fixed periarticular drug mixture.

The stated tourniquet pressure and time limits, tourniquet-pain treatment recipe, fixed TXA regimen, blood-loss estimate, and claim that BCIS is rare specifically in TKA were not established by the supplied evidence and are omitted.

The sources contain differing and sometimes conflicting comparisons of neuraxial and general anesthesia and of regional analgesia techniques. The draft presents options and limitations rather than declaring a universally superior anesthetic.
The orthopedic blood-pressure review discusses cemented arthroplasty and tourniquet use broadly; its content does not establish a TKA-specific protocol or incidence estimate.
No source supports mandatory Foley placement, cell-saver use, warming setup, routine invasive arterial monitoring, or a universal airway device for TKA; these are not presented as standards.
The supplied procedure-specific sources do not establish a TKA room layout, positioning protocol, or vascular-access plan.
evidenceGaps: A current, procedure-relevant source for TKA-specific tranexamic-acid use and blood-management implementation is not included; the supplied TKA review explicitly lacks fluid regimens and blood-loss thresholds.

A current TKA thromboprophylaxis pathway, including selection and timing in relation to neuraxial or peripheral catheters, is not established by the supplied material; use applicable current specialty guidance.
The supplied reviews do not provide a complete patient-selection algorithm for neuraxial versus general anesthesia or detailed TKA-specific airway and positioning protocols.
setup: This is a source-scope limitation, not a clinical setup recommendation; moved out of the clinical section.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that spinal anesthesia is categorically preferred over general anesthesia; evidence comparisons are described as conflicting and choice is individualized.
Removed unverified drug doses, concentrations, timing, infusion rates, and fixed analgesic recipes from the Base44 fields.
Removed fixed tourniquet inflation pressures and time limits and the associated tourniquet-pain management recipe.
Removed the fixed TXA regimen, asserted blood-loss range, transfusion claim, and TKA-specific BCIS frequency statement because these were not supported by the supplied sources.
Corrected the motor-sparing block claim: ACB generally has less quadriceps effect than femoral block, but motor impairment and fall risk still require attention.

reports.title: Trigger Finger Release
reviewNotes: Source 0 is useful for describing one WALANT workflow and setting comparisons, but its retrospective cost design does not compare clinical outcomes or establish that a setting or anesthetic is safer.
Source 1 supplies procedural technique and hazards, not an anesthesia protocol. Its no-comparison retrospective series should not be treated as proof that a technique prevents complications.
