corrections: Removed the asserted undescended-testis rationale and fertility/cancer-risk benefit because the supplied sources do not substantiate those claims for this adult reference.

Removed pediatric age ranges, parental-induction advice, pediatric room and equipment setup, pediatric airway choices, sevoflurane/propofol/fentanyl/rocuronium recipes, and pediatric thermoregulation claims.

Removed the caudal-block recommendation and bupivacaine concentration/volume, as well as the specified oral analgesics and other medication list; no supplied source supports these as adult orchiopexy recommendations.
Corrected any implication that the acute-torsion fixation description or anesthesia choices establish routine adult elective orchiopexy practice.
Retained quantitative TOF recovery guidance only conditionally, when neuromuscular blockade is used; it is not a requirement for local or neuraxial cases without blockade.

reports.title: Partial Nephrectomy (Open / Robotic / Laparoscopic)
reviewNotes: The supplied Base44 fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. Mannitol 0.5 g/kg as standard renal protection conflicts with the procedure-specific review, which says mannitol preconditioning is not recommended and no agent reliably protects against ischemia-reperfusion injury.

The Base44 warm-ischemia target of <25 minutes and assertion of significant nephron loss beyond 30 minutes are not reproduced as universal clinical rules. The surgical review distinguishes expected warm-ischemia intervals from situations where cold ischemia may be valuable; it does not establish an anesthetic clamp-time target.

The supplied claims for routine arterial line, fixed crystalloid volumes, mandatory crossmatch, universal ETT, and a prescribed postoperative drug regimen are not established for all patients and approaches in the sources.

Ketorolac evidence cited in the urologic review comes from live-donor nephrectomy and does not establish routine safety after partial nephrectomy; NSAID use should not be presented as categorically safe or prohibited.

The available evidence does not establish comparative anesthesia protocols for open versus laparoscopic versus robotic partial nephrectomy. Generic laparoscopic/robotic physiology is identified as such rather than presented as procedure-specific evidence.

The laparoscopic/robotic source is a general reference rather than a partial-nephrectomy-specific anesthesia source; its PONV recommendation is supported for laparoscopy generally, not as a procedure-specific regimen.
evidenceGaps: A current, procedure-specific anesthesia guideline or comparative evidence addressing anesthetic technique and monitoring across open, laparoscopic, and robotic partial nephrectomy is not present.
The sources do not establish case-specific renal perfusion targets or an anesthetic protocol for managing renal hilar clamping and unclamping.
Partial-nephrectomy-specific evidence for analgesic selection, regional block choice, and PONV regimen is limited in the supplied sources.
corrections: Removed the unverified claim that mannitol 0.5 g/kg before clamping is standard renal protection; the procedure-specific review reports against mannitol preconditioning.
Replaced fixed warm-ischemia thresholds with the open-surgery review’s qualified discussion of expected ischemia duration and selective cold ischemia.
Removed fixed fluid-volume, arterial-line, crossmatch, and blood-availability prescriptions because the supplied evidence does not establish them universally.
Reframed NSAID use: the general review describes both nephrotoxicity concerns and limited ketorolac evidence in donor nephrectomy, not a universal rule for partial nephrectomy.
Removed the unverified assertion that a specific airway, extubation plan, or postoperative analgesic regimen applies to every partial-nephrectomy approach.

reports.title: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
reviewNotes: The Base44 assertion that spinal anesthesia is preferred is unsupported by the fetched evidence. The procedure review specifies general anesthesia; neuraxial anesthesia appears in a single case report without comparative data.

Base44-specific spinal, sedation, and drug recipes; the proposed fixed fluid volume; and a mandatory stool-softener/opioid-avoidance plan are not established by the supplied procedure-specific evidence and were not carried into the clinical reference.

Base44's stated supine/lithotomy position and preferred airway options are not specified in the procedure source. The reference explicitly preserves this limitation rather than selecting a position or airway.

A penile/perineal local anesthetic block and the stated ketorolac/acetaminophen plan are not supported as a procedure-specific regimen by these sources. The general urologic review's analgesia material addresses other procedures and should not be transferred as a penile-prosthesis recommendation.

The source describes infection prevention measures and targeted preoperative parenteral antibiotics, but notes uncertainty about optimal prophylaxis. No specific antibiotic regimen is presented here as a universal standard.
The 2025 spinal-anesthesia case report is used only to qualify a possible vasovagal hazard. Its isolated event and treatment do not establish routine incidence, prevention, or response protocols.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific comparative evidence to guide selection among general, neuraxial, and other anesthetic techniques.
Procedure-specific airway and anesthetic maintenance recommendations, including whether any patient subgroup or operative approach requires a distinct plan.
Procedure-specific estimates or guidance for blood loss, systemic fluid management, and perfusion; the source explicitly does not provide these.
Procedure-specific evidence for postoperative analgesia and PONV prevention.
corrections: Removed the claim that spinal anesthesia is preferred; corrected to general anesthesia specified in the procedure review, with spinal use supported only by a case report.
Removed unverified fixed anesthetic doses, sedation instructions, fluid totals, and analgesic prescriptions from Base44.
Removed the asserted supine/lithotomy position and airway-device plan because the procedure-specific source does not state them.
Removed the claim that stool softeners are mandatory and that opioid avoidance is required; these statements are not substantiated in the supplied sources.
Removed a procedure-specific penile/perineal block recommendation and fixed ketorolac/acetaminophen plan because available sources do not establish them.

reports.title: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
reviewNotes: This is a source-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan or an approved clinical protocol. The PCNL evidence is mainly narrative-review evidence, with a selected single-center anesthesia trial and general standards covering narrower domains.
The sources support prone positioning as standard and describe GA and regional techniques; they do not support Base44's claims that GA and an ETT are mandatory for every PCNL.
No supplied PCNL source establishes routine pre-prone arterial-line placement, a fixed team size for turning, pressure-controlled ventilation or a particular PEEP strategy as universal requirements.

The specific Base44 fluid total, routine warming of all irrigation fluid, mandatory return to supine before extubation, and specified analgesic/block regimen are not established in the fetched evidence.
The source discussion of severe infection, hemorrhage, fluid absorption, and pleural injury supports risk recognition and escalation, but not a universal treatment algorithm.
The source is a narrative review, not a formal guideline; it gives both a general description of stones generally larger than 2 cm and a reported indication range of >1.5–2 cm.
evidenceGaps: Adult PCNL-specific, evidence-based criteria for selecting airway technique and for monitoring ventilation during prone positioning and renal access.
PCNL-specific emergence and extubation guidance, including how positioning affects timing and assessment.
PCNL-specific protocols for severe hemorrhage, fluid absorption, and sepsis; the supplied review discusses these complications but is not a formal management guideline.
PCNL-specific criteria for arterial access or other invasive monitoring are not established in the supplied sources.
corrections: Removed the claim that general anesthesia and endotracheal intubation are mandatory for PCNL; regional anesthesia is also described.
Removed routine arterial-line placement as a requirement; the supplied sources do not establish it as standard for every case.
Removed fixed fluid-volume and warmed-irrigation instructions; no universal total or warming requirement is supported by the fetched evidence.
Removed the absolute instruction to return supine before extubation; the PCNL sources provide no specific extubation protocol.
Removed prescribed ketorolac, acetaminophen, TAP/ESP block, or PCA regimen; the sources do not establish these as a PCNL-specific standard.

Qualified the infection discussion: the cited sources support assessment and vigilance but do not establish the Base44 statement that an obstructed infected kidney is necessarily an emergency in this context.
Removed fixed positioning-team size, universal ventilation settings, and other procedural targets not established in the provided evidence.

reports.title: Prostate Biopsy (TRUS / MRI-Fusion)
reviewNotes: Base44 claims about holding anticoagulation, fluoroquinolone resistance, and institution-specific prophylaxis are not established by the supplied biopsy sources as actionable protocols; individualize and consult current local guidance.
The Base44 MAC drug combination, propofol infusion, natural airway, atropine, and specific postoperative analgesic plan are unsupported as routine biopsy management and were not carried forward.
The claim that transperineal biopsy has lower infection risk than transrectal biopsy is not substantiated by the supplied excerpts; route-specific infection comparison was not asserted.

The supplied antibiotic evidence is summarized in a 2008 narrative review, whereas the newer technical report does not establish a prophylaxis regimen. Current agent selection remains unresolved here.
The ASA basic-monitoring and postanesthesia standards apply when anesthesia care is provided; they do not establish a prostate-biopsy-specific anesthetic technique.
evidenceGaps: Current, procedure- and institution-relevant antibiotic prophylaxis guidance, including selection in the context of local antimicrobial resistance.
Biopsy-specific anticoagulant and antiplatelet management guidance, including individualized interruption and resumption decisions.
A current post-biopsy infection/sepsis recognition and escalation pathway, including how fever or systemic symptoms should be evaluated.
corrections: Removed the unsupported blanket statement that anticoagulation must be held; no stop or restart timing is supplied.
Removed the claim that fluoroquinolone resistance is increasing and the implication that a particular institutional protocol is specified by these sources.
Removed fixed MAC anesthetic drugs, infusion plan, and natural-airway plan because the biopsy references do not establish them as routine.
Removed the blanket assertion of lower infection risk with transperineal biopsy because the supplied evidence does not support that comparison.
Replaced the fixed rapid-recovery claim with a qualified statement: local anesthesia may minimize recovery time, while biopsy-specific emergence and observation protocols are not provided.

reports.title: Pyeloplasty (Open / Robotic)
reviewNotes: Adult scope retained. The procedure study includes children, but pediatric dosing, premedication and caudal/epidural recommendations from the unverified case fields are not carried into this adult reference.
The cohort supports reporting general anesthesia and open/laparoscopic surgical approach, not the Base44 airway, induction, maintenance, fluid-volume or extubation recipes.

The analgesic study has an internal attribution limitation: its methods assign drugs by age, while its summary associates mean requirements with surgical approach. The draft does not convert this into an adult regimen.
Generic laparoscopic/robotic physiology is distinguished from pyeloplasty-specific evidence. Robotic pyeloplasty is not separately characterized in the supplied comparative study.
No claim is made that the draft is complete, clinically approved or production ready.

The supplied pyeloplasty study is retrospective and reports surgical outcomes and analgesic use, but does not provide procedure-specific anesthetic protocols, fluid guidance, or anesthetic-complication management.
evidenceGaps: Adult-specific anesthesia outcomes and a procedure-specific anesthetic pathway for open and robotic pyeloplasty are not established by the supplied sources.
The sources do not establish adult pyeloplasty-specific airway/ventilation management, intraoperative renal-perfusion strategy, or emergence pathway.
The supplied evidence does not support the case-field assertions about crossing-vessel handling, repair kinking, nephrostomy use, mandatory stent-placement confirmation, or fixed fluid volumes.
complications: This is a limitation of the supplied evidence rather than a supported clinical complication-management bullet.
fluids: Recasts the source limitation as an evidence note and removes migration commentary.
corrections: Removed the unsupported fixed crystalloid total and the claim that blood loss is typically minimal; the pyeloplasty study reports no fluid volumes or measured blood loss.
Removed the pediatric caudal/epidural, pediatric temperature, pediatric dosing and age-specific premedication recommendations from the adult clinical content.
Removed unsupported pyeloplasty-specific claims about vascular crossing vessels, repair kinking, nephrostomy tubes and mandatory stent confirmation.
Did not retain the unverified induction and maintenance drug recipes, mandatory ETT/NMB, or suggested adult PCA plan as case-specific standards.
Qualified analgesic findings because the study’s methods assign analgesics by age rather than surgical approach.

reports.title: Radical Cystectomy with Urinary Diversion
reviewNotes: Base44 content was treated as unverified and not used as evidence. Claims of a universal ETT, pre-induction arterial line, CVP, routine ICU admission, fixed multi-liter crystalloid volume, MAP or urine-output targets, mandatory epidural, and TXA benefit are not established by the supplied sources.
The source evidence does not support a universal case duration, blood-product requirement, cell-saver use, or a single position and monitoring setup.
The review’s transfusion associations are observational and conflicting; they do not establish a causal cancer-outcome effect or a transfusion threshold.

Epidural use varies by approach: the ERAS review describes it chiefly for open surgery and reports consensus for omission in many robot-assisted cases. The small nonrandomized SpEA study should not be used to set routine practice.
The provided source on postoperative standards permits PACU-equivalent care and does not make ICU admission standard for every patient.
The supplied sources do not establish cystectomy-specific positioning precautions or routine invasive-monitoring choices.
evidenceGaps: Cystectomy-specific airway-device selection, ventilation strategy, and emergence criteria are not established in the supplied sources.
Case-specific positioning, vascular-access, invasive-monitoring, and operative-room setup recommendations are not established.
The sources do not provide a cystectomy-specific hemorrhage recognition and escalation protocol or a validated approach to intraoperative coagulation management.
The evidence does not resolve which ERAS components have the greatest effect or provide a unified approach across open and robot-assisted cystectomy.

setup: This is a source-limitation note, not a supported setup recommendation. The advice to determine precautions from the planned approach and patient-specific considerations is not stated in the supplied sources.
corrections: Removed unsupported Base44 claims that an endotracheal tube, thoracic epidural, arterial line before induction, CVP, cell saver, Level 1 infuser, and ICU admission are universal requirements.
Removed unsupported fixed fluid volume, MAP target, urine-output target, TXA administration, and routine transfusion assumptions.
Corrected the claim that thoracic epidural is essential for all cases: available review evidence distinguishes open from robot-assisted approaches and supports individualized technique selection.
Corrected the claim that ICU admission is standard: ASA postanesthesia standards require PACU or equivalent care, with disposition determined for the patient and circumstances.
Did not include unsupported routine ileal-conduit/neobladder selection details, a universal bowel preparation regimen, or fixed antibiotic redosing interval.

reports.title: Robot-Assisted Prostatectomy (RALP)
reviewNotes: Reconciled differing fluid-restriction suggestions as context-dependent practice rather than a single target. The older institutional series and later narrative review do not establish a universal total.
The source-0 blood-loss and complication figures come from a single-institution historical series; they are not individualized predictions.

The provided RALP sources do not support an RALP-specific obturator nerve stimulation/leg-movement warning. Obturator reflex evidence in source 1 pertains to transurethral bladder resection, not RALP.

Sources support airway edema, ocular pressure effects, and pulmonary complications as hazards, but do not establish blanket contraindications based on COPD, glaucoma, elevated intracranial pressure, or obesity.
No case-specific PONV prophylaxis evidence was supplied.
evidenceGaps: RALP-specific PONV prevention and management evidence was not provided.
A procedure-specific robotic emergency response and undocking/conversion protocol was not provided; local institutional procedures are needed for that operational detail.
analgesia: This is a source-scope note rather than a clinical recommendation.
corrections: Removed the unsupported claim that obturator nerve stimulation routinely causes leg movement during RALP; the supplied obturator-reflex evidence is for TURB.
Removed unsupported recommendations for an armored endotracheal tube, awake fiberoptic intubation, a universal RSI approach, and a fixed airway device.
Removed blanket claims that severe COPD, CHF, glaucoma, elevated ICP, or obesity make the procedure contraindicated; sources describe relevant risks but do not establish these absolute exclusions.
Removed the claim that phenylephrine is the preferred vasopressor and omitted fixed drug regimens, infusion rates, and reversal dosing not established as universal RALP practice.
Removed the claim that trocar injury to iliac vessels is a documented RALP-specific event in the supplied sources.
Replaced fixed fluid totals and a universal deep-block target with individualized fluid management and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring when blockade is used.

reports.title: Robotic Nephrectomy (Partial or Radical)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not as evidence. The supplied material does not support a fixed crystalloid volume, routine arterial line, routine mannitol before hilar clamping, steep Trendelenburg for nephrectomy, or the proposed ETT and drug recipe as case-specific standards.
The partial-nephrectomy position is supported as lateral decubitus with flank elevation; the source does not supply a matching radical-nephrectomy robotic setup or a steep Trendelenburg requirement.

The source describes both NSAID nephrotoxicity concerns and selected ketorolac evidence without reduced renal function in live donors. Neither supports a universal NSAID prohibition nor universal use.

The source on robotic surgery is a narrative review and identifies limited procedure-specific detail for robotic partial nephrectomy. Emergency detachment is a general robotic-access priority, not a nephrectomy-specific rescue algorithm.
The 6.6% positioning-injury figure is from a center's adult robot-assisted urologic procedures and is not presented as a nephrectomy-specific risk estimate.
This is an evidence-grounded draft, not a complete, clinically approved, or production-ready reference.

The supplied nephrectomy evidence does not establish a fixed crystalloid volume; the robotic review’s example fluid restriction concerns radical prostatectomy and should not be transferred to nephrectomy.
evidenceGaps: Case-specific evidence for partial-nephrectomy hilar clamp and renal-protection management, including whether and when mannitol is appropriate.
Nephrectomy-specific guidance for fluid and blood-management strategy, beyond individualization to patient and operative factors.
Procedure-specific airway, ventilation, and emergence/extubation recommendations for robotic partial and radical nephrectomy.
Nephrectomy-specific postoperative surveillance recommendations, including how to assess urinary leak.
fluids: The bullet is migration commentary, and the supplied nephrectomy sources do not establish a nephrectomy-specific fixed crystalloid volume.
corrections: Removed the unsubstantiated fixed 1–2 L crystalloid recommendation and any implication that it is a standard target.
Removed routine arterial-line placement as a case requirement; monitoring should follow applicable standards and patient-specific needs.
Removed the unsubstantiated routine mannitol-before-hilar-clamp instruction.
Corrected the steep Trendelenburg position claim: the supplied robotic nephrectomy evidence describes lateral decubitus, with flank elevation for partial nephrectomy.
Removed the unsupported claim that a cuff-leak test is routinely indicated for prolonged positioning in robotic nephrectomy.
Did not endorse the Base44 induction, maintenance, analgesic, PONV, or emergence drug recipe as a procedure-specific standard.
Reframed NSAIDs from blanket avoidance to individualized consideration because the nephrectomy review presents both renal-risk concerns and limited postoperative ketorolac evidence.

reports.title: Suprapubic Tube (SPT) Placement
reviewNotes: Base44’s assertion that ultrasound guidance is mandatory for every percutaneous placement is not supported by the supplied procedure source. It describes ultrasound, fluoroscopy, or CT guidance and says radiographic guidance for Seldinger placement is desirable but optional; imaging may reduce bowel-injury risk.

Base44’s specified MAC drug recipe, light-sedation instruction, brief propofol infusion, postoperative acetaminophen/opioid plan, and claim of rapid recovery are not established by the supplied SPT anesthesia evidence. Omit rather than present these as routine guidance.
Do not generalize the T-SPeC case series’ general-anesthesia technique or favorable outcomes to open, trocar, or Seldinger placement. The series involved four adult men and a specific device.

The source lists nondistended bladder, suspected or confirmed bladder cancer, and uncorrected coagulopathy as contraindications to percutaneous placement. Preserve the stated approach-specific scope; do not imply a universal contraindication to all suprapubic access.

The procedural source is a narrative clinical overview, not a procedure-specific anesthesia guideline. The generic urologic anesthesia review and the ASA standards support relevant background requirements but do not supply SPT-specific anesthetic recipes.
The supplied sources do not establish SPT-specific emergence, recovery-room, or discharge criteria.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific evidence comparing local, monitored, regional, and general anesthesia, including criteria for selecting among them.
SPT-specific airway strategy, anesthetic drug regimen, analgesia and PONV protocol, and recovery or discharge criteria.
corrections: Removed the unsupported claim that ultrasound is mandatory for every percutaneous placement; retained the source-supported role of imaging and its potential to reduce bowel-injury risk.
Removed the unverified MAC drug recipe, propofol maintenance claim, fixed pain regimen, and rapid-recovery assertion.
Corrected categorical implications about contraindications by identifying the listed contraindications as specific to percutaneous placement.
Did not treat the four-patient T-SPeC general-anesthesia experience as evidence for routine management of other suprapubic catheter techniques.

reports.title: TURBT (Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor)
reviewNotes: The unverified case fields are not treated as evidence. In particular, the supplied sources do not support the listed spinal dose, routine fluid volume, blood availability rule, postoperative drug regimen, or claimed choice of succinylcholine or rocuronium as a standard.

Sources 0 and 1 support the lateral-wall obturator-reflex hazard but describe surgical prevention measures as well as anesthetic blockade. Source 1 reports conflicting bipolar-versus-monopolar findings; do not state one modality guarantees prevention.
Source 2 discusses TURB anesthesia and summarizes selected studies, but it is a narrative review. Its findings do not establish a universal TURBT technique or patient-specific anesthetic plan.
The ASA basic-monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general standards, not TURBT-specific recommendations. Quantitative TOF recovery guidance applies when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.
The sources do not substantiate classifying bladder perforation as extra- versus intraperitoneal in this reference, nor do they provide a TURBT-specific perforation response algorithm.

The broad comparative analgesia and PONV claim is not supported by the supplied TURBT-specific evidence. The sources include general urologic analgesia findings and a selected outpatient laser report, but these do not establish routine TURBT analgesia or PONV recommendations.
evidenceGaps: TURBT-specific airway selection and criteria for choosing spinal versus general anesthesia beyond the obturator-reflex context.
A TURBT-specific fluid-absorption recognition and management protocol, including how to distinguish clinically important absorption from other causes of intraoperative change.
Procedure-specific bleeding assessment, transfusion criteria, and management of significant postoperative hematuria or clot retention.
A supported TURBT-specific analgesia and PONV regimen, including evidence for bladder-spasm treatment.
A detailed postoperative catheter, irrigation, and discharge protocol.
complications: This is an evidence-scope limitation rather than a clinical complications bullet.
analgesia: Retain the supported source limitation without internal-import commentary or an unsupported PONV claim.
analgesia: The supplied sources do not establish the full claim about TURBT-specific comparative analgesic selection, opioid requirements, and PONV prevention.
corrections: Removed the unverified spinal bupivacaine dose and general-anesthetic drug recipe; the sources do not establish these as routine TURBT regimens.
Removed the unverified crystalloid total and routine blood-availability instruction; no source provides a universal fluid or blood-management protocol.

Removed routine neuromuscular-blocker claims and any implication that spinal anesthesia alone prevents obturator reflex. Blockade is relevant when selected to mitigate the reflex and requires general anesthesia.
Removed the unverified Foley placement, oxybutynin, ketorolac, acetaminophen, and minimal-opioid regimen as prescribed routine care; available TURBT evidence does not establish that regimen.
Corrected the implication that the case-field monitoring and recovery statements are TURBT-specific standards; general ASA standards are identified separately.

reports.title: TURP (Transurethral Resection of the Prostate)
reviewNotes: This is a source-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan, approved protocol, or claim of clinical completeness.

The supplied Base44 fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. In particular, the claims that anticoagulation must be held, a specific PSA review is required, and a type-and-screen or blood availability is routine are not established by the supplied TURP sources.

Removed the fixed spinal drug/dose recipe, propofol infusion plan, and blanket ETT-if-spinal-contraindicated formulation: sources allow spinal or general anesthesia but do not establish these recipes as routine.

Removed fixed irrigation-deficit alert thresholds and fixed sodium-correction rates. Source recommendations differ in thresholds and hypertonic-saline details; this draft does not convert them into a universal protocol.
The source describing a 24-hour postoperative presentation supports vigilance for delayed symptoms, but does not establish a universal observation duration.
Bipolar saline reduces risk of classic hypotonic-irrigant TURP syndrome but does not eliminate absorption-related complications; do not equate saline irrigation with absence of risk.
The stated incidence estimates vary across the supplied reviews and retrospective series; they are not presented as a single settled rate.
The supplied TURP-specific source does not provide an analgesia, emergence, or TURP-specific PONV prevention plan.
evidenceGaps: The supplied sources do not provide a TURP-specific approach to perioperative anticoagulant and antiplatelet management; decisions require applicable medication and specialty guidance.
The sources do not establish TURP-specific blood-loss estimates, transfusion thresholds, or routine blood-ordering criteria.
TURP-specific PONV prevention and a standardized postoperative analgesic regimen are not detailed.
The supplied material does not provide a single validated protocol for diagnosing and managing TURP syndrome across irrigation types and clinical severities.
analgesia: This is a source limitation rather than a clinical analgesia recommendation; the claim about a TURP-specific PONV plan and advice to individualize are not directly supported.
corrections: Removed the Base44 assertion that anticoagulation must be held as a universal requirement; the supplied sources do not provide stop or restart guidance.
Removed the specified intrathecal bupivacaine and fentanyl doses, propofol infusion, and fixed anesthetic regimen because these are unsupported by the supplied sources.

Removed fixed irrigation-fluid deficit alerts (>1 L monopolar or >2 L bipolar) and the instruction to check fluid deficit every 10–15 minutes; source thresholds and measurement recommendations differ.

Removed the Base44 instruction for sodium correction at a fixed 1–2 mEq/hr and its bundled furosemide/hypertonic-saline treatment recipe; the sources describe differing approaches that require severity- and context-specific clinical judgment.
Removed routine type-and-screen/blood-availability claims, a mandatory fluid-restriction prescription, and a named bladder-spasm drug regimen as unsupported universal TURP requirements.
Reframed spinal anesthesia as an often-favored option rather than an absolute requirement; general anesthesia is also described as a viable approach.

reports.title: Ureteral Stent Placement / Removal
reviewNotes: Base44's lithotomy position is not established specifically for ureteral stent placement or removal by the available sources; the textbook chapter mentions lithotomy only as a general urologic positioning consideration.

The proposed MAC/natural airway for removal, spinal or LMA for placement, propofol-fentanyl induction, propofol infusion, and rapid recovery are not substantiated as case-specific recommendations by these sources.
The claims that tamsulosin significantly reduces stent symptoms and that phenazopyridine or acetaminophen constitute a specific postoperative plan are unsupported by the provided evidence.
Vasovagal events are listed in Base44 but are not supported by the supplied case-specific sources. Perforation, failed access, haematuria, infection, displacement, and pain are supported concerns.
Reported anesthetic proportions from urgent obstructive-stone placement and non-OT study regimens are descriptive evidence, not comparative recommendations for routine placement or removal.
evidenceGaps: Removal-specific procedural technique, anesthetic options, and comparative outcomes.
Stent-specific positioning and airway/ventilation recommendations across routine placement settings.
Procedure-specific analgesia, PONV prevention, and postoperative discharge criteria.
corrections: Removed a universal lithotomy-position claim; available positioning evidence is general to urologic surgery, not specific to stenting.
Removed fixed anesthetic drug combinations, maintenance infusion, and airway-device choices as recommendations; source reports are descriptive or absent.
Removed the unsupported tamsulosin, phenazopyridine, and acetaminophen treatment claims.
Qualified urgent-cohort anesthesia proportions and mortality associations as observational findings, not guidance or causal estimates.
Retained ureteral perforation and access failure as documented procedural hazards; did not retain vasovagal events as a sourced case-specific concern.

reports.title: Ureteroscopy (URS)
reviewNotes: Base44 was treated as unverified. Its fixed anesthetic drug recipe, assertion that paralysis is needed, ETT/LMA options, routine crystalloid volume, and specific analgesic/PONV plan are not established by the supplied URS evidence and were not carried forward as recommendations.

The supplied sources support lithotomy, fluoroscopy with minimized exposure, infection assessment, cautious irrigation, and awareness of stent discomfort. They do not support treating an obstructed infected kidney as a reason to proceed immediately; the URS review instead says active UTI must be treated and resolved before ureteroscopy.

The procedure-specific StatPearls source is an educational review, not an anesthesia guideline. The anesthesia review is narrative; the ASA standards address general monitoring and recovery, while the neuromuscular-blockade source applies only when blockade is used.

The source discussion of an alternative anesthetic technique does not establish that it is preferred for all patients. Airway device, anesthetic agents, need for neuromuscular blockade, IV fluid strategy, and analgesia/PONV choices remain clinician- and context-dependent.
The supplied sources do not establish a ureteroscopy-specific perfusion target.
evidenceGaps: URS-specific comparative evidence or a detailed anesthetic guideline establishing airway technique, ventilation approach, and when neuromuscular blockade is beneficial or necessary.
Procedure-specific IV fluid, blood-loss, and perfusion guidance; the URS review explicitly does not provide fluid-resuscitation or transfusion guidance.
A URS-specific analgesia and PONV strategy, including comparative evidence for routine postoperative pain management.
fluids: This is a source-limitations statement rather than a clinical fluid-management recommendation.
corrections: Removed the unverified Base44 claim that a particular propofol, fentanyl, and rocuronium regimen is the induction plan; the sources do not establish that regimen.
Removed the claim that paralysis is required or significantly aids ureteral access as routine URS management; the supplied URS sources do not establish a routine need for neuromuscular blockade.
Removed the fixed 500–1000 mL crystalloid amount and the assertion that it is a procedure-specific fluid plan; the URS review provides no fluid-resuscitation guidance.

Removed the unverified routine ETT/LMA choice, PONV prophylaxis, ketorolac/acetaminophen regimen, and routine alpha-blocker prescription. The source supports alpha-blockers as an option for stent discomfort but not the Base44 regimen or a universal prescription.

Corrected the source-independent implication that infected obstruction should not delay ureteroscopy: the supplied procedure-specific source says active UTI must be treated and resolved before ureteroscopy and advises postponement when purulent urine is encountered.

reports.title: Urethral Dilation / Stricture Repair
reviewNotes: The two stricture-specific sources differ in how they characterize the preferred anesthetic setting: one review calls general anesthesia ideal or suggests spinal/epidural, while the technical report describes office intraurethral lidocaine and operating-room sedation, spinal, or general anesthesia. Neither supports a universal technique.

The direct-vision balloon source is a technical article with limited author experience and no comparative outcome data; it cannot establish routine safety, superiority, or a standard balloon approach.
The supplied general anesthesia standards support monitoring and recovery requirements, but do not resolve procedure-specific airway, drug, or physiologic management.

The source reports on outcomes and complications vary substantially with stricture characteristics, follow-up, and definitions of success; avoid presenting a single success estimate as predictive for an individual.
The supplied procedure sources do not address vasovagal events or atropine-at-bedside practice; no replacement clinical guidance is supported.
evidenceGaps: No procedure-specific anesthesia source establishes airway selection, ventilation strategy, or anesthetic drug regimen for urethral dilation or DVIU.
No supplied source establishes whether vasovagal events are common during urethral instrumentation or supports routine atropine-at-bedside practice.
Procedure-specific evidence does not establish an anesthesia analgesia/PONV plan or a postoperative urinary-retention assessment and management protocol.
complications: The bullet is internal commentary rather than a clinical statement, and the supplied sources do not support vasovagal events or an atropine-at-bedside practice as routine guidance.
corrections: Removed the Base44 propofol, fentanyl, midazolam, volatile-agent, and ETT recipes because the procedure sources do not provide anesthetic drug regimens.
Removed the claim that vasovagal response is common and that atropine should routinely be at bedside; these claims are not supported by the supplied procedure-specific evidence.
Replaced the asserted minimal fluid/blood-management plan with a transparent statement that procedure-specific fluid-volume and blood-loss guidance is unavailable.
Qualified routine postoperative catheter placement and duration: catheter use is common, but the review reports no definitive consensus.
Did not present dysuria, urinary retention, rapid emergence, or minimal opioid use as established procedure-specific recovery or analgesia guidance.

reports.title: AV Fistula Creation / Revision
reviewNotes: The Base44 fields are unverified and were not used as evidence. Removed unsupported details include the specified arm position, block drug/concentration/volume and adjuncts, sedation doses, fluid types or totals, potassium thresholds, dialysis timing rules, access thrill/bruit checks, block analgesia duration, and claims that a particular anesthetic is ideal.

The supplied procedure-specific evidence primarily concerns primary AVF creation. The registry includes elective AV access creation but does not establish a distinct anesthetic plan for fistula revision; revision-specific content is therefore limited.

The systematic review reports favorable pooled outcomes for some regional-versus-local comparisons, but its own limitations and absence of a universal guideline standard preclude presenting regional anesthesia as mandatory or universally superior.

The general anesthesia monitoring standards and postanesthesia standards are applicable across anesthesia settings, but they are not AVF-specific. Neuromuscular-monitoring guidance applies only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.
The clinical draft is evidence-limited and is not a patient-specific plan, a complete protocol, or a clinical approval.
evidenceGaps: AVF revision-specific anesthetic selection, operative considerations, and postoperative access surveillance.
AVF-specific airway and positioning guidance, fluid/perfusion strategy, analgesia/PONV regimen, and recovery access-assessment protocol.
setup: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a clinical setup recommendation; removed the internal-import commentary.
corrections: Removed the claim that regional anesthesia is the ideal or universal technique; the sources describe multiple anesthetic approaches and state that regional anesthesia is not an established universal standard.
Removed unsupported ESRD-specific potassium testing thresholds, dialysis timing, fluid restrictions, crystalloid preferences, and hyperkalemia treatment instructions.
Removed unsupported routine fistula-arm access restrictions, thrill/bruit checks, and return-to-operating-room triggers.
Removed unsupported block drug recipes, doses, durations, and claims of guaranteed complete anesthesia or prolonged analgesia.
Corrected the scope from AVF creation/revision as a uniform evidence base to evidence chiefly addressing primary creation, with revision-specific guidance unresolved.

reports.title: Carotid Artery Stenting (CAS) — Anesthesia Support
reviewNotes: The anesthesia-type cohort does not establish causation, does not distinguish MAC from conscious sedation, and does not specify patient-selection criteria or detailed protocols. Its findings should not be converted into a universal anesthetic preference.
The cohort does not specify patient ages; it cannot alone establish adult-specific effects. General ASA standards apply to anesthesia care but do not fill CAS-specific gaps.
The functional-outcome report has a timing inconsistency between the stated 90-day secondary outcome and the 30-day results comparison.

The available basic monitoring, preanesthesia, and postanesthesia standards are general standards; the vascular book excerpt and peripheral vascular review excerpt are limited-scope pages rather than CAS management protocols.

Unverified case-field assertions not retained as established guidance include dual-antiplatelet loading details, specific sedative regimens, carotid-sinus reflex management, arterial-line preference, contrast hydration, procedural anticoagulation, access-site specifics, and hyperperfusion management.

Focused source supplementation resolved the empty analgesia section using CIRSE 2024 CAS standards and the SVS TCAR/TFCAS sedation statement. Earlier gap notes describe the initial source set. No CAS-specific PONV regimen was inferred.
The CAS source is a brief prospective cohort abstract, not a detailed anesthesia-management reference; it does not provide CAS-specific perioperative protocols.
The cohort findings are associations and do not establish causation.
evidenceGaps: CAS-specific adult patient-selection and preoperative risk assessment, including how anatomy and comorbidities modify anesthetic approach.
Procedure-specific technique, access, positioning, critical phases, and hemodynamic risks or targets.
Supported CAS-specific antiplatelet and anticoagulation management, including coordination with the procedural team.
Detailed recognition and escalation pathways for neurologic, hemodynamic, access-site, and other CAS complications.
Procedure-specific fluid, bleeding, analgesia, emergence, and neurologic recovery recommendations.
setup: This is a source-scope note, not a supported setup recommendation; the sources do not establish suite requirements or a need for invasive monitoring.
fluids: The available evidence supports a limitation note, not a CAS-specific fluid, blood-loss, contrast-protection, or perfusion recommendation.
analgesia: The source supports only the absence of analgesia information, not a regimen or drug recommendation.
corrections: Removed fixed MAC drug choices, doses, and infusion rates because the CAS cohort reports no anesthetic drug protocols.
Removed assertions that dexmedetomidine is ideal or that propofol should be avoided; neither is established by the supplied CAS evidence.

Removed the claims that carotid-sinus manipulation predictably causes profound bradycardia/asystole and that atropine must be prepared for stent deployment; the supplied sources do not document these claims.
Removed claims requiring an arterial line, contralateral-arm NIBP, particular suite equipment, or a specific access route; these are not supported by the available CAS sources.
Removed fixed fluid volumes, contrast pre-hydration instructions, and procedural heparin details; no CAS-specific regimen is provided.
Removed unverified dual-antiplatelet loading instructions and specific postoperative hyperperfusion or imaging pathways; the supplied evidence does not establish these recommendations.

reports.title: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA)
reviewNotes: The supplied case fields are unverified and were not treated as evidence. In particular, the asymptomatic stenosis threshold, delay after recent stroke, medication-continuation instructions, and specific anesthetic drug recipes are not established by these sources.

Do not treat the proposed ipsilateral-arm restriction, EEG change as an automatic shunt indication, fixed MAP threshold, carotid-sinus lidocaine infiltration, routine protamine reversal, or fixed PACU neurological-check interval as validated universal practice.

The source review describes pressure augmentation during clamping but also flags myocardial ischemia and cardiovascular workload; the draft therefore presents pressure management as individualized rather than prescribing a fixed target.

The 2015 review is older and reports uncertainty; the 2022 review is more directly guideline-oriented but acknowledges low-quality evidence and unresolved monitoring, shunting, reversal, and postoperative blood-pressure questions.

No specific airway, positioning, access, routine fluid, postoperative analgesia, or PONV protocol is established by the CEA sources. General ASA monitoring standards are used only within their stated scope.
This is a source-grounded draft for professional review, not a patient-specific plan, checklist, or clinically approved reference.
The supplied sources do not describe a CEA-specific PONV-prevention strategy; this is a source-coverage gap, not evidence that none exists.
evidenceGaps: A current, detailed CEA-specific preoperative selection and optimization protocol, including management decisions for recent TIA or stroke, is not supplied.
The sources do not establish validated decision thresholds for instrumental cerebral monitoring or a definitive shunt strategy under general anesthesia.
The supplied material does not provide a CEA-specific postoperative observation duration or a detailed protocol for evaluation of neck hematoma and new neurological deficit.
setup: This is a source-scope note rather than a clinical setup instruction.
analgesia: This is a source-scope note, not a patient-facing analgesic recommendation.
corrections: Removed the case-field thresholds of greater than 80% stenosis for asymptomatic patients; the supplied review says the indication for asymptomatic high-grade stenosis is less clear and conditional.
Removed the proposed fixed 2–6 week delay after stroke; no supplied source establishes that timing rule.
Removed specific induction drug doses, paralytic choice, and blanket avoidance of succinylcholine; these recipes are not established by the supplied evidence.
Removed the asserted routine arterial-line placement, ipsilateral-arm restriction, NIRS requirement, and fixed MAP above 80; the sources do not establish these as universal CEA standards.
Removed the rule that any sudden EEG change on clamping mandates shunt placement; monitoring methods have limitations and the evidence does not establish a single universal shunt trigger.
Removed fixed heparin dosing and routine protamine reversal; the supplied review finds no definitive reversal strategy.

Removed the proposed carotid-body denervation claim, carotid-sinus infiltration recipe, fixed q15-minute neurological checks, and routine cervical plexus analgesia plan because the supplied evidence does not substantiate those as standard care.

reports.title: Dialysis Graft Placement
reviewNotes: Base44-specific anesthetic recipes—including named block approach and concentration, sedative regimen, and stated block-analgesia duration—are not established by the supplied evidence and were not carried forward.
The claim that grafts are usable within a stated short interval, and that block-induced vasodilation improves anastomosis quality, is unsupported by the supplied sources.

The supplied sources do not establish that absent thrill alone proves technical failure; the older procedure series describes an augmentation test and considers it more reliable than thrill palpation.
Graft kinking or malposition as a named intraoperative concern and a specific graft-versus-fistula comparative hierarchy are not substantiated in the provided sources.
The old PTFE series describes routine systemic heparinization in that practice; this draft does not convert it into a universal recommendation.
Source 0 contains broad fluid guidance and a specific caution about lactated Ringer’s in hyperkalemia; this does not support a blanket prohibition of all potassium-containing fluids.
evidenceGaps: Contemporary procedure-specific recommendations for choosing graft configuration and access site based on patient anatomy and prior access history.
Current graft-placement-specific anesthesia evidence comparing local anesthesia, MAC, peripheral nerve block, and general anesthesia, including selection factors and block-specific risks.
Current procedure-specific standards for intraoperative graft-flow assessment and troubleshooting an abnormal completion examination.
Contemporary graft-specific estimates and management guidance for thrombosis, infection, and other access complications.
corrections: Removed unsupported exact regional-block drugs, concentrations, approaches, sedation choices, and block-duration claims from the unverified Base44 fields.
Removed the unsupported claim that PTFE grafts can be cannulated within a specified number of weeks and the unsupported claim that regional-block vasodilation improves anastomosis quality.
Corrected the claim that absent thrill establishes technical failure; the supplied older series describes an augmentation assessment and says it was more reliable than thrill palpation.
Removed unsupported graft-kinking/malposition claims and did not assert a comparative fistula-versus-graft complication rate or preference not established by these sources.
Qualified heparinization as described in a historical single-center series rather than a universal intraoperative rule.
Did not carry forward a blanket instruction to avoid all potassium-containing fluids; the ESRD source specifically cautions against lactated Ringer’s in hyperkalemia.

reports.title: Embolectomy / Thrombectomy (Peripheral)
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. Its airway/RSI recipe, mandatory arterial line/CVP, fluid rates, mannitol, bicarbonate, calcium, diuretic, and reperfusion-management assertions are not established by the supplied sources and were omitted.
The two procedure-specific articles are historical; their anesthesia preferences conflict and their case outcomes cannot establish present-day technique selection or comparative benefit.
ASA basic monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general requirements, not evidence for procedure-specific invasive monitoring, positioning, recovery targets, or vascular complication treatment.
The vascular anesthesia book page and peripheral vascular review abstract provide broad scope only; neither supplies the detailed embolectomy protocols claimed in the unverified case fields.
The embolectomy sources are historical reports and do not establish contemporary procedure-specific anesthetic or postoperative protocols.
evidenceGaps: Contemporary procedure-specific guidance comparing open and endovascular approaches and informing anesthetic technique selection.
Current perioperative antithrombotic/anticoagulation management applicable to peripheral embolectomy, including coordination with the chosen anesthetic technique.
Modern evidence for recognition, monitoring, and management of reperfusion-related complications and post-revascularization compartment syndrome.
corrections: Removed claims that endotracheal intubation, RSI, general anesthesia, neuromuscular blockade, an arterial line, or CVP monitoring are universally required.
Removed unsupported fixed fluid rates, urine-output targets, and routine mannitol, bicarbonate, calcium, or diuretic treatment recipes.
Removed unsupported claims about routine ICU admission, fixed hourly limb checks, compartment-pressure monitoring, and bedside fasciotomy thresholds.
Reframed historical local, regional, and spinal anesthesia descriptions as noncontemporary and conflicting rather than standards of care.
Restricted quantitative TOF guidance to cases in which neuromuscular blockade is used.

reports.title: Endovascular Aortic Repair (EVAR)
reviewNotes: The sources disagree on anesthetic preference: one review says no technique has a demonstrated overwhelming outcome advantage and describes GA as practical; another favors avoiding GA whenever possible. The evidence is limited, so neither is presented as a universal rule.
ACT targets differ between the EVAR anesthesia review and the broader aortic-repair review. This draft reports monitoring as described but does not adopt a universal anticoagulation target.
The Base44 claim that LMA is preferred, its fixed induction and maintenance drug recipes, heparin dose, and awake-OR extubation instruction are not established by the supplied evidence.

The Base44 claims that spinal or epidural anesthesia is uniformly hemodynamically favorable, and that ketorolac or N-acetylcysteine should be used for renal protection, are not supported as routine recommendations. The EVAR review reports no compelling evidence for N-acetylcysteine and identifies NSAIDs among nephrotoxic drugs.
The source recommending a fixed two-unit crossmatch does not establish that quantity for every patient; preparation should reflect case risk and local practice.
This is a source-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan or a clinically approved or production-ready reference.
The supplied sources do not establish universal EVAR extubation criteria or support individualizing analgesia specifically to renal function; those assertions were omitted.
evidenceGaps: Patient-specific anatomy, urgency (including rupture status), comorbidities, renal function, access plan, and procedural complexity are not supplied; these materially affect anesthetic and recovery planning.
The supplied sources do not provide a detailed EVAR-specific PONV prevention strategy.
A detailed, current endoleak surveillance and imaging schedule is not established in the supplied material.
corrections: Removed the unverified LMA-preferred airway claim; the EVAR review gives no routine airway-device specification.
Removed fixed anesthetic drug regimens and fixed heparin dosing because the supplied sources do not validate the Base44 recipes, and the EVAR review describes a different heparin approach.
Replaced the fixed ACT target with an explicit note that sources differ and that no universal target is adopted here.
Removed routine N-acetylcysteine and ketorolac recommendations; the EVAR review finds no compelling evidence for N-acetylcysteine and identifies NSAIDs as nephrotoxic.
Reframed fixed crossmatch quantity and mandatory awake-OR extubation as case-dependent rather than universal.

reports.title: Femoral-Popliteal Bypass
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as a source. Removed its fixed spinal, sedation, and epidural recipes; heparin dose, ACT, and protamine instructions; and claims that regional anesthesia is preferred or guarantees improved graft patency.
Removed unsupported routine setup claims, including mandatory Foley catheter, arterial line, warming blanket, and fluoroscopy. Monitoring and access should be selected for the case and patient.

Removed unsupported clamp/declamp hyperkalemia, acidosis, bicarbonate treatment, Doppler schedule, compartment-syndrome warning, and wound-healing claims as routine guidance; the supplied sources do not establish these case-specific recommendations.

Reconciled conflicting graft-outcome studies: some neuraxial studies favor graft outcomes, but other trial findings differ, meta-analysis cannot conclude on limb outcomes, and the review identifies important design limitations.

The older peripheral-vascular abstract's broad medication statements are not presented as current drug instructions. Current perioperative medication decisions require applicable contemporary guidance.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific perioperative guidance for antithrombotic management around neuraxial or deep regional anesthesia, including drug-specific interruption and resumption decisions.
A current, procedure-specific protocol for graft/limb assessment and escalation after infrainguinal bypass; the available review explicitly does not specify postoperative monitoring.
Detailed case-specific anesthetic setup and airway/access recommendations, which are not established by the supplied sources.
Procedure-specific guidance for intraoperative clamp-related physiology, anticoagulation monitoring/reversal, and management of graft compromise.
corrections: Removed the Base44 assertion that spinal anesthesia is preferred and that sympathectomy improves graft patency as a reliable clinical outcome; evidence is mixed and no ideal anesthetic is established.
Removed all Base44 anesthetic drug doses, sedation rates, heparin dosing, ACT targets, and routine protamine-reversal instructions.
Removed unsupported fixed equipment, positioning, catheter, and invasive-monitoring requirements.

Removed Base44 claims of routine reperfusion hyperkalemia/acidosis, bicarbonate treatment, and specified Doppler or compartment-syndrome protocols because these are not established in the provided infrainguinal sources.
Corrected recovery content to distinguish general postanesthesia standards from bypass-specific vascular surveillance, for which the supplied sources provide no standard protocol.

reports.title: Iliac Artery Bypass / Aortobifemoral Bypass
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and not used as evidence. The sources do not support its specific induction drug doses, mandatory pre-induction arterial line, TEE or PA catheter use, fixed fluid volume, TXA use, or specified cross-clamp and clamp-release drug strategy.

The claim that thoracic epidural is the gold standard and dramatically reduces pulmonary complications or ICU stay is not established for this operation by the supplied evidence. Neuraxial techniques are discussed in a limited peripheral vascular review, with antithrombotic risk requiring individual assessment.

The supplied sources do not substantiate the case-field postoperative graft-thrombosis time window, hourly femoral-pulse schedule, urgent colonoscopy rule, or specific postoperative pulse-loss response. These were not presented as clinical recommendations.

There is no direct comparative or guideline-level evidence in the supplied material establishing the routine anesthetic technique, invasive monitoring, aortic clamp physiology management, or postoperative disposition for open bypass of aortoiliac occlusive disease.
The supplied sources do not define diagnostic thresholds or a general troubleshooting sequence for suspected perfusion compromise.
evidenceGaps: Direct procedure-specific evidence for open aortobifemoral bypass for occlusive disease, including operative anatomy and anesthetic technique, is absent.
The supplied sources do not establish aortic cross-clamp and release physiology, associated management priorities, or procedure-specific invasive monitoring indications.
The supplied sources do not establish a procedure-specific plan for graft surveillance, early recognition of graft compromise, or evaluation of postoperative bowel or limb ischemia.
corrections: Removed the unverified Leriche syndrome indication and symptom description because the sources do not establish them for this reference.
Removed specific anesthetic drug doses, neuraxial test-dose timing, and a mandatory epidural-general technique because these are not supported by the supplied sources.
Removed the fixed crystalloid/colloid amount and routine TXA, cell-saver, blood-product, and protamine instructions; no source supports these as universal practice for this operation.
Corrected ICU observation in the small case series to an observed study practice, not a universal postoperative disposition.

Excluded claims of mandatory clamping or routine inferior mesenteric artery sacrifice and related specific surveillance instructions because the supplied evidence does not establish them for this procedure.

reports.title: Lower Extremity Amputation (BKA / AKA)
reviewNotes: Do not present neuraxial anesthesia as universally preferred. The amputation chapter describes GA and RA as options and recommends case-by-case selection; comparative outcome evidence is mixed.

The regional-anesthesia review is narrative and primarily focused on peripheral nerve blocks. Its pooled RA findings often combine neuraxial and peripheral techniques, limiting conclusions about a specific technique.
The 2003 peripheral-vascular review is old, abstract-only evidence; its medication statements are not a basis for a contemporary universal perioperative regimen.

The source material does not validate the Base44 anesthetic drug doses, spinal recipe, sedation regimen, fluid total, arterial-line indication, or blanket tourniquet practice. These are not carried forward as reference recommendations.

Claims that a pre-emptive sciatic catheter, gabapentin, or ketamine prevents phantom limb pain are not established as universal practice by these sources. The regional review describes mixed or limited long-term evidence.

Mortality estimates differ between the supplied reviews and are not presented as a single predictable patient-specific risk. The available evidence supports describing this as a high-risk population, not promising a particular outcome.
The amputation sources provide no procedure-specific invasive-monitoring requirement, universal anesthetic target, or standardized critical-phase protocol.
evidenceGaps: No supplied source establishes a procedure-specific airway-management or ventilation strategy for BKA or AKA.
No supplied source provides a current, procedure-specific fluid, transfusion, or bleeding-management protocol.
No supplied source establishes an optimal anesthetic technique or validated selection criteria that resolve GA versus neuraxial or peripheral regional anesthesia for an individual amputation.
setup: This is a statement about the scope of the available evidence, not a supported clinical instruction for the setup section.
intraop: The source describes limits on its intraoperative guidance but does not support the clinical instruction to respond to physiology or escalate concerns.
corrections: Removed the Base44 claim that spinal anesthesia is preferred over general anesthesia as a universal recommendation; supplied sources support individualized technique selection and report conflicting comparative outcomes.
Removed specific intrathecal drug doses, sedative choices and doses, GA drug recipes, and infusion rates because the supplied evidence does not support those regimens as recommendations.
Removed the fixed crystalloid volume and routine phenylephrine infusion claim; no supplied source supports a universal fluid total or vasopressor regimen.
Removed a routine arterial-line recommendation, Foley requirement, and blanket blood-product availability instruction; the supplied sources do not establish these as universal requirements.
Corrected the claim that tourniquet use is routine: the surgical chapter says use is appropriate only in some cases and unnecessary when there is no vascular inflow.
Qualified the claimed phantom-pain benefit of pre-emptive sciatic block or catheter; the review reports limited or mixed evidence for long-term phantom-pain relief.
Removed the implication that ketamine, gabapentin, or epidural analgesia should be prepared routinely; the sources describe possible multimodal approaches but do not establish one required regimen.
Did not retain a blanket claim that regional anesthesia reduces 30-day cardiac events or respiratory complications; available sources describe heterogeneous, conflicting observational evidence.

reports.title: Mesenteric Revascularization (Open / Endovascular)
reviewNotes: This draft is not patient-specific, clinically approved, or a complete management protocol. The strongest procedure-specific source is focused on acute mesenteric ischemia; its applicability to chronic mesenteric ischemia is limited.

Base44 claims for routine RSI, ketamine induction, ketamine TIVA, epidural-general anesthesia, mandatory arterial line before induction, CVP/PA catheter, cell saver, TXA, named vasopressors as a standard regimen, routine ICU intubation, and a fixed analgesic plan are not established by the supplied procedure-specific evidence and have not been retained as recommendations.

The WSES guideline advises caution with vasopressors and notes potential intestinal microcirculatory harm with vasopressin in the postoperative hypotension context. This does not establish a universal alternative regimen; the Base44 blanket vasopressin suggestion is therefore not adopted.

The Base44 claim that TPN is needed until bowel function returns is not supported as a universal rule. The source prefers enteral feeding while noting parenteral nutrition may be needed after short-bowel resection or intestinal failure.

The WSES source describes postoperative systemic heparin in its AMI care discussion, but this draft omits a regimen or target: it should not be generalized without case-specific vascular/surgical direction.
Basic ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards are general standards, not mesenteric-specific guidance. The neuromuscular-blockade guidance applies only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.

Source 0 is an acute mesenteric ischemia guideline, not an anesthesia reference. It supports the surgical reassessment statements but does not specify how reassessment or anticipated repeat surgery should determine anesthesia recovery planning.
evidenceGaps: Mesenteric-specific adult anesthetic technique and airway strategy, including differences between open, endovascular, hybrid, acute, and chronic cases.
Chronic mesenteric ischemia-specific perioperative evidence, including procedure selection and anesthesia-related risk modifiers.
Procedure-specific positioning, vascular access, invasive monitoring selection, and monitoring targets.
Mesenteric revascularization-specific analgesia and PONV evidence.
Procedure-specific emergence, extubation, and postoperative ventilation recommendations.
corrections: Removed unsupported universal airway claims, including routine RSI and mandatory endotracheal intubation for every approach.

Removed unsupported induction and maintenance drug recipes, including ketamine as an established agent of choice, ketamine-based TIVA, and routine propofol/fentanyl/neuromuscular-blocker combinations.
Removed unsupported routine epidural, arterial-line timing, central venous or pulmonary artery catheter, cell-saver, TXA, and fixed blood-product recommendations.

Corrected the blanket vasopressin recommendation: the source urges caution and notes possible intestinal microcirculatory impact in a specified postoperative context, without establishing a universal vasopressor prescription.
Corrected blanket TPN language: source supports enteral feeding preference, with parenteral nutrition as a possible need in short-bowel resection or intestinal failure.
Did not present lactate as a sole intraoperative decision rule or a fixed intervention threshold.
Did not generalize postoperative anticoagulation details from the AMI guideline into a universal mesenteric revascularization protocol.

reports.title: Open AAA Repair (Elective)
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not used as evidence. Its exact sex-specific size thresholds are oversimplified: the supplied review distinguishes men and women, describes intervention consideration for men at 5.0–5.4 cm and women at 5.0 cm, and states a growth criterion for intervention.

Corrected the implication that an arterial line, TEE/PAC, epidural, cell saver, or ICU intubation is mandatory for every elective case. The anesthesia chapter describes monitoring options and conditional PAC use; extubation timing is not a universal protocol.

The supplied evidence does not establish Base44’s fixed induction drugs, epidural test-dose timing, dexamethasone use, ACT greater than 200, routine protamine reversal, TXA, mannitol, or a mandatory norepinephrine strategy. These were not carried forward as instructions or standard regimens.

The chapter’s statements about beta-blocker/aspirin continuation and epidural benefits should not be converted into blanket medication or neuraxial rules. Its epidural discussion explicitly reports disagreement over intraoperative use and increased fluid/vasopressor requirements in some practice.

The supplied material does not support the Base44 claim that epidural is the gold standard or that it dramatically reduces ICU stay. The source reports better analgesia and associations with selected outcomes, while describing intraoperative use as disputed.

The review’s numerical outcome estimates and recommendations reflect cited studies and guidelines; they do not establish individual risk or replace current assessment. The 2003 peripheral vascular review is abstract-only and not a procedure-specific open-AAA source.
The open-AAA chapter mentions metoclopramide only within its description of a fast-track elective-repair approach; it does not establish a general PONV prophylaxis regimen.
evidenceGaps: A current, procedure-specific adult elective open-AAA anesthesia guideline or detailed evidence review establishing indications and comparative outcomes for elective airway/ventilation approaches is not included.
The supplied sources do not establish elective open-AAA-specific PONV prophylaxis or a preferred regimen.
The sources describe heparin use and discuss coagulation management, but do not establish a universal elective open-AAA ACT target or heparin reversal protocol.
The sources do not establish an elective open-AAA-specific evidence-based protocol for mannitol or other renal-protection interventions during suprarenal clamping.
airway: This is a source-scope limitation rather than a clinical recommendation; retain it in the evidence section.
analgesia: This is an evidence-scope note, not a clinical-section recommendation.
corrections: Removed the unsourced universal ETT, pre-induction arterial line, thoracic epidural placement, TEE/PAC, and cell-saver requirements; monitoring and technique are presented as individualized options.
Removed fixed induction drug choices and doses, epidural test-dose timing, and routine dexamethasone.
Removed ACT greater than 200 and routine protamine reversal; no universal target or reversal protocol is established in the supplied evidence.
Removed routine TXA, mannitol 12.5–25 g, and fixed vasopressor/volume recipes because the provided sources do not substantiate them as universal elective practice.
Corrected 'ICU intubated' to individualized emergence and recovery: ICU care is usual, but the source does not specify universal extubation timing.

Qualified the epidural claim: it may improve analgesia and is associated with favorable reported outcomes, but source evidence describes intraoperative use as disputed and does not establish a mandatory gold standard.
Removed unsupported PONV drug claims and a universal postoperative ketorolac plan.

reports.title: Peripheral Angiogram / Diagnostic Arteriogram
reviewNotes: Base44 fields were treated as unverified and were not used as clinical evidence. The PAD review primarily covers endovascular interventions; diagnostic-only application is limited.

The ASA monitoring standards support general monitoring requirements, not the proposed Base44-specific setup details. The sources do not establish nasal-cannula ETCO2 as the only method or contralateral-arm blood-pressure placement.

The supplied evidence does not support the Base44 fluid regimen for CKD, a metformin hold interval, a specific steroid-antihistamine contrast-allergy schedule, low-dose propofol infusion, or claims about contrast-induced nephropathy prevention.

The supplied sources do not establish the Base44-specific access-site warning signs, urgent imaging instruction, distal-pulse protocol, or rapid-recovery claim. Pseudoaneurysm is discussed in the intervention review, but that does not validate those additional instructions.
The review's intervention-specific anticoagulation and access-cocktail details should not be generalized into diagnostic angiography orders or universal ACT targets.
evidenceGaps: A procedure-specific adult diagnostic peripheral arteriography source addressing renal risk and contrast-associated kidney injury prevention.
A diagnostic-case source defining post-access observation and assessment, including how to evaluate suspected access-site or retroperitoneal bleeding.
corrections: Removed the unverified NS prehydration rate and duration, contrast-volume instruction, and metformin hold interval; these are not established by the supplied sources.
Removed the exact contrast-allergy premedication recipe; the relevant review describes general premedication approaches but does not provide the asserted regimen.
Removed the proposed propofol infusion and specific midazolam/fentanyl doses; the source describes titrated conscious sedation but the requested reference excludes numerical drug dosing.
Removed the asserted radial-access safety comparison and the instruction that the patient must be very still with the arm extended; these claims are not supported by the supplied evidence.

Removed the asserted retroperitoneal-hematoma symptom-and-CT pathway, routine distal-pulse checks, and access-site pressure-dressing direction; these details are not established in the supplied sources.

reports.title: Peripheral Angioplasty / Arterial Stenting
reviewNotes: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as evidence. Its specific claims about renal prehydration, contrast nephropathy, routine access-site or limb-pulse checks, access-site closure, a particular sedation recipe, balloon-timed fentanyl, and vessel rupture/conversion planning are not established by the supplied sources and were not carried forward as standards.

The supplied evidence supports conscious sedation for most interventions and identifies respiratory risk with sedative-opioid combinations; it does not support imposing a routine airway device, general anesthesia, or a fixed anesthetic regimen.

ACT values appear in the medication review as customary practices, including variation by intervention. They are not presented here as a universal target; the procedural team must determine the applicable anticoagulation plan.

The older peripheral vascular surgery review (source 3) concerns high-cardiac-risk peripheral surgery and provides only an abstract; it does not establish recommendations for endovascular angioplasty or stenting.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific postintervention access-site and distal limb-perfusion assessment and escalation protocol.
Renal-risk assessment and contrast-associated kidney injury prevention or management specific to peripheral angioplasty/stenting.
A procedure-specific approach to recognition and escalation for major endovascular complications, including vessel injury or acute limb-threatening events.
fluids: This is a limitation of the supplied evidence rather than a clinical-section recommendation.
emergence: This is an evidence-scope limitation, not a vascular-specific postoperative protocol.
corrections: Removed Base44's routine prehydration-for-CKD assertion: the supplied sources provide no general fluid-management recommendations and do not establish a renal-protection protocol.
Removed the claim that distal pulse checks are a specified postprocedure standard: the available sources do not supply a vascular-specific recovery assessment protocol.
Removed a fixed midazolam/fentanyl or dexmedetomidine plan and pre-inflation fentanyl timing; sources describe general sedation approaches and pain risk, not a universal case recipe.
Removed unsupported claims that vessel rupture is a stated common procedural concern, that a nearby hybrid OR is required, or that a particular conversion plan is established by the supplied sources.
Did not treat aspirin/clopidogrel use, a specific access route, heparin/ACT values, or any drug regimen as universally required.

reports.title: Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (rAAA)
reviewNotes: The Base44 material is unverified and was not treated as evidence. This draft does not adopt its fixed induction drug recipe, universal RSI, vasopressor timing, central access requirement, or instruction that monitoring follow clamping.

The supplied sources support balanced component resuscitation as an approach, but do not establish rAAA-specific transfusion thresholds. The Base44 numerical hemoglobin, INR, platelet and fibrinogen targets, calcium schedule, and warming temperature are not included.

The Base44 fixed systolic pressure target conflicts with the source review’s caution about very low pressure and its account of differing guidance. Blood-pressure strategy requires clinical individualization.
Routine TXA is not supported by the supplied evidence; the review describes limited evidence and states that NICE recommends use only within clinical trials.

The source review and institutional protocol do not establish a single anesthesia technique for all rAAA repairs. Local anesthesia is an option for selected endovascular cases; open repair in the protocol uses general anesthesia.
evidenceGaps: No supplied source establishes an rAAA-specific emergence or extubation protocol.
No supplied source establishes a PONV prevention or treatment approach specific to rAAA repair.
No supplied evidence resolves the comparative outcome question for EVAR versus open repair or establishes universal blood-pressure or transfusion targets.
corrections: Removed the Base44 fixed ketamine–succinylcholine induction recipe, mandatory RSI, and universal norepinephrine-before-induction instruction; these are not established by the supplied sources.
Removed the Base44 claim that all patients require central access, CVP monitoring, or a specific invasive-monitoring sequence; access and invasive monitoring must not delay hemorrhage control.
Removed fixed permissive-hypotension values as universal targets; the supplied sources give differing, context-dependent perspectives.
Removed the Base44 TXA dose and routine-use instruction; the review reports limited evidence and controversy.
Removed unsubstantiated fixed calcium, component-threshold, temperature, and laboratory targets from the Base44 material.
Replaced the Base44 routine ICU-intubation instruction with critical-care recovery planning; the review explicitly states that it provides no specific extubation protocol.

reports.title: Varicose Vein Procedures (EVLA / Phlebectomy / Stripping)
reviewNotes: Base44 details were treated as unverified. Its tumescent lidocaine maximum, drug regimens, fluid-absorption estimate, laser-safety instructions, Trendelenburg positioning, and immediate compression claims were not adopted because the supplied sources do not substantiate them as stated.
The sources describe differing RFA generator temperatures and device protocols; this draft avoids turning either device-specific description into a universal setting.
The 2005 narrative review and undated StatPearls page are limited for contemporary anesthetic protocols. General ASA standards were used only for general monitoring and recovery statements.
Pregnancy is listed as a relative contraindication in the RFA review; no universal pregnancy rule or pregnancy-specific perioperative management is inferred.
This is a source-grounded draft, not a patient-specific plan or a clinically approved reference.
evidenceGaps: Procedure-specific anticoagulation management and thrombosis-prophylaxis recommendations, including how to individualize them for the intervention and patient.
A detailed, validated approach to recognition and management of local-anesthetic systemic toxicity for these procedures.
Contemporary procedure-specific anesthetic protocols for extensive bilateral phlebectomy and open stripping, including airway and recovery criteria.
corrections: Removed the unsupported universal tumescent lidocaine maximum and specified drug doses or infusion rates.
Removed the assertion that tumescent fluid absorption is approximately 30% and any associated fluid-balance prescription.
Removed unsupported mandatory Trendelenburg positioning, laser eyewear/wet-drape instructions, and a claim that compression stockings must be applied before the patient stands.

Corrected the implication that every procedure uses local anesthesia or MAC: the review says GSV stripping is usually performed under general anesthesia, while RFA and phlebectomy may use local/tumescent approaches.
Did not adopt a universal monitoring minimum for local-only procedures beyond applicable general anesthesia standards.
